# METHOD-SELECTION — the analyst's rule-based decision tree

> The economist's reasoning **as code**. Method selection is rule-based, not an
> opinion; the preconditions are **hard gates** that block an invalid result. Authority:
> `CLAUDE.md` §6 (determinism principles) + `PROJECT-SCOPE.md` §5.2 (METHOD-SELECTION as an
> explicit deliverable). In a conflict, the charter (`CLAUDE.md`) prevails. Every rule here carries a
> **source** (vignette/ or textbook/paper); anything uncertain is marked [TO VERIFY].

---

## §0.1 What METHOD-SELECTION is

`METHOD-SELECTION.md` encodes **the macro analyst's reasoning as a decision tree** —
"if the series are I(1) and cointegrated ⇒ VECM; otherwise VAR in differences", not as prose but
as an explicit, checkable rule with a source. It is the deliverable that **bridges L2 and L3**
(`PROJECT-SCOPE.md` §3, §5.2): the L3 tool descriptions (Phase 4, `tool`) are written
**FROM** this document — the LLM reads the what/why/when/how encoded here and does not
invent it at call time.

The correctness guarantee is **structural, not probabilistic** (`CLAUDE.md` §2, §6;
`PROJECT-SCOPE.md` §1):

| Principle | What it means here | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Rule-based selection** | The "which method" decision is an encoded rule, not improvisation by the LLM. | `CLAUDE.md` §6 |
| **Gates = hard blockers** | Every violated precondition → an explicit `stop` in the wrapper; an invalid result never escapes. | `CLAUDE.md` §5.4; `PROJECT-SCOPE.md` §5.2 |
| **Never guess** | Every rule is documented with a source; the "never guess from memory" of §4 applies to knowledge too, not only to the API. | `PROJECT-SCOPE.md` §5.2 step 1 |
| **Reproducible** | Stochastic steps carry a seed; non-convergent → does not escape without an override. | `PROJECT-SCOPE.md` §6 |

The LLM **presses ready-made, validated buttons** — it does not do the mathematics. METHOD-SELECTION tells it
*which* button, *when*, *under which preconditions*, and *how the output is read*.

---

## §0.2 How to read this document

Two levels of reading, from the general to the specific:

1. **Master decision trees (§2)** — the large branchings that cut the whole problem:
 *univariate vs multivariate*, *stationary vs I(1)*, *cointegrated vs not*, *causal
 inference design*, *volatility/regime*. Every task starts here; the output of the tree points
 to the appropriate **category card**.
2. **Per-category method cards (§3+)** — one section per category folder (`01-preparation-prechecks`,
 … `15-model-evaluation`), where each method of the catalog (`Wrappers-sources.md`) becomes
 a card with a fixed skeleton.

**Method-card skeleton (invariant):**

| Field | What it contains |
|---|---|
| **When / When NOT** | The triggering question and the explicit limits of application (when the method is the wrong choice). |
| **Preconditions + tool** | The assumptions that *must* hold, and which tool of category `01`/`15` checks them before the method runs (e.g. stationarity ⇒ `Urca-wrapper`/`unit_root_normality`). |
| **Alternatives + criterion** | Which other methods solve the same thing, and the **explicit criterion** for choosing between them. |
| **Reading the output + traps** | What each field of the named-list output means, and the typical interpretation traps (e.g. IRF sign convention, prob-of-rejection sign). |
| **Sources** | vignette/ + textbook/paper for every rule of the card. |

The LLM reader follows: **§2 tree → card → Preconditions (runs the check tools) →
selects a method → reads the output with the traps in mind.**

---

## §0.3 Source convention

Every rule carries documentation — **never "I think so"** (`PROJECT-SCOPE.md` §5.2 step 1). Two
kinds of source, often together:

- **Textbook / paper** — for the econometric rule itself (when I(1), when VECM, how a
 bounds test is read). Inline **surname convention**:

 | Citation | Typically covers |
 |---|---|
 | **Enders** (*Applied Econometric Time Series*) | unit roots, cointegration, VAR/VECM, GARCH, TAR/STAR — the introductory rule. |
 | **Hamilton** (*Time Series Analysis*) | asymptotic theory, Kalman/state-space, spectral, regime-switching. |
 | **Lütkepohl** (*New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis*) | VAR/SVAR identification, IRF/FEVD, lag-order, cointegration rank. |
 | **Johansen** (1988/1995) | trace/max-eigen rank test, VECM deterministic terms. |
 | **Pesaran-Shin-Smith** (2001) | ARDL bounds test, level relationships without pre-classification I(0)/I(1). |
 | **KPSS 1992** (Kwiatkowski-Phillips-Schmidt-Shin) | stationarity-null test (complementary to ADF). |
 | **Adrian-Boyarchenko-Giannone / ABG** (2019) | Growth-at-Risk, quantile regression in macro. |

 Others as the case requires (e.g. Jordà 2005 for Local Projections, Callaway-Sant'Anna 2021 for
 staggered DiD, Uhlig 2005 for sign restrictions) are introduced in the corresponding card.

- **Package vignette / URL** — when the rule is **package-specific** (default args,
 what the function returns, which gates the package itself enforces). Format:
 `<pkg>` + ` (as in `Wrappers-sources.md`).
 Live API verification with **btw** (`CLAUDE.md` §8) — never from memory.

**Uncertainty:** if a citation is not certain (page, year, exact wording of the
rule), it is marked **[TO VERIFY]** next to it — a source is **never** invented. The
document passes an **adversarial review** (`PROJECT-SCOPE.md` §5.2 step 2) that hunts exactly for
wrong/invented rules.

---

## §0.4 Legend — glyphs

Fixed symbols across all cards:

| Glyph | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ✅ | Precondition holds / valid choice for the scenario. |
| ⛔ | **Hard gate** — violation → `stop` in the wrapper; the method does not run. |
| ⚠️ | Interpretation trap or requirement that passes silently if not watched. |
| → | Decision-tree flow / cross-reference to the next card or check tool. |
| ⤷ | Alternative method with its selection criterion. |
| 🔒 | Determinism point: requires a seed / convergence gate (`PROJECT-SCOPE.md` §6). |
| 📖 | Textbook/paper citation (surname convention, §0.3). |
| 📦 | Package-specific rule (vignette/ URL, §0.3). |
| [TO VERIFY] | Citation/rule whose verification is pending — it has not "locked". |

## §0.5 Link to L3 (Phase 4)

This document is the **source of truth for the L3 tool descriptions**. When the
`tool` adapter is written (`PROJECT-SCOPE.md` §5.3 step 2), every `description` field of a tool
**is drawn from the corresponding card** here — the "When / When NOT" and the "traps" become the
text the LLM reads before calling the tool. Flow:

```
METHOD-SELECTION card → tool(description = "<when/why/how + traps>")
 (knowledge, here) (L3 adapter, Phase 4)
```

This way the reasoning lives **once**, encoded and documented, and L3 exposes it —
it neither reproduces nor improvises it. Completion criterion for METHOD-SELECTION (before
L3 starts): **every method of the catalog covered, every rule with a source, review with no
open CRITICAL/HIGH** (`PROJECT-SCOPE.md` §5.2).

## §1 — preconditions layer: the shared gate vocabulary

> This layer is the **entry gate** of every macro time-series analysis. Before
> any model runs (VAR, ARDL, etc.), the LLM presses the "buttons" of the
> `01-preparation-prechecks` category to **establish the assumptions** on
> which the model rests (order of integration, structural stability, seasonality,
> outliers). After estimation, the "buttons" of the `15-model-evaluation` category
> **check ex post** that the residual assumptions are not violated.
> Correctness is **structural**: every precondition maps to a rule-based tool
> with hard gates; the LLM does not judge the mathematics, it only reads the verdict.

The most frequent human (and LLM) error at this layer is the **polarity
confusion** between unit-root tests and stationarity tests. This
section encodes the shared vocabulary so that the error becomes impossible.

---

## 1.1 Unit-root / stationarity polarity table

Two families of test with an **opposite null hypothesis**. The interpretation of a rejection
is inverted — this is the critical trap.

| Test | Family | H0 (null) | H1 (alternative) | Rejecting H0 ⇒ | Source |
|---------|-----------|---------------|------------------|----------------|------|
| **ADF** (Augmented Dickey-Fuller) | unit-root | **unit root** (non-stationary) | stationary / explosive | **stationary — I(0)** | Dickey-Fuller 1979; Hamilton 1994; Enders |
| **PP** (Phillips-Perron) | unit-root | **unit root** (non-stationary) | stationary / explosive | **stationary — I(0)** | Phillips-Perron 1988; Hamilton 1994 |
| **ERS / DF-GLS** (Elliott-Rothenberg-Stock) | unit-root | **unit root** (non-stationary) | stationary | **stationary — I(0)** | Elliott-Rothenberg-Stock 1996 |
| **Zivot-Andrews** | unit-root (+1 break) | **unit root** with 1 endogenous break | stationary around a break | **stationary with structural change** | Zivot-Andrews 1992 |
| **KPSS** (Kwiatkowski-Phillips-Schmidt-Shin) | **stationarity** | **stationarity** (level or trend) | unit root | **NON-stationary / unit root** | KPSS 1992; Hamilton 1994 |

> ⚠️ **POLARITY TRAP (commit it to memory).** **KPSS has the OPPOSITE polarity**
> to ADF/PP/ERS. In ADF/PP/ERS "rejection = good news (stationary)"; in KPSS
> "rejection = bad news (non-stationary)". KPSS does **not** prove stationarity when
> it rejects — the opposite. A large KPSS statistic means *unit root*, a
> large (negative) ADF statistic means *stationarity*.

**Sign note (ADF-type).** The ADF/PP/ERS-DF-GLS statistics (`tau` type)
are **negative**; rejection happens when the statistic is **more negative**
than the critical value (`teststat < cval`). The KPSS statistic is **positive**;
rejection happens when `teststat > cval`. In the `unit_root_normality` wrappers this is already
built into the `decision` field via the p-value; in the `unit_root_suite` wrappers it is a
**manual comparison** (see §1.3).

---

## 1.2 The confirmatory-pair rule (ADF + KPSS)

No single unit-root test is reliable: ADF has
**low power** near the unit boundary (it struggles to separate a root ≈1 from a
strongly autoregressive stationary series), while KPSS reverses the hypothesis roles.
The professional standard (Enders; Hamilton 1994) is to **combine one
test from each family** — "confirmatory analysis" — and to conclude only
when they agree:

| ADF | KPSS | Conclusion | Action |
|-----|------|-----------|----------|
| **rejection** (stationary) | **no rejection** (stationary) | **I(0)** — safe stationarity | proceed to the model in levels |
| **no rejection** (unit root) | **rejection** (unit root) | **I(1)** — safe unit root | take first differences / check for cointegration |
| rejection | rejection | **uncertain / contradictory** | look for a possible break (Zivot-Andrews), try ERS (higher power), fractional integration |
| no rejection | no rejection | **uncertain / low power** | increase the sample; ERS/DF-GLS; examine trend vs drift spec |

The two "diagonals" (first two rows) give a clean conclusion; the two
"anti-diagonals" require further investigation — typically a **structural break** or the more
powerful ERS/DF-GLS test.

> **Practical implementation rule.** The "both reject" anti-diagonal is a
> classic symptom of **structural change** in the deterministic part: ADF sees a
> spurious unit root because of the ignored break, while KPSS rejects constant
> stationarity. Next step → `wrap_ur_za` (Zivot-Andrews) or `run_breakpoints`.

---

## 1.3 urca: no p-value — teststat vs critical values

A critical package-specific difference. The tests of **`unit_root_normality`** (`adf.test`,
`kpss.test`, `pp.test`) return a **p-value** (with a warning when it falls outside
the internal table of critical values). The tests of **`unit_root_suite`** (`ur.df`,
`ur.kpss`, `ur.pp`, `ur.ers`, `ur.za`) **do not return a p-value**: they return
`teststat` and a `cval` table with critical values at **10% / 5% / 1%**. The
decision is taken by **direct comparison** at the desired significance level.
(Source: Pfaff, `unit_root_suite` — )

| urca test | decision slot | H0 | rejection rule |
|-----------|---------------|-----|-------------------|
| `wrap_ur_df` (`ur.df`) | `teststat` vs `cval` (`tau`,`phi`) | unit root | `tau < cval` (more negative) |
| `wrap_ur_pp` (`ur.pp`) | `teststat` vs `cval` | unit root | `teststat < cval` |
| `wrap_ur_ers` (`ur.ers`) | `teststat` vs `cval` | unit root | `teststat < cval` |
| `wrap_ur_kpss` (`ur.kpss`) | `teststat` vs `cval` | **stationarity** | `teststat > cval` (positive) |
| `wrap_ur_za` (`ur.za`) | `teststat` vs `cval` + `bpoint` | unit root with 1 break | `teststat < cval` |

`wrap_ur_kpss` **keeps the same opposite polarity** as `kpss.test`
— H0 = stationarity (`type="mu"` level, `type="tau"` trend) — merely expressed as
`teststat > cval` instead of as a small p-value.

---

## 1.4 Mapping precondition → tool

Every assumption that must be checked maps to a **specific wrapper**. The LLM
does not choose mathematics — it chooses the button that fits the assumption.

| Precondition (what I want to establish) | Tool / file | Functions | Note |
|-----------------------------------|---------------|-------------|----------|
| **Stationarity — fast** (p-value) | `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.py` | `run_adf_test`, `run_kpss_test`, `run_pp_test` | + `run_jarque_bera_test` (residual normality) |
| **Stationarity — full** (teststat/cval) | `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_suite.py` | `wrap_ur_df`, `wrap_ur_kpss`, `wrap_ur_pp`, `wrap_ur_ers` | ERS/DF-GLS = higher power; §1.3 |
| **Structural break — unit root with a break** | `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_suite.py` | `wrap_ur_za` | Zivot-Andrews, 1 **endogenous** break; `model` = intercept/trend/both |
| **Structural breaks — multiple / test** | `c01_preparation_prechecks/structural_change.py` | `run_breakpoints` (Bai-Perron), `run_efp` (CUSUM/MOSUM), `run_Fstats` + `run_sctest` (Chow/supF) | see §1.5 for the distinction |
| **Seasonal unit root / stability** | `c01_preparation_prechecks/seasonal_unit_roots.py` | `run_hegy_test` (HEGY), `run_ch_test` (Canova-Hansen) | requires a `ts` with `frequency > 1` |
| **Seasonal adjustment (removing seasonality)** | `c01_preparation_prechecks/seasonal_adjustment_13arima.py` | `run_seas` (X-13ARIMA-SEATS), `get_series`, `check_x13` | + `qs` seasonality diagnostic |
| **Time-series outliers** | `c01_preparation_prechecks/automatic_outlier_detection.py` | `run_tso` | AO/LS/TC/IO/SLS (Chen-Liu 1993) |
| **Panel unit root** | `c01_preparation_prechecks/panel_unit_root.py` | `run_purtest` (LLC/IPS/Fisher/Hadri), `run_cipstest` (Pesaran CIPS) | `make_pdata_frame` for preparation |

**Detail on the seasonal tests (uroot).** Two opposite hypotheses — the same pattern as
§1.1 in a seasonal setting:

- **HEGY** (`run_hegy_test`): H0 = **seasonal unit root** at the given
 frequency; rejection ⇒ there is *no* unit root there (seasonally stationary at
 that root). It returns t/F statistics per root/frequency. Source:
 Hylleberg-Engle-Granger-Yoo 1990; `seasonal_unit_roots` —
- **Canova-Hansen** (`run_ch_test`): H0 = **stable seasonal pattern**; rejection ⇒
 *changing / unstable* seasonality. Opposite polarity to HEGY, exactly as
 KPSS vs ADF. Source: Canova-Hansen 1995 (confirmed by the help page: "null
 hypothesis of a stable seasonal pattern").

**Detail on the panel tests (plm).** Two generations:

- **First generation** (`run_purtest`): LLC (Levin-Lin-Chu), IPS (Im-Pesaran-Shin),
 Fisher-type (Maddala-Wu / `madwu`, `Pm`, `invnormal`, `logit`), Hadri. H0
 is typically a unit root (exception: Hadri, H0 = stationarity — opposite
 polarity). They assume **cross-sectional independence**.
- **Second generation** (`run_cipstest`): CIPS (Pesaran), **robust to
 cross-sectional dependence** (common factors across units) via
 `model="cmg"`. Use it when the countries/units share common
 macro shocks. Source: Pesaran 2007; `panel_unit_root` —

---

## 1.5 strucchange: which break tool when

Three distinct questions, three tools (Bai-Perron 2003; Zeileis et al.,
`structural_change` — ):

| Question | Tool | What it returns |
|---------|------|----------------|
| "Where are the breaks and how many?" (endogenous, multiple) | `run_breakpoints` | break positions/dates (min-BIC) + confidence intervals |
| "Is there *general* parameter instability?" (fluctuation) | `run_efp` → `run_sctest` | empirical fluctuation process (CUSUM/MOSUM) + p-value |
| "Is the break at a given/unknown point significant?" (Chow/supF) | `run_Fstats` → `run_sctest` | F-statistics per candidate break + supF/aveF/expF p-value |

`run_sctest` accepts a **raw** `Fstats` or `efp` object (not the wrapper's
list) and produces the p-value that settles the decision.

---

## 1.6 Post-estimation diagnostics (category 15)

Once a model is estimated, we check that the **residuals** respect the assumptions.
A violation ⇒ the model is mis-specified ⇒ the standard errors / forecasts are
unreliable. Every diagnostic has a clear trigger (when it runs):

| Diagnostic | Tool / file | Function | H0 | When it runs |
|-------------|---------------|-----------|-----|-------------|
| **Residual autocorrelation** | `c15_model_evaluation/breusch_godfrey_breusch.py` | `run_bg_test` (Breusch-Godfrey) | no serial correlation | **always** after OLS/regression with time series — the i.i.d. error assumption |
| **Heteroskedasticity** | `c15_model_evaluation/breusch_godfrey_breusch.py` | `run_bp_test` (Breusch-Pagan) | homoskedasticity | after a regression; rejection ⇒ use robust SE |
| **ARCH effects** (conditional variance) | `c15_model_evaluation/arch.py` | `run_arch_test` (Engle ARCH-LM) | no ARCH | on residuals/returns; **rejection ⇒ precondition for GARCH** (go to 12-distribution-risk) |
| **Wrong functional form** | `c15_model_evaluation/breusch_godfrey_breusch.py` | `run_reset_test` (Ramsey RESET) | correctly specified (linear) form | when you suspect non-linearity / omitted variables |
| **Residual normality** | `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.py` | `run_jarque_bera_test` | normality | for valid inference in small samples |
| **Forecast-accuracy comparison** (2 models) | `c15_model_evaluation/diebold_mariano_tscv.py` | `eval_dm_test` (Diebold-Mariano) | equal forecast accuracy | when you choose between **two** competing forecasts |
| **Backtest (rolling-origin CV)** | `c15_model_evaluation/diebold_mariano_tscv.py` | `eval_tsCV` | — | out-of-sample RMSE/MAE/ME per horizon |
| **Comparison of many models** (>2) | `c15_model_evaluation/confidence_set.py` | `run_mcs_procedure` (Model Confidence Set) | — | when you keep "the set of the best" out of **many** models |

**Logical chain (typical flow).**
1. `run_bg_test` → if there is autocorrelation, the model is losing dynamics (add
 lags) — for a VAR use the serial-correlation test of `reduced_form_var`
 (Lütkepohl 2005, multivariate Breusch-Godfrey/Portmanteau).
2. `run_bp_test` → heteroskedasticity ⇒ robust covariance.
3. `run_arch_test` → **if it is rejected, the variance is time-varying** — this
 is the trigger criterion for moving to a GARCH model (ARCH-LM is a
 *precondition* of GARCH, not a plain diagnostic).
4. `run_reset_test` → wrong form ⇒ re-specify (log/non-linear terms).
5. Choice between models: **two** → `eval_dm_test`; **many** → `run_mcs_procedure`;
 out-of-sample performance → `eval_tsCV`.

**DM vs MCS distinction.** **Diebold-Mariano** (Diebold-Mariano 1995) compares
**exactly two** forecast-error series (pairwise). The **Model Confidence Set**
(Hansen-Lunde-Nason 2011) generalises to **many** models at once, returning
the subset that contains the "best" at a given confidence — avoid multiple
pairwise DM (multiple-comparison problem). `run_mcs_procedure` is fed by
`compute_loss_level` (SE/AE point-forecast loss) or `compute_loss_vol`
(SE1/SE2/QLIKE/R2LOG/AE1/AE2 volatility loss).


---

## §2 — Master decision trees

> The core of METHOD-SELECTION. Every node of a tree answers one question,
> names the **exact tool** (wrapper function + file) that checks or
> implements it, and carries a **source** (textbook/paper inline convention + package
> vignette/ URL where the rule is package-specific). The routing rules
> are rule-based — the LLM does NOT improvise; it presses ready-made, gated buttons.
>
> **Reading convention:** `tool` = wrapper function; `[folder/file]` =
> where it lives; "gate" = hard blocker (`stop`) inside the wrapper; every stochastic
> step has a mandatory seed (PROJECT-SCOPE §6 INVARIANTS).
>
> §1 (order-of-integration / stationarity toolkit) is the **prerequisite**
> of every multivariate tree; it is referred to here as "§1".

---

### Tree A — Univariate forecasting (cat. 02)

**When:** one series, target a point/interval forecast (without structural interpretation).

**Precondition — stationarity OPTIONAL.** `auto.arima` differences *endogenously*:
it selects `d` with successive KPSS tests and `D` with a seasonal-unit-root test,
so no manual stationarity check is required beforehand (Hyndman-Khandakar
2008; forecast vignette, ). The seasonality
check HOWEVER determines the routing (seasonal branch) → run the seasonal
unit-root test `run_hegy_test` / `run_ch_test` [c01_preparation_prechecks/seasonal_unit_roots.py]
(HEGY: Hylleberg-Engle-Granger-Yoo 1990; Canova-Hansen 1995) or rely on the
`seasonal.test` of `run_auto_arima` (default "seas").

```
Tree A — univariate forecast
│
├─ Q1: is there seasonality? → run_hegy_test/run_ch_test [c01_preparation_prechecks/seasonal_unit_roots.py]
│ or seasonal.test in run_auto_arima [c02_univariate_forecasting/forecast.py]
│
├─ NON-SEASONAL
│ ├─ small/medium sample, want an automatic and robust baseline
│ │ → run_auto_arima [c02_univariate_forecasting/forecast.py] (ARIMA, differencing endogenous)
│ │ or run_fable_arima [c02_univariate_forecasting/fable.py] (same engine, tidy API)
│ ├─ purely exponential-smoothing dynamics (trend/level, no AR structure)
│ │ → run_ets [c02_univariate_forecasting/forecast.py] (ETS state-space)
│ │ or run_fable_ets [c02_univariate_forecasting/fable.py]
│ └─ fast, robust benchmark (M3 winner)
│ → run_theta [c02_univariate_forecasting/forecast.py]
│
├─ SEASONAL
│ ├─ ONE seasonal pattern, stable
│ │ → run_auto_arima(seasonal=TRUE) or run_ets
│ ├─ MULTIPLE / high-frequency seasonalities (e.g. daily+weekly+yearly),
│ │ non-integer period
│ │ → run_tbats [c02_univariate_forecasting/forecast.py] (trig. seasonality, Box-Cox)
│ └─ MULTIPLE seasonalities + holidays/events + known structural changepoints
│ → run_prophet [c02_univariate_forecasting/prophet.py] (holidays/changepoints)
│ validation: run_prophet_cv
│
├─ BREAKS / structural instability (see strucchange, §1)
│ → prophet (explicit changepoints) or ADAM with explanatory vars
│ → run_adam/run_auto_adam [c02_univariate_forecasting/smooth.py]
│
└─ GENERALISED framework (ARIMA+ETS+regression in one, with multiple
 error distributions, intermittent demand, xreg)
 → run_auto_adam [c02_univariate_forecasting/smooth.py] (ADAM; Svetunkov 2023,
 )
 → run_ces/run_auto_ces (Complex Exponential Smoothing)
```

| Method | tool | when it is preferred | source |
|---|---|---|---|
| ARIMA (auto) | `run_auto_arima` / `run_fable_arima` | default; AR/MA structure, endogenous `d`/`D` | Box-Jenkins; Hyndman-Khandakar 2008 |
| ETS | `run_ets` / `run_fable_ets` | trend/seasonal exponential smoothing | Hyndman et al. 2008 (FPP3 ch.8) |
| Theta | `run_theta` | cheap robust benchmark | Assimakopoulos-Nikolopoulos 2000; Hyndman-Billah 2003 (Theta ≡ SES+drift) |
| TBATS | `run_tbats` | multiple/non-integer seasonalities | De Livera-Hyndman-Snyder 2011 |
| prophet | `run_prophet` | many seasonalities + holidays + changepoints | Taylor-Letham 2018; prophet docs |
| ADAM/CES | `run_auto_adam`/`run_auto_ces` | unified ARIMA+ETS+reg, alternative distributions | Svetunkov 2023 (smooth) |

**Reading the output / traps:** ARIMA intervals presuppose a correct `d` — if
the residuals show autocorrelation (check with `run_bg_test` [15]) the model
is under-differenced. Theta/ETS point forecasts may coincide but the
intervals differ (state-space vs analytic).

---

### Tree B — MULTIVARIATE analysis (FLAGSHIP)

> This is the critical tree. The central error it prevents: **a VAR in levels
> on I(1) non-cointegrated series ⇒ spurious regression** (Granger-Newbold
> 1974; Enders 2015 ch.6; Hamilton 1994 ch.18). The routing is rule-based and
> is not bypassed.

#### Step 1 — Order of integration per series (confirmatory ADF + KPSS)

For **EVERY** series separately, run **both** confirmatory tests (§1):

- `run_adf_test` [c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.py] — H0: unit root (Dickey-Fuller 1979)
- `run_kpss_test` [c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.py] — H0: stationarity (KPSS 1992)
- (alternative/confirmatory: `wrap_ur_ers` DF-GLS, higher power —
 Elliott-Rothenberg-Stock 1996; `wrap_ur_za` for a unit root with an endogenous break
 — Zivot-Andrews 1992; all [c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_suite.py])

**Confirmatory logic** (Enders 2015; KPSS 1992 — the two tests have inverse
H0, so that agreement is decisive):

| ADF | KPSS | Conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| rejects (stationary) | does NOT reject (stationary) | **I(0)** — clear |
| does NOT reject | rejects (non-stationary) | **I(1)** — clear; test the 1st difference to confirm I(1) and not I(2) |
| rejects | rejects | contradictory → possible break/short sample; `wrap_ur_za` |
| does NOT reject | does NOT reject | unclear (low power) → enlarge the sample / DF-GLS |

> Check for I(2): if the 1st difference is still non-stationary, the series is I(2) —
> **neither ARDL bounds nor classical Johansen** hold as they stand (Pesaran-Shin-Smith
> 2001 explicitly requires I(0)/I(1) regressors, not I(2)).

#### Step 2 — Routing based on the order of integration

```
Tree B — multivariate routing (after Step 1)
│
├─ (A) ALL series I(0)
│ → VAR IN LEVELS
│ 1. lag selection: vr_varselect [c03_multivariate_nowcasting/reduced_form_var.py] (AIC/HQ/SC/FPE)
│ 2. estimation: vr_var [c03_multivariate_nowcasting/reduced_form_var.py]
│ 3. stability GATE: vr_var.stable (all |roots|<1; Lütkepohl 2005)
│ stable=FALSE ⇒ IRF/FEVD unreliable
│ 4. diagnostics: vr_serial_test / vr_arch_test / vr_normality_test
│ → structural: Tree B2
│
├─ (B) ALL series I(1) → Johansen cointegration rank test
│ tool: wrap_ca_jo [c05_cointegration/johansen_restricted_vecm.py] (trace or max-eigen)
│ or vecm_rank_test [c05_cointegration/vecm_estimate_johansen.py] — REQUIRES estim="ML" (gate)
│ Sequential comparison of teststat vs cval, STARTING from r=0 (Johansen 1988/1991):
│ │
│ ├─ r = 0 (no cointegration)
│ │ → VAR IN FIRST DIFFERENCES (diff each series, then vr_var)
│ │ ⚠ NEVER a VAR in levels here — spurious (Enders 2015; Hamilton 1994)
│ │
│ ├─ 0 < r < K (cointegration)
│ │ → VECM
│ │ wrap_cajorls [c05_cointegration/johansen_restricted_vecm.py] (restricted VECM at rank r)
│ │ or vecm_estimate [c05_cointegration/vecm_estimate_johansen.py] (2OLS/ML)
│ │ → IRF/FEVD: bridge to a level VAR
│ │ vr_vec2var(z, r) [c03_multivariate_nowcasting/reduced_form_var.py] (Lütkepohl 2005 §6.3)
│ │ vec2var feeds vr_irf/vr_fevd [c04_structural_shocks/svar_irf_fevd.py]
│ │
│ └─ r = K (full rank)
│ → the series were essentially I(0) — RE-CHECK stationarity (Step 1)
│ (Johansen 1995: full rank ⇒ stationary VAR in levels)
│
└─ (C) MIXED order I(0)/I(1) (none I(2))
 → ARDL bounds test (Pesaran-Shin-Smith 2001)
 estimation: ardl_fit / ardl_auto [c05_cointegration/ardl_uecm_estimation.py]
 bounds: ardl_bounds_f (F) + ardl_bounds_t (t) [stochastic→seed]
 or dmac_ardl + dmac_pssbounds [c05_cointegration/dynardl_ardl_ecm.py]
 Decision (F-stat, single regressand):
 F > upper bound ⇒ cointegration (long-run relationship)
 F < lower bound ⇒ NO cointegration
 lower ≤ F ≤ upper ⇒ inconclusive (the order of integration is uncertain)
 → long-run: ardl_multipliers; ECM: ardl_recm/ardl_coint_eq
```

**Johansen decision table (node B):**

| Comparison (from r=0) | rank | Model | tool |
|---|---|---|---|
| trace/max-eigen < cval at r=0 | r=0 | VAR in differences | `vr_var` on diff |
| exceeds cval up to r*, then not | 0<r*<K | VECM | `wrap_cajorls`/`vecm_estimate` |
| exceeds cval at every step | r=K | (stationary) re-check | `run_adf_test` again |

**Interpretation traps:**
- **trace vs max-eigen** may disagree; trace is more robust to
 non-normality (Lütkepohl-Saikkonen-Trenkler 2001) — on disagreement, prefer
 trace and check the residuals. `wrap_ca_jo(type=..)` returns ONLY the
 selected test type per call — `.teststat`/`.cval` hold trace **or**
 max-eigen, not both. To compare trace vs max-eigen, call it TWICE
 (`type='trace'` and `type='eigen'`). (By contrast, `vecm_rank_test` of tsDyn
 gives trace AND eigen p-values together in one `.table` — a single call.)
- The `ecdet`/`type` (const/trend, longrun/transitory) of `ca.jo` must
 match the deterministic terms of your hypothesis — a wrong choice changes
 the cval (Johansen 1995; urca vignette, ).
- `vecm_rank_test` on a 2OLS-fitted VECM ⇒ **gate stop** (rank.test needs ML);
 the root cause is documented in the [c05_cointegration/vecm_estimate_johansen.py] footer.
- The ARDL `case` (1.5 / n,rc,uc,ucrt,ucut) determines the deterministic terms and the
 bounds — a wrong case ⇒ wrong critical values (Pesaran-Shin-Smith 2001 Table CI(i)-CI(v)).

#### Step 3 — Structural analysis → **Tree B2**

Once you have a valid reduced-form VAR/VECM (stable), the "which shock causes what"
requires **identification** → Tree B2.

---

### Tree B2 — SVAR identification (cat. 04)

**When:** you have a reduced-form VAR (`vr_var.model`, class `varest`) and you want
structural IRF/FEVD/HD. The question: **how you go from reduced-form residuals to
structural shocks** (matrix B). The choice = which *theoretical restrictions* you are
willing to impose.

```
Tree B2 — identification
│
├─ I have a clear theoretical ORDERING (contemporaneous recursive causality)
│ → Cholesky / recursive
│ vr_svar(Amat/Bmat) [c04_structural_shocks/svar_irf_fevd.py] or svar_id_chol [c04_structural_shocks/driven_svar_identification.py]
│ ⚠ the ordering IS an assumption — it changes the IRF (Sims 1980; Christiano-
│ Eichenbaum-Evans 1999). Test robustness under alternative orderings.
│
├─ I have a LONG-RUN restriction (e.g. a demand shock neutral on output in the long run)
│ → Blanchard-Quah
│ vr_bq [c04_structural_shocks/svar_irf_fevd.py] (LRIM; Blanchard-Quah 1989)
│
├─ I have a-priori response SIGNS (theory gives signs, not zero restrictions)
│ → sign restrictions
│ vsr_uhlig_reject/vsr_uhlig_penalty/vsr_rwz_reject [c04_structural_shocks/svar_irf_fevdignr.py]
│ (Uhlig 2005; Rubio-Ramírez-Waggoner-Zha 2010; Bayesian→seed)
│
├─ I do not want / do not have theoretical restrictions → data-driven statistical ID
│ ├─ known regime/structural break in the vol → changes-in-volatility
│ │ svar_id_cv(SB=..) [c04_structural_shocks/driven_svar_identification.py] (Rigobon 2003; Lanne-Lütkepohl-
│ │ Maciejowska 2010)
│ ├─ shock independence (least-dependent innovations) → distance covariance
│ │ svar_id_dc [c04_structural_shocks/driven_svar_identification.py] (Matteson-Tsay 2017; seed)
│ └─ non-Gaussian shocks → non-Gaussian ML
│ svar_id_ngml [c04_structural_shocks/driven_svar_identification.py] (Lanne-Meitz-Saikkonen 2017; seed)
│ → CI: svar_wild_boot/svar_mb_boot (Gonçalves-Kilian 2004;
│ Brüggemann-Jentsch-Trenkler 2016; seed)
│
└─ I worry about VAR misspecification / I want an external instrument
 → Local Projections (robust to misspecification; Jordà 2005)
 lp_linear [c04_structural_shocks/local_projections_lp.py] (Cholesky-identified)
 lp_linear_iv [c04_structural_shocks/local_projections_lp.py] (LP-IV, external instrument;
 Stock-Watson 2018)
 lp_nonlinear (state-dependent, two regimes)
```

| Strategy | tool | selection criterion | source |
|---|---|---|---|
| recursive/Cholesky | `vr_svar`/`svar_id_chol` | clear contemporaneous ordering | Sims 1980 |
| long-run BQ | `vr_bq` | theory gives long-run neutrality | Blanchard-Quah 1989 |
| sign restrictions | `vsr_*` | theory gives signs, not zeros | Uhlig 2005; RWZ 2010 |
| changes-in-vol | `svar_id_cv` | known break/regime in the variance | Rigobon 2003 |
| distance-cov | `svar_id_dc` | statistical independence of the shocks | Matteson-Tsay 2017 |
| non-Gaussian ML | `svar_id_ngml` | non-normal shocks | Lanne et al. 2017 |
| local projections | `lp_linear(_iv)` | robustness / external IV / nonlinearity | Jordà 2005; Stock-Watson 2018 |

**Traps:** IRF from `boot=TRUE` require a stable VAR (otherwise the bands open
without bound); the data-driven IDs (`id.dc`/`id.ngml`) do not attach an **economic
label** to the shocks — the interpretation (which shock = monetary) is made ex post from
the impact signs. LP-IV requires a valid (relevant + exogenous) instrument.

---

### Tree C — Volatility / regimes (cat. 06)

**Precondition — ARCH effects.** Before any GARCH, document
conditional heteroskedasticity: `run_arch_test` [c15_model_evaluation/arch.py]
(Engle 1982 ARCH-LM). Without ARCH effects, GARCH is over-parameterisation.

```
Tree C — volatility / regimes
│
├─ Q0 (precondition — ONLY for the GARCH family): run_arch_test [c15_model_evaluation/arch.py]
│ required BEFORE univariate GARCH / DCC-GARCH / MS-GARCH; if there is no ARCH
│ ⇒ stop FOR THOSE (over-parameterisation). The MS-mean (msw_fit) &
│ SETAR/LSTAR paths do NOT require ARCH — they model the mean/dynamics, not the conditional
│ variance; for those, stationarity (SETAR/LSTAR) + a linearity/break test suffice
│ (SETAR: setar_test; MSwM: break-test motivation).
│
├─ ONLY the conditional variance of one series (vol clustering)
│ → univariate GARCH
│ ga_spec → ga_fit → ga_forecast [c06_volatility_regimes/univariate_garch_family.py]
│ (Bollerslev 1986; sGARCH/eGARCH/gjrGARCH; rugarch vignette,
│ )
│
├─ MANY series, time-varying correlations (contagion, correlation spillovers)
│ → multivariate DCC-GARCH
│ dcc_spec/dcc_multispec → dcc_fit → dcc_forecast [c06_volatility_regimes/dcc_mgarch.py]
│ (Engle 2002 DCC)
│
├─ Abrupt changes in the MEAN/dynamics (business-cycle regimes, expansions/recessions)
│ → Markov-switching (mean/AR)
│ msw_fit [c06_volatility_regimes/markov_switching.py] (Hamilton 1989; MSwM: MSM.lm/MSM.glm)
│
├─ Regime switching IN the variance as well (vol regimes)
│ → MS-GARCH
│ msg_spec → msg_fit_ml/msg_fit_mcmc → msg_risk [c06_volatility_regimes/markov_switching_garch.py]
│ (Haas-Mittnik-Paolella 2004; MCMC→seed)
│
└─ Nonlinear threshold dynamics (asymmetry around a threshold)
 → SETAR (abrupt) / LSTAR (smooth)
 A linearity test COMES FIRST: setar_test [c06_volatility_regimes/threshold.py]
 setar_fit/lstar_fit/star_fit; setar_select for lag/threshold
 (Tong 1990 SETAR; Teräsvirta 1994 LSTAR)
```

| Method | tool | when | source |
|---|---|---|---|
| univariate GARCH | `ga_fit` | vol clustering, 1 series | Bollerslev 1986 |
| DCC-GARCH | `dcc_fit` | time-varying correlations | Engle 2002 |
| MS-mean/AR | `msw_fit` | discrete regimes in the dynamics | Hamilton 1989 |
| MS-GARCH | `msg_fit_ml` | regimes in the vol | Haas et al. 2004 |
| SETAR/LSTAR | `setar_fit`/`lstar_fit` | threshold nonlinearity | Tong 1990; Teräsvirta 1994 |

**Traps:** the linearity test (`setar_test`) is mandatory before a threshold model —
otherwise you over-fit on linear data (Teräsvirta 1994). MS-GARCH MCMC without a seed
= non-reproducible (gate/seed). DCC requires all univariate specs to have
converged (dcc_fit gate).

---

### Tree D — Causality / policy (cat. 07)

> **Design-based tree.** The choice is NOT made by statistics but by the
> *research design* (the source of exogeneity). ⚠ Critical trap: **Granger causality =
> predictive, NOT structural/causal** (Granger 1969; "Granger-cause" ≠ "cause").
> For predictive precedence → `vr_causality` [c03_multivariate_nowcasting/reduced_form_var.py]; for a *causal
> effect* use the designs below.

```
Tree D — causal identification (ask: where does the exogeneity come from?)
│
├─ Randomization (RCT / natural experiment with randomisation)
│ → simple comparison / OLS with controls (fx_feols [c07_causality_policy/fixed_effects_ols.py])
│
├─ Sharp cutoff in a running variable (eligibility threshold)
│ → RDD
│ wrap_rdrobust/wrap_rdbwselect [c07_causality_policy/rdd_robust.py] (sharp & fuzzy;
│ Calonico-Cattaneo-Titiunik 2014)
│ or wrap_rdd_reg_np/wrap_rdd_bw_ik [c07_causality_policy/rdd.py] (Imbens-Kalyanaraman 2012)
│
├─ Treatment at DIFFERENT points in time (staggered adoption)
│ → Callaway-Sant'Anna group-time ATT
│ wrap_att_gt → wrap_aggte [c07_causality_policy/staggered_did.py] (Callaway-Sant'Anna 2021)
│ or the imputation estimator
│ wrap_did_imputation [c07_causality_policy/staggered_didimputation.py] (Borusyak-Jaravel-Spiess 2021)
│ (both correct the TWFE bias under heterogeneous timing —
│ Goodman-Bacon 2021)
│
├─ ONE treated unit + donor pool (comparable untreated units)
│ → Synthetic Control
│ wrap_dataprep→wrap_synth [c07_causality_policy/synthetic_control.py] (Abadie-Diamond-Hainmueller 2010)
│ inference: wrap_scest/wrap_scpi [c07_causality_policy/synthetic_control_prediction.py] (Cattaneo et al. 2021)
│ tidy API: wrap_synthetic_control [c07_causality_policy/synthetic_control_2.py]
│ multiple treated / interactive FE: wrap_gsynth [c07_causality_policy/generalized_synthetic_control.py] (Xu 2017)
│
├─ A valid instrument (relevant + exclusion)
│ → IV / 2SLS
│ wrap_ivreg [c07_causality_policy/iv_2sls.py] (Wooldridge) or fx_feols(..|iv) [c07_causality_policy/fixed_effects_ols.py]
│
├─ High-dim controls / heterogeneity, I want a √n-consistent effect
│ → Double/Debiased ML
│ wrap_doubleml_data→wrap_doubleml_plr/_irm [c07_causality_policy/double_debiased.py]
│ (Chernozhukov et al. 2018)
│ → heterogeneous treatment (CATE)
│ wrap_causal_forest→wrap_average_treatment_effect [c07_causality_policy/causal_forests_grf.py]
│ (Wager-Athey 2018; Athey-Tibshirani-Wager 2019)
│
└─ Time-series intervention at a known moment (single series, counterfactual)
 → CausalImpact (BSTS counterfactual)
 run_causal_impact [c07_causality_policy/counterfactual_intervention.py] (Brodersen et al. 2015)
```

| Design | tool | requirement | source |
|---|---|---|---|
| RDD | `wrap_rdrobust` | sharp/fuzzy cutoff | CCT 2014 |
| staggered DiD | `wrap_att_gt`/`wrap_did_imputation` | parallel trends, variable timing | Callaway-Sant'Anna 2021; BJS 2021 |
| synthetic control | `wrap_synth`/`wrap_scpi`/`wrap_gsynth` | 1(+) treated, donor pool | Abadie et al. 2010; Xu 2017 |
| IV | `wrap_ivreg`/`fx_feols` | valid instrument | standard |
| DML / causal forest | `wrap_doubleml_*`/`wrap_causal_forest` | high-dim controls / CATE | CCDDHNR 2018; Wager-Athey 2018 |
| TS intervention | `run_causal_impact` | known moment, good predictors | Brodersen et al. 2015 |
| **Granger (predictive)** | `vr_causality` | NOT structural; precedence only | Granger 1969 |

---

### Tree E — Distribution / risk (cat. 12)

**When:** the question concerns the *tail* or the whole *conditional distribution*, not the
conditional mean.

```
Tree E — distribution / risk
│
├─ Conditional distribution of a macro variable / downside macro risk (Growth-at-Risk)
│ → STEP 1: quantile regression
│ qr_growth_at_risk(formula, data, tau=..) [c12_distribution_risk/quantile_regression.py]
│ (Koenker-Bassett 1978; Adrian-Boyarchenko-Giannone/ABG 2019 AER)
│ helpers: qr_regression; qr_conditional_quantiles; qr_slope_equality
│ → STEP 2 (full ABG): fit a skew-t to the conditional quantiles → FULL density + ES
│ st_fit_quantiles(probs, quantiles) → st_density/st_shortfall [c12_distribution_risk/skew_fit_fitted.py]
│ (ABG 2019; Azzalini-Capitanio 2003; #95) alpha<0 ⇒ vulnerable-growth downside
│
└─ Portfolio / returns tail risk (VaR / Expected Shortfall)
 → pa_var/pa_expected_shortfall [c12_distribution_risk/value_risk_expected.py]
 (methods: historical/gaussian/modified-Cornish-Fisher)
 pa_downside_risk; pa_component_var (Boudt-Peterson-Croux 2008)
```

| Question | tool | source |
|---|---|---|
| GaR / conditional quantiles (step 1) | `qr_growth_at_risk` | ABG 2019; Koenker-Bassett 1978 |
| GaR full density + ES (step 2) | `st_fit_quantiles`→`st_density`/`st_shortfall` | ABG 2019; Azzalini-Capitanio 2003 |
| VaR / ES (raw returns) | `pa_var`/`pa_expected_shortfall` | PerformanceAnalytics; Cornish-Fisher for "modified" |

**Traps:** quantile crossing at extreme tau (non-monotone quantiles) — check
`qr_conditional_quantiles`; the skew-t fit (`#95`) **rejects** non-monotone quantiles (gate).
"modified" VaR (Cornish-Fisher) becomes unreliable under extreme skew/kurtosis; "historical"
needs a sufficient sample in the tail.

---

### Tree F — Trend / cycle / output gap (cat. 10)

**When:** decomposition into trend + cycle (output gap, credit gap, potential output).
The choice is governed by **real-time vs full-sample** and model-free vs model-based.

```
Tree F — trend / cycle extraction
│
├─ Two-sided smoothing, known ex post (in-sample cycle)
│ → HP filter
│ mfl_hp_filter(lambda) [c10_trend_cycle_statespace/hp_baxter_king.py] (Hodrick-Prescott 1997;
│ lambda=1600 quarterly, Ravn-Uhlig 2002)
│ ⚠ END-POINT BIAS + spurious cycles (Hamilton 2018); band-pass alternatives:
│ mfl_bk_filter (Baxter-King 1999); mfl_cf_filter (Christiano-Fitzgerald 2003)
│
├─ Real-time / one-sided (policy, does not see the future; Basel credit gap)
│ → one-sided HP
│ hp_one_sided(lambda) [c10_trend_cycle_statespace/sided_hp_filter.py]
│ (Basel III credit-to-GDP gap: lambda=400000;
│ Drehmann-Borio-Tsatsaronis 2011)
│
├─ Avoiding HP spurious-cycle artefacts entirely
│ → Hamilton regression filter
│ hf_filter/hf_glm [c10_trend_cycle_statespace/hamilton_regression_filter.py] (Hamilton 2018:
│ "Why You Should Never Use the HP Filter")
│
├─ Model-based unobserved components (trend/cycle as a state, with CI)
│ → structural time-series / Kalman
│ kf_trend_cycle/kf_local_linear_trend [c10_trend_cycle_statespace/kalman_filter_smoother.py] (Harvey 1989; KFAS)
│ or dl_trend_cycle/dl_local_level [c10_trend_cycle_statespace/dynamic_linear.py] (Petris et al., dlm)
│
└─ Multivariate trend / common factor (NAIRU-style, many indicators → 1 trend)
 → dynamic factor analysis
 marss_dfa(m=..) [c10_trend_cycle_statespace/multivariate_state_space.py] (Holmes-Ward-Wills 2012; MARSS)
 marss_forecast; marss_param_cis
```

| Filter | tool | one/two-sided | source |
|---|---|---|---|
| HP (two-sided) | `mfl_hp_filter` | two-sided; end-point bias | Hodrick-Prescott 1997 |
| band-pass | `mfl_bk_filter`/`mfl_cf_filter` | two/one-sided | BK 1999; CF 2003 |
| one-sided HP | `hp_one_sided` | one-sided (real-time) | Drehmann et al. 2011 (BIS) |
| Hamilton filter | `hf_filter` | regression-based | Hamilton 2018 |
| UC / Kalman | `kf_trend_cycle`/`dl_trend_cycle` | model-based, with CI | Harvey 1989 |
| DFA / NAIRU | `marss_dfa` | multivariate common trend | Holmes et al. 2012 |

**Traps:** HP end-point bias means that the most recent gap is revised
drastically as new data arrive — NEVER use a two-sided HP for real-time policy (use
`hp_one_sided`). Lambda controls the smoothing; a wrong lambda ⇒ a wrong cycle (Ravn-Uhlig 2002).

---

### Tree G — Panel data (cat. 08 + #6)

**When:** you have a panel `i × t` (countries/regions × time) and you want to estimate
an effect. The choice is governed by **static vs dynamic**, **small T vs large-T macro
panel**, and **cross-sectional dependence**.

```
Tree G — panel estimation
│
├─ 1. Poolability: are there individual effects at all?
│ → pd_poolability_test [c08_panel_data/static_panel_estimators.py] (Breusch-Pagan LM 1980;
│ H0: no effects -> reject => you need FE/RE, not pooled OLS)
│ + pd_effects_ftest (F within vs pooling)
│
├─ 2. FE vs RE: are the effects correlated with the regressors?
│ → pd_hausman_test [c08_panel_data/static_panel_estimators.py] (Hausman 1978;
│ reject H0 => FE consistent/RE inconsistent -> choose FE; otherwise RE is more efficient)
│ estimation: pd_fit(model="within"|"random")
│
├─ 3. Dynamic panel (lagged y as a regressor); small T & large N => Nickell bias
│ → GMM (NOT FE: within on a dynamic panel is biased O(1/T))
│ pd_gmm_fit [c08_panel_data/static_panel_estimators.py] (Arellano-Bond 1991, difference-GMM)
│ POST-GATES (mandatory): pd_gmm_autocorr_test [AR(2)/m2 NOT rejected]
│ pd_gmm_sargan_test [overidentification, H0 valid instruments]
│
├─ 4. Panel unit roots — ONLY for macro panels (large T)
│ → run_purtest [c01_preparation_prechecks/panel_unit_root.py] (LLC/IPS/Fisher/Hadri)
│ (small-T micro panels: skip; the order of integration is meaningless)
│
└─ 5. Cross-sectional dependence (CSD) — common shocks across units?
 → run_cipstest [c01_preparation_prechecks/panel_unit_root.py] (Pesaran 2007 CIPS,
 second generation; model="cmg" = Common Correlated Effects Mean Group, Pesaran 2006)
 (first-generation purtest is size-distorted under CSD -> prefer CIPS)
```

| Step | tool | rule / source |
|---|---|---|
| poolability | `pd_poolability_test`/`pd_effects_ftest` | Breusch-Pagan 1980; Baltagi |
| FE vs RE | `pd_hausman_test` | Hausman 1978 (reject => FE) |
| dynamic / Nickell bias | `pd_gmm_fit` + `pd_gmm_autocorr_test`/`pd_gmm_sargan_test` | Nickell 1981; Arellano-Bond 1991 |
| panel unit roots (large T) | `run_purtest` | Levin-Lin-Chu; Im-Pesaran-Shin |
| cross-sectional dependence | `run_cipstest` (CIPS/CMG) | Pesaran 2006, 2007 |

**Traps:** (1) **Nickell bias** — FE `within` on a dynamic panel (lagged y) is
biased O(1/T); with small T ⇒ GMM, NOT FE. (2) GMM without the m2/Sargan post-gates
is unreliable (instrument proliferation; an AR(2) rejection ⇒ invalid instruments).
(3) `hadri` has the **opposite** polarity (H0=stationarity, like KPSS). (4) First-generation
panel unit-root tests break down under CSD ⇒ CIPS.

---

### Tree H — Forecast workflow (cat. 15 / 17)

**When:** you have one or many forecasting models and you want **end-to-end evaluation
and selection** — from in-sample diagnostics to out-of-sample density scoring.

```
Tree H — forecast evaluation & selection
│
├─ 1. In-sample diagnostics (is the model adequate at all?)
│ → run_bg_test/run_bp_test/run_reset_test [c15_model_evaluation/breusch_godfrey_breusch.py]
│ (Breusch-Godfrey serial corr; Breusch-Pagan hetero; RESET functional form)
│ + run_arch_test [c15_model_evaluation/arch.py] (ARCH effects -> volatility model)
│
├─ 2. Out-of-sample backtest (rolling-origin)
│ → eval_tsCV [c15_model_evaluation/diebold_mariano_tscv.py] (per-horizon RMSE/MAE, Hyndman)
│
├─ 3. Point-forecast comparison of 2 models
│ → eval_dm_test [c15_model_evaluation/diebold_mariano_tscv.py] (Diebold-Mariano 1995;
│ H0: equal accuracy -> reject => one dominates)
│
├─ 4. MANY models -> which set is statistically equivalent-best?
│ → run_mcs_procedure [c15_model_evaluation/confidence_set.py] (Model Confidence Set;
│ Hansen-Lunde-Nason 2011; trimmed to a (1-alpha) set)
│
├─ 5. Combination (instead of selecting one)
│ → run_hybrid [c17_forecast_combination/ensemble_forecast_combination.py] (Bates-Granger 1969;
│ Timmermann 2006; equal/insample/CV weights)
│
└─ 6. DENSITY forecast (posterior/ensemble draws) -> proper scoring, NOT point
 → sr_crps_sample/sr_logs_sample [c15_model_evaluation/density_forecast_evaluation.py] (#94;
 CRPS/LogS negatively oriented; Gneiting-Raftery 2007); sr_pit_sample calibration
```

| Step | tool | rule / source |
|---|---|---|
| in-sample diagnostics | `run_bg_test`/`run_bp_test`/`run_reset_test`/`run_arch_test` | Breusch-Godfrey/Pagan; Engle 1982 |
| backtest (tsCV) | `eval_tsCV` | Hyndman-Athanasopoulos |
| point comparison (DM) | `eval_dm_test` | Diebold-Mariano 1995 |
| model set (MCS) | `run_mcs_procedure` | Hansen-Lunde-Nason 2011 |
| combination | `run_hybrid` | Bates-Granger 1969; Timmermann 2006 |
| **density scoring** | `sr_crps_sample`/`sr_logs_sample`/`sr_pit_sample` | Gneiting-Raftery 2007 (#94) |

**Traps:** (1) **point ≠ density** — DM/MCS apply to point forecasts; for distributions
use CRPS/LogS (#94), NOT DM. (2) CRPS/LogS are **negatively oriented**
(LOWER=BETTER). (3) in-sample fit ≠ out-of-sample: always tsCV/holdout before
concluding. (4) MCS does not say "which is best" — it says "which are not excluded".

---

### Recipes (composition of wrappers — chaining; not a new method)

Compositions of existing tools into known macro pipelines. Every step points to an existing
tool; the recipe is read self-contained by L3.

**FAVAR — Factor-Augmented VAR** (Bernanke-Boivin-Eliasz 2005):

```
Recipe FAVAR — factors → augmented VAR → IRF/FEVD
│
├─ 1. Extract K factors from a LARGE panel of indicators (informational summary)
│ → df_dfm [c03_multivariate_nowcasting/dynamic_factor_nowcasting.py] (#15;
│ Stock-Watson 2016 diffusion index; static/dynamic factors; .factors = the F_t)
│
├─ 2. Augment the VAR: [factors, key observables (e.g. the policy rate)] as a system
│ → vr_var [c03_multivariate_nowcasting/reduced_form_var.py] (#11 reduced-form VAR
│ on the factors+observables)
│
└─ 3. Structural transmission analysis: IRF / FEVD of the system
 → vr_irf/vr_fevd [c04_structural_shocks/svar_irf_fevd.py] (#19; recursive/Cholesky)
```

**When FAVAR instead of a large BVAR (#12):** when you have **dozens to hundreds** of indicators
(e.g. 120 monthly series) and want to condense the information into a few factors —
FAVAR solves the degrees-of-freedom problem of the VAR without Bayesian shrinkage.
Prefer **BVAR (#12)** when the variables are few to moderate (e.g. <20) and you want
full posterior uncertainty without the two-step generated-regressor problem.

**Trap (generated regressors):** the two-step FAVAR uses **estimated**
factors as regressors in the VAR — it ignores the **estimation uncertainty** of the factors
(generated-regressors problem; Pagan 1984). The IRF standard errors are
understated; strict inference requires a bootstrap over the factor step as well,
or a one-step Bayesian FAVAR (outside the current surface).

**Sources:** Bernanke, Boivin & Eliasz 2005 *QJE* 120(1):387-422 (Measuring the Effects
of Monetary Policy: A FAVAR Approach); Stock & Watson 2016 (Handbook of Macroeconomics,
Dynamic Factor Models); Pagan 1984 *Int. Econ. Rev.* 25 (generated regressors).

### Supplementary trees (analysed in the method cards — §3)

One line each; the full routing + output reading is in the corresponding cards.

- **Panel data (cat. 08):** static → `pd_fit` FE/RE + `pd_hausman_test` (FE vs RE; Hausman 1978); dynamic/endogeneity → `pd_gmm_fit` (Arellano-Bond 1991) + `pd_gmm_sargan_test`/`pd_gmm_autocorr_test` [c08_panel_data/static_panel_estimators.py]. Source: Wooldridge; plm vignette.
- **Cross-section / networks (cat. 09):** input-output & multipliers, GVAR, connectedness (Diebold-Yılmaz 2012), spatial regression (Anselin 1988), graph metrics — see the cat. 09 cards.
- **Decomposition / accounting (cat. 11):** productivity (Malmquist/DEA; Färe et al. 1994) + Oaxaca-Blinder wage-gap decomposition (Oaxaca 1973; Blinder 1973) [11]. ⚠ DEA is silently wrong on negative/zero inputs.
- **Bayesian toolkit (cat. 14):** BVAR/Minnesota priors, brms/rstan HMC, convergence gates (Rhat/ESS; Vehtari et al. 2021) — see the cat. 14/03 cards.
- **Model evaluation (cat. 15):** forecast comparison `eval_dm_test` (Diebold-Mariano 1995); `run_mcs_procedure` (MCS; Hansen-Lunde-Nason 2011); `eval_tsCV`; regression diagnostics `run_bg_test`/`run_bp_test`/`run_reset_test` [15].
- **Limited dependent (cat. 16):** binary/count outcomes → `run_feglm_binom` (logit/probit) [c16_limited_dependent/binomial_glm_recession.py]; ROC/AUC `run_roc` [c16_limited_dependent/roc_auc_binary.py] (⚠ level inversion). Source: Wooldridge.
- **Yield curve (cat. 18):** term-structure fit → `fit_nelson_siegel` (Nelson-Siegel 1987); `fit_svensson` (Svensson 1994) [c18_yield_curve/nelson_siegel_svensson.py].
- **Business-cycle dating (cat. 19):** peak/trough dating → `date_business_cycles` (Bry-Boschan 1971) + `average_over_phases` [c19_business_cycle_dating/harding_pagan_bbq.py]. Change-point detection → `detect_changepoints` (PELT/BinSeg/SegNeigh/AMOC, `change_point_detection`) + `changepoint_segments` [c19_business_cycle_dating/change_point_detection.py]; Bayesian PPM `detect_change_points` [c19_business_cycle_dating/bayesian_change_point.py]; energy-stats multivariate `detect_changepoints_divisive`/`detect_changepoints_agglo` [c19_business_cycle_dating/energy_statistics_nonparametric.py].
- **Inequality (cat. 22):** Gini/Theil/Atkinson → `compute_inequality`; Lorenz `lorenz_curve` [c22_inequality/inequality_indices_lorenz.py] (Gini 1912; Cowell 2011). Extended/S-Gini, Atkinson, GEI + subgroup decomposition `ic2_sgini`/`ic2_decomp_gei` [c22_inequality/tax_progressivity_redistribution.py]; RIF regressions/decomposition `rif_regression`/`gini_decomposition` [c22_inequality/drivers_inequality_change.py]; survey-aware `svy_inequality`/`svy_poverty` [c22_inequality/complex_survey_aware.py]; GB2 fit `fit_gb2` [c22_inequality/gb2_parametric_income.py]; affluence/richness `richness_index` [c22_inequality/affluence_richness_indices.py] (Kakwani 1977; Firpo-Fortin-Lemieux 2009).

## §3. Data utilities — the everyday data layer — `c00_data_utilities/`

when this category applies: **in almost every task, BEFORE any econometric method** — it is the "everyday data layer". Here you (a) bring the series into the canvas as input — **only** from a **user upload** (reader nodes) — one single data source, (b) move it to a common class/frequency and apply basic transformations (`time_series_class` #78), (c) fill gaps (`imputeTS` #80), (d) change the frequency up/down (`temporal_aggregation_series` #79), (e) produce ACF/PACF/CCF/rolling/corr descriptives (`descriptive_statistics` #81) and (f) apply the deterministic macro identities growth/annualize/deflate/rebase/per-capita/contributions (`macro-arithmetic` #82). None of these estimates a stochastic model (exception: `temporal_aggregation_series`, which is regression-based) — it is the preparatory/accounting layer on top of which every other category runs.

---

### #78 Unifying time-series classes + basic transformations — `time_series_class` (`c00_data_utilities/time_series_class.py`)
**Functions:** `ts_convert` [`ts_ts`/`ts_xts`/`ts_tsibble`/`ts_df`], `ts_transform` [`ts_diff`/`ts_pc`/`ts_pcy`/`ts_pca`], `ts_rebase` [`ts_index`], `ts_standardize` [`ts_scale`], `ts_lag_series` [`ts_lag`], `ts_aggregate` [`ts_frequency`], `ts_limit_span` [`ts_span`], `ts_fill_regular` [`ts_regular`], `ts_combine` [`ts_c`/`ts_bind`], `ts_stats` [`ts_summary`]

**When:** immediately after data entry (the user's upload), as the unified "everyday" data layer — conversion between class systems (ts/xts/tsibble/df) and the standard analyst transformations (diff, % changes, index/rebase, z-scores, lag, aggregation to a lower frequency, span restriction, materialising gaps, combining series, per-series descriptives). `time_series_class` locates the time column FROM THE CLASS (Date/POSIXct), so a long df (upload) works as it stands.

**When NOT:** for charts (all `ts_plot`/`ts_ggplot`/`theme_*` are omitted — the JS frontend draws them); for **increasing** the frequency (disaggregation) → `temporal_aggregation_series` #79 (`ts_aggregate` goes ONLY to a lower frequency); for NA imputation → `imputeTS` #80 (`ts_fill_regular` merely materialises the implicit gaps as NA, it does NOT fill them with values).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** no formal statistical precondition (mechanical transformations). Gates: every input `ts_boxable` and non-empty; `ts_aggregate` has a **hard gate that the target is of lower frequency** than the current one (comparison of periods-per-year via `ts_summary.freq`, otherwise a cryptic data.table error); `ts_lag_series` accepts a finite integer or a string offset; `ts_rebase` rejects `base=NA`; `ts_limit_span` requires ≥1 of start/end + a post-gate that it did not empty the series.

**Alternatives + criterion:** `macro-arithmetic` #82 for the same operations with **explicit, checked conventions** (growth with an annualize convention, deflate, rebase with base_value≠1, per-capita, contributions with an additivity check) — prefer it when you need the macro semantics and the post-checks, not merely the class-agnostic transformation. `time_series_class` is preferred when the issue is **class conversion / frequency plumbing**.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- Every wrapper: `series` (the converted/transformed object — `ts`→`{values,start,frequency}`, `mts`/matrix→nested rows, `DataFrame`→records, `tbl_ts`→records) + `class`/`n`/`freq` + the arguments that were applied.
- `ts_transform`: `pc`=period-over-period %, `pcy`=year-over-year % (same period of the previous year), `pca`=annualized % of pc, `diff`=simple difference.
- **`ts_rebase`/`ts_index` trap**: the index is set **= 1** (NOT 100) at the `base` date; `base` is a **DATE** (string/Date), NOT a numeric value — `base=100` errors. For a base=100 index use `macro_rebase` (#82). Two dates → the mean of the range = 1.
- **`ts_aggregate` trap**: only to a lower frequency; `aggregate="last"` ≠ end-of-period value if observations are missing.

**Sources:** tsbox reference/vignette (`ts_index`, `ts_frequency`, `ts_scale`, `ts_pc`/`ts_pcy`/`ts_pca`, `ts_summary`) — Sax, "tsbox: Class-Agnostic Time Series" <https://docs.ropensci.org/tsbox/> / <

---

### #79 Temporal (dis)aggregation of series — `temporal_aggregation_series` (`c00_data_utilities/temporal_aggregation_series.py`)
**Functions:** `td_disaggregate` [`td` + `predict`], `td_aggregate` [`ta`]

**When:** when you must change the **frequency with sum/mean consistency** — `td_disaggregate` for low→high (e.g. annual GDP → quarterly, with or without a high-frequency indicator), `td_aggregate` for high→low (the deterministic inverse, sum/average/first/last). The model is specified lm-like: `low ~ indicator(s)` (GLS Chow-Lin/Fernandez/Litterman) or `low ~ 1` (pure Denton/Denton-Cholette interpolation, in which case `to` is required).

**When NOT:** for plain aggregation without a consistency requirement → `ts_aggregate` (#78) suffices; for filling scattered NA (not a frequency change) → `imputeTS` (#80); it is not a forecasting tool (extrapolation happens ONLY when the indicator extends beyond the low-freq series in time — and here it is **deliberately blocked**, see the trap).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** the **high-frequency indicator must COVER the low-frequency series in time** — a critical gate (`.tda_coverage` + escalation of the "Discarding/shorter than/Extrapolat" warning to `stop`): otherwise `td` silently discards low-freq observations or extrapolates, corrupting the data with ONLY a warning. Also: `formula` a valid formula; `truncated.rho ∈ [-1,1]`; `|fixed.rho|<1` (only for the `*-fixed` methods); `h ∈ {0,1,2}` (Denton differencing); `to` unique (numeric → a positive integer frequency ratio); a post-gate that `fr` (the high:low ratio) is a positive integer and that `predict`/`ta` return a `ts`.

**Alternatives + criterion:** **default = `chow-lin-maxlog`** (recommended by the documentation, good over a wide range); `fernandez`/`litterman-*` when the underlying series is I(1)/random-walk-like; `denton-cholette` (or `fast`, a shortcut of `chow-lin-fixed` with rho≈1) when you have **no indicator** and want a smooth interpolation; `ols`/`uniform` as benchmarks. For non-regular cases (e.g. months→days) tsbox must be installed.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `disaggregated` (`ts` high-frequency, →`{values,start,frequency}`) — the main result; `low_span`/`high_span` = requested vs realized ranges (data integrity, explicit in the output).
- `coefficients`/`std_errors`/`rho`/`method`/`conversion`/`fr` + regression stats `r_squared`/`adj_r_squared`/`logl`/`aic`/`bic`/`rss`/`tss`/`s_2`/`s_2_gls`/`rank`/`df`; `residuals`/`fitted_low`/`actual` are **low-frequency** (at the level of the input, not of the disaggregated output).
- **Interpretation traps**: (1) the **Denton methods leave the regression stats NULL→NA** (`.tda_or_na`) — do not read them as a "bad fit"; there is no regression there. (2) `conversion` must match the meaning of the series (flow→`sum`, index/rate→`average`, stock→`last`/`first`); a wrong conversion gives a consistent but WRONG result. (3) `rho` close to the truncation bound (0) indicates a weak indicator.

**Sources:** tempdisagg help (`help("td","tempdisagg")`, `ta`) — Sax & Steiner, "Temporal Disaggregation of Time Series", 5(2):80-88, 2013 <https://doi.org/10.32614/RJ-2013-028>; Chow & Lin 1971 (*Review of Economics and Statistics* 372-375); Denton 1971 (*JASA* 66(333):99-102); Fernández 1981; Litterman 1983; Santos Silva & Cardoso 2001 (*Economic Modelling* 18:269, dynamic Chow-Lin).

---

### #80 Replacing missing values (NA) in time series — `imputeTS` (`c00_data_utilities/replacement_missing_values.py`)
**Functions:** `imputets_kalman` [`na_kalman`], `imputets_interpolation` [`na_interpolation`], `imputets_seadec` [`na_seadec`], `imputets_statsna` [`statsNA`]

**When:** when a series has scattered/internal NA and you need a complete series for methods that do not tolerate gaps (VAR, filters, ACF). First `imputets_statsna` to **map the NA pattern** (count, gaps, longest/most-weighty), then choose the imputer: Kalman/state-space (default, best for structured series), interpolation (linear/spline/stine), or seasonal decomposition (deseasonalize → impute → reseasonalize).

**When NOT:** when the "gap" is in fact a frequency difference (e.g. quarterly vs annual) → `temporal_aggregation_series` #79, not imputation; when the WHOLE tail is missing (extrapolation/forecast) → forecasting methods (cat. 02), not interpolation; for merely materialising implicit gaps as NA (without filling) → `ts_fill_regular` #78.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** `x` a numeric vector/one-dimensional `ts` (not matrix/df), **≥2 non-NA observations**, not all-NA (`.its_check_x`); `maxgap` positive (Inf allowed); `model`/`option`/`algorithm` via `match.arg`. **`imputets_seadec` requires a seasonal `ts` (frequency>1, ≥2 complete periods)** unless `find_frequency=TRUE` — otherwise the stl error "series is not periodic".

**Alternatives + criterion:** `na_kalman` (default) for series with trend/seasonality and medium gaps; `na_interpolation` (linear/spline/stine) for a fast, model-free filling of small gaps; `na_seadec` when strong seasonality dominates and you want to preserve it. **`maxgap` protects against over-imputation**: long NA runs beyond `maxgap` stay NA (you handle them separately).

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `imputed` (`ts`/numeric →`{values,start,frequency}`) + `method`/parameters; **`n_imputed`** = positions that were NA and were filled, **`n_remaining_na`** = remaining NA (>maxgap).
- `na_report` (`statsNA` as data): `length_series`, `number_NAs`, **numeric `percentage_NAs`** (the raw field is the string "28.6%"), `number_na_gaps`, `average/longest/most_frequent/most_weighty_na_gap`, `gap_distribution`.
- **Interpretation traps**: (1) `n_remaining_na > 0` is NOT an error — it is the deliberate `maxgap` cut-off. (2) `algorithm="random"` in `na_seadec` is stochastic → the wrapper enforces a **seed (default 42L)** for reproducibility; two calls without a seed would give different numbers. (3) `bins` affects ONLY the (non-returned) binned print table; `gap_distribution` is UNBINNED (per exact gap length). (4) imputed values carry no uncertainty — do not treat them as observations in inference without care.

**Sources:** imputeTS help (`na_kalman`, `na_interpolation`, `na_seadec`, `statsNA`) — Moritz & Bartz-Beielstein, "imputeTS: Time Series Missing Value Imputation ", 9(1):207-218, 2017 <https://doi.org/10.32614/RJ-2017-009>; Harvey 1990 *Forecasting, Structural Time Series Models and the Kalman Filter* (Kalman/StructTS); Hyndman & Khandakar 2008 (*JSS* 26(3), auto.arima state-space).

---

### #81 Descriptive statistics as data (ACF/PACF/CCF/rolling/corr + per-pair correlation inference) — `stats`+`zoo` (`c00_data_utilities/descriptive_statistics.py`)
**Functions:** `desc_acf` [`acf`], `desc_pacf` [`pacf`], `desc_ccf` [`ccf`], `desc_rolling` [`rollapply`], `desc_correlations` [`cor`], `desc_cor_test` [`cor.test` + `p.adjust`]

**When:** exploration/diagnosis before the model — autocorrelation (ACF) and partial autocorrelation (PACF) for ARMA order identification and serial dependence, cross-correlation (CCF) for lead/lag relationships between two series, rolling-window statistics (mean/sd/…) for changing volatility/trend, a correlation matrix for cross-sectional relationships. All return **numeric data (never a plot)** — the frontend draws. `desc_cor_test` when you need **INFERENCE** (p-values/CI) per pair with a **multiplicity correction**.

**When NOT:** as a formal stationarity test (the ACF is indicative, not a test — for a decision use ADF/KPSS in cat. 01); as causality (CCF correlation ≠ Granger — see the multivariate categories); for **partial/conditional** correlation (conditioning on third variables → regression, cat. 06/07); on **autocorrelated** series without prewhitening (the i.i.d. null of `cor.test` is violated → inflated Type I error).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** the input numeric, non-empty, **without NA/NaN/Inf** (`.dsc_check_numeric_vec` — this is why you run `imputeTS` #80 first if there are NA); `lag.max` a positive integer `< length(x)`; `width ≤ length(x)`; `n≥3` for acf/pacf/ccf; `x,y` of the same length for ccf; `data` a numeric matrix/df with ≥2 columns and ≥2 rows. **Stationarity**: for an interpretable ACF/PACF the series must be stationary → run a unit-root test first (cat. 01, ADF/KPSS); on a non-stationary series the ACF decays slowly and linearly (an artefact, not structure).

**Alternatives + criterion:** ACF vs PACF — an **ACF cut-off** indicates the MA(q) order, a **PACF cut-off** indicates the AR(p) order (Box-Jenkins); use both together. `method="pearson"` (default, linear) vs `"spearman"`/`"kendall"` (rank-based, robust to non-linearity/outliers). `desc_rolling` `align="right"` (causal, default) vs `"center"` (smoothing, non-causal).
**`desc_correlations` vs `desc_cor_test` (delimitation):** `desc_correlations` gives **POINT** estimates (a p×p matrix, no hypothesis, no p-value) → exploration/heatmap; `desc_cor_test` gives **INFERENCE** per pair (`statistic`, df, p-value, conf.int) + a **MANDATORY** multiplicity correction. The point estimates are **IDENTICAL** (test-covered) — the difference is **ONLY** the inference.
**`p.adjust.method="BH"` (default) vs `holm`/`bonferroni`:** BH controls the **FDR** (more powerful, for screening many pairs); `holm`/`hochberg`/`hommel`/`bonferroni` control the **FWER** (when EVERY false positive is costly). `bonferroni` is **dominated** by `holm` → use `holm`. The alias `"fdr"` is NOT exposed (identical to BH).
**`use="pairwise.complete.obs"` (default) vs `"complete.obs"`:** pairwise = maximum n per pair but a **DIFFERENT sample per pair** (the p-values are not strictly comparable); `complete.obs` = listwise drop, a **COMMON** sample across all pairs (comparable, smaller n); `na.fail` = a hard stop on any NA.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `acf`/`pacf`/`ccf` (numeric vectors) + `lag` + `n_used` + **`ci_upper`/`ci_lower` = ±1.96/√n** (white-noise 95% band): a spike outside the band = statistically significant (at roughly the 5% level).
- `desc_ccf`: **direction trap** — under the `ccf(x, y)` convention (as the wrapper calls it) lag k estimates `cor(x[t+k], y[t])`, so **negative** lags mean that x **leads** y (x leads; the peak appears at lag<0), while **positive** lags mean that x **lags** (y leads). Always confirm the lag-sign convention on the raw object before concluding lead/lag.
- `desc_rolling`: `rolled` (index-aligned, `fill=NA` at the edges) + `index`; the NA at the edges are structural (the window does not fit), not missing data.
- `desc_correlations`: `correlation` (matrix →nested rows+dimnames), `n`=**the rows that were supplied** (NOT per-pair complete!), `n_pairwise`=the actual sample size per pair. **Trap**: with `use="pairwise.complete.obs"` and NA, the scalar `n` OVERSTATES the per-pair sample — read `n_pairwise` for a meaningful interpretation; a strong correlation with a small `n_pairwise` is fragile.
- `desc_cor_test`: `pairs` = tidy records **PER PAIR** (`var1`, `var2`, `n`, `estimate`, `statistic`, `statistic_name`, `parameter`, `p_value`, `p_adjusted`, `conf_low`, `conf_high`, `ties`, `exact_used`). **ALWAYS read `p_adjusted`, NOT `p_value`.**
- `desc_cor_test`: `pair_order` = an **EXPLICIT deterministic** order (upper triangle by **COLUMN INDEX** (1,2),(1,3),…,(p−1,p) — **NOT alphabetically**), so that stored workflows reproduce (charter §5).
- `desc_cor_test`: `n_rows_input` / `n_rows_used` / `n_missing_cells` (`n_missing_cells` is measured **BEFORE** the listwise drop); `any_ties` / `any_exact_fallback` / `warnings` = degradation flags.
- **Trap** `desc_cor_test` (kendall/spearman): neither `conf.int` **NOR** df is defined — the wrapper returns an **explicit NA** in `conf_low`/`conf_high`/`parameter` (NEVER a silently omitted field). Source: `the cor.test documentation` "conf.int … Currently only given for Pearson's … at least 4 complete pairs" (live-verified: `is.null(conf.int)==TRUE` for kendall and spearman).
- **Trap** `desc_cor_test` (ties): `cor.test` **SILENTLY DOWNGRADES** the exact p-value to an asymptotic approximation and ONLY warns ("cannot compute exact p-value with ties"). The wrapper exposes this as **DATA**: `ties` / `exact_used` / `any_exact_fallback` / `warnings` (each warning carries its pair). Look at `exact_used` before trusting small p-values.
- **Trap** `desc_cor_test` (spearman, n>1290): AS 89 is abandoned **silently (WITHOUT a warning)** in favour of the t-approximation. `the cor.test documentation` says "n < 1290" while the `stats` code checks "n <= 1290" — the wrapper encodes the **CODE** (live-verified), which is why `exact_used` is reliable.
- **Trap** `desc_cor_test` (constant column): `cor.test` does **NOT** error — it ONLY warns ("the standard deviation is zero") and returns an NA estimate/p-value (live-verified for all 3 methods). The wrapper makes this a **HARD GATE**, per column **AND** per pair (a column may have variance overall yet be constant on the common non-NA rows of a pair).
- **Trap** `desc_cor_test` (pearson): `cor.test` **SILENTLY** ignores `exact`/`continuity` (live-verified: identical p-value, no warning) → the wrapper makes them a **hard gate** so that the user does not believe they took effect.
- **Trap** `desc_cor_test` (time series): the i.i.d. null of `cor.test` is violated on autocorrelated macro series → inflated Type I error. For lead/lag on time series use `desc_ccf` (with prewhitening) or Granger (cat. 06), **NOT** `desc_cor_test` on raw levels.
- **Trap** `desc_cor_test` (n): the single gate `n>=4` is **DELIBERATELY** stricter than the per-method minimum (pearson n≥3, kendall/spearman n≥2 — live-verified) so that the output shape does not change silently with the method; at n=2/3 kendall/spearman return a degenerate |r|=1 with p=1.

**Sources:** base `stats` help (`acf`, `pacf`, `ccf`, `cor`) & zoo help (`rollapply`) < Box, Jenkins & Reinsel *Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control* (ACF/PACF order identification); Enders 2015 *Applied Econometric Time Series* 4th ed. §2 (correlogram); white-noise band ±1.96/√n; `the cor.test documentation` (version 4.6.1) — exact rules (kendall n<50; spearman AS 89), `conf.int` only for pearson with ≥4 complete pairs, + the `cor.test.default` source (the DEFINITION of ties, cutoff `n <= 1290`); `the p.adjust documentation` (version 4.6.1) — BH/BY/holm/hochberg/hommel/bonferroni, "BH (or its alias fdr)"; Benjamini & Hochberg (1995) *JRSS-B* 57(1):289-300 [doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x] (FDR — the BH default); Holm (1979) *Scand. J. Statist.* 6:65-70 (step-down FWER; dominates Bonferroni); Benjamini & Yekutieli (2001) *Ann. Statist.* 29(4) [doi:10.1214/aos/1013699998] (FDR under dependence — BY).
