### #118 Parametric distributions as a numeric grid (fan-chart data) — `parametric_distributions_numeric` (`c00_data_utilities/parametric_distributions_numeric.py`)
**Functions:** `dist_fan_quantiles` [`dist_normal`/`dist_student_t` + `quantile`], `dist_prob_cdf` [`cdf`], `dist_density_grid` [`density`], `dist_moments` [`mean`/`variance`]

**When:** when a forecast/scenario is described by PARAMETERS (mean/sd, df) and you need NUMERIC data for the frontend: quantile bands per horizon (a fan chart), a CDF (P(X≤q), e.g. P(inflation>target)), a density curve (ridgeline/pdf), or moments. `family`∈{normal, student_t (location-scale, fat tails)}. Recycling: every parameter of length 1 or of a common length L (e.g. increasing `mu`/`sigma` per forecast horizon → a widening fan).

**When NOT:** for density-forecast evaluation (CRPS/LogS/PIT) → `scoringRules` #94; for empirical quantiles FROM a sample → `quantile` / `caTools` #110; for FITTING a distribution to data → #12 (the wrapper does NOT fit — it TAKES parameters). No drawing here — numeric grids only.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** `mu`/`sigma` finite and non-empty; **`sigma` strictly >0** (=0 is degenerate, <0 is a pkg error); **student_t: `df` mandatory and >0**; **`probs` strictly in (0,1)** (probs>1 → a silent WARN 'NaNs produced'; 0/1 → ±Inf — a hard gate BEFOREHAND); `at` finite and non-empty; incompatible lengths → a clean stop (otherwise the cryptic vctrs 'Can't recycle').

**Alternatives + criterion:** `dist_fan_quantiles` for fan bands; `dist_prob_cdf` for tail probabilities; `dist_density_grid` for a ridgeline/pdf; `dist_moments` for mean/var/sd. student_t instead of normal when the scenario has fat tails (a small `df` → heavier tails; df→∞ → normal). For the same family but density-forecast SCORING → `scoringRules` #94.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `dist_fan_quantiles`: `quantiles` (an n_dist × n_probs matrix: row=distribution/horizon, column=band) + `probs`/`family`/`params` + `mean`/`sd`.
- `dist_prob_cdf`: `cdf` (n_dist × n_at) in [0,1]; `dist_density_grid`: `density` (n_dist × n_at) ≥0.
- `dist_moments`: `mean`/`variance`/`sd` per distribution.
- **Trap**: the Student-t variance is INFINITE for df≤2 (and the mean undefined for df≤1) → `to_mcp` serialises it to null; do NOT read that as 0. **Trap**: `sigma` is a scale, NOT the sd for t (sd = sigma·√(df/(df-2)) for df>2).

**Sources:** the distributional reference/pkgdown (`dist_normal`/`dist_student_t`/`cdf`/`variance`; the generics `quantile`/`density`) v0.8.1 — <https://pkg.mitchelloharawild.com/distributional/> / <
### #119 US NBER recession chronology (shading + dummy) — `nber_recession_chronology` (`c00_data_utilities/nber_recession_chronology.py`)
**Functions:** `nber_recessions` [`nberDates`, overlap-clipped to [from,to]], `nber_recession_flag` [a per-date 0/1 recession dummy from the NBER windows]

**When:** when you want the official NBER recession intervals (Business Cycle Dating Committee, peak→trough) as NUMERIC data — either for recession-shading bands that the frontend draws over any chart (`nber_recessions`), or as a 0/1 recession-dummy regressor aligned to the time index of a macro series (`nber_recession_flag`). A static, deterministic US chronology (34 recessions, 1857→the 2020 COVID one).

**When NOT:** for DRAWING the bands (nberShade/ymdShade/romerLines — omitted; the JS frontend draws them); for non-US business cycles or for data-driven turning-point dating (the NBER chronology is fixed, NOT estimated); for the Romer monetary-policy dates (not exposed).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** no statistical precondition (a static lookup). Gates: `from`/`to` accept a Date / an ISO string / a yyyymmdd integer and REJECT anything that does not parse into a real date (this catches a bare-year `from=2020`, "2020-13-40", NA, a fractional/non-finite numeric — NEVER a silent NA); a hard gate `from<=to`; `nber_recession_flag(dates)` a non-empty vector with every element a valid date (anyNA => stop, NO silent drop); `as_date` strictly TRUE/FALSE.

**Alternatives + criterion:** reader/data nodes + `time_series_class` #78 when you need the series itself/transformations rather than a recession reference; `nber_recession_flag` when you want a 0/1 dummy per date instead of intervals for shading. The recession chronology is a unique fixed reference — there is no alternative estimation.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `nber_recessions`: `recessions` a records df (`start`,`end` = the business-cycle PEAK→TROUGH; a yyyymmdd integer by default, or a Date if `as_date=TRUE`) + `n_recessions`/`from`/`to`/`as_date`. The filtering is by OVERLAP (end>=from & start<=to) — the correct semantics for shading a chart range.
- `nber_recession_flag`: `flags` a records df (`date`, `in_recession` 0/1) + `n`/`n_recession_periods`/`as_date`.
- **Boundary trap**: the recession window is INCLUSIVE at both ends (the Start=peak and End=trough belong to the recession); the day AFTER the trough => 0.
- **Empty-window trap**: a recession-free [from,to] => 0 rows (valid, NOT an error); to_mcp => an empty table.
- **yyyymmdd trap**: `20200101` is a yyyymmdd INTEGER, NOT a year; `from=2020` errors (it is not an 8-digit date).

**Sources:** tis reference — `the nberDates documentation` ("a matrix with two yyyymmdd columns, Start/End, of the recessions defined by the NBER"; live docs_help_page nberShade.Rd), Hallman, "tis: Time Indexes and Time Indexed Series" < the NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee <https://www.nber.org/research/business-cycle-dating>.
### #120 Numeric rescaling + axis-break positions + label strings — `numeric_rescaling_axis` (`c00_data_utilities/numeric_rescaling_axis.py`)
**Functions:** `scale_rescale` [`rescale`], `scale_rescale_mid` [`rescale_mid`], `scale_breaks` [`breaks_extended`/`breaks_log`], `scale_labels` [`label_number`/`label_percent`]

**When:** a pure DATA-helper layer of the canvas — when you need (a) a linear (min-max) rescale of a numeric series into a target range c(min,max) (e.g. [0,1] for normalisation/visual comparison of heterogeneous series, or around a midpoint for diverging data such as growth around 0), (b) the computation of axis-break positions as DATA (Wilkinson extended, linear or logarithmic) that the frontend will use for its axes, (c) the formatting of numbers into label strings (number/percent). It returns ONLY numeric/string data — no ggplot scale, no chart.

**When NOT:** for a macro-semantic rebase (index base=100, deflate, per capita) → `macro-arithmetic` #82 / `ts_rebase` #78 (`scale_rescale` is a mechanical min-max, WITHOUT economic semantics); for the chart drawing itself / colour palettes / ggplot scale objects → frontend (ALL `col_*`/`alpha`/`*_trans`/`scale_*`/`pal_*`/`show_col` are deliberately omitted); for z-score standardization → `ts_standardize` #78 (`scale_rescale` is range-based, NOT mean/sd).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** no statistical precondition (deterministic mechanical transformations). Gates (ALL live-probed on scales 1.4.0): the input numeric and non-empty with ≥1 finite value; `to`/`from` numeric of EXACTLY length 2 and finite — **a silent-wrong trap: `to`/`from` of length 1 => `zero_range` => it returns `mean(to)` for EVERY element** (and a `to` with Inf => Inf/NaN); `mid` a finite number of length 1 (length 2 => silent recycling); `n` an integer ≥ 1 (**n=0/negative => `extended` enters an infinite loop — a live-confirmed hang**); `base` > 1 (base ≤ 1 => `breaks_log` enters an infinite loop); type='log' requires POSITIVE values (otherwise the cryptic `missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed`); `accuracy` a positive number of length 1 or NULL; `big_mark` a string of length 1; a post-gate: an empty breaks vector (a non-finite range) => stop.

**Alternatives + criterion:** `ts_standardize` #78 (z-scores via center/scale) when you want normalisation by mean/sd instead of a min-max range; `macro_rebase` #82 (base=100, date-anchored) for indices with an economic base instead of a mechanical [0,1]; `ts_transform` #78 for %/diff transformations. `numeric_rescaling_axis` is preferred purely for range normalization + axis-break positions + label formatting on numeric data.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `scale_rescale`/`scale_rescale_mid`: `values` (numeric, the same length as x; NA are preserved as NA/null) + `to`/`from`(/`mid`)/`n`. **Trap:** a constant series (a zero-range `from`) => all values = `mean(to)` (the documented `zero_range` behaviour — NOT an error).
- `scale_breaks`: `breaks` (the numeric positions), `n_breaks`, `type`(, `base`). The positions are "nice" readability-optimised numbers — `n_breaks` ~ `n`, NOT exactly `n` (`n` is a target).
- `scale_labels`: `labels` (character; NA => "NA"/null in JSON), `type`, `n`. percent = ×100 + '%'.

**Sources:** the scales reference/help pages (`rescale`/`rescale_mid`: `to=c(0,1)`, `from=range(x,na.rm,finite)`, `mid=0`; `breaks_extended(n)`/`breaks_log(n,base)`; `label_number`/`label_percent(accuracy,big.mark)`) — Wickham & Seidel, "scales: Scale Functions for Visualization" < / < Wilkinson extended breaks: Talbot, Lin & Hanrahan (2010), "An Extension of Wilkinson's Algorithm for Positioning Tick Labels on Axes".
### #121 Analytical OLS: a deterministic trend / named predictors — `stats` + `broom` (`c00_data_utilities/analytic_ols_closed.py`)
**Functions:** `ols_trend(y, trend)` [`lm` on a CLOSED trend formula via `reformulate` — `linear`=1+t, `quadratic`=1+t+t^2 — + the DETRENDED series = the residuals of the trend fit], `ols_regress(data, response, predictors)` [`lm` on named numeric predictor columns of a DataFrame]. The output of both: the `tidy` coefficient table (term/estimate/std.error/statistic/p.value), `glance` (r.squared/adj.r.squared/sigma/AIC/BIC/…), `fitted`, `residuals`, `model` (the producer handle).

**When:** for a fast, deterministic (analytical QR, WITHOUT a seed) linear model at the data layer — (a) removing a deterministic trend from a series (`analytic_ols_closed` → `detrended`), or (b) a simple linear regression on **explicitly named** numeric columns (`ols_regress`). The formula is always CLOSED (an enum or bare column names), built internally with `reformulate` — NEVER a free user string (no arbitrary term syntax is executed).

**When NOT:** for charts (the JS frontend draws them); for a **stochastic trend / unit root** — OLS detrending is valid ONLY if the series is trend-stationary; if it has a unit root it needs **differencing** (see the unit-root tests #2, `unit_root_suite`), not a deterministic detrend (a spurious trend); for categorical/factor predictors or interactions/WLS/offset (a numeric-only closed design here — another node); for residual diagnostics → pass the `model` handle to `breusch_godfrey_breusch`/`FinTS` (#76).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** `y`/the columns numeric and finite (without NA/NaN/Inf — a hard gate, otherwise `lm` SILENTLY applies `na.omit` and changes the sample size); `n > k` (a positive residual df — a saturated fit ⇒ `sigma=NaN` is blocked); a full-rank design (`any(is.na(coef))` ⇒ collinearity, `lm` SILENTLY produces an `NA` coefficient ⇒ stop); `ols_regress`: `data`=a DataFrame, `response`=ONE existing non-empty name, `predictors`=a non-empty vector of existing names without duplicates, `response ∉ predictors`. The statistical validity of the detrend: trend stationarity (KPSS/ADF, #2).

**Alternatives + criterion:** `#82 macro-arithmetic` — when you need explicit macro conventions (growth/deflate/rebase) instead of a model; `mFilter`/HP (#56) trend-cycle — when you want a **flexible/non-parametric** trend instead of a low-order polynomial; `quantile_regression` (#64, GaR) — when you want conditional quantiles instead of a conditional mean; the unit-root tests (#2) — when the question is whether detrending or differencing is the right tool.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `coefficients` (DataFrame→records): `term`/`estimate`/`std.error`/`statistic` (t)/`p.value`. `glance` (DataFrame→records): `r.squared`/`adj.r.squared`/`sigma`/`statistic` (F)/`AIC`/`BIC`/`logLik`/`df.residual`/`nobs`.
- `fitted`/`residuals` numeric vectors; `analytic_ols_closed` additionally `detrended` (= the residuals of the trend fit — the detrended series). `n`/`k` = observations/parameters.
- **NA trap**: the gates reject NA/Inf up front; there is NO silent `na.omit`. Impute (#80) first if needed.
- **Detrend vs difference trap**: `analytic_ols_closed` removes a DETERMINISTIC trend; on a series with a unit root the residuals remain non-stationary — use differencing.
- **Collinearity trap**: perfectly collinear predictors ⇒ `lm` gives an `NA` coefficient SILENTLY; here it is blocked (a rank-deficient stop).
- `model` = the producer handle (RDS): pass it to diagnostic/prediction nodes.

**Sources:** stats `lm`/`reformulate` (the reference base docs, r-btw `docs_help_page`); broom `tidy.lm`/`glance.lm` ( broom 1.0.x, `docs.ropensci.org/broom`); Wooldridge, *Introductory Econometrics* (deterministic trend and detrending); Hamilton, *Time Series Analysis* ch.3 (trend-stationary vs difference-stationary — the detrend caveat).

### #122 Bootstrap unit-root tests (robust to heterogeneity/volatility/missing data) — `bootUR` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/bootstrap_unit_root.py`)
**Functions:** `bur_boot_adf` [`boot_adf`], `bur_boot_union` [`boot_union`], `bur_boot_panel` [`boot_panel`], `bur_order_integration` [`order_integration`]

**When:** testing stationarity/unit roots when the asymptotic critical values (adf.test/ur.df #1/#2) do NOT apply — heteroskedasticity, non-stationary volatility, structural changes in the variance, or an inability to trust the tables of critical values; bootUR builds the H0 distribution with a residual bootstrap instead of fixed tables (Smeekes & Wilms 2023). `bur_boot_adf`: one series, an explicit choice of deterministics/detrending. `bur_boot_union`: one series, the union of 4 specs (intercept/trend × OLS/QD) — robust to an arbitrary choice of deterministics/detrending (the preferred default for the univariate case). `bur_boot_panel`: a Group-Mean panel test, H0 = ALL series have a unit root. `bur_order_integration`: estimates the order of integration I(d) PER series and returns the appropriately differenced/stationarised data (`diff_data`) — a feeder for the VAR/VECM/cointegration nodes.

**When NOT:** fixed asymptotic critical values + complete tables suffice → `unit_root_suite` #2 (ur.df/ur.ers/ur.pp/ur.kpss); a fast classical test → `unit_root_normality` #1 (adf/kpss/pp); SEASONAL unit roots → `seasonal_unit_roots`/HEGY #89; a stationarity test with H0=stationarity (instead of a unit root) → KPSS (#1/#2); panel unit roots with fixed-N asymptotics → `purtest`/`cipstest` #6; charts (frontend). The raw multivariate joint/FDR tests `boot_ur`/`boot_sqt`/`boot_fdr` are NOT exposed here as direct nodes (they are reached only internally via the `method=` of `bur_order_integration`).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** a complete series WITHOUT NA (a hard gate — bootUR SILENTLY TRIMS leading/trailing NA and errors on an internal NA; align/fill first with imputeTS #80); >=20 observations per series (short series run silently with an unreliable result); a non-constant series (var>0; otherwise the cryptic `inv_sympd: singular`); `B>=99` (otherwise the cryptic "iterations too low"); the single-series functions reject multivariate input (→ `bur_boot_panel`); panel/order require >=2 columns. **STOCHASTIC → `seed` MANDATORY** (set.seed before every draw; do_parallel=FALSE; verified reproducible across processes).

**Alternatives + criterion:** `bur_boot_union` over `bur_boot_adf` — prefer the union when you do not want to commit to a specific deterministics/detrending choice (robust to that nuisance choice); use boot_adf when you have an a-priori specification (e.g. trend + QD ⇒ DF-GLS). Bootstrap method: `AWB` (default, autoregressive wild — robust, general) · `MBB`/`SB` do NOT handle unbalanced/missing data (they error) · `SB`/`SWB` are not recommended for panels (invalid for joint testing — a warning is issued). `detrend=QD` ⇒ more powerful (DF-GLS) near unity. `criterion=MAIC` (Ng-Perron, the default) for lag selection; `AIC/BIC` are the classical ones.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `bur_boot_adf`/`bur_boot_union`: `statistic`, `p_value`, `estimate` (gamma — the coefficient on the lagged level; **NA for the union** by construction), `stationary` (bool), `decision`, `selected_lag`(adf)/`selected_lags`(union, 4 combos), `alpha`, `bootstrap`/`B`/`criterion`/`seed`.
- `bur_boot_panel`: `statistic` (Group-Mean), `p_value`, `some_stationary`, `individual_statistics`/`individual_pvalues`/`individual_estimates`/`selected_lags` (N×specs matrices, nested arrays with dimnames), `series_names`.
- `bur_order_integration`: `order_int` (a named integer I(d) per series), `classification` ("I(0)"/"I(1)"…), **`diff_data`** (the stationarised (T×N) matrix — a PRODUCER, register→Parquet, feeding downstream VAR/cointegration).
- **POLARITY TRAP (critical):** the bootUR ADF/union/panel tests have **H0 = a unit root** ⇒ `p<alpha ⇒ STATIONARY (I(0))` — the OPPOSITE of KPSS, where a rejection ⇒ NON-stationary. Do not confuse the two polarities when combining tests (ADF-reject=stationary vs KPSS-reject=nonstationary).
- **Panel trap:** H0 = ALL series have a unit root; a rejection ⇒ **SOME** are stationary (NOT all) — run the individual single tests to identify them (the per-series details are returned).
- **Union estimate trap:** `estimate=NA` is not an error — a single gamma is not defined across the 4 combinations.

**Sources:** bootUR reference/JSS vignette (`boot_adf`, `boot_union`, `boot_panel`, `order_integration` — r-btw docs-verified, bootUR 1.0.5) — Smeekes, S. & Wilms, I. (2023), "bootUR: An the reference Package for Bootstrap Unit Root Tests", *Journal of Statistical Software* 106(12), 1-39 <https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v106.i12> / < Palm, Smeekes & Urbain (2011, *J. Econometrics* 163:85-104, the panel GM test); Harvey, Leybourne & Taylor (2012); Ng & Perron (2001, MAIC); Smeekes & Wijler (2020, the order of integration).

### #123 Covariate-Augmented Dickey-Fuller (CADF) unit-root test — `CADFtest` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/covariate_augmented_dickey.py`)
**Functions:** `run_cadf(y, X, type, max.lag.y, min.lag.X, max.lag.X, criterion, alpha)` → `CADFtest`. Without `X` (NULL) = a plain ADF; with stationary covariates `X` = CADF (Hansen 1995), which INCREASES the power of the test.

**When:** testing for a unit root in a univariate series WHEN you have one or two **stationary** covariates correlated with the innovations of the series — then CADF has substantially higher power than plain ADF against the H0 of a unit root. With `X=NULL` it works as an alternative ADF with full asymptotic p-values (Costantini-Lupi-Popp) and automatic lag selection (AIC/BIC/HQC/MAIC).

**When NOT:** if you do NOT have a genuinely stationary covariate → use plain ADF/PP (`unit_root_normality` #1) or ADF/ERS with full critical values (`unit_root_suite` #2); for an H0 of STATIONARITY (the inverse polarity, confirmatory) → KPSS (`unit_root_normality`/`unit_root_suite`); for a seasonal unit root → HEGY/Canova-Hansen (`seasonal_unit_roots` #89); for a structural break under a unit root → Zivot-Andrews (`ur.za`). The covariates must be stationary — a non-stationary `X` invalidates the asymptotic theory.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** `y` must be a univariate `ts`, without NA, of sufficient length (≥15) and with non-zero variance; the covariates `X` must be **stationary** (check that first with ADF/KPSS #1) and **aligned** with `y` (the same `nrow`). Gates (hard `stop`): y is.ts/univariate/no-NA/length≥15/var>0; type and criterion via `match.arg`; `max.lag.y`,`max.lag.X` non-negative integers; `min.lag.X` an integer (negative=a lead) AND ≤ `max.lag.X`; X numeric+aligned+no-NA; effective observations > parameters (which excludes degenerate fits).

**Alternatives + criterion:** `ur.df/ur.ers` #2 when you want the classical tables of critical values without covariates; `adf.test/pp.test` #1 for fast univariate screening; **prefer CADF** only when a genuinely stationary, correlated covariate exists (otherwise you gain no power). For lag selection: `criterion="AIC"/"BIC"` (max/min as the upper/lower bounds); the default `"none"` = a fixed `max.lag.y`.

**Reading the output** (L2 `to_mcp`): `method` ("ADF test"|"CADF test"), `statistic` (+`statistic_label`, e.g. "CADF(0,2,0)"), `p_value` (the Costantini-Lupi-Popp surface), `rho2` (a nuisance parameter — CADF ONLY, `NULL` for ADF), `estimate`/`null_value`, `alternative`="less", the (se)lected `max_lag_y`/`min_lag_X`/`max_lag_X`, `info_criteria` {AIC,BIC,HQC,MAIC}, `decision`, `warnings`.
- **Polarity trap:** H0 = a UNIT ROOT, the alternative = stationarity (one-sided). **Rejecting H0 (p<alpha) => STATIONARITY** — the OPPOSITE of KPSS (where a rejection => non-stationarity). Do not confuse them.
- **Silent-wrong trap (gated):** the package silently drops NA in `y`, accepts NA/misaligned `X`, and at many lags throws a cryptic `subscript out of bounds` / `NAs are not allowed` — all blocked by gates.
- **Small-sample trap:** the message "Specified sample size may be too small" is PRINTED to stdout (it is NOT an the reference warning) → it is exposed via `warnings`; on such small samples the p-value is less reliable.
- `min.lag.X<0` = leads (a documented feature) — CADF can also use leads of the covariates.

**Sources:** CADFtest reference `CADFtest` (r-btw docs) — Hansen BE (1995) "Rethinking the Univariate Approach to Unit Root Testing", Econometric Theory 11(5):1148-1171; Costantini-Lupi-Popp (2007) Panel-CADF (asymptotic p-values); Lupi C (2009) "Unit Root CADF Testing with the reference", JSS 32(2) <http://www.jstatsoft.org/v32/i02/>.
### #124 General-to-Specific (GETS) + Indicator Saturation — `general_specific_selection` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/general_specific_selection.py`)
**Functions:** `gts_arx` [`arx` — the AR-X GUM, producer→`model`], `gts_getsm` [`getsm` — a multi-path GETS simplification of the mean specification of an `arx`], `gts_isat` [`isat` — IIS/SIS/TIS indicator saturation, producer→`model`]

**When:** automatic, rule-based model selection and detection of structural anomalies at the preparation stage. Set up a General Unrestricted Model with `gts_arx` (intercept + AR lags + conditioning regressors), then (a) `gts_getsm` for a parsimonious final model via a multi-path GETS with PET encompassing, or (b) `gts_isat` for the **automatic detection of outliers (IIS), mean shifts (SIS) and trend shifts (TIS)** as saturating indicators. Deterministic (an OLS multi-path search, no seed).

**When NOT:** for a break test at a **known/unknown single point** with a formal sup-F/CUSUM → `structural_change` #3 (`breakpoints`/`Fstats`/`efp`); for outliers via an ARIMA intervention → `automatic_outlier_detection`; for the **log-variance (ARCH) GETS** (`getsv`) — omitted here, the button targets the mean specification; for charts (frontend).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** a sufficiently specified GUM (enough AR lags for the residuals to be ~white noise — see Ljung-Box); `y` univariate numeric with ≥10 obs and without **interior** NA (leading/trailing ones are allowed via `na.trim`). Gates: `mxreg` **aligned** (NROW==length(y) — silent-wrong if it is longer); `t.pval`/`wald.pval` **strictly in (0,1)** (silent-wrong: the package accepts 1.5); `isat` requires ≥1 of iis/sis/tis; `vcov.type` ∈ {ordinary,white,newey-west} (getsm: the documented surface is {ordinary,white}). For a stationarity diagnosis of `y` first → ADF/KPSS #2.

**Alternatives + criterion:** `structural_change` #3 when you want a **hypothesis-driven** break test (sup-F, OLS-CUSUM) instead of an **automatic multiple selection** of indicators; `isat` is preferred when you do not know the number/position of the breaks and want data-driven saturation with a controlled gauge (set a **tight** `t.pval`, e.g. 0.001, so that the false-detection rate ≈ `t.pval·n`). `getsm` is preferred for variable selection with encompassing when you have many candidate regressors.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- Every wrapper: `coefficients` (named) + `mean_results` (a tidy df: `term/coef/std_error/t_stat/p_value`) + `sigma`/`rss`/`logl`/`r_squared` + `fitted`/`residuals` (numeric chart-data) + `n`/`k`/`df`.
- `gts_arx`/`gts_isat`: they additionally return `model` — the fitted `arx`/`isat` object (**a producer**, register→an RDS blob; `to_mcp` turns it into a **stub** `@mcp_serialized=FALSE`, the extracted values live in the sibling fields).
- `gts_isat`: `is_names` (the selected indicators, e.g. `sis41`), `n_indicators`, `isat_dates.iis/.sis/.tis` (per mechanism a df: `breaks/date/index/coef/coef.se/coef.t/coef.p`) — **this is where you read the break points**.
- **Direction trap:** `sisNN` = a **step** shift starting at observation NN (a permanent level change); `iisNN` = an **impulse** (an isolated outlier at NN); `tisNN` = a **trend** shift. Do not confuse them.
- **Gauge trap:** a tighter `t.pval` ⇒ fewer false detections but also lower power; the `isat` default `t.pval=0.001` (NOT 0.05) exists exactly for this.
- **Empty-model trap:** `gts_getsm` may end at the empty model (no variable significant) → `empty_model=TRUE`, `coefficients` of length 0 (structured, NOT a silent NULL).

**Sources:** the `general_specific_selection` reference (`arx`, `getsm`, `isat`, `isatdates`, `rsquared`) — Pretis, Reade & Sucarrat (2018), "Automated General-to-Specific (GETS) Regression Modeling and Indicator Saturation for Outliers and Structural Breaks", *Journal of Statistical Software* 86(3), doi:10.18637/jss.v086.i03; Sucarrat (2020), ** 12(2):388-401; Hendry & Doornik (2014), *Empirical Model Discovery and Theory Evaluation* (MIT Press).
### #125 Seasonality tests — `seasonality` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/seasonality.py`)
**Functions:** `run_isseasonal` [`isSeasonal`, a boolean dispatcher, test ∈ {combined,qs,fried,kw,seasdum,welch,ocsb}], `qs_test` [`qs`], `fried_test` [`fried`], `kw_test` [`kw`], `seasdum_test` [`seasdum`], `welch_test` [`welch`], `ocsb_test` [`ocsb`]

**When:** at the preparation/prechecks stage, AFTER the stationarity tests (#1/#2) and BEFORE seasonal adjustment (#3 X-13/#4) or seasonal-aware modelling — to decide structurally whether a monthly/quarterly/weekly series is seasonal. `run_isseasonal` = the fast boolean gate (a faithful mirror of `isSeasonal`, with the WO combined rule by default). The individual tests (`qs/fried/kw/seasdum/welch`) when you need the statistic + p-value of one specific test. `ocsb_test` for a SEASONAL UNIT ROOT (how many seasonal differences are needed — the nsdiffs convention).

**When NOT:** for non-seasonal stationarity → tseries/urca (#1/#2); for the seasonal adjustment itself (deseasonalising) → seasonal/X-13 (#3) — seastests only DETECTS, it does not remove seasonality; for frequency=1 (annual/without a seasonal period) — a hard gate; for charts (the frontend draws).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** a univariate `ts` with **frequency > 1** (a hard gate: freq=1 → a cryptic pkg error); **without NA** (a hard gate: seastests SILENTLY accepts NA and returns a wrong decision — live-confirmed); **≥ 3 complete seasonal cycles** (n ≥ 3·freq; fewer than 3 cycles → the cryptic "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed" in combined/qs/welch); a non-constant series (var>0). The input is normalised to a genuine `ts` (welch fails live with "object 'intra' not found" on a plain numeric vector).

**Alternatives + criterion:** `seasonal_unit_roots`/`nsdiffs` for deciding the number of seasonal differences (`ocsb_test` covers the OCSB part); `seas` (#3) when the target is deseasonalisation rather than detection; among the seastests: `combined` (WO) as the default combined rule; `qs` for TRAMO-SEATS-style seasonal autocorrelation; `seasdum` for explicit deterministic seasonal dummies; `ocsb` when you suspect a seasonal UNIT ROOT (stochastic seasonality) rather than a deterministic one.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- Every wrapper: `test`, `null_hypothesis`, `statistic`, `p_value`, `alpha`, `is_seasonal` (boolean), `decision` (text), `freq`, `n_obs` (+ the echoed args; `run_isseasonal(combined)`: `statistic=NA`, `p_values` = the 3 named WO p-values; ocsb: `method/augmentations/nrun/seed`).
- **POLARITY TRAP (critical):** `combined/qs/fried/kw/seasdum/welch` have **H0 = no seasonality** → a SMALL p (< alpha) ⇒ SEASONAL. **`ocsb` has H0 = a SEASONAL UNIT ROOT** → the INVERSE polarity: a SMALL p ⇒ REJECTING the unit root (seasonally stationary); a LARGE p (≥ alpha, fail to reject) ⇒ a seasonal unit root IS PRESENT ⇒ `is_seasonal=TRUE` (the nsdiffs convention). This is why `null_hypothesis` is ALWAYS returned — the meaning of the p-value is structurally explicit.
- **`combined` trap:** the `.stat` of combined_test is a LOGICAL decision (the WO rule: QS p<0.01 OR KW p<0.002), NOT a numeric statistic; `alpha` does NOT affect the decision.
- **Residual-based trap:** a pure deterministic sine is NOT detected by `combined` (the residuals of the auto-ARIMA are white noise); it needs a seasonal structure that survives (a seasonal AR / seasonal means).
- **`isSeasonal` trap:** `isSeasonal` itself does NOT support test='ocsb' (it leaves 'seasonal' undefined → "object 'seasonal' not found"); `run_isseasonal` routes ocsb DIRECTLY.

**Determinism:** deterministic throughout; only OCSB has a Monte Carlo simulation of the H0 distribution → **`seed` MANDATORY** (the same seed ⇒ the same p-value, live-verified) ⇒ it stays cacheable.

**Sources:** seastests reference (`isSeasonal`, `combined_test`, `qs`, `fried`, `kw`, `seasdum`, `welch`, `ocsb`) — Ollech (2021), seastests 0.15.4 < Webel & Ollech (2019), "An overall seasonality test", Deutsche Bundesbank Discussion Paper; Osborn, Chui, Smith & Birchenhall (1988), "Seasonality and the order of integration for consumption", Oxford Bull. Econ. Stat. 50(4):361-377 (OCSB).
### #126 Feature extraction + time-series decomposition — `time_series_decomposition` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/time_series_decomposition.py`)
**Functions:** `fst_stl` [`STL(value ~ trend + season(window=))` -> trend/seasonal/remainder + the STL strengths, PRODUCER `decomp` = a mable], `fst_classical` [`classical_decomposition(value ~ season, type=additive|multiplicative)`, PRODUCER `decomp` = a mable], `fst_features` [`features(value, list(feat_stl, feat_acf, feat_spectral))` -> a single row of features].

**When:** at the preparatory stage, when you want to **see the structure** of a seasonal series before modelling — to isolate trend/seasonal/remainder (STL: robust, loess-based, preferable; classical: a plain centred moving average for educational/checking use) or to summarise the series into numeric features (trend/seasonal strength, ACF features, spectral entropy) for screening/comparing/clustering series. The input `ts` handle is converted internally into a tsibble (a class-derived index).

**When NOT:** for a non-seasonal series (frequency == 1) — the seasonal decomposition is **deliberately blocked** (see the trap); use a trend filter (HP/BK/CF, cat. 10) or state space. For forecasting/model fitting (ARIMA/ETS) → cat. 02 (fable). For graphs (gg_season/autoplot) — the JS frontend draws them. For a Box-Cox/guerrero transformation — those are transforms, not here. For multiple seasonal periods — a univariate `ts` carries one frequency.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** a regular univariate `ts`; no NA (STL/classical with NA -> `<NULL model>` -> a cryptic error; gated + run `imputeTS` #80 first); a non-constant series (var>0). fst_stl/fst_classical: a **hard gate frequency > 1 AND n >= 2*frequency** (>= 2 complete seasonal periods). fst_classical multiplicative: **strictly positive values (>0)**. A post-gate: `is_null_model` catches a failed fit as an explicit stop. fst_features: n >= max(10, 2*freq).

**Alternatives + criterion:** STL (`fst_stl`) vs classical (`fst_classical`) — prefer **STL** (robust to outliers, to changing seasonality, with a loess trend; `s_window="periodic"` for a fixed pattern, an odd numeric >=7 for a flexible one); classical (fixed seasonality, NA at the edges because of the centred MA) only as an educational/baseline option. For a non-seasonal trend → HP/Baxter-King/Christiano-Fitzgerald (cat. 10). For seasonality based on X-13/SEATS → `seasonal_adjustment_13arima` #4. `fst_features` (a tidyverts feature row) vs plain ACF/PACF (`descriptive_statistics` #81) — feasts gives **unified, comparable** metrics (trend/seasonal strength ∈ [0,1], spectral entropy) for screening many series.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- fst_stl/fst_classical: `components` = a canonical DataFrame **{index, observed, trend, seasonal, remainder, season_adjust}** (parquet-able; the index -> strings); fst_stl additionally `strength` = {trend, seasonal} ∈ [0,1]; `decomp` = the mable [PRODUCER, register field="decomp" -> the RDS bucket (an opaque `mdl_df`)].
- fst_features: `features` = a named numeric list (one row), `feature_names`, `n_features`.
- **Naming trap**: STL names the column `season_year`/`remainder`, classical names it `seasonal_adjustment_13arima`/`random` — the wrapper **unifies** them into `seasonal_adjustment_13arima`/`remainder` (do not look at the raw feasts names).
- **frequency==1 trap**: STL SILENTLY drops the seasonal component (trend+remainder only) — which is why it is blocked (the frequency>1 gate); do not read that as "no seasonality".
- **Classical trend NA trap**: a centred moving average => NA in the first/last ~frequency/2 points (expected, NOT an error).
- **Multiplicative trap**: non-positive values give a (silently) inconsistent decomposition — blocked (>0).
- **Interpreting strength**: a trend/seasonal strength close to 1 => a strong component, close to 0 => negligible.

**Sources:** feasts reference (`STL`, `classical_decomposition`, `feat_stl`, `feat_acf`, `feat_spectral`; live the interpreter help/args introspection, feasts 0.5.0 / fabletools 0.8.0 / tsibble 1.2.0); the reference.B. Cleveland, W.S. Cleveland, McRae & Terpenning (1990), "STL: A Seasonal-Trend Decomposition Procedure Based on Loess", J. Official Statistics 6:3-73; Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, *Forecasting: Principles and Practice* 3e, ch. 3 (decomposition and feature strengths) <https://otexts.com/fpp3/>.

### #127 Data-driven locally weighted seasonal-trend decomposition (IPI bandwidth) — `driven_locally_weighted` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/driven_locally_weighted.py`)
**Functions:** `des_deseats` [`driven_locally_weighted` with a data-driven (IPI) bandwidth; internally `set_options`, `detrend`, `deseasonalize`]

**When:** when you have an equally spaced seasonal time series (frequency > 1) and want a non-parametric decomposition into **trend + (slowly changing) seasonality + remainder** without setting the smoothing window yourself: the bandwidth is selected **deterministically** by the iterative plug-in (IPI) algorithm (minimising the AMISE, Feng-Gries-Fritz 2020) under short memory in the errors. It additionally provides ready-made detrended (obs−trend) and seasonally adjusted (obs−seasonality) series as numeric chart-data.

**When NOT:** for non-seasonal data (frequency ≤ 1) → use a pure trend filter (`mFilter`/HP #… or `loess`); for **official** model-based seasonal adjustment (X-13ARIMA-SEATS) → `Seasonal-run_seas` (#4); for STL with explicit (non data-driven) loess windows or robustness to outliers → `fst_stl` (#126); for charts (the frontend draws them).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** an equally spaced `ts` with frequency > 1 (a hard gate); a complete series without NA (a hard gate — otherwise the cryptic "Convergence … failed"); ≥ 2 complete seasonal cycles (length ≥ 2·frequency, a hard gate); a non-constant series (var > 0). Confirm that there is seasonality worth decomposing with `c01_preparation_prechecks/seasonality.run_isseasonal` (seasonality present).

**Alternatives + criterion:** `fst_stl` (#126) — when you want STL (loess) with **explicit** trend/seasonal windows or a robust estimate under outliers instead of a data-driven optimal bandwidth; `Seasonal-run_seas` (#4, X-13ARIMA-SEATS) — when you need **official** model-based seasonal adjustment (RegARIMA + SEATS) instead of a non-parametric locally weighted regression.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `non_parametric_trend`/`seasonal_adjustment_13arima`/`remainder`/`observations`: `ts` (→ `{values,start,frequency}`) — from the `Trend`/`Seasonality`/`Rest`/`Observations` columns of `fit@decomp` (an mts).
- `detrended` = observations − trend; `adjusted` = seasonally adjusted = observations − seasonality (from `detrend`/`deseasonalize`).
- `bwidth`: the **relative** ([0,1]) data-driven bandwidth chosen by the IPI — NOT a number of observations; `sum_autocov`: the estimated sum of the error autocovariances.
- `model`: the S4 fitted `driven_locally_weighted` (a producer → an RDS pointer) for downstream use.
- **Trap:** `driven_locally_weighted` **silently** accepts a matrix/mts (silent-wrong) — the wrapper blocks it; also, the decomposition concerns **slowly** changing seasonality (not abrupt changes in the seasonal shape).

**Sources:** deseats reference (`driven_locally_weighted`, `set_options`, `deseasonalize`, `detrend`) — Feng, Gries & Fritz (2020), "Data-driven local polynomial for the trend and its derivatives", J. Nonparametric Statistics 32(2):510-533; Feng (2013), J. Applied Statistics 40(2):266-281; Bühlmann (1996), J. Time Series Analysis 17(3):247-270. <
### #128 BFAST — Detecting structural breaks in trend and seasonality + near-real-time monitoring — `detection_structural_breaks` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/detection_structural_breaks.py`)
**Functions:** `bf_bfast` [`detection_structural_breaks` — an iterative STL decomposition + `breakpoints` on the trend (Vt) and seasonal (Wt) components; it returns the breakpoint indices→dates, CI, and the magnitude/timing of the largest trend change; a **producer** `model`], `bf_monitor` [`bfastmonitor` — near-real-time detection of a disturbance at the END of the series with a fixed model `response ~ trend + harmon`]

**When:** you have a seasonal time series (`ts`, frequency > 1) and want to locate **when** the **trend** and/or the **seasonality** changed structurally (retrospectively, multiple breaks with dates — `bf_bfast`), or to monitor in **near real time** whether new observations at the end deviate from the stable historical pattern (`bf_monitor`). Appropriate when trend and season coexist and you want to separate them before forecasting/regime analysis.

**When NOT:** non-seasonal series (frequency = 1 → the seasonal component is meaningless; use pure break dating); **only** unit root yes/no (→ tseries #1 / urca #2); one break in a unit-root setting (→ urca `ur.za` #2); probabilistic regimes (Markov switching); maps (the frontend draws them — all `plot` calls are omitted). For NA without an explicit `decomp='stlplus'` the node blocks (a silent-fallback gate).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** a regular `ts` with frequency > 1 and ≥ 2 complete periods (n ≥ 2·frequency) — hard gates. Make the series regular first: `c00_data_utilities/time_series_class.ts_fill_regular` (materialise the gaps as a regular ts) and `c00_data_utilities/time_series_class.ts_convert` (to `ts`); for NA: `c00_data_utilities/replacement_missing_values.imputets_kalman` (filling) or an explicit `decomp='stlplus'`, which accepts NA.

**Alternatives + criterion:** `c01_preparation_prechecks/structural_change.run_breakpoints` — when you want Bai-Perron dating **only** on one relationship/trend (a regression) without a simultaneous seasonal decomposition and seasonal breaks; `c01_preparation_prechecks/driven_locally_weighted.des_deseats` — when you want a **smooth** (data-driven bandwidth) trend+seasonal decomposition **without** break detection; `bf_monitor` — when the target is online detection of a new disturbance at the end, not a full retrospective break history.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `bf_bfast`: `trend_breaks`/`seasonal_breaks` = `{n, indices, dates, confint}`; `dates` in decimal time (e.g. 2005.167 = Feb 2005); `magnitude` = the largest change in the **trend**, `time_of_change` its timing; `trend_component`/`seasonal_component`/`remainder_component` = `ts` (the chart-data of the last iteration); `model` = the full `detection_structural_breaks` fit (a producer; it becomes a stub in to_mcp).
- `bf_monitor`: `breakpoint` = the date of the disturbance **or NA** (none); `disturbance` = a logical; `magnitude` = median(data − prediction) over the monitoring period; `history_period`/`monitor_period` = start/end.
- **Breakpoint-indices trap:** the breakpoints are indices into `na.omit(as.numeric(component))`, NOT raw positions — the node already maps them to dates via the non-NA time stamps; do not read them as integer positions.
- **No-break trap:** when `nobp$Vt/Wt == TRUE`, `bp.Vt/bp.Wt` is an atomic `NA` (NOT a breakpoints object) → `n=0`, empty (do not try `.breakpoints`).
- **Magnitude/timing trap:** they concern **ONLY** the trend (Vt), not the seasonality.
- **NA trap:** `decomp='stl'` falls back SILENTLY to stlplus (a warning only); here it is blocked — set `decomp='stlplus'` explicitly.

**Sources:** bfast reference/vignette (`the bfast documentation`, `the bfastmonitor documentation`, bfast 1.7.2 — `Yt` requires a `ts` with frequency > 1; breakpoints via `strucchangeRcpp`) — Verbesselt, Hyndman, Newnham, Culvenor (2010) "Detecting trend and seasonal changes in satellite image time series", *Remote Sensing of Environment* 114(1):106-115; Verbesselt, Hyndman, Zeileis, Culvenor (2010) *RSE* 114(12):2970-2980; Verbesselt, Zeileis, Herold (2012) "Near real-time disturbance detection using satellite image time series", *RSE* 123:98-108.
### #129 Regularisation/decomposition and analysis of space-time series — `regularisation_decomposition_space` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/regularisation_decomposition_space.py`)
**Functions:** `ps_turnpoints` [`turnpoints`: peaks/pits + the Kendall information], `ps_stat_desc` [`stat.desc`: a full table of descriptives including normality (skewness/kurtosis/Shapiro-Wilk)], `ps_decompose` [`decdiff` = a differencing trend filter · `decloess` = an STL trend-seasonal decomposition, method-switched]

**When:** at the preparatory/diagnostic layer BEFORE model estimation — (a) `ps_stat_desc` for a full descriptive table of one or many series with normality criteria (skew.2SE/kurt.2SE >1 ⇒ significantly ≠0, normtest.p), (b) `ps_turnpoints` for locating peaks/troughs and testing randomness (the Kendall information — fewer turning points than expected ⇒ a more monotone/more "informative" series), (c) `ps_decompose` for a quick trend removal (diff) or a seasonal STL decomposition (loess) as a precheck before stationarity/seasonality.

**When NOT:** for charts (the frontend draws them — all plot./lines./identify. are omitted); for formal stationarity/unit-root tests → `unit_root_normality`/`unit_root_suite` #1/#2; for seasonal tests (HEGY/Canova-Hansen) → `seasonal_unit_roots` #89; for a multiplicative seasonal decomposition (X-13/census) → `seasonal_adjustment_13arima` #4 / `deccensus` (out of scope); for irregular→regular resampling (`regul`/`unit_root_normality`) — OMITTED (outside the macro scope).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** a numeric univariate series without NA; `ps_turnpoints` requires ≥3 obs AND ≥3 UNIQUE values (otherwise turnpoints emits the warning "Less than 3 unique values" and a degenerate result); `ps_decompose` with method=loess requires a **regular ts with frequency>1 and ≥2 complete periods** and additive ONLY. Make the series regular/fill the gaps first: `c00_data_utilities/time_series_class.ts_fill_regular` (materialise gaps → a regular ts) and `c00_data_utilities/replacement_missing_values.imputets_interpolation` (filling NA before the decomposition).

**Alternatives + criterion:** `#81 descriptives` for ACF/PACF/rolling/correlation descriptives (`stat.desc` gives the static summary table per series); `#1 tseries`/`#2 urca` when you need a formal stationarity p-value instead of a visual/turning-point precheck; `#4 seasonal` (X-13) or a fuller STL when you want a complete seasonal adjustment instead of a quick decdiff/decloess.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `ps_turnpoints`: `n_turns` (=n_peaks+n_pits), `first_is_peak`, `tppos` (the positions of the turning points in the original series, with ex-aequos), `peak_positions`/`pit_positions`, and (if `calc_proba=TRUE`) `proba`/`info` per turning point; **info = -log2(P)** — larger ⇒ fewer turning points than random ⇒ a more "informative"/monotone series.
- `ps_stat_desc`: `stats_table` records with the label column `statistic` (THE STATISTIC NAMES are kept explicitly, they are not lost in serialization) + one column per variable; the critical cells: `coef.var`=std.dev/mean (meaningless near mean≈0), `skew.2SE`/`kurt.2SE` (>1 ⇒ significantly ≠0), `normtest.p` (Shapiro-Wilk).
- `ps_decompose`: `components` = an mts (→{values,dim,dimnames,start,frequency}) with columns depending on the path — diff: `filtered`,`residuals`; loess with trend=TRUE: `non_parametric_trend`,`seasonal_adjustment_13arima`,`residuals`; loess with trend=FALSE: `deseasoned`,`seasonal_adjustment_13arima`.
- **Trap (silent-wrong)**: `stat.desc` on NON-numeric input silently returns ALL NA; `decdiff` on NA input SILENTLY fills them (ends="fill") — both are blocked by hard gates.

**Sources:** pastecs reference/vignette — `turnpoints`, `stat.desc`, `decdiff`, `decloess` (Grosjean & Ibanez, "pastecs: Package for Analysis of Space-Time Ecological Series", <); Kendall, M.G. 1976, *Time-series* (2nd ed.), Griffin (the turning-points test); Ibanez, F. 1982, *J. Exp. Mar. Biol. Ecol.* 4:619-632 (the turning-points information); Cleveland, the reference.B. et al. 1990, *STL: A Seasonal-Trend Decomposition based on Loess*, J. Official Stat. 6:3-73.
### #130 Robust descriptives + correlation prechecks — `Hmisc` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/robust_descriptives_correlation.py`)
**Functions:** `hm_describe` [`describe` — per-variable stats records: n/missing/distinct/Info/Mean/pMedian/Gmd + weighted quantiles], `hm_rcorr` [`rcorr` — a Pearson/Spearman correlation matrix + a matrix of p-values + a matrix of pairwise n], `hm_wtd` [`wtd.mean`/`wtd.var`/`wtd.quantile` — the weighted mean/variance/quantiles]

**When:** at the preparatory layer, BEFORE modelling — a fast, robust description of numeric variables (`hm_describe`: robust location pMedian/Hodges-Lehmann + robust dispersion Gmd/Gini, a distinct count, a missing report, a quantile grid), checking correlations **with significance** (`hm_rcorr`: p-values + the pairwise-complete n per pair, Pearson or Spearman rank), and weighted statistics when the observations carry sampling/frequency weights (`hm_wtd`).

**When NOT:** for charts (the spike-histogram/dot-chart plot/latex/html methods are omitted — the JS frontend draws them); for formal stationarity → `unit_root_normality`/`unit_root_suite` cat. 01 (describe/rcorr are exploratory, not inference under time dependence); for causality/lead-lag → CCF (`descriptive_statistics` #81) / Granger; for class-agnostic transformations → `time_series_class` #78.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** no formal statistical precondition (these are the prechecks themselves). Gates: the input a numeric matrix/df with numeric-only columns and non-empty (`hm_describe`/`hm_rcorr`); `hm_rcorr` has a **hard gate of >=2 columns and >=5 rows** (rcorr needs >4 obs, otherwise the cryptic "must have >4 observations"); `hm_wtd` **hard gates: weights of the same length as x** (LIVE: a mismatch → silent recycling/NA), **non-negative** (LIVE: negatives silently accepted → a wrong result), **sum(weights)>0** (LIVE: all zeros → NaN), without NA/Inf, `probs`∈[0,1].

**Alternatives + criterion:** `c00_data_utilities/descriptive_statistics.desc_correlations` when you want a correlation matrix **without** p-values/significance — `hm_rcorr` is preferred when you need asymptotic p-values + the pairwise n; `hm_rcorr (type=spearman)` = rank-based, robust to outliers/non-linearity, vs `type=pearson` (linear); `hm_wtd` when the observations carry weights (survey/frequency) vs the unweighted `hm_describe`; `var_method=ML` (Gaussian MLE) vs `unbiased` (Bessel, the default).

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `hm_describe`: `stats` = a named list per variable; each element a named numeric (n/missing/distinct/Info/Mean/pMedian/Gmd + the quantiles.05/.10/.25/.50/.75/.90/.95). **Trap:** the quantiles appear ONLY for continuous variables (>10 distinct); discrete ones → only n/missing/distinct/Info/Mean/pMedian/Gmd. The values are rounded to `digits` significant digits (default 4 — raise it for precision). `pMedian`=the pseudomedian (Hodges-Lehmann, robust); `Gmd`=the Gini mean difference (robust dispersion).
- `hm_rcorr`: `r`/`P`/`n` = matrices (→ nested rows + dimnames). **`P` trap:** the diagonal = **NA** (there is no self-correlation p-value); **pairwise deletion** → a different `n` per pair (a strong correlation with a small `n` is fragile — read the `n` matrix). Spearman = Pearson on the ranks (midranks under ties).
- `hm_wtd`: `weighted_mean`/`weighted_var`/`weighted_sd`/`weighted_quantiles` (named). **Trap:** `wtd.var` defaults to unbiased (Bessel); `ML` = the Gaussian MLE; n=1 effective obs → var=NaN (the warning → a message, it does not crash).

**Sources:** Hmisc reference (`the describe documentation`, `the rcorr documentation`, `the wtd.stats documentation` — describe.matrix/DataFrame, rcorr type=pearson/spearman, wtd.mean/wtd.var method=unbiased|ML/wtd.quantile probs) < Harrell, *Regression Modeling Strategies* 2nd ed. (describe/pseudomedian/Gini); Hollander & Wolfe, *Nonparametric Statistical Methods* 1973 (the rcorr midrank Spearman).
### #131 Non-parametric trend and change-point tests — `non_parametric_trend` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/non_parametric_trend.py`)
**Functions:** `tr_mk` [`mk.test`] — the Mann-Kendall trend test (a rank-based monotone trend); `tr_sens` [`sens.slope`] — the Theil-Sen slope + CI (the size of the linear change); `tr_pettitt` [`pettitt.test`] — a single change point in the central tendency (rank-based, non-parametric); `tr_smk` [`smk.test`] — the Seasonal Mann-Kendall (Hirsch-Slack) for seasonal series (frequency>1).

**When:** for detecting a **monotone trend without a distributional assumption** (MK is rank-based — robust to outliers/non-normality, it assumes neither linearity nor normal errors, only monotonicity). `tr_mk` for the significance of the trend, `tr_sens` for its **magnitude** (a robust slope, the median of the pairwise slopes) + a confidence interval. `tr_pettitt` when you suspect **one** change point (a structural shift) in the mean/median and want its position K. `tr_smk` for monthly/quarterly series with seasonality (it sums MK per season, so that seasonality does not contaminate the trend test).

**When NOT:** for a **unit root / stationarity** → `unit_root_normality` #1 (ADF/KPSS/PP) or `unit_root_suite` #2 — MK is not a unit-root test (it tests monotonicity, not I(1)); for **multiple** breakpoints or parametric (regression-based) structural breaks → `structural_change` #3 (`run_breakpoints`); for graphical output (the frontend draws — we expose numeric chart-data); under **strong autocorrelation** the MK p-values are unreliable (over-rejection) — prewhiten or use a block-bootstrap alternative.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** complete observations (no NA — `non_parametric_trend` works "for complete observations only", live: `missing values in object`); a non-constant series (var>0; a constant one ⇒ p-value=NaN — a hard gate); length≥3 (`mk.test` requires "at least 3 elements"); `tr_smk`: a `ts` object with frequency>1 (≥2 seasons — otherwise the cryptic `'x' must have at least 2 seasons`). No formal distributional precondition (rank-based). Precondition tools: [] (independence/no autocorrelation is an interpretive caveat, not a blocking tool).

**Alternatives + criterion:** `tr_sens` when you want the **magnitude** of the trend (slope + CI) and not only the significance from `tr_mk`; `tr_smk` when the series is seasonal (frequency>1) — plain `tr_mk` on a seasonal series confounds seasonality with trend; `c01_preparation_prechecks/structural_change.run_breakpoints` for **multiple/parametric** breakpoints instead of the single non-parametric `tr_pettitt`; `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_kpss_test` when the question is trend **stationarity** (I(0) around a trend) and not a monotone direction.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `tr_mk`: `statistic` = the normal z-quantile, `p_value`, `S` (the Kendall score), `varS`, `tau` (∈[-1,1], the sign=the direction, the magnitude=the strength), `decision`.
- `tr_sens`: `slope` = the **median** of the pairwise slopes d(k)=(x_j−x_i)/(j−i) (per time unit; NOT a % — deseasonalise/rescale yourself); `conf_low`/`conf_high` at `conf_level`; `p_value`/`statistic` come from MK.
- `tr_pettitt`: `change_point_index` = the position K (**an integer index 1.n**, not a date — map it onto your own time column); `statistic` = U*; `Uk` = the |U[k]| series (chart-data for locating it); the approximate p is valid only for p≤0.5.
- `tr_smk`: `statistic`/`p_value` = the **overall** values (all seasons summed); `season_S`/`season_varS`/`season_pvalue`/`season_z` = per-season vectors of length=frequency (chart-data — they show which seasons drive the trend).
- **Trap**: MK/Sens test **monotonicity**, not linearity — a U-shaped series may give a non-significant MK despite strong non-monotone variation. **Trap**: on autocorrelated data the p is understated (a spurious trend).

**Sources:** trend 1.1.7 reference — the help pages `mk.test`/`sens.slope`/`pettitt.test`/`smk.test` (r-btw docs lookup); Hipel & McLeod (1994) *Time Series Modelling of Water Resources and Environmental Systems*; Sen (1968) *JASA* 63:1379-1389 (Theil-Sen); Pettitt (1979) *Appl. Statist.* 28:126-135; Hirsch, Slack & Smith (1982) *Water Resources Research* 18:107-121 (the seasonal MK).

### #132 Time-series (non-)linearity tests — `nonlinearTseries` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/linearity_battery_linearity.py`)
**Functions:** `nlt_nonlinearity` [`nonlinearityTest` — a battery of 6 tests: Teraesvirta ANN / White ANN / Keenan / McLeod-Li (ARCH) / Tsay / LR-threshold (TAR)], `nlt_surrogate` [`surrogateTest` + `FFTsurrogate`, with the discriminating statistic `timeAsymmetry`/`timeAsymmetry2`]

**When:** as a precheck AFTER the stationarity tests, to decide whether a stationary series can be modelled with LINEAR tools (ARIMA/VAR) or whether there is genuine non-linearity requiring threshold/regime-switching/nonlinear methods. `nlt_nonlinearity` = a fast parametric battery (the H0 of each test: linearity); `nlt_surrogate` = a model-free test with FFT phase-randomised surrogates (H0: a gaussian linear stochastic process).

**When NOT:** for charts/attractor reconstruction/fractal dimensions (`corrDim`/`maxLyapunov`/`rqa`/`dfa`/`recurrencePlot` — out of scope; the frontend draws the plots); BEFORE you have established stationarity (the tests assume a stationary series); on very small samples (< 50 obs the battery fails cryptically); it is not an estimation tool — a diagnosis only.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** a stationary univariate series — run `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test` (+ `run_kpss_test`) for stationarity first. Gates (`.nlt_check_series`): numeric and univariate; NO NA (`surrogateTest` silently accepts NA and returns `data.statistic=NA` — silent-wrong); NO Inf/NaN (otherwise the cryptic `var(x)==NaN`); length >= 50 (live: a cryptic "subscript out of bounds" on small samples); `var>0` (otherwise "0 (non-NA) cases"); `alpha`/`significance` in (0,1). `nlt_surrogate`: `seed` MANDATORY (stochastic); `K`/`tau` positive integers; `statistic`/`alternative` via `match.arg`. **NOTE:** `nlt_nonlinearity` is stochastic too (random ANN weights) ⇒ `seed` is mandatory.

**Alternatives + criterion:** `nlt_surrogate` when you want one unified, model-free surrogate test (H0: gaussian linear) instead of a battery of parametric tests with multiple (and dependent) p-values; `nlt_nonlinearity` when you want the parametric battery with per-test statistics/p-values and an overall verdict. If non-linearity is detected → threshold/regime-switching models (SETAR/Markov switching, other categories); if only McLeod-Li rejects → ARCH/GARCH (volatility), not nonlinear-mean models.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `nlt_nonlinearity`: `tests` (a named list per test: `statistic`/`p_value`/`reject_linearity`/`decision` + extras); `summary` (a 6-row DataFrame); `p_values` (a named numeric — chart-data); `n_reject`/`reject_tests`/`overall_nonlinear`/`verdict`. Rejecting H0 (p<alpha) ⇒ evidence of non-linearity.
- `nlt_surrogate`: `data_statistic` vs `surrogates_statistics` (a vector — chart-data histogram); `n_surrogates`; `reject_linearity`/`direction`/`decision`.
- **McLeod-Li trap**: it returns a VECTOR of p-values (one per lag); the decision uses the MINIMUM (`statistic=NA`); it tests ARCH (conditional heteroscedasticity), NOT a nonlinear mean — a rejection ONLY from McLeod-Li = volatility clustering.
- **ANN stochasticity trap**: White/Teraesvirta use random weights — without a `seed` the p-value varies across identical calls (hence the mandatory seed).
- **`surrogateTest` trap**: it does NOT return a p-value; the decision is rank-based (the data.statistic among the K smallest/largest of the set); H0 = a gaussian LINEAR process (a rejection ⇒ nonlinearity/non-gaussianity, not necessarily chaos); when `one.sided=FALSE` the `alternative` is ignored.

**Sources:** nonlinearTseries reference (`the nonlinearityTest documentation`, `the surrogateTest documentation`, `the timeAsymmetry documentation`) — Garcia & Sawitzki, "nonlinearTseries: Nonlinear Time Series Analysis" < Teraesvirta/Lin/Granger 1993 & Lee/White/Granger 1993 (the ANN linearity tests); Keenan 1985 (*Biometrika* 72:39); McLeod & Li 1983; Tsay 1986 (*Biometrika* 73:461); Schreiber & Schmitz 2000, "Surrogate time series", *Physica D* 142(3):346-382.

### #133 nnfor (neural-network univariate forecasting) — `nnfor` (`c02_univariate_forecasting/nnfor.py`)
**Functions:** `mlp` → `nnf_mlp` (an automatic MLP ensemble), `elm` → `nnf_elm` (an Extreme Learning Machine); common: `diebold_mariano_tscv` (→ `forecast.mlp`/`forecast.elm`).

**When:** non-linear univariate forecasting when you suspect non-linearities/interactions that ARIMA/ETS (#7) do not capture. `nnf_mlp`: a multilayer perceptron ensemble (full backpropagation via `neuralnet`); `nnf_elm`: an Extreme Learning Machine (random hidden weights, an output layer with lasso/ridge/step/lm — far faster). Both perform automatic lag selection (`sel.lag`), automatic differencing (`difforder=NULL`) and deterministic seasonal dummies; they return an ensemble of `reps` networks.

**When NOT:** a small sample / interpretability / a linear DGP → #7 forecast (auto.arima/ets) or #10 smooth (ADAM); multivariate → 03-multivariate-nowcasting; without reproducibility (a seed) the node is uncacheable — which is forbidden.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** no formal statistical precondition (the NN learns non-parametrically; mlp/elm perform differencing/lag selection internally). Gates: `y` a **ts/msts** with ≥2 obs (nnfor rejects a plain vector: "Input y must be of class ts or msts"); **`seed` MANDATORY**, a single finite integer (random weight initialisation → without a seed the node is non-deterministic/uncacheable); `h` (if supplied) a positive integer; `hd`/`reps` positive integers; `level` within (0,100); `xreg` NOT a data frame.

**Alternatives + criterion:** #7 `auto.arima`/`ets` for the linear/interpretable route (lightweight, with analytical PI); #10 `adam` for state-space ETS+ARIMA (non-gaussian/intermittent). Between mlp and elm: `nnf_elm` when you want speed (closed-form output weights, no backpropagation iterations); `nnf_mlp` when you want full training of the hidden weights.

**Reading the output:**
- `mean` — the point forecasts (the ensemble combination via `comb`, a ts).
- `all.mean` — an h×reps matrix of ALL the ensemble members.
- `lower`/`upper` — **EMPIRICAL** PI (h×length(level)): the per-horizon quantiles of the ensemble members. **NOT analytical** — nnfor gives no PI; it requires `reps>1` for a meaningful range.
- `accuracy` — the in-sample ME/RMSE/MAE/MAPE from the network residuals (the `forecast.net` object does not include it — it is computed here).
- `model` — the whole mlp/elm object → a **producer** (register field=`model`, bucket=rds) for re-use in `diebold_mariano_tscv`; a compact stub in `to_mcp`.
- `hd`/`lags`/`difforder`/`reps`/`seed`/`n` — what was finally selected + the locked seed (the cache key).
- **Interpretation traps:** (1) the `seed` is part of the cache key — the same seed ⇒ identical output (live-verified); a different seed ⇒ a different forecast. (2) the PI are empirical ensemble quantiles, NOT frequentist/Bayesian intervals — do not read them as such. (3) `xreg` must cover the in-sample period + the horizon (length ≥ n+h). (4) the defaults `reps=2`/`hd=3` are curated-cheap (the docs say reps=20); raise them deliberately for quality.

**Sources:** Kourentzes, `nnfor` reference (`mlp`, `elm`, `forecast.mlp`, `forecast.elm`); Ord, Fildes & Kourentzes (2017) *Principles of Business Forecasting* 2e, Ch.10; Kourentzes, Barrow & Crone (2014) neural network ensemble operators (*Expert Systems with Applications* 41(9)); Huang, Zhou & Ding (2006) Extreme Learning Machine (*Neurocomputing* 70(1)).

### #135 Intermittent / sparse-demand forecasting (Croston / SBA-SBJ / TSB / iMAPA / decomposition) — `intermittent_sparse_demand` (`c02_univariate_forecasting/intermittent_sparse_demand.py`)
**Functions:** `tsi_croston` [`crost` — Croston + the optimised variants `type ∈ {croston,sba,sbj}`], `tsi_tsb` [`tsb` — Teunter-Syntetos-Babai], `tsi_imapa` [`imapa` — the Multiple Aggregation Prediction Algorithm, with automatic model selection per AL], `tsi_decomp` [`crost.decomp` — a demand-size / inter-demand-interval decomposition]

**When:** **demand series with many zeros** (intermittent / sparse demand — spare parts, rare events, low-volume sales) where classical ARIMA/ETS fail because they model continuous demand. `crost`/`tsb` give a constant out-of-sample **demand rate**; `imapa` selects automatically (Croston/SBA/SES) per aggregation level (robust); `crost.decomp` splits the series into demand sizes + intervals (a diagnostic/preprocessing step).

**When NOT:** for **dense** series (no zeros) → standard forecasting (`diebold_mariano_tscv` #7); for charts (ONLY the frontend draws them — `outplot` is forced to FALSE); for continuous macro series (GDP/inflation) — they are not intermittent.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** no formal statistical precondition — mechanical gates (hard `stop`): a non-negative numeric/ts univariate series; **intermittent** (≥1 zero, otherwise dense → #7) AND ≥2 non-zero values (a hard requirement of crost/tsb/imapa; decomp needs ≥1); `h` a positive integer; the enums `type`/`init`/`cost`/`comb` via `match.arg` (`crost` does **NOT** validate `type` — silently wrong); `nop ∈ {1,2}`; `minimumAL ≥ 1`; `maximumAL ≥ minimumAL`; an NA → `stop` if `na.rm=FALSE` (otherwise the cryptic "missing value where TRUE/FALSE").

**Alternatives + criterion:** `tsi_croston (type=sba)` = bias-corrected Croston (SBA; the default choice in the literature for less positive bias; sbj = Shale-Boylan-Johnston); `tsi_tsb` when demand is **declining / obsolescing** (it models the probability of demand, not the interval); `tsi_imapa` when you want **automatic, robust** model selection (a combination across ALs, without a manual choice); `c02_univariate_forecasting/forecast.run_ets` when the series is **not** intermittent (dense).

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- The forecasters (`tsi_croston`/`tsi_tsb`/`tsi_imapa`): `diebold_mariano_tscv` = the **out-of-sample demand rate** (`frc.out`, of length `h`, a CONSTANT per-period rate — NOT discrete demand events); `fitted` = the in-sample rate (`frc.in`, with leading `NA`); `weights`/`initial` = the smoothing and init parameters; `model` = the selected model.
- **Demand-rate trap**: the `diebold_mariano_tscv` is a **demand rate per period** (e.g. 0.19 units/period), not a forecast of an individual order; sum it over the horizon for the total expected demand.
- `tsi_imapa`: `summary` = a matrix per AL (`AL`/`n`/`p`=the average inter-demand interval/`cv2`/`model` 1=Croston·2=SBA·3=SES/`use`); `model_fit` = the parameters per AL. ALs with `use=0` (<4 obs) are ignored.
- `tsi_croston`: `components` = `c.in`/`c.out` (the demand and interval vectors) + `coeff` (the scaling for sba/sbj). `tsi_decomp`: `demand` (the non-zero sizes) + `interval` (the inter-demand intervals) — of equal length.
- **Determinism**: purely optimisation-based (no seed; fully cacheable). The method returns the forecast DIRECTLY (there is no downstream `diebold_mariano_tscv`) → no registry producer.

**Sources:** tsintermittent 1.10 reference (`crost`/`tsb`/`imapa`/`crost.decomp` — the formals and outputs live-probed). Kourentzes 2014, "On intermittent demand model optimisation and selection", Int. J. Production Economics 156:180-190 <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpe.2014.06.007>; Petropoulos & Kourentzes 2015, "Forecast Combinations for Intermittent Demand", JORS <https://doi.org/10.1057/jors.2014.62>; <
### #136 Long memory / fractional integration (ARFIMA long memory) — `long_memory_fractional` (`c02_univariate_forecasting/long_memory_fractional.py`)
**Functions:** `fdf_fit` [`long_memory_fractional`], `fdf_gph` [`fdGPH`], `fdf_sperio` [`fdSperio`], `fdf_diffseries` [`diffseries`]

**When:** when the series shows **slowly (excessively slowly) decaying autocorrelation** — neither purely I(0) nor purely I(1) — that is, fractional integration I(d), 0<d<0.5 (stationary long memory) or d≥0.5 (non-stationary). `fdf_gph`/`fdf_sperio` for a fast **semi-parametric** estimate of the memory parameter d (a log-/smoothed-periodogram regression, with an SE); `fdf_fit` for a **parametric** ML estimate of the whole ARFIMA(p,d,q) (d + AR/MA jointly); `fdf_diffseries` to **fractionally difference** the series at the estimated d so as to obtain an I(0) input for later methods.

**When NOT:** for integer integration (standard unit-root/differencing) → ADF/KPSS + `diff` in cat. 01 (ARFIMA is overkill if d≈0 or d≈1); for a forecasting workflow with automatic orders → forecast/fable/smooth (#7-10) (fracdiff does NOT produce a forecast object — only the fit/d/filtered series); for GARCH long memory (volatility) → cat. 06.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** a univariate numeric/`ts` series **without NA/NaN/Inf** (`.fdf_check_series` — run `c00_data_utilities/replacement_missing_values.imputets_kalman` first if there are NA); evidence of long memory before the fit: a **slowly decaying ACF** (`c00_data_utilities/descriptive_statistics.desc_acf` — a linear/ultra-slow decay) and a **non-rejection of a unit root together with weak stationarity** (`c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_suite.wrap_ur_df` (ADF) + `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_suite.wrap_ur_kpss` (KPSS) — an ambiguous result ⇒ possible fractional integration). Gates: `nar`/`nma` non-negative integers, `M≥1`, `drange` an increasing numeric of length 2 (`fdf_fit`); `bandw.exp` (and `beta`) **strictly in (0,1)** (`fdf_gph`/`fdf_sperio` — at 0, fdGPH SILENTLY returns d=NA/sd=Inf); `d` a single finite number (`fdf_diffseries`).

**Alternatives + criterion:** `fdf_gph` (GPH) = the classical, fast semiparametric estimator — the **exploration default**; `fdf_sperio` (Reisen 1994, a smoothed periodogram) = more robust to short-run dynamics/noise (a Parzen window); `fdf_fit` (ML ARFIMA) = the full parametric model when you need AR/MA jointly with d and an SE (but it is sensitive to mis-specification, and the cov/SE may be inaccurate). Strategy: estimate d semi-parametrically → `fdf_diffseries(x, d)` → check that the result is I(0) → model it.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `d` = the memory parameter; **`d_reading`** maps it: d≈0 short memory (I(0)); d<0 anti-persistent (intermediate/negative memory); 0<d<0.5 **stationary** long memory; d≥0.5 **non-stationary**. `fdf_gph`/`fdf_sperio`: `sd_asymptotic`/`sd_regression` = two SE estimators for d (use them for a CI/the significance of d≠0).
- `fdf_fit`: `d`/`ar`/`ma`/`sigma`/`log_likelihood`/`std_errors` (order: d, ar, ma)/`covariance`/`correlation` + the full `model` (a producer, rds). **Trap**: the `drange` default = `c(0,0.5)` **restricts** the estimated d to [0,0.5] — for d>0.5 (non-stationary) widen `drange` explicitly.
- `fdf_diffseries`: `series` = the fractionally differenced series (it preserves the ts attributes if the input was a ts). **MA sign trap**: `long_memory_fractional` uses the S-plus convention with **reversed** signs on the MA coefficients relative to `arima`/Wikipedia — do not compare `ma` directly with arima output.

**Sources:** fracdiff help (the live Rd, fracdiff 1.5.4: `long_memory_fractional`, `fdGPH`, `fdSperio`, `diffseries`) — Haslett & Raftery (1989) *Applied Statistics* 38:1-50 (the ML approximation); Geweke & Porter-Hudak (1983) *J. Time Series Analysis* 4(4):221-238 (GPH); Reisen (1994) *J. Time Series Analysis* 15(1):335-350 (the smoothed periodogram); Jensen & Nielsen (2014) *J. Time Series Analysis* 35(5):428-436 (the fast fractional difference, doi:10.1111/jtsa.12074).

### #137 Distributed-lag & ARDL regression (finite / Koyck / autoregressive / polynomial) — `dLagM` (`c02_univariate_forecasting/distributed_lag_ardl.py`)
**Functions:** `dlm_finite` [`dynamic_linear` — a finite DL], `dlm_koyck` [`koyckDlm` — the infinite geometric/Koyck model, IV], `dlm_ardl` [`ardlDlm` — an autoregressive DL(p,q)], `dlm_poly` [`polyDlm` — an Almon polynomial DL]

**When:** modelling the lag-distributed effect of a predictor X on Y — the short-run and long-run multipliers. `dlm_finite` for an explicit finite lag order q (several predictors via a closed formula). `dlm_koyck` when the effect decays geometrically to infinity (parsimony: one decay rate phi). `dlm_ardl` when you need AR dynamics of Y as well as the lags of X. `dlm_poly` when many lags create multicollinearity and you want to impose a smooth (polynomial) shape on the lag weights.

**When NOT:** purely univariate forecasting without an exogenous X → #7 `diebold_mariano_tscv`/#8 `fable`. Non-linear relationships. When the series are I(1) and you ask for a **long-run cointegration/ECM** → ARDL bounds (05-cointegration). Structural shocks/IRF → 04.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** a DL/ARDL regression on **level** series that are I(1) and NOT cointegrated is spurious. Test the stationarity of x and y first. Gates (hard): x/y numeric with ≥3 finite values (dLagM used to accept char/NA silently); x/y of the **same length** (a mismatch is not accepted SILENTLY → a wrong fit); q,p,k positive integers ≥1 (q=0 → "subscript out of bounds"; a non-integer → silent rounding); q,p < nobs (q≥n → a cryptic replacement error); `dlm_poly` k ≤ q (k>q → computationally singular); the formula mode is **closed** (the formula is built from y_col ~ x_cols with `reformulate`, NEVER a free formula string; the columns must exist, be numeric and be free of NA/Inf).

**Alternatives + criterion:** `c05_cointegration/ardl_uecm_estimation.ardl_bounds_f` — when x,y are I(1): a bounds test for a long-run relationship + an ECM instead of a level DL regression. `dlm_koyck` — infinite geometric decay instead of an explicit q. `dlm_poly` — Almon smoothing of the lag weights under multicollinearity. `dlm_ardl` — adding AR dynamics of Y.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- Common: `coefficients` (a named numeric: the intercept + the lag terms), `fitted`, `residuals`, `diagnostics` (`r_squared`/`adj_r_squared`/`sigma`/`df_residual`/`nobs`/`aic`/`bic`).
- Method-specific: `q`/`k` (finite/poly), `order`=c(p,q) (ardl), `geometric_coefficients` alpha/beta/phi (koyck), `beta`+`beta_tvalue`/`beta_pvalue` (poly), `formula`/`removed`/`k` (the multi-predictor formula mode).
- **Koyck trap:** what is interpretable is `geometric_coefficients` (alpha, beta, **phi**=the decay rate) — NOT the raw ivreg delta coefficients. `aic`/`bic` = **NA** for `dlm_koyck` (ivreg: logLik is undefined) — do not compare them with the lm-based models.
- **Poly trap:** `beta` (the original per-lag weights) is what is interpretable; `coefficients` are the gammas of the z-transformed polynomial, NOT per-lag effects.
- **nobs trap:** a q loses q initial observations (nobs = n − q).

**Sources:** dLagM reference / the help pages `dynamic_linear`/`koyckDlm`/`ardlDlm`/`polyDlm` (Demirhan, v1.1.13) — < theory: the reference.C. Hill, W.E. Griffiths, G.G. Judge, *Undergraduate Econometrics* (Wiley); B.H. Baltagi, *Econometrics* 5th ed. (Springer).
