### #148 Bayesian Structural VAR identified through heteroskedasticity/non-normality (SV / Markov switching / Student-t) + IRF/FEVD/HD/structural shocks + SDDR identification — `bayesian_structural_var_identified_through` (`c04_structural_shocks/bayesian_structural_var_identified_through.py`)
**Functions:** `bsv_estimate` (an MCMC Gibbs estimation, model∈{sv,msh,t} → a PRODUCER posterior 'PosteriorBSVAR*'); `bsv_irf` (impulse responses, the posterior mean+bands); `bsv_fevd` (the forecast error variance decomposition); `bsv_hd` (the historical decomposition); `bsv_shocks` (the structural shocks per period); `bsv_verify` (the Savage-Dickey Density Ratio — a test of identification through heteroskedasticity/non-normality)

**When:** you have a multivariate series (K≥2) and want a **Bayesian** structural VAR where the identification of the shocks rests NOT on theoretical exclusion/sign restrictions but on **statistical structure**: `sv`=stochastic volatility (a time-varying shock variance), `msh`=Markov-switching heteroskedasticity (discrete variance regimes, M regimes), `t`=Student-t (non-normal shocks). You obtain posterior IRF/FEVD/HD/structural shocks with full credible bands, and you check with the SDDR WHETHER the heteroskedasticity/non-normality really identifies the model (`bsv_verify`).
**When NOT:** linear/time-invariant reduced-form dynamics suffice → `reduced_form_var` (#11); **frequentist** data-driven identification (changes in volatility à la Rigobon, distance covariance, non-Gaussian ML) → `driven_svar_identification` (#20); theoretical A/B or Blanchard-Quah restrictions → `SVAR`/`vr_bq` (#19); sign-restriction set identification → `VARsignR` (#21); regime-dependent **dynamics** (not only the variance) → `smooth_transition_threshold` (#150).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- `data`: a multivariate numeric `matrix`/`ts`/`mts` (**K≥2**, **≥3 rows**), **without NA/Inf** (a hard gate in the wrapper; bsvars rejects missing values).
- The stationarity/order of integration of the inputs (a VAR in levels vs differences) → `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test` (+ `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_kpss_test`).
- **A check that the heteroskedasticity/non-normality really identifies** (otherwise B is only recursively point-identified) → `bsv_verify` (SDDR).
- Stochastic MCMC → a **mandatory `seed`** (`bsv_estimate`). `model='msh'` → `M≥2`.

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| `c04_structural_shocks/driven_svar_identification.svar_id_cv` #20 | **Frequentist** changes-in-volatility (Rigobon) identification instead of Bayesian; you want a point estimate + wild/MB bootstrap bands |
| `c04_structural_shocks/driven_svar_identification.svar_id_chol` #20 | A simple recursive (Cholesky) identification without a Bayesian machinery |
| `c03_multivariate_nowcasting/reduced_form_var.vr_var` #11 | Reduced-form dynamics/forecasting suffice (no structural identification) |
| `bsv_verify` | Before interpreting the IRF/FEVD: confirm that the statistical structure identifies (a negative logSDDR) |

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `bsv_estimate`: `model` = the fitted posterior ('PosteriorBSVAR*', the producer handle → it feeds the analysis functions); `B_mean`/`A_mean` (the posterior-mean structural/autoregressive matrices); `model_type`/`p`/`K`/`S`/`burnin`/`thin`/`n_draws`/`seed`/`converged`.
- `bsv_irf`/`bsv_fevd`: a long-format `DataFrame` (`response`/`variable` × `shock` × `horizon` + `mean`/`lower`/`upper`) — the posterior mean + quantile bands (default 16%/84%). Horizon 0 = the impact.
- `bsv_hd`: a long df (`variable` × `shock` × `time` + `mean`/`lower`/`upper`) — the historical contribution of each shock per period (time = the actual ts time).
- `bsv_shocks`: a long df (`shock` × `time` + `mean`/`lower`/`upper`) — the estimated structural disturbances.
- `bsv_verify`: `logSDDR` (SV/MSH: a **per-shock** vector of length K; t: a scalar) + `logSDDR_se` (SV/MSH) or the `SDDR` ratio (t); `identified` (a per-shock boolean = `logSDDR < 0`); `type`/`degenerate`.

*Interpretation traps:* (1) **The sign of the SDDR**: a **negative** `logSDDR` is evidence AGAINST a lack of identification (i.e. the shock IS identified through heteroskedasticity/non-normality); a positive one means it adds no identification beyond the default lower-triangular structure. `-Inf` is VALID strong evidence (the t model), NOT an error; `NaN/NA` = degenerate (the SDDR failed) → block. (2) **The default identification is a lower-triangular B** (recursive; the variable ORDER matters); the heteroskedasticity allows the exclusion restrictions to be TESTED/relaxed, it does not replace the recursive structure by default. (3) **Degenerate diagnostics = non-convergence** (the Bayesian lesson): non-finite posterior draws (`bsv_estimate`) or a `NaN/NA` logSDDR (`bsv_verify`) → a hard `stop` unless `allow_nonconvergence=TRUE`. (4) **TINY defaults** (`S=100`, `burnin=50`): production MUST raise the draws; without a `seed` it is not reproducible (`bsv_estimate` calls `set.seed`, covering the burn-in + retained draws across two sequential `estimate` calls). (5) `bsv_hd` returns the actual ts time as `time` (as.numeric of the labels — as.integer would TRUNCATE 1.25→1 and destroy the axis).
**S3 collision:** the generics `estimate`/`compute_impulse_responses`/`compute_variance_decompositions`/`compute_historical_decompositions`/`compute_structural_shocks`/`verify_identification` CLASH with same-named ones in vars/svars/BVAR/bayesianVARs; the wrapper does NOT call `library(bsvars)` — `requireNamespace` + a fully qualified everywhere (bullet-proof dispatch; sibling safety live-verified with `driven_svar_identification` loaded).

**Sources:** Lütkepohl H., Woźniak T. 2020, *Bayesian Inference for Structural Vector Autoregressions Identified by Markov-Switching Heteroskedasticity*, Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control 113, 103862; Lütkepohl H., Shang F., Uzeda L., Woźniak T. 2024, *Partial Identification of Heteroskedastic Structural VARs*, arXiv:2404.11057; Woźniak T. 2024, *bsvars: Bayesian Estimation of Structural Vector Autoregressive Models*, the reference package; `bayesian_structural_var_identified_through` v3.2 < (the help pages `specify_bsvar_sv`/`estimate`/`compute_impulse_responses`/`verify_identification` + live introspection on version 4.6.1).
### #149 Bayesian Structural VAR with SIGN + ZERO + NARRATIVE restrictions (set-identified; importance sampling) — `bsvarSIGNs` (`c04_structural_shocks/bayesian_structural_var_identified_throughigns.py`)
**Functions:** `bss_estimate` (specify + Gibbs sampling → a producer `'PosteriorBSVARSIGN'`); `bss_irf` (the set-identified IRF bands); `bss_fevd` (the FEVD median-share bands); `bss_forecast` (predictive + conditional forecast bands)

**When:** you have a multivariate series (N≥2) and want to identify structural shocks with **theoretically justified restrictions** instead of a statistical identification: the signs of the impulse responses (**sign restrictions**, e.g. "a demand shock ⇒ inflation and output ↑"), zero responses (**zero restrictions**, e.g. "no contemporaneous effect on productivity"), or restrictions on specific historical periods (**narrative sign restrictions**, Antolín-Díaz & Rubio-Ramírez). The model is **set-identified** (Bayesian): the output is a posterior distribution of responses ⇒ credible bands, not a point IRF. Zero restrictions are written as `0` in the `sign_irf` array; they activate importance sampling (Arias et al. 2018).
**When NOT:** you have an **exclusion/recursive** identification (a known ordering) or a statistical identification from heteroskedasticity/non-Gaussianity → `driven_svar_identification` (#20, frequentist data-driven) / `SVAR` (#19); purely reduced-form forecasting/nowcasting without a structural ID → `reduced_form_var` (#11) / BVAR (#12); regime-dependent (nonlinear) structural dynamics → `smooth_transition_threshold` (#150).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- `data`: a multivariate numeric `matrix`/`ts` (**N≥2**), `(T+p) x N`, **without NA/Inf** (a gate in the wrapper; ts/mts/DataFrame → coerced to a matrix).
- The stationarity/order of integration of the inputs (the identification concerns shocks in a stationary VAR, or a VAR in levels with cointegration awareness) → `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test` (+ `run_kpss_test`).
- **≥1 substantive restriction** (`sign_irf`/`sign_structural` non-NA or `sign_narrative`) — a **hard gate**: without restrictions the SVAR is NOT identified.
- `sign_irf` values only `{-1,0,1,NA}`, conformable `NxNxH`; `sign_structural` `{-1,1,NA}` `NxN`. Gates in the wrapper.
- Stochastic (Gibbs + predictive sampling) → a **mandatory `seed`** (`bss_estimate` and `bss_forecast`).

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| `c04_structural_shocks/driven_svar_identification.svar_id_chol` #20 | a frequentist data-driven ID (heteroskedasticity/non-Gaussianity) or a recursive Cholesky — there are no theoretical sign/zero restrictions |
| `c03_multivariate_nowcasting/reduced_form_var.vr_var` #11 | purely reduced-form (forecasting/Granger) without structural shock identification |
| `c04_structural_shocks/smooth_transition_threshold.sst_girf` #150 | regime-dependent (nonlinear/smooth-transition) structural dynamics |
| `bss_forecast` vs `bss_irf` | predictive/conditional forecast bands versus structural IRF/FEVD bands |

**Reading the output:**
- `bss_estimate`: `model` = a `'PosteriorBSVARSIGN'` (the producer handle → it feeds the analysis functions); `B_median` (the posterior median contemporaneous B), `ess` (the importance-sampling effective sample size), `n_draws`, `ess_ratio`, `converged`, `restrictions` (which are active), `K`/`p`/`S`/`seed`.
- `bss_irf`: `irf` = a tidy long DataFrame (`response`, `shock`, `horizon`, `median`, `lower`, `upper`) — the **set-identified band per (response,shock,horizon)** (chart-data).
- `bss_fevd`: `fevd` = tidy long (`variable`, `shock`, `horizon`, `median` share + `lower`/`upper`).
- `bss_forecast`: `diebold_mariano_tscv` = tidy long (`variable`, `horizon`, `median`, `lower`, `upper`); `conditional=TRUE` when a conditional_forecast was supplied.

*Interpretation traps:* (1) **Set identification, NOT point identification**: the IRF is a posterior *distribution* — read it as a median + credible band, NEVER as a single "true" response; the band reflects BOTH identification uncertainty AND estimation uncertainty. (2) **The ESS is a degeneracy indicator** (mirroring rstan/MARSS): for sign-only restrictions `ess == n_draws` (uniform rotations); under zero/narrative restrictions `ess < n_draws` (importance reweighting); a **very low `ess/n_draws`** means the restrictions leave very few valid rotations ⇒ the posterior is dominated by a handful of draws ⇒ **unreliable** — the wrapper BLOCKS (`ess_min_ratio`, overridable with `allow_nonconvergence=TRUE`). (3) **Zero restrictions** are written as `0` in the same `sign_irf` array (NOT as a separate argument); they activate importance sampling. (4) **Impossible/excessive restrictions** → the sampler spends an enormous amount of time searching for a valid rotation Q (the L1 default `max_tries=Inf` can hang; the node uses a finite default). (5) **Stochasticity**: `bss_estimate` (Gibbs) and `bss_forecast` (predictive sampling) require a `seed` (identical draws were verified); `bss_irf`/`bss_fevd` are deterministic transformations of the draws.
**S3 collision:** the generics `estimate`/`compute_impulse_responses`/`compute_variance_decompositions`/`diebold_mariano_tscv` clash with those of `reduced_form_var`/`driven_svar_identification`/`local_projections_lp`/`BVAR`/`bayesianVARs`/`fable`/`diebold_mariano_tscv` — there is NO `library(bsvarSIGNs)`; only `specify_*` + `getS3method(generic, class, asNamespace("bsvarSIGNs"))` (`conflicts(detail=TRUE)` is empty; co-sourcing with `driven_svar_identification` was verified without cross-breakage).

**Sources:** Wang X. & Woźniak T. (bsvarSIGNs: Bayesian SVARs with sign, zero & narrative restrictions, v2.0 <); Rubio-Ramírez, Waggoner & Zha 2010 (*Structural VARs: Theory of Identification & Algorithms*, Review of Economic Studies 77:2, 665-696); Arias, Rubio-Ramírez & Waggoner 2018 (*Inference Based on SVARs Identified with Sign & Zero Restrictions*, Econometrica 86:2, 685-720); Antolín-Díaz & Rubio-Ramírez 2018 (*Narrative Sign Restrictions for SVARs*, American Economic Review 108:10, 2802-29); Waggoner & Zha 2003 (*A Gibbs sampler for structural VARs*, JEDC 28:2, 349-366); Giannone, Lenza & Primiceri 2015 (*Prior Selection for VARs*, REStat 97:2, 436-451); the bsvarSIGNs 2.0 Rd reference + live introspection (`specify_bsvarSIGN.new`, `estimate.BSVARSIGN`, `compute_impulse_responses/variance_decompositions.PosteriorBSVARSIGN`, `forecast.PosteriorBSVARSIGN`, `specify_narrative`).
### #151 Gaussian / Student's-t Mixture VAR (regime switching through mixture weights) — `gaussian_student_mixture` (`c04_structural_shocks/gaussian_student_mixture.py`)
**Functions:** `gmv_fit` [`fitGSMVAR` — a PRODUCER 'gsmvar'], `gmv_girf` [`GIRF`], `gmv_gfevd` [`GFEVD`], `gmv_linear_irf` [`linear_IRF`]

**When:** a multivariate series (d>=2) where the dynamics SWITCH between M regimes with **mixing weights that depend on the past** (low/high volatility, recession/expansion, a monetary regime). The regimes are Gaussian (GMVAR), Student's-t (StMVAR, heavy tails) or mixed (G-StMVAR). You want regime-/state-dependent generalized impulse responses (a GIRF), a generalized FEVD, or the linear IRF of one regime, with an optional structural identification through conditional heteroskedasticity (the matrix W).

**When NOT:** linear/time-invariant dynamics suffice -> vars #11 / BVAR #12; a **smooth-transition / threshold / (m)logistic** transition (INSTEAD of mixture-density weights) -> sstvars #150 (the most direct successor); smooth CONTINUOUS temporal variation of the coefficients (NOT discrete regimes) -> shrinkTVPVAR #146 / bvarsv #14; a linear data-driven structural shock ID -> svars #20; univariate (d=1) -> uGMAR (outside the surface).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** a multivariate series with d>=2 and without NA/Inf (`.gmv_check_data`); the series must be **stationary** and on a **similar scale** (otherwise the GA struggles to find an appropriate solution). Gates: `p/M/ncalls/ncores/maxit/N/R1/R2/bootstrap_reps/regime` positive integers; `M` of length 1 (GMVAR/StMVAR) or length 2 (G-StMVAR); `model/parametrization/initval_type` enums; `structural_W` a numeric d x d matrix; `which_shocks` in [1,d]; `regime <= sum(M)`; `ci` in (0,1); `shock_size` non-zero. **CONVERGENCE (the post-gate `.gmv_check_convergence`):** degenerate estimates (no round converged or a non-finite loglik) => `stop`, unless `allow_nonconvergence=TRUE`.

**Alternatives + criterion:** `c04_structural_shocks/smooth_transition_threshold.sst_fit` — when the transition is smooth-transition/threshold/(m)logistic/exogenous (not mixture-density weights); `c03_multivariate_nowcasting/reduced_form_var.vr_var` — linear time-invariant dynamics suffice (cheaper); `c04_structural_shocks/driven_svar_identification.svar_id_chol` — a linear structural VAR in one regime; `gmv_linear_irf` — the linear IRF of one fixed regime instead of the regime-dependent GIRF (`gmv_girf`).

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `gmv_fit`: `model` (the producer 'gsmvar' handle) + `loglik`/`IC` (AIC/HQIC/BIC) + `params`/`std_errors` + `mixing_weights` (the T x M path of regime probabilities, chart-data) + `M`/`d`/`p`/`model_type`/`structural`/`converged`/`n_converged`.
- `gmv_girf`: `girf` (a named list per shock: `point_est` [(N+1) x vars] with the first row = the impact at n=0, + `conf_ints`) + `which_shocks`/`N`/`R1`/`R2`/`ci` — the **non-linear generalized responses**.
- `gmv_gfevd`: `gfevd` (a 3D array [(N+1) x variables x shocks]) + `initval_type`/`N`.
- `gmv_linear_irf`: `point_est` (a 3D array [variables x shock x (N+1)], slice 1 = the impact) + `conf_ints` (4D wild-bootstrap bands [vars x shock x (N+1) x 2] or NULL) + `regime`/`N`.

**Interpretation traps:**
- **The GIRF is NON-LINEAR and NON-SYMMETRIC**: the response depends on the size/sign of the shock AND on the initial state (init_regimes) — not like a linear IRF.
- **linear_IRF/GIRF on a reduced-form model -> an automatic lower-triangular recursive (Cholesky) ID** (the variable ORDER matters); for a genuine structural ID supply `structural_W` (which requires M>=2).
- **linear_IRF bootstrap ci: bands ONLY for models with linear AR dynamics** (M==1 or the AR parameters constrained identical); with genuine regime switching -> use the GIRF.
- **The GFEVD `seeds` length DEPENDS on `initval_type`** (a live-verified trap): `nrow(data)-p+1` for 'data' (one GIRF per p-history), `R2` for 'random'; the wrapper computes it automatically.
- **A stochastic GA with a multimodal log-likelihood**: a small `ncalls` (the default is TINY=2) -> a local maximum; production raises `ncalls` (the recommendation is (M+1)^5). The `seed` is MANDATORY (without it, it is not reproducible).
- **StMVAR/G-StMVAR** models: degrees of freedom (df) of the Student's-t regimes near the bound (megap) => effectively Gaussian; G-StMVAR requires `M=c(M1,M2)` (M1 Gaussian + M2 Student's-t regimes).

**Sources:** Kalliovirta L., Meitz M., Saikkonen P. 2016. Gaussian mixture vector autoregression. *Journal of Econometrics*, 192:2, 485-498. · Virolainen S. 2022. A mixture autoregressive model based on Gaussian and Student's t-distributions. *Studies in Nonlinear Dynamics & Econometrics*, 26:4, 559-580. · Virolainen S. 2025. A statistically identified structural vector autoregression with endogenously switching volatility regime. *Journal of Business & Economic Statistics*, 43:1, 44-54. · Lanne M., Nyberg H. 2016. Generalized Forecast Error Variance Decomposition for Linear and Nonlinear Multivariate Models. *Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics*, 78:4, 595-603. · Herwartz H., Lütkepohl H. 2014. Structural vector autoregressions with Markov switching. *Journal of Econometrics*. · gmvarkit v2.2.1 (the fitGSMVAR/GIRF/GFEVD/linear_IRF reference + live introspection).

### #89 Seasonal unit roots and seasonal stability (HEGY / Canova-Hansen) — `seasonal_unit_roots` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/seasonal_unit_roots.py`)
**Functions:** `run_hegy_test` [`hegy.test` (+`hegy.boot.pval`)], `run_ch_test` [`ch.test`]

**When:** when you have a **seasonal** series (frequency > 1) and the question is whether the **seasonality is stochastic/non-stationary** (it needs an `s`-order seasonal difference) or **deterministic/stable** (seasonal dummies suffice). Two complementary tests:
- `run_hegy_test` (**HEGY**, H0: a seasonal **unit root** at the root frequency): t-stats at the zero and Nyquist frequencies + F-stats at the seasonal harmonics. A rejection ⇒ there is **no** unit root there.
- `run_ch_test` (**Canova-Hansen**, H0: **stable** seasonality): a rejection ⇒ the seasonality **changes/is non-stationary** (the OPPOSITE polarity to HEGY, as KPSS is to ADF).

**When NOT:** (a) a non-seasonal series, or when you want only a **level** unit root → `#1/#2`. (b) When you want to **remove** seasonality (adjustment) instead of **testing** it → `#4 seasonal`. (c) Panels → `#6`.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** strict gates (`.hgy_check_seasonal_ts`): `x` a **`ts`, univariate, frequency > 1, without NA/Inf, of length ≥ 2 complete seasonal cycles** (`stop` otherwise). `deterministic` = a length-3 vector of 0/1; **`c(0,0,0)` is forbidden** (it breaks the package; include at least a constant). `bootstrap=TRUE` ⇒ **`lag.method="AICc"` is forbidden** (`hegy.boot.pval` does not support it). For `ch.test`, `xreg` must have `nrow == length(x)` without NA/Inf.

**Alternatives + criterion:**
- **`run_hegy_test` + `run_ch_test` confirmatory** — HEGY (H0: a unit root) + Canova-Hansen (H0: stability) together, exactly as ADF+KPSS in the non-seasonal case.
- **`#4 seasonal (X-13)`** — if the end goal is an adjusted series (X-13 has its own seasonal diagnostics too).
- **A plain ADF on a seasonally differenced series** — a quick fix, but HEGY distinguishes AT WHICH frequency the root sits (ADF does not).

**Reading the output** (L2 `to_mcp`): class `HEGYtest`/`CHtest` (S3) objects are returned — the wrapper extracts the numeric fields (the `test.object`/`fitted.model` are **stubbed**):
- `statistics` — a **named numeric vector** of statistics per root/frequency (e.g. `t_1`, `t_2`, `F_3:4` for quarterly data); `pvalues` — the corresponding p-values; `statistic_names` — the labels.
- `pvalue.method` — `"RS"` (response surface, the default), `"raw"` (tables), or `"bootstrap"` (the CPU path; **deterministic via `seed`**). `lag.method`/`lag.order`/`strdet`/`deterministic` — the specification of the regression.
- **Polarity trap:** HEGY H0 = a seasonal unit root (a small p ⇒ there is **NO** root, stationary at that frequency); Canova-Hansen H0 = stable seasonality (a small p ⇒ **changing/non-stationary**). They are OPPOSITE — do not read them in the same direction.
- **Multiple-frequency trap:** HEGY does not give ONE verdict; you check EACH frequency separately — there may be a unit root at the seasonal harmonic but not at the zero frequency. `bootstrap=TRUE` ⇒ reproducible p-values only because of the `set.seed(seed)` inside the function.
- **Package trap:** the `pvalue="bootstrap"` of `hegy.test` ITSELF was removed with the CUDA release (v2.1-0) and throws an error — the wrapper exposes the official CPU path `hegy.boot.pval` via `bootstrap=TRUE`.

**Sources:** `seasonal_unit_roots` (`help("hegy.test")`, `ch.test`) — López-de-Lacalle (package) < Hylleberg, Engle, Granger & Yoo 1990 (*J. Econometrics* 44(1):215, HEGY); Beaulieu & Miron 1993 (*J. Econometrics* 55:305, monthly HEGY); Smith, Taylor & del Barrio Castro 2009 (*Econometric Theory* 25:527, general regressors); Canova & Hansen 1995 (*JBES* 13(3):237, seasonal stability); Burridge & Taylor 2004 (*J. Econometrics* 123:67, the bootstrap HEGY); Díaz-Emparanza 2014 (*CSDA* 76:237, response-surface p-values).

### #246 Multivariate outlier detection (Mahalanobis vs robust MCD) — `stats` + `robustbase` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/multivariate_outlier_detection.py`)

**Functions:** `mv_mahalanobis` [`mahalanobis`] — the **classical** squared distances D² with the sample mean/cov **or with SUPPLIED** `center`/`cov` (an out-of-sample apply) + a chi-square(p) cutoff + flags. `mv_covmcd` [`covMcd`, `h.alpha.n`] — the **Minimum Covariance Determinant**: robust center/cov from the "cleanest" subset h = h(alpha,n,p), robust distances, the best subset, the weights. `mv_outliers` — the **classical AND robust distances side by side** at the same chi-square quantile + a **MASKING / SWAMPING** diagnosis (the "main" node of the card).

**When:** when the input is a numeric **observations × variables** matrix (countries × macro indicators, periods × variables) and the question is **which rows are outlying in the joint space**. This is something **no univariate test can see**: a country may have "normal" inflation **and** "normal" unemployment, but an impossible *combination*. Flow: `mv_outliers` (the decision: classical vs robust + masked/swamped) → `mv_covmcd` (only the robust center/cov/h/best subset, e.g. as fitted params) → `mv_mahalanobis` (the baseline, or **scoring new observations** with supplied center/cov).

**When NOT:** for **one** variable (`p ≥ 2` is a hard gate — univariate capping/trimming → #114 `dt_winsorize`/`dt_trim`); for **time-series** outliers of *type* AO/LS/TC/IO → #5 `run_tso` (`automatic_outlier_detection`); on **levels of non-stationary** series (§3b gate 3 — supply differences explicitly); with **missing** data (impute first, cat. 00); for **clustering** instead of outlier detection → cat 29 (#241 `km_kmeans`/`km_pam`, #244 `mb_mclust`); for **robust regression** (`ltsReg`/`lmrob`) — another family; charts: **frontend only** (§5).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** a numeric **matrix/DataFrame**, rows = observations, columns = variables; **all** columns numeric; **without NA/NaN/Inf**; **p ≥ 2**; **no** column of zero variance; **no** collinearity (`rcond(cov) ≥.Machine.double.eps`, exposed as `cov_rcond`); a sample size of **n ≥ p+1** for the classical `cov` and **n ≥ p+2** for the MCD; `quantile` strictly in (0,1); `alpha` in **[0.5, 1)**; `seed` an integer. Exception: when **both** `center` **and** `cov` are supplied, **n ≥ 1** suffices (scoring a single new observation). Checking tools: **`data-dp_quality_flags`** — the blockers `constant` / `p_ge_n` / `infinite_values` are *exactly* these gates; **`imputets_interpolation`** for the NA; **`mv_mahalanobis`** as a cheap algebraic pass that reveals collinearity via `cov_rcond` before the MCD runs.

**Alternatives + criterion:** `mv_outliers` is the **default** path — the *comparison* of the two distances is the result. `mv_covmcd(alpha = 0.5)` = **maximum robustness** (h ≈ n/2, breakdown ≈ (n−h+1)/n); `alpha = 0.75` = **higher efficiency** when you know the contamination is < 25% — `alpha` controls exactly this trade-off. `mv_mahalanobis` without `center`/`cov` **only** on a demonstrably clean sample (or as a baseline). `mv_mahalanobis(center =, cov = )` for an **out-of-sample apply**. #114 when the target is univariate tail cleaning; #5 when the input is a time series and outliers of a *type* are wanted.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `mv_mahalanobis`: `distance` (the named D² per observation — the main chart-data) + `distance_sqrt`, `outlier`/`outlier_index`/`outlier_labels`, `n_outliers`/`share_outliers`, `cutoff = qchisq(quantile, df = p)`, `center`/`cov`/`cov_rcond` and **`center_source`/`cov_source`** (`"sample"` vs `"supplied"` — showing whether the result is in-sample or an apply).
- `mv_covmcd`: **`center`/`cov`** (robust; fit/apply), `distance` (after the reweighting) vs `raw_distance` (before), `raw_center`/`raw_cov`, **`h`** = `h.alpha.n(alpha,n,p)` / `h_share` / `best_subset` / `in_best_subset`, `mcd_weight` (binary 0/1) / `n_zero_weight`, `crit` = the **log** determinant of the MCD, `cnp2`/`raw_cnp2` (**of length 2**: consistency + finite-sample), `method`, `nsamp = "deterministic"`, `i_best` ∈ 1:6, `n_csteps` (one per initial subset), `small_sample` (n < 2p).
- `mv_outliers`: **`distance_table`** (n×2 "classical | robust" — the central chart-data), `masked` / `swamped` / `both` (+ counts + labels), `order_robust`/`ranked_labels` (descending robust D², with a tie-break on the name), and the center/cov of **both** estimators.
- All flags/distances are **named per row** (`observations`; if rownames/colnames are missing, `obs1.obsN` / `v1.vP` are generated).

**Critical traps:**
- **MASKING/SWAMPING is the point of the node.** The classical mean/cov is computed *from* the outlying points themselves ⇒ an outlier hides itself (**masked**) and clean points get "hit" (**swamped**). In the shipped test: the classical method found **2 of the 4** planted multivariate outliers, the MCD found **all 4** — and **no** univariate test would have seen any of them (their maximum absolute value is *smaller* than that of the clean data). Read `n_masked`/`n_swamped`, not just the classical result.
- **`alpha` ∈ [0.5, 1) — a hard gate.** `covMcd(alpha = 0.2)` **does not error**: only the warning "subsample size h < n/2 may be too small", h = 9/30 (live-verified) ⇒ a breakdown > 50%, and the "robust" subset may be **entirely outlying**. The help page says explicitly "Allowed values are between 0.5 and 1".
- **`alpha = 1` = degeneracy (a separate gate).** "alpha = 1: The minimum covariance determinant estimates … are equal to the classical estimates" **and** the object is returned **without any** `mah`/`best`/`iBest` (live-verified, robustbase 0.99.7). Zero robustness *and* no distances.
- **Determinism (§5).** `nsamp = "deterministic"` is **PINNED** (DetMCD: it starts from the h most central points of **six** deterministic estimators) — the default `nsamp = 500` is subsampling. The `seed` is a **safety net** for `n > nmini*kmini` (=1500), where the help page says that "the initial search uses only a subsample"; it runs with `set.seed` **and restores** the caller's `.Random.seed`. `covMcd(seed=)` is never passed (it wants an entire `.Random.seed`). Tests: `identical` over 2 runs **and** identical distances with a *different* seed.
- **`mcd_weight` ≠ `outlier`.** The `mcd.wt` values are tied to the **fixed 0.975** of `wgtFUN = "01.original"`, independently of our `quantile` ⇒ with `quantile ≠ 0.975`, `n_zero_weight` does **not** equal `n_outliers`.
- **Silent-wrongs that are blocked:** `p = 1` (covMcd without `mah`/`best`); a character column in a DataFrame (it operates on the **factor codes**, live `crit = -2.300799`); NA (a **silent** dropping of rows, live `n.obs = 29/30`); `n ≤ p` / `n = p+1` (cryptic covMcd messages); a constant column or collinearity (the cryptic "system is … singular").
- **No standardisation, no `transform` argument (§3b gate 2):** D² is **affine equivariant** (`D²(x) = D²(Ax+b)`) — `scale(X)` gives **identical** distances (live-verified, both classical *and* MCD). A `transform` knob would be a no-op implying a non-existent option.
- **Non-stationarity (§3b gate 3):** the node is **cross-section/panel**. In I(1) levels the population mean is undefined and the sample cov diverges with T ⇒ the distances are **uninterpretable**; the user supplies differences **explicitly** — never a silent correction here.
- **fit/apply externalization (§3b gate 6):** `center`/`cov` (classical **and** MCD) are returned as numbers **and** accepted as input ⇒ reproducible out-of-sample scoring (the KNIME "Normalize Model" pattern). A **TERMINAL** node: no `register`/handle chaining.
- **Package masking:** `library(robustbase)` is not called — it masks `plot` (live `conflicts(detail = TRUE)`) ⇒ `requireNamespace` + `covMcd`/`h.alpha.n` (the CLAUDE.md §3.a exception).

**Sources:** `robustbase` 0.99.7 `the covMcd documentation` (live, version 4.6.1) — "Allowed values are between 0.5 and 1 and the default is 0.5", `nsamp = "deterministic"` ⇒ "starts from the h most central observations of *six* (deterministic) estimators", "When `nmini*kmini < n`, the initial search uses only a *subsample* of size `nmini*kmini`", `quan = h.alpha.n(alpha,n,p)`, `length(best) == quan`, `iBest` ∈ 1:6, `cnp2` = the consistency + finite-sample factors, `wgtFUN = "01.original"`; Rousseeuw & Van Driessen (1999), *Technometrics* **41**, 212-223 (FastMCD); Hubert, Rousseeuw & Verdonck (2012), *JCGS* **21**, 618-637 (DetMCD = the PINNED `nsamp`); Pison, Van Aelst & Willems (2002), *Metrika* **55**, 111-123 (the finite-sample corrections; the efficiency of the reweighting); Rousseeuw & Leroy (1987), *Robust Regression and Outlier Detection*, Wiley (the breakdown point); the `mahalanobis`/`qchisq`/`cov` the reference help (version 4.6.1); Hamilton, Ma & Xi, NBER WP 32068 (§3b gate 3); `the normative gate spec` §3b live-verified gates + determinism ("covMcd ⇒ `nsamp="deterministic"`"); wrapper footer *IMPLEMENTATION NOTE* (all the silent-wrongs, the `conflicts` baseline, the affine-equivariance verification).

### #247 Battery of normality tests (AD / CvM / Lilliefors / Pearson chi-square / Shapiro-Francia) — `battery_normality_edf` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/battery_normality_edf.py`)

**Functions:** `nt_normality_battery` — **all** the requested tests in one call → a tidy table + a `consensus` summary. `nt_ad_test` [`ad.test`] — Anderson–Darling (an EDF omnibus test, **the recommended one** per Stephens 1986; it weights the **tails**). `nt_cvm_test` [`cvm.test`] — Cramér–von Mises (EDF, the "second choice"). `nt_lillie_test` [`lillie.test`] — Lilliefors (KS with **estimated** mu, sigma). `nt_pearson_test` [`pearson.test`] — Pearson chi-square on **equiprobable** classes. `nt_sf_test` [`sf.test`] — Shapiro–**Francia** (correlation-based, Royston 1993).

**When:** when the input is **one** numeric univariate series — typically **model residuals**, returns or a macro series — and the question is whether its **distribution** is normal with the parameters **unknown** (a composite hypothesis). The battery is the default path: a single test is fragile, because the five have **different power against different departures** (tails vs centre vs classes). The five individual functions are for when you want one specific test or when `n` rules some of them out.

**When NOT:** for **Jarque–Bera** (moment-based: skewness + kurtosis) → it **already exists**, #1 `run_jarque_bera_test` — it is not duplicated here (and note the **incompatible NA policy**, below); for a **descriptive** Shapiro–Wilk inside a descriptives table (`normtest.W`/`normtest.p`, without gates/decision) → #129 `ps_stat_desc`; for **descriptive moments** per column → #248 `dp_profile`; for **several columns** (a hard gate against a matrix/DataFrame — run the node **per column**); with **missing** values (impute first, cat. 00); for **stationarity** (#1/#2) or **autocorrelation** (#81 `desc_acf`) — a different hypothesis; for **multivariate** outlyingness → #246; `qqnorm`/plots: **frontend only** (§5).

**Delimitation (grep-verified, no overlap):** `run_jarque_bera_test` (#1) tests **moments**, the EDF tests here test the **distribution function** — they are **complementary**. `shapiro.test` (Shapiro-**Wilk**) is **not** exposed as inference by any node and does **not** belong to `battery_normality_edf`; what is exposed here is Shapiro-**Francia**, a different test (the squared correlation with the expected normal quantiles, without Wilk's weight matrix). `ps_stat_desc` (#129) gives Shapiro-Wilk **as one descriptive cell**, not gated inference with a decision at alpha.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** a **univariate** numeric vector or `ts` (a matrix/DataFrame/array ⇒ stop); **n ≥ 1**; **no NA/NaN** (a hard stop — see the policy); **no Inf**; **non-zero variance**; `alpha` in the open interval (0,1); `series_name` a non-empty string of ≤ 100 characters. And — critically — a **min-n PER TEST, never one global n**: `ad`/`cvm` **n > 7**, `lillie` **n > 4**, `sf` **5 ≤ n ≤ 5000** (which excludes *large* samples as well), `pearson` has **no gate in the package** ⇒ ours (df ≥ 1, `n/k ≥ min_expected`, an integer `n_classes`, no observation outside the classes). Checking tools: **`dp_quality_flags`** (#248) — the flags `constant` / `infinite_values` / `few_rows` are *exactly* these gates (`few_rows` reports the same min-n values); **`imputets_interpolation`** for the NA.

**Alternatives + criterion:** `nt_normality_battery` for a **cross-checked decision**. `nt_ad_test` when the target is **fat tails** (returns, crises) — it gives more weight to the tails. `nt_sf_test` as the second choice (but it is **ruled out** for n > 5000). `nt_cvm_test` when you want an EDF test without tail emphasis. `nt_lillie_test` when the reader/the literature asks for it explicitly — **and** as the only feasible one for 5 ≤ n ≤ 7. `nt_pearson_test` **twice** (`adjust = TRUE` and `FALSE`), because the correct p-value lies **in between**. #1 `run_jarque_bera_test` for the moment-based test.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `table` = tidy records `{test, test_label, method, statistic, statistic_name, p_value, df, n_classes, expected_per_class, n, alpha, reject, decision}` — the main chart-data. The **row order is canonical** (`ad, cvm, lillie, pearson, sf`) **irrespective** of the order the user gave in `tests` (determinism).
- The summary: `statistic`/`p_value`/`reject` (named **per test**), `n_tests`/`n_reject`/`share_reject`/`reject_any`/`reject_all`, **`consensus`** ∈ {`reject_all`, `fail_to_reject_all`, `mixed`}, `min/max/median_p_value`, **`primary_test`**/`primary_p_value`/`primary_reject`, `alpha`/`n`/`mean`/`sd`/`series`/`na_policy = "error"`, and `results` (the full per-test output, including the raw `htest`).
- The fields `df`/`n_classes`/`expected_per_class`/`adjust`/`min_expected` are **NA** for every test except `pearson` — they indicate non-applicability, not missingness.
- `decision` ∈ {`reject_normality`, `fail_to_reject`} + a ready `interpretation`.

**Critical traps:**
- **An incompatible NA policy — an explicit project decision.** `battery_normality_edf` states "Missing values are allowed" and silently applies `complete.cases` (live: `ad.test(c(rnorm(20), NA))` returns a normal result), whereas the **existing** Jarque–Bera node **errors** ("NAs in x"). On the same input the two normality nodes would give **a result from one and an error from the other**, and the reported `n` would not be the n of the input ⇒ a wrong reading of the min-n gates. **The choice: one policy, the stricter one — a HARD STOP**, with a message pointing to the imputation path (cat. 00). `na_policy = "error"` is always returned.
- **No silent skipping in the battery.** If a requested test does not meet its min-n, the call **stops** and says which one to remove (`blocked-by-gate`, §5) — never "I skipped it".
- **`pearson.test` has no validity checks at all.** Live-verified silent-wrongs that are blocked here: `n_classes = 3` + `adjust` ⇒ **df = 0 ⇒ p = 0 exactly, for any data**; `n_classes = 2` + `adjust` ⇒ df = −1 ⇒ "NaNs produced", p = NA; a **non-integer** `n_classes` (4.7) is accepted silently; **n/k < 5** ⇒ the chi-square approximation does not hold (Cochran 1954; Moore 1986) and **the reference never warns here**; an **extreme value** with `pnorm == 1` ⇒ `tabulate` **drops** the observation (live: `sum(counts) = 199` for n = 200, with no warning). Each is a hard gate, with the **permitted range** of `n_classes` in the message.
- **`adjust`: neither of the two p-values is the correct one.** "this is not (!) the correct p-value, lying somewhere between the two" (`the pearson.test documentation`). The `statistic` is **the same**; only `df` (k−3 vs k−1) and the p change. Read them as **bounds**.
- **Lilliefors ≠ `ks.test`.** The same statistic, a **different p-value** — "it is not correct to use the p-value from the latter for the composite hypothesis of normality … since the distribution of the test statistic is different when the parameters are estimated" (`the lillie.test documentation`).
- **Shapiro-Francia ≠ Shapiro-Wilk.** A different test; Wilk appears **only descriptively** in #129.
- **`primary_test` is not arbitrary:** `ad > sf > cvm > lillie > pearson`, taken from the **Notes of the help pages themselves** ("recommended EDF test by Stephens (1986)" · "known to perform well … Royston (1993)" · "as second choice" · "known to perform worse" · "usually not recommended … inferior power properties"). It is the first available one of that order within the selected subset.
- **`consensus = "mixed"` is a normal result.** Live in the tests: with an `alpha` between the p of `ad` (9.73e-05) and that of `cvm` (4.59e-04), **only** `ad` rejects (`n_reject = 1`, `share_reject = 0.2`). Read `primary_test` **and** the whole table, never one cell.
- **`fail_to_reject` does not prove normality** (the `interpretation` itself says so). `alpha` changes **only** the `decision` column, never the `p_value`.
- **Other silent-wrongs:** with `Inf`, `ad`/`cvm`/`lillie` error cryptically, but `sf` → W = NaN/p = NaN and `pearson` → a **normal-looking** P = 21 / p = 0.00032, **without** an error or a warning; **zero variance** ⇒ `pearson` returns a spuriously "significant" result out of nothing (the worst of the family).
- **Determinism (§5):** no RNG in any test (closed formulas/tables) ⇒ **no seed**; `identical` over 2 runs and identical output irrespective of the order of `tests`.
- **`series_name` = a label, not data:** it replaces the `data.name` of the `htest` (which `battery_normality_edf` fills with `deparse(substitute(x))` — in the node path that would serialise the **entire** vector into the JSON). A **TERMINAL** node, no `register`. **Masking:** `library(nortest)` is safe — `conflicts(detail = TRUE)` is **identical** before/after, with zero S3 registration (`.__S3MethodsTable__.` = `character(0)`); nevertheless all calls are / qualified.

**Sources:** the `battery_normality_edf` 1.0.4 help pages (live, version 4.6.1): `the ad.test documentation` ("the recommended EDF test by Stephens (1986) … Cramer-von Mises test (as second choice) … more weight to the tails"), `the lillie.test documentation` ("known to perform worse" + the warning about `ks.test`), `the sf.test documentation` ("known to perform well, see also the comments by Royston (1993)"; `qnorm(ppoints(x, a = 3/8))`), `the pearson.test documentation` (`n.classes = ceiling(2 * (n^(2/5)))` "due to Moore (1986)"; "usually not recommended … inferior power properties"; "not (!) the correct p-value, lying somewhere between the two"); Stephens, M.A. (1986) *Tests based on EDF statistics*, in D'Agostino & Stephens (eds), **Goodness-of-Fit Techniques**, Marcel Dekker; Dallal & Wilkinson (1986), *The American Statistician* **40**, 294-296; Royston (1993), *Statistics in Medicine* **12**, 181-184; Moore, D.S. (1986) *Tests of the chi-squared type*, ibid.; Cochran (1954), *Biometrics* **10**(4), 417-451 (the minimum expected frequency ⇒ `min_expected = 5`); Thode Jr., H.C. (2002) **Testing for Normality**, Marcel Dekker (§5.2); `the normative gate spec` §3b live-verified gates ("nortest min-n **per test**: ad/cvm n>7 · lillie n>4 · sf 5≤n≤5000"; "`jarque.bera.test`: NAs in x — an **incompatible NA policy**"); wrapper footer *IMPLEMENTATION NOTE*.

### #248 Data profiling / data-quality report — `base` + `stats` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/profiling_quality_report.py`)

**Functions:** `dp_profile` — a tidy profile **per column** (type/missing/uniqueness/moments) + a **dataset-level** summary. `dp_column_profile` — **one** column in depth: a quantile grid + a **histogram** (numeric) or a **top-N frequency table** (categorical/logical/date), as pure numeric chart-data. `dp_quality_flags` — a **rule-based** report: structured `blocker`/`warning` flags with a **rule, a detail and a value**, not prose.

**When:** as **the first node of every workflow**, before any statistical method runs: "what are these data and what is wrong with them?". Flow: `dp_profile` (the picture of the whole dataset) → `dp_column_profile` (depth on the suspect column) → `dp_quality_flags` (**the decision**: what will break downstream and why). It works on **mixed types** (`numeric`/`integer`/`logical`/`character`/`factor`/`Date`/`POSIXct`) — the non-numeric columns are **not lost** and are **not** coerced.

**When NOT:** for **transformation/imputation/standardisation** — the node **diagnoses, it does not alter** (§3b gate 2; imputation → cat. 00 `imputeTS`); for **cross-variable** missingness patterns (which columns are missing *together*) → #249 `missing-pattern` ("one wrapper = one node"); for **normality tests** with a p-value/decision → #247 `battery_normality_edf` / #1 Jarque–Bera (here the moments are **descriptive**); for **correlations + p-values** → #130 `hm_rcorr`; for **multivariate outliers** → #246; for **time-series descriptives** (ACF/PACF/rolling) → #81; for the `stat.desc` table with normality criteria → #129; charts: **frontend only** (§5) — the node supplies `breaks`/`counts`/`mids`.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** a `DataFrame` or an **atomic** `matrix` (rows = observations); **≥ 1 row** and **≥ 1 column**; column names **non-empty, non-NA and without duplicates** (an ambiguous profile otherwise); **no** list column / DataFrame column / matrix column / `POSIXlt` / `complex` / **unknown S3 class**; `quantile_type` an integer in **1.9**; `bins`/`top_n`/`min_rows` positive integers; `max_missing_pct` ∈ [0,100]; `max_unique_ratio` ∈ (0,1]. **There is no precondition tool** — *this* is the precondition node: `dp_quality_flags` is the checking tool for #246 (`constant`/`p_ge_n`/`infinite_values`) and #247 (`constant`/`infinite_values`/`few_rows`).

**Alternatives + criterion:** `dp_profile` = a cheap first pass; `dp_column_profile` = depth on one column; `dp_quality_flags` = a decision instead of numbers. `moment_type = "type2"` (SAS/SPSS, unbiased under normality, requires n ≥ 3 / n ≥ 4); `"type3"` (MINITAB/BMDP — **and** the default of `e1071`); `quantile_type ≠ 7` when you need a specific Hyndman & Fan algorithm. #249 when the question is missingness *patterns*.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `dp_profile.profile` = tidy records **per column**: `{column, type, n, n_missing, pct_missing, n_infinite, n_valid, n_unique, is_constant, n_zeros, min, q1, median, mean, q3, max, iqr, sd, skewness, kurtosis}` — the main chart-data.
- `dp_profile.dataset` = `{rows, cols, complete_rows, incomplete_rows, pct_complete_rows, duplicate_rows, distinct_rows, n_cells, n_missing_cells, pct_missing_cells, n_constant_cols, n_all_missing_cols, n_cols_with_missing, n_cols_with_infinite}` + `type_counts` (a named integer over the 7 types) + `columns`.
- `dp_column_profile` = the same fields for the single column + `quantiles` (named `p0…p100`) + `histogram` `{breaks, counts, mids, bins, degenerate}` (**numeric only**; otherwise `NULL`) + `frequency` (top-N `{value, count, pct}`, **non-numeric only**) + `n_levels`/`levels` (**factor only**).
- `dp_quality_flags.flags` = tidy records `{scope, column, issue, severity, detail, value}` **sorted** (blocker < warning < info → issue → column) + `n_flags`/`n_blockers`/`n_warnings`/`has_blocker`/`blocked_columns` + `profile` + `dataset` + `thresholds`.
- **Always:** `quantile_type`, `moment_type`, `kurtosis_excess = TRUE` — **§3b gate 6**: two profiles are comparable **only** under the same estimator.

**The exact moment estimator (explicit, with a source):** Joanes & Gill (1998), **the same typology as `e1071`**, over `m_r = (1/n)·sum((x_i − x̄)^r)` (the **moment** estimator, divisor **n**, not n−1):

| type | skewness | kurtosis (**excess**) | defined for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `type1` (**default**, moment-based) | `g1 = m3 / m2^(3/2)` | `g2 = m4 / m2² − 3` | n ≥ 2, m2 > 0 |
| `type2` (SAS/SPSS) | `G1 = g1·√(n(n−1))/(n−2)` | `G2 = ((n+1)g2 + 6)(n−1)/((n−2)(n−3))` | n ≥ 3 / n ≥ 4 |
| `type3` (MINITAB/BMDP) | `b1 = g1·((n−1)/n)^(3/2)` | `b2 = (g2+3)(1−1/n)² − 3` | n ≥ 2, m2 > 0 |

The **kurtosis is always excess** (normal ⇒ 0) in all **three** types — it is stated explicitly as `kurtosis_excess = TRUE`. The tests pin the identity against an **independent recompute** *and* against `e1071` for all 3 types.

**Critical traps:**
- **Estimator comparability.** Our default is `type1`, whereas `e1071` defaults to **`type = 3`** (the `the skewness documentation` usage). Two "skewness" values on the same data can differ because the **estimator** changed, not the data — hence `moment_type`/`quantile_type`/`kurtosis_excess` are always returned.
- **No silent coercion (§3b gate 2).** The non-numeric columns get the count fields and **NA** for the moments. An **unknown S3 class ⇒ a hard stop**: it was live-verified that `difftime` is a `double`, so without the gate it would be profiled as "numeric" with moments in **unknown units** (days/secs). The same holds for `ts`/`units`/`labelled`/`AsIs`.
- **Never NaN/Inf in the output** (a post-check): `min`/`max` on an **all-NA** column ⇒ the standard library returns **Inf/−Inf + a warning** "no non-missing arguments to min; returning Inf" (here `NA_real_`); moments on a **constant** column ⇒ 0/0 = NaN (here `NA_real_`); **arithmetic overflow** `c(1e308, −1e308)` ⇒ `sd = Inf` with no error (here it **blocks**).
- **`NaN` counts as missing** (`is.na(NaN) == TRUE`), **`Inf` does not** — it is counted in `n_infinite`, excluded from the moments **and** flagged as a blocker. `n_unique` counts the **distinct non-missing** values — for a factor, the **present** levels, not `nlevels` (that is the separate `n_levels`).
- **Boundary behaviours (documented + tested):** all-NA ⇒ `n_unique = 0`, `is_constant = NA` (**not** FALSE); n = 1 valid value ⇒ `iqr = 0`, `sd = NA`, the moments NA; a constant column ⇒ `sd = 0` **but** the moments NA (m2 = 0); `n_zeros = NA` for non-numeric columns.
- **The moments are descriptive, not inference.** On an **autocorrelated** series they are neither evidence of normality nor a basis for a test (cf. §3b gate 4: autocorrelation inflates the Type I error) ⇒ a normality decision belongs to #247/#1, and inference under autocorrelation → HAC (`hac_robust_standard`, cat 07).
- **The histogram is not `hist`.** The "Sturges" breaks are *pretty*-adjusted (an unpredictable number of bins); here they are **exactly equal width**, `seq(min, max, length.out = bins+1)` ⇒ reproducible. A constant column ⇒ **one** degenerate bin. A post-check: `sum(counts)` = the number of values.
- **The rules of `dp_quality_flags` are explicit and sourced:** `all_missing` (a blocker); `high_missing` > `max_missing_pct` (a warning, default 10% — the Bennett 2001 rule, as the `detail` itself cites); `constant` (a blocker: `cor` → **NA with only a warning**; `scale` divides by 0); `infinite_values` (a blocker); `high_cardinality` (a warning: it looks like an **id**, not a variable); `duplicate_rows` (a warning: it breaks `kmeans` with "more cluster centers than **distinct** data points" and `isoMDS` with "zero or negative distance"); `few_rows` (a warning: the **per-test min-n** of the normality tests); `p_ge_n` (a blocker: a singular cov ⇒ `mahalanobis` "system is computationally singular"; `Mclust` **does not even error**); `no_complete_rows` (a blocker). `all_missing` **excludes** `high_missing` (an else-if) ⇒ one missingness flag per column.
- **`dp_quality_flags` does not halt execution:** it produces structured flags that the frontend displays **educationally** (`blocked-by-gate` as a *state*, not an error); the hard `stop` calls are only for **structurally invalid** input.
- **Determinism (§5):** no RNG/seed, no sampling; an **explicit tie-break** everywhere — flags: severity → issue → column with `method = "radix"` (locale-independent); `frequency`: a descending count with a lexicographic tie-break. `identical` over 2 runs (the wrapper **and** the node path).
- **`df_handle`, not `matrix_handle`:** `.mcp_to_matrix` would **drop** the non-numeric columns — which is precisely what the profiling is obliged to **report** (silent data loss). **TERMINAL** nodes, no `register`.

**Sources:** Joanes, D.N. & Gill, C.A. (1998), "Comparing measures of sample skewness and kurtosis", *The Statistician* (JRSS-D) **47**, 183-189 — the type 1/2/3 typology; `e1071` `the skewness documentation`/`the kurtosis documentation` (live, version 4.6.1) for the **exact** formulas ("Used in SAS and SPSS", "Used in MINITAB and BMDP", "Only G2 (`type = 2`) is unbiased under normality") **and** for the e1071 default `type = 3`; Hyndman, the reference.J. & Fan, Y. (1996), "Sample Quantiles in Statistical Packages", *The American Statistician* **50**(4), 361-365, [doi:10.1080/00031305.1996.10473566](https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.1996.10473566) — the 9 types of `quantile` (as cited by `the quantile documentation`), with `type = 7` (the the classical statistical packages default) explicitly pinned; the `quantile`/`sd`/`.bincode`/`tabulate`/`duplicated`/`order(method="radix")` the reference help (version 4.6.1); `the normative gate spec` §3b live-verified gates (which reproduce `few_rows`/`p_ge_n`/`duplicate_rows`/`constant`) **and** §3b REJECTED ("DataExplorer/skimr/naniar/mice/VIM as dependencies … `md.pattern(plot=TRUE)` draws by default ⇒ a §5 violation; the `naniar.order` inconsistent default ⇒ a determinism risk") + gates 2/6; Bennett, D.A. (2001), "How can I deal with missing data in my study?", *Australian and New Zealand Journal of Public Health* — the ">10% ⇒ possible bias" rule, as the `detail` of `high_missing` cites it; wrapper footer *IMPLEMENTATION NOTE*.

### #249 Analysis of missingness PATTERNS (cross-variable missingness) — `base` + `stats` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/missingness_patterns_pattern.py`)

**Functions:** `mp_pattern` — a **pattern matrix** (1 = observed / 0 = missing, one row per **distinct** pattern) + counts per pattern + NA per variable + complete cases + a **monotonicity check**. `mp_runs` — the **NA runs/spans** per variable (`start`/`end`/`length`/`position`): the real case of macro panels — **mixed frequency** (internal gaps) and a **ragged edge** (trailing NA from publication lags). `mp_pairs` — the **per-pair** co-missingness `rr`/`rm`/`mr`/`mm` (the semantics of `md.pairs`).

**When:** when the question is **not** "how many are missing per column" (that is #248) but "**which combinations** of variables are missing **together**". 10% missing across 5 variables may be **one** common pattern (the same 10 countries) or **5 unrelated** ones (⇒ 40% incomplete rows) — two entirely different problems with the same per-column profile. Flow: `mp_pattern` (how many distinct patterns, how many complete cases, **monotonicity**) → `mp_runs` (**where** the gaps sit in time: leading / internal / trailing) → `mp_pairs` (which **pairs** are missing together, which never share an observation). It works over **mixed column types**: the criterion is **only** `is.na`, with no coercion.

**When NOT:** for **imputation / dropping / any alteration** — the node **diagnoses** (§3b gate 2; filling NA in a time series → `imputeTS` #80); for a **per-column** profile/moments/types/quality flags → #248 `dp_profile` ("one wrapper = one node"); for **estimation** with a ragged edge / mixed frequency instead of a **diagnosis** → `dynamic_factor_nowcasting` #15 / `mixed_frequency_bayesian` #17 / `midas_regression` #18 / `sparseDFM` #144; for an **MCAR test** (Little 1988) — it is **not exposed** (it requires normality + EM, and the autocorrelation of macro panels violates the assumptions — cf. §3b gate 4); charts: **frontend only** (§5) — the node supplies 0/1 matrices, counts and spans.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** a `DataFrame` or an **atomic** `matrix` (rows = observations/**time**, columns = variables); **≥ 1 row** and **≥ 1 column**; column names **non-empty, non-NA and without duplicates** (otherwise the patterns are ambiguous); **no** list column / matrix column / DataFrame column / `POSIXlt` / `complex`. If a `time` argument is supplied: an existing **atomic** `numeric`/`character`/`Date`/`POSIXct` column, **without NA**, **strictly increasing**, and with ≥ 1 variable left after its removal. Checking tools: **#248 `dp_profile`** (how many are missing per column) and **`mp_pattern`** (`n_patterns`/`n_complete_cases`/`monotone.is_monotone` decide whether `mp_runs`/`mp_pairs` are needed at all).

**Alternatives + criterion:** `mp_pattern` = the **structure** of the missingness (and the critical `monotone`, which determines which imputation mechanism is permissible); `mp_runs` = the **position** of the gaps in time — the pattern matrix does **not** distinguish a ragged edge from an internal gap; `mp_pairs` = the **pairs** (if `rr = 0` for a pair, no pairwise correlation is defined). `sort_by = "missingness"` when you want the `mice` semantics ("increasing amounts of missing information"); the default `"count"` = the most **frequent** pattern first. `time = <column>` when a strictly increasing axis exists and you want `start_time`/`end_time` labels on the spans.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `mp_pattern`: `pattern_matrix` (n_patterns × n_cols, an **integer 0/1** matrix, dimnames `pattern_i` × the column name — **the main chart-data**) + `pattern_counts` + `pattern` (tidy records `{pattern_id, pattern_key, count, pct, n_missing_vars, n_observed_vars, missing_vars, is_complete_case}`) + `variables` + `row_missing_counts` + `monotone {is_monotone, order, order_index, n_violating_rows, pct_violating_rows, first_violating_row}` + `summary` (including `n_patterns`, `n_complete_cases`, `pct_missing_cells`, `any_missing`).
- `mp_runs`: `runs` = tidy records **one per NA span** `{variable, run_id, start, end, length, position ∈ leading|internal|trailing|all, start_time, end_time}` + `variables` (`n_runs`, `longest_run`, `leading_na`, `trailing_na`, `n_internal_runs`, `first_obs`/`last_obs` + `*_time`) + `summary` with the decision field **`ragged_edge`** (and `balanced_start`/`balanced_end`, `n_vars_internal_gaps`).
- `mp_pairs`: `rr`/`rm`/`mr`/`mm` = **four p × p integer matrices** with dimnames (chart-data) + `pairs` (records `i<j`, `{both_observed, both_missing, only_1_missing, only_2_missing, pct_both_missing}`).
- **§3b gate 6:** `columns` (**always** in input order), `time_name`, `sort_by`, `time_labels` are always returned ⇒ two runs are **comparable without ambiguity**. **TERMINAL** nodes: no `register`/chaining.

**Critical traps:**
- **Why the standard library and not `mice` (the normative gate spec §3b REJECTED).** We take the **semantics** of `md.pattern`/`md.pairs` **without** the dependency, because (a) `mice` **masks** both `filter` **and** `complete` in the shared `source` env (CLAUDE.md §3.a) and (b) `md.pattern` has **`plot = TRUE` as its default** — that is, it **draws**, violating charter §5. We keep the encoding (1/0) and the `rr/rm/mr/mm` quantities; we **reject** the drawing.
- **Two deliberate deviations from `mice`:** the counts are **not** appended as the last row/column of the same matrix (they would contaminate the chart-data with non-binary values) — they are **separate** fields; and the **columns are never reordered** (`mice` sorts them by missingness ⇒ the same shape + different data = **a different column order**).
- **An explicit deterministic ordering rule** (no RNG anywhere): **columns** always in input order; **pattern rows** by **three** keys — `"count"` (default): DESCENDING `count` → ASCENDING `n_missing_vars` → ASCENDING `pattern_key`; `"missingness"`: ASCENDING `n_missing_vars` → DESCENDING `count` → ASCENDING `pattern_key`. `pattern_key` is **unique** per pattern ⇒ a **total** ordering, with no unresolved tie (`mice` does **not** define a tie-break). `runs`: input order → ascending `start`. `pairs`: DESCENDING `both_missing` → ASCENDING `i` → ASCENDING `j`. All with `method = "radix"` (the C locale ⇒ **locale-independent**; live-verified: `order(c("a","B"), method="radix")` = 2,1 whereas the `en_US` default gives 1,2).
- **Monotonicity — why the check is exact, not heuristic.** The definition is Van Buuren's (FIMD §4.1.1). Equivalently the sets `M_j = {i : Y_ij missing}` are **nested**; nested sets have **increasing** cardinality, and nested sets of equal cardinality are **equal** ⇒ if *some* monotone ordering exists, then "ascending |M_j|" is **also** monotone. **One** candidate ordering is checked — the tests verify this against a **brute force over all p! orderings**.
- **`NaN` counts as missing, `±Inf` does not** (`is.na(NaN) == TRUE`, `is.na(Inf) == FALSE` — live-verified). An explicit, documented choice; for `Inf` diagnostics → #248.
- **A strictly increasing time column is a hard gate.** The spans are defined **only** if "row order = time order"; with an unsorted or **duplicated** (= a panel, not a series) column the runs are meaningless **with no error at all** (silent-wrong). The check uses `order(method="radix")` + `anyDuplicated`, **not** `is.unsorted` on a character (which is locale-dependent).
- **Column-type gates — an essential difference from #248:** here unknown *atomic* S3 classes (`difftime`/`ts`/`units`/`labelled`) **are allowed**, because `is.na` is type-agnostic and **no** moment is computed; what is blocked is **exactly** the structures where `is.na` does not give a vector of length `nrow` (a matrix/DataFrame column → a **matrix**; `POSIXlt` → internally a list of 9 fields; a list column → it checks the *content*, not the cell) and `complex` (not JSON-safe).
- **Post-checks as mutation guards** (structurally impossible to trigger from valid input ⇒ the tests call them **directly**): sum(counts) == `nrow`; the complete cases from the patterns == a direct count; the sum of the run lengths per variable == its number of missing values; `rr+rm+mr+mm == nrow` in **every** cell.
- **Boundary cases (documented + tested, never an error):** zero missing ⇒ **one** pattern (all 1), `monotone = TRUE`, 0 runs; an all-NA column ⇒ **one** run with `position = "all"`, `first_obs/last_obs = NA`, and it does **not** break monotonicity; an all-NA dataset ⇒ one pattern (all 0); `nrow == 1` ⇒ `vapply(df, is.na)` returns a **vector** (live-verified) ⇒ an explicit `matrix` fallback; `ncol == 1` ⇒ `mp_pairs` = 0 pairs with the correct shape.
- **Masking / handles:** no `library` (base/stats only, always attached) ⇒ **zero** masking — `conflicts(detail = TRUE)` is **identical** before and after the `source` (live-verified). Conversely, **all** calls are / qualified because *other* wrappers in the shared env mask basic generics (`proxy` → `as.matrix`, `sn` → `sd`). At the node layer the data are passed as a **`df_handle`, not a `matrix_handle`**: `.mcp_to_matrix` would drop the non-numeric columns, that is, it would **hide exactly the missing values** the node counts.

**Sources:** van Buuren, *Flexible Imputation of Missing Data*, 2nd ed., **§4.1.1** ("A missing data pattern is said to be monotone if the variables Y_j can be ordered such that if Y_j is missing then all variables Y_k with k>j are also missing"); the **`mice` package documentation** (`md.pattern`/`md.pairs`: "1=observed, 0=missing"; "Rows and columns are sorted in increasing amounts of missing information"; "Default is plot = TRUE"; the `rr`/`rm`/`mr`/`mm` definitions) — **`mice` is not a dependency and is not installed**; the semantics are reproduced and recorded verbatim in the wrapper footer; `the normative gate spec` §3b **REJECTED** (the packages `DataExplorer/skimr/naniar/mice/VIM` — "we TAKE the feature (the standard library)", `mice` masking `filter`/`complete`, `md.pattern(plot=TRUE)` ⇒ a §5 violation) + §3b gates 2 & 6; the `rle` the reference help ("Missing values are regarded as unequal to the previous value"); the `is.na` / `order(method="radix")` / `crossprod` / `tabulate` the reference help (version 4.6.1, live-verified); Little (1988), *A Test of Missing Completely at Random for Multivariate Data with Missing Values*, **JASA 83(404), 1198-1202** (why the MCAR test is **not** exposed here); wrapper footer IMPLEMENTATION NOTE (`c01_preparation_prechecks/missingness_patterns_pattern.py`).
