### #250 Battery of parametric mean tests (t · ANOVA · Welch) — `stats` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/battery_parametric_mean.py`)

**Functions:** `tp_t_test` [`t.test`] — one-sample (`mu`), two-sample **Welch** (the default), two-sample **Student pooled** (`var_equal = TRUE`), **paired**. `tp_anova` [`aov` + `summary.aov`] — a one-way ANOVA **with** the equal-variance assumption, with the **ANOVA table as numeric chart-data** + `eta_squared`. `tp_welch` [`oneway.test`] — a one-way test of equal means **without** the equal-variance assumption (Welch 1951); `var_equal = TRUE` gives the classical F **as a test** (without a table).

**When:** a fast test of **means** on **cross-sectional** data (countries, firms, households, survey respondents) **before** a heavy model is deployed: "does the mean growth rate differ from 2%?" (one-sample) · "do euro vs non-euro differ?" (two-sample — **Welch is the default**) · "did something change before/after the reform in the **same** units?" (paired) · "do three or more regions differ?" (`tp_anova` for the ANOVA table/eta-squared; `tp_welch` when the variances are unequal or the `n_i` are very unbalanced).

**When NOT:** on **time series / temporally dependent data** — a **hard gate** (see the Preconditions); the HAC path is **#35 `hac_robust_standard`** (cat. 07, `wrap_vcov_hac`/`wrap_vcov_cl`/`wrap_vcov_panel`). On **non-normal or very small** samples → **#251** `tests-nonparametric` (the rank-based counterparts of the same designs). For a **normality decision** → #247 `battery_normality_edf` / #1 Jarque–Bera. For **two categorical** variables → **#257** `categorical-assoc` (chi-square/Fisher). For **multi-factor / repeated-measures** designs (`Error` strata, weights, contrasts, multi-response) — they are **not exposed**: **one-way only** here. Post-hoc tests (`TukeyHSD`/`model.tables`) are not exposed. Charts: **frontend only** (§5).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **NORMATIVE GATE 4 — CROSS-SECTION ONLY** (the normative gate spec §3b): every exported function calls the **shared** `gate_cross_section_only` (`the reference/wrapper_gates` — written **once**, shared with #251 and #257; it is **not** copied). Two branches, both hard `stop`: **(a)** an explicit rejection of the classes `ts/mts/msts/xts/zoo/zooreg/irts/timeSeries/tis/its/fts/tsibble/tbl_ts`; **(b)** a **Ljung–Box whiteness precheck** with `lag = min(10, n/5)` (`gate_alpha` default 0.05, `fitdf = 0` because the input is **data**, not residuals) — it runs **only** when `ordered = TRUE`. Autocorrelation **inflates the Type I error** ⇒ spuriously significant p-values. The diagnostics are always returned as `cross_section_gate` (with `gate_alpha`, `ordered`, `branch`). **Consequence:** the minimum n is 3; for n < 5 the rule gives `lag < 1` ⇒ an explicit `tested = FALSE`, `decision = "pass-untested"` (**never** a silent pass).
- **`gate_alpha` (default 0.05) — DECOUPLED from the `alpha` of the test.** `alpha` determines **only** the `reject`/`decision` fields of the output; the level of the gate is its **own** argument. **Reason:** the Ljung–Box precheck is a **test of size `gate_alpha`**, so **by construction it blocks a small share of valid i.i.d. input** (a false block). Live-measured (version 4.6.1, `rnorm`, 5000 replications): `n = 200` → **1.6% / 5.7% / 10.1%** and `n = 60` → **2.3% / 6.7% / 10.8%** for `gate_alpha = 0.01 / 0.05 / 0.10`. If the level were tied to the test's `alpha`, a "t-test at 10%" would raise the gate's false-block rate to ~10% with no statistical justification.
- **`ordered` (default `TRUE`) — an EXPLICIT declaration about row order.** Ljung–Box is a **function of the order**: **the same numbers** pass unsorted and are **blocked sorted** (live-verified: 60 `rnorm` values → pass, `sort` of the same → blocked) — and sorted is exactly how a cross-sectional CSV arrives (countries alphabetically, firms by size). `t.test`/`aov`/`oneway.test` are **permutation-invariant**, so the order does not change their result. `ordered = FALSE` ⇒ the user **declares** that the rows carry no order, branch (b) is **explicitly skipped** (`branch = "skipped-by-declaration"`, `decision = "pass-unordered"`, `tested = FALSE` throughout) and **all** the structural checks (NaN/Inf, `n ≥ 3`, zero variance) **remain**. Branch **(a)** applies **always** (`branch: class-rejected`): an explicitly time-classed object is never a cross-section. `lb_lag` **together with** `ordered = FALSE` ⇒ a hard `stop` (contradictory — it would be a silent no-op).
- **`tp_t_test` input:** plain **numeric vectors** (not a matrix/DataFrame/array), non-empty, **without Inf/-Inf/NaN**, **non-constant**, `n ≥ 2` **per sample** (and ≥ 3 from the gate); `mu` a single finite number; `conf_level`/`alpha` in the **open** interval (0,1); `x_name`/`y_name` labels of ≤ 100 characters and **different**; `paired = TRUE` requires a `y` of **equal length**; `var_equal` applies **only** to the two-sample unpaired design.
- **`tp_anova`/`tp_welch` input:** a non-empty `DataFrame`; `response` ≠ `group`, **both existing column names**; `response` a **numeric vector**; **`group` a factor or character** (a hard gate — see the traps); `k ≥ 2` levels and `n_i ≥ 2` per level; no group of zero variance (`tp_welch`) / not **all** constant (`tp_anova`).
- **Checking tools:** **#247** `nt_normality_battery` (parametric vs #251), **#248** `dp_quality_flags` (`constant`/`infinite_values`/`few_rows` = exactly the gates that will block here), and **`tp_welch`** — if `tp_anova` and `tp_welch` **disagree**, the problem is the equal-variance assumption.

**Alternatives + criterion:** `var_equal = FALSE` (**the default**, Welch/Satterthwaite) is the safe choice; `TRUE` (Student pooled, `df = n1+n2−2`) only if the variances really are equal. `paired = TRUE` when the **same** units were measured twice. `tp_anova` when you want the **full** ANOVA table + `eta_squared`; `tp_welch` when the variances are **unequal** or the `n_i` are very unbalanced (a generalisation of the 2-sample Welch test to arbitrarily many samples); `tp_welch(var_equal = TRUE)` = the classical F **as a test**, with a statistic **identical** to that of `tp_anova` (pinned in the tests). #251 when normality fails; **#35 `hac_robust_standard`** when the data *are* temporally dependent — **never** bypass the gate.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `tp_t_test`: a tidy htest → `method`, `statistic`(+`statistic_name`), `parameter` (df), `p_value`, `estimate`, `conf_low`/`conf_high`/`conf_level`, `null_value`, `stderr`, `alternative` + `alpha`/`reject`/**`decision`** (`reject_H0` | `fail_to_reject_H0`) + **`design`** (`one_sample` | `two_sample_welch` | `two_sample_student_pooled` | `paired`) + `n_used`/`n_na`/`na_action`/`sample_names`.
- `tp_anova`: **`anova_table`** = `{term = c("group","Residuals"), df, sum_sq, mean_sq, f_value, p_value}` as **numeric columns** (chart-data) + `statistic` (F), `parameter` (`num df`, `denom df`), `p_value`, `eta_squared` (= `SS_group/SS_total`), `ss_total`, `df_residual`, `grand_mean`.
- `tp_welch`: a tidy htest (F + a **non-integer** Welch–Satterthwaite `denom df`) + `test` (`oneway_welch` | `oneway_f`).
- **Common per-group chart-data:** `levels` (canonically sorted), `k`, `n`, `n_na`, `n_by_group`, `mean_by_group`, `sd_by_group`, `grand_mean`, `response`, `group`.
- **`cross_section_gate`** = `{groups, lb_statistic, lb_p_value, lb_lag, n, n_na, alpha, tested, decision}` — **always** in the output, purely numeric.

**Critical traps** (all live-verified, version 4.6.1):
- **Exactly where the gate runs** — statistically precise, not mechanical: *one-sample* on `x`; *two-sample* on `x` **and** `y` **separately** (each sample has its own mean and variance); *paired* **only on the differences** `d = x − y` (autocorrelation that **cancels** in the difference does not inflate the Type I error — a gate on `x`/`y` would reject **valid** analyses); *anova/welch* **per group**.
- **⚠️ A documented limit of the gate:** in `tp_anova`/`tp_welch` the column is split into groups **before** it reaches the gate, and `[` on a `ts` returns an unclassed numeric ⇒ the "time-series class" branch does **not** see a `ts` column inside a `DataFrame`. The **substantive** branch (Ljung–Box per group) stays fully active. In `tp_t_test` both branches are active.
- **The gravest silent-wrong:** with a **numeric or logical** grouping column `aov` **does not do an ANOVA — it does a linear regression** (`Df = 1` instead of `k−1`) **with no error or warning**; `oneway.test` likewise accepts numeric groups ⇒ a **hard gate**: `factor`/`character` only.
- `t.test` on **non-numeric** input **does not error** — only warnings ("argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA") and it returns `NA`; with muffled warnings it would pass **entirely silently** ⇒ a hard type gate.
- **Incompatible behaviour on `Inf`:** `t.test` and `oneway.test` **do not error** (they return `NaN`/`NaN` — `the t.test documentation`: "no longer errors and returns a still not very useful result"), whereas `aov` **errors** ("NA/NaN/Inf in 'y'") ⇒ **one** unified policy: a hard stop everywhere.
- `t.test(c(1,2), 3, var.equal = TRUE)` **does not error** — pooled Student accepts a sample with `n = 1` (whose variance is not even defined); and with `n_i = 1` in an ANOVA you get `df.residual = 0` and the table comes back **without** the "F value"/"Pr(>F)" columns, with no error ⇒ an explicit shape check.
- **Zero variance — two different policies:** `tp_welch` (`zero_var="any"`): Welch weights by `w_i = n_i/s_i²` ⇒ **a single** constant group gives `NaN`/`NaN` (and with `var_equal=TRUE` → `F = Inf`, `p = 0`); `tp_anova` (`zero_var="all"`): if **all** groups are constant, the residual SS is ~1e-31 and `aov` returns **F ≈ 1.83e+31, p ≈ 4.4e-93** (numerical garbage). It runs **before** the shared gate so that the message is test-specific.
- **An explicit NA policy:** `the t.test documentation` — "Missing values are silently removed (in pairs if `paired` is TRUE)"; `aov` → `na.omit`. So the reported `n` is **not** the n of the input and the balance of the design is altered ⇒ `na_action = "fail"` (**default**) | `"omit"` with a **count** (`n_na` always in the output; pairs in the paired design, **rows** in anova/welch).
- **No `formula` on the surface (security):** a one-way design has **exactly one** term ⇒ a formula adds no expressiveness, only attack surface. The column names are validated with `%in% names(data)` and used **only** as a `[[` index; the formula is **literally written in the code** (`.tp_value ~.tp_group`). **Zero** user-string → `parse`/`eval` path (.claude/rules/security.md). The table comes back with **canonical** labels `c("group","Residuals")` (+ `raw_rownames`).
- **Determinism (§5):** no RNG (closed-form t/F + the Welch–Satterthwaite df) ⇒ **no seed**. The order of the levels is **canonical** (`sort(unique(g))`, **not** order of appearance) and the `factor` is built explicitly with it ⇒ the ANOVA table, `mean_by_group`/`sd_by_group` and the Welch statistic do **not** depend on how the rows are sorted (tests: `identical` over 2 runs **and** over shuffled rows).
- **Post-checks (a defensive "second net",** covered by **direct** calls in the tests**):** the class `htest`/`aov`; a finite statistic of length 1; a finite p-value in [0,1]; `df.residual ≥ 1`; **all 5** columns of the ANOVA table present, **exactly 2** rows.
- **Masking / handles:** no `library` — only `stats` (always attached) ⇒ **zero** new masking surface (`conflicts(detail = TRUE)` identical before/after the `source`; no S3 method is registered); all calls are qualified. Node layer: `x`/`y` as a **`raw_handle`** (**not** a `series_handle` — that would imply exactly the **forbidden** input, and `resolve_handle(as="ts")` rejects a numeric vector), `data` as a `df_handle`, `response`/`group`/`x_name`/`y_name` = **names and labels**, never data. **TERMINAL** nodes: no `register`; the fitted `aov` is **not** returned (it carries `terms`/`call`/an environment).

**Sources:** version 4.6.1 `the t.test documentation` ("Missing values are silently removed (in pairs if 'paired' is TRUE)"; "the Welch modification to the degrees of freedom is used"; "'mu' must be a single number"; "not enough 'x' observations"; "data are essentially constant"); `the oneway.test documentation` ("an approximate method of Welch (1951) is used, which generalizes the commonly known 2-sample Welch test to the case of arbitrarily many samples"); `the aov documentation` + `summary.aov`; **Welch, B.L. (1951)**, *On the Comparison of Several Mean Values: An Alternative Approach*, **Biometrika 38(3/4), 330**, doi:10.2307/2332579 (the reference `the oneway.test documentation` itself gives); **Ljung & Box (1978)**, *On a Measure of Lack of Fit in Time Series Models*, **Biometrika 65(2), 297-303**, doi:10.1093/biomet/65.2.297 + the `?Box.test` Note "Missing values are not handled"; **Hyndman & Athanasopoulos**, *FPP* 3rd ed. **§5.4** — the rule `lag = min(10, n/5)`, identical to the documented default of `checkresiduals` (live-verified: "If missing, it is set to `min(10, n/5)` for non-seasonal data"); `the normative gate spec` **§3b normative gate 4** ("to be written ONCE as a shared helper, not 3 times"); `.claude/rules/security.md` (the ban on `eval(parse)`) + CLAUDE.md §5; the wrapper footers IMPLEMENTATION NOTE (`c01_preparation_prechecks/battery_parametric_mean.py`, `the reference/wrapper_gates`).

---

### #251 Battery of non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon · Mann–Whitney · Kruskal–Wallis · Friedman) — `stats` (`c01_preparation_prechecks/battery_non_parametric.py`)

**Functions:** `tn_wilcox` [`wilcox.test`] — the Wilcoxon **signed rank** test (one sample or paired) **and** the Wilcoxon **rank sum / Mann–Whitney** test (two independent samples), with an optional non-parametric **CI + Hodges–Lehmann estimator**. `tn_kruskal` [`kruskal.test`] — Kruskal–Wallis, `k ≥ 2` **independent** groups (a non-parametric one-way ANOVA). `tn_friedman` [`friedman.test`] — Friedman on an **unreplicated complete block design** (a non-parametric repeated-measures test), in **WIDE** or **LONG** form.

**When:** the rank-based **counterparts** of the parametric battery **#250**, when **normality does not hold** (#247 `battery_normality_edf`) or the sample is very small: two **independent** groups of countries/firms → `tn_wilcox` (rank sum / Mann–Whitney); **before/after** on the **same** units → `tn_wilcox(paired = TRUE)`; `k ≥ 2` **independent** groups → `tn_kruskal`; `k` methods/treatments **measured on the same blocks** (e.g. 3 forecasting methods × 6 countries) → `tn_friedman`.

**When NOT:** on **time series / temporally dependent data** — a **hard gate** (see the Preconditions); the HAC path is **#35 `hac_robust_standard`** (cat. 07). When normality **does** hold and you want more power, an ANOVA table or eta-squared → **#250** `tests-parametric`. When **no** variable is continuous — two **categorical** answers per unit ⇒ a contingency table (chi-square/Fisher/Cramér's V) → **#257** `categorical-assoc`. For a **normality decision** → #247 / #1. `quade.test` (Friedman weighted by the block range) is **not** exposed — a different test, with its own card if requested. An incomplete or **replicated** block design is not Friedman. Charts: **frontend only** (§5) — the node supplies `rank_means`/`rank_sums`/`within_block_ranks`.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **NORMATIVE GATE 4 — CROSS-SECTION ONLY** (the normative gate spec §3b): all three tests presuppose **independent** observations. The rule is implemented **once** in the **shared** `gate_cross_section_only` (`the reference/wrapper_gates`, shared with #250 and #257) and **called** here — it is **not** copied: **(a)** an explicit rejection of `ts/mts/msts/xts/zoo/zooreg/tsibble/…`; **(b)** a **Ljung–Box whiteness precheck** per group with `lag = min(10, n/5)`, at level **`gate_alpha`** (default 0.05) and **only** when `ordered = TRUE`. Autocorrelation **inflates the Type I error** ⇒ spuriously significant p-values; the message points explicitly to the **HAC path** (`hac_robust_standard`, cat. 07: `wrap_vcov_hac`/`wrap_vcov_cl`/`wrap_vcov_panel`). **⚠️ Live-verified:** `friedman.test` accepts a matrix of class `mts` **without complaint** — **only** the gate stops it. **Consequence:** the minimum `n` **per group** rises to **3** (stricter than `stats`, deliberately); for `n < 5` ⇒ `tested = FALSE`, `decision = "pass-untested"`.
- **`gate_alpha` (default 0.05) — the level belongs EXCLUSIVELY to the gate.** The three non-parametric tests have **no** `alpha` of their own (no `decision` column), which is why the argument is called `gate_alpha` and **not** `alpha`. **The precheck is a test of size `gate_alpha`** ⇒ by construction it blocks a small share of **valid i.i.d.** input; live-measured (version 4.6.1, `rnorm`, 5000 replications): `n = 200` → **1.6% / 5.7% / 10.1%**, `n = 60` → **2.3% / 6.7% / 10.8%** for `0.01 / 0.05 / 0.10`.
- **`ordered` (default `TRUE`) — an EXPLICIT declaration about row order.** Ljung–Box depends on the **order** (live-verified: the same 60 numbers pass unsorted and are blocked `sort`ed), whereas `wilcox.test`/`kruskal.test`/`friedman.test` are **permutation-invariant** (Friedman with respect to the order of the **blocks**). `ordered = FALSE` ⇒ an explicit skip of branch (b) (`branch = "skipped-by-declaration"`, `decision = "pass-unordered"`), with **all** the structural checks (NaN/Inf, `n ≥ 3`, zero variance) and branch **(a)** (`branch: class-rejected`) **active**. `lb_lag` together with `ordered = FALSE` ⇒ a hard `stop`.
- **Input:** numeric vectors **without dimensions**, non-empty, **without Inf/-Inf**; `mu`/`conf_level` finite (`conf_level ∈ (0,1)`); `digits_rank` a positive number or `Inf`; `exact` `NULL`/logical; `paired = TRUE` requires a `y` of **equal length**. `tn_kruskal`: a **named list** / a numeric `matrix` (columns = groups) / a `DataFrame` of numeric columns, **≥ 2 groups**, names **non-empty and unique**, no **empty** group. `tn_friedman`: **≥ 2 columns** and **≥ 2 rows**; in the LONG form `groups` **and** `blocks` together, of equal length to `y`, without NA/empty labels, with **no replication** and **no empty** `(block, group)` combination.
- **Checking tools:** **#247** `nt_normality_battery` (you come here when normality was rejected) and **#248** `dp_quality_flags` (`constant`/`infinite_values`/`few_rows`).

**Alternatives + criterion:** `tn_wilcox(y = NULL)` = the one-sample signed rank test (H0: **symmetry** around `mu`); `tn_wilcox(y, paired = FALSE)` = rank sum / Mann–Whitney (H0: a **location shift** equal to `mu`); `tn_wilcox(paired = TRUE)` = the signed rank test of the differences (NA removed **pairwise**); `conf_int = TRUE` when you want the **magnitude** and not only a p-value. `tn_kruskal` for **independent** groups; `tn_friedman` when the groups are **not** independent (all were measured in every block ⇒ the ranks are computed **within block**, removing the block effect). **#250** when normality holds; **#257** for two categorical variables; **#35 `hac_robust_standard`** when the data *are* temporally dependent — **never** bypass the gate.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- **Common:** `tests` = a tidy **single-row** record (`test`, `method`, `statistic_name`, `statistic`, (`df`), `p_value`, `alternative`, `n_*`, `n_omitted`, `exact_used`, `normal_approximation`, `ties_present`, …) **and** the same fields as atomic scalars.
- `tn_wilcox`: `test ∈ {rank_sum, signed_rank_one_sample, signed_rank_paired}` + `statistic` (W or V) + `rank_means`/`rank_sums`/`group_sizes` (**chart-data**: the groups `"x"`,`"y"` in the rank sum test; `"positive"`,`"negative"`,`"zero"` in the signed rank test) + **exact/asymptotic transparency**: `exact_requested`, `exact_used`, `normal_approximation`, `continuity_correction`, `ties_present`, `zeroes_present`. With `conf_int = TRUE`: `conf_int`, `conf_level` (**as requested**), `conf_level_achieved`, `conf_int_finite`, `estimate`/`estimate_name` (Hodges–Lehmann).
- `tn_kruskal`: `statistic` (the Kruskal–Wallis chi-squared), `df = k−1`, `p_value`, `rank_means`/`rank_sums`/`group_sizes` **per group**, `groups`, `n_groups`, `n_total`, `n_omitted`.
- `tn_friedman`: `statistic` (the Friedman chi-squared), `df = k−1`, `p_value`, `rank_means`/`rank_sums` (the **within-block** ranks per group), **`within_block_ranks`** (a blocks × groups numeric matrix), `groups`/`blocks`, `n_blocks_dropped`, `input_form ∈ {wide, long}`.
- **`cross_section_gate`** = `{groups, statistic, p.value, lag, n, n_na, alpha, tested, decision}` — the numeric diagnostics of normative gate 4.

**Critical traps** (all live-verified, version 4.6.1):
- **Why there is no `as.numeric` before the gate:** the **class** must survive intact until the gate (it is the **only** holder of the "reject ts/xts/zoo" rule) ⇒ the gate comes **last** before the test and the conversion happens afterwards. **⚠️ A known limitation:** when `na_action = "omit"/"drop_blocks"` **removes** values, the subset **loses** its class ⇒ a `ts` **with NA** + an explicit omit is checked only by the Ljung–Box branch; in the LONG form of Friedman the gate sees the **reconstructed wide** matrix (which is correct: a stacked long vector is **not** a time series).
- **An incompatible documented policy for non-finite values:** `the wilcox.test documentation` says "Non-finite (e.g., infinite or missing) values will be omitted", **but** in the two-sample branch `Inf` values are **kept** as "very large" ⇒ **the same `Inf` changes meaning** depending on the branch ⇒ a hard gate: no `Inf/-Inf` anywhere.
- **An explicit NA policy:** `wilcox.test`/`kruskal.test` remove NA **silently** (live: `kruskal.test(list(c(x,NA), y))` runs normally); `friedman.test` removes **whole blocks** ("if `y` contains `NA`s, corresponding blocks are removed") ⇒ silent data loss. Here: `"fail"` (**default**) | `"omit"` | `"drop_blocks"`, **always** with a count (`n_omitted`/`n_blocks_dropped`) and a check that ≥ 2 blocks remain.
- **A documented change in the reference ≥ 4.6.0 (a deviation from older knowledge):** there is no longer a silent fallback to the normal approximation with the warning "cannot compute exact p-value with ties" — "If there are ties, exact inference is performed using the conditional/permutation distribution given the observed ranks, using an implementation of the **Streitberg–Röhmel shift algorithm**" (contributed by Torsten Hothorn). The node **exposes it anyway** as fields (`exact_used`/`normal_approximation`/`continuity_correction` read **from the `method` string itself** — the release notes: "If exact computations are used, the result now has "exact" in the method element") ⇒ if a future version falls back again, it **shows** in the JSON instead of hiding.
- **The same sample, two Vs:** in the signed rank test with **zero** differences, `stats` builds the statistic in **two** ways — *exact*: `r <- rank(abs(x)); V <- sum(r[x > 0])` (zeros **in**); *asymptotic*: `if (ZERO) x <- x[x != 0]` **first** (zeros **out**). Measured: `x = c(.6,1,1.4,.5,1.3,1.2,1.3,1.9)`, `mu = 1` → **V = 22** (exact) vs **17** (`exact = FALSE`). The node exposes `zeroes_present` + `exact_used` **together** **and** builds `rank_means`/`rank_sums` **from the path that actually ran**.
- **A post-check of the chart-data ↔ statistic identity** (if it breaks, the frontend would draw **different** numbers from the p-value ⇒ a hard stop): rank sum → `rank_sums["x"] − n_x(n_x+1)/2 == W` (the reference **subtracts** `m(m+1)/2` — the `the wilcox.test documentation` Note: "the engine subtracts"); signed rank → `rank_sums["positive"] == V`; Kruskal → `sum(rank_sums) == N(N+1)/2`; Friedman → `sum(rank_sums) == n_blocks·k(k+1)/2`.
- **Silent-wrong degeneracies (all hard-gated):** all differences from `mu` zero → `V = 0`, `p = 1` **with no error**; a pooled sample that is entirely constant → `p = 1` / `chi-squared = NaN` and `p = NaN` **with no error** (0/0 in the tie correction); **every** block with identical values → `friedman.test` → `NaN`/`NaN`.
- **A silent drop avoided structurally:** `the kruskal.test documentation` documents "`g` … **Ignored with a warning** if `x` is a list" ⇒ the input is **always normalised** into a named list of groups, so that `g` can never be silently ignored.
- **Friedman = an unreplicated COMPLETE block design** ("exactly one observation in `y` for each combination of levels of `groups` and `blocks`") ⇒ our gates: no **replication**, no **empty** combination, ≥ 2×2 (otherwise the cryptic "dim(X) must have a positive length"), no NA label. The ranks are **within block** — they are **not** compared across blocks.
- **`conf.int` only where it is documented:** it exists **only** in `tn_wilcox`; `kruskal.test`/`friedman.test` do not document `conf.int`/`estimate` and it is **not invented**. A live trap: with a small `n` the **achieved** level differs from the requested one (0.95 → **0.9609375**) and the interval may come out as `(-Inf, Inf)` **with no warning** ⇒ the explicit `conf_level` / `conf_level_achieved` / `conf_int_finite`.
- **`digits_rank` / `correct`:** if finite, the ranks are computed on `signif(r, digits_rank)` — this stabilises tie detection when differences of order 1e-16 hide them (`the wilcox.test documentation`: "it may be advisable to … set `digits.rank = 7`"). `correct` is exposed **only as a logical**: the integer form 0–3 (Edgeworth terms) is **not** recorded in the `method` string (live: `correct = 2` gives **the same** "with continuity correction") ⇒ the output would be **unverifiable**, and the `adapters` kind `"number"` would convert `TRUE` into `1` = "1 Edgeworth term" (a silent change of meaning).
- **Determinism (§5):** **no** RNG path — no seed, no Monte Carlo/permutation approximation; the exact distributions are closed-form (`psignrank`/`pwilcox`) or, under ties, the **deterministic** shift algorithm. `identical` over 2 runs is pinned in the tests (wrapper **and** node path).
- **Masking / handles:** no `library` — only base+stats (always attached) ⇒ **zero** masking, but all calls are / qualified (other wrappers in the shared env mask generics: `proxy` → `as.matrix`/`dist`, `sn` → `sd`, `ARIMA` → `ARIMA`). Node layer: **all** data as a **`raw_handle`** (not a `matrix_handle`/`num_array`) — `resolve_handle(as="raw")` returns the object **as it is**, so that the **class** reaches the gate intact (with a `matrix_handle` the gate would be **blinded**); `groups`/`blocks` = **labels** (`series_codes`), not data. **TERMINAL** nodes: no `register`/chaining.

**Sources:** version 4.6.1 `the wilcox.test documentation` ("Non-finite (e.g., infinite or missing) values will be omitted"; "an exact p-value is computed if the samples contain less than 50 finite values"; "If there are ties, exact inference is performed … using an implementation of the Streitberg–Röhmel shift algorithm … contributed by Torsten Hothorn"; "set `digits.rank = 7`"; the Note "the engine subtracts"); `the kruskal.test documentation` ("If `x` is a list, its elements are taken as the samples"; "`g` … Ignored with a warning if `x` is a list"); `the friedman.test documentation` ("exactly one observation in `y` for each combination of levels of `groups` and `blocks`"; "if `y` contains `NA`s, corresponding blocks are removed"); **Streitberg & Röhmel (1986)**, *Statistical Software Newsletter* 12(1), 10-17 and **(1987)**, *EDV in Medizin und Biologie* 18(1), 12-19; **Hollander & Wolfe (1973)**, *Nonparametric Statistical Methods*, Wiley, pp. 27-33 / 68-75 (the pseudomedian, p. 34); **Bauer (1972)**, *Constructing Confidence Sets Using Rank Statistics*, **JASA 67(339), 687-690**; **Ljung & Box (1978)**, **Biometrika 65(2), 297-303** + the `?Box.test` Note "Missing values are not handled"; **Hyndman & Athanasopoulos**, *FPP* 3rd ed. **§5.4** — `lag = min(10, n/5)`, identical to the documented default of `checkresiduals` (live-verified); `the normative gate spec` **§3b normative gate 4** + `docs/catalog/merge-wrapper.md` (the node's row: "gate: `friedman.test` requires a matrix/blocks"); the wrapper footers IMPLEMENTATION NOTE (`c01_preparation_prechecks/battery_non_parametric.py`, `the reference/wrapper_gates`).

## §5. Univariate forecasting — `c02_univariate_forecasting/`

> **when this category applies:** when we want point + interval forecasts of **one** series (a single endogenous y) from its own history (+ optionally calendar/exogenous regressors), without modelling structural relationships between several variables (for that → `04-multivariate-timeseries` VAR/VECM) or causal interventions.

**The common selection logic inside the category (a decision rule):**

| Data issue | Preferred tool |
|---|---|
| a clean `ts`, single/no seasonality, I want an automatic ARIMA **or** ETS | `#7 forecast` (`auto.arima`/`ets`) |
| I want a tidy pipeline / many models on a tsibble / a `<distribution>` output | `#8 fable` |
| multiple/non-integer seasonalities (weekly+yearly, 24×7) | `#7 tbats` |
| calendar effects, holidays, a daily/high-frequency series with gaps | `#9 prophet` |
| ETS+ARIMA+regression unified, intermittent demand, non-normal distributions | `#10 smooth` (ADAM) |
| a very short series / a fast robust baseline | `#7 theta_model` (Theta) |

**Preconditions — the general rule:** the automatic tools (`auto.arima`, `ETS`, ADAM, prophet) do **not require** a manual stationarity check — they perform unit-root testing and differencing internally. The formal tests (`c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test` + a confirmatory KPSS) are needed **only** when we specify `d`/`pdq` **manually** or want to document the order of integration before forecasting. Watch the **opposite KPSS polarity**: a KPSS *rejection* (a small p) ⇒ **non-stationary** — the opposite sign to ADF, where a *rejection* ⇒ **stationary** (KPSS 1992; Enders 2015).

---

### #7 forecast (ARIMA/ETS/Theta/TBATS) — `diebold_mariano_tscv` (`c02_univariate_forecasting/forecast.py`)
**Functions:** `auto.arima` → `run_auto_arima`, `ets` → `run_ets`, `theta_model` → `run_theta`, `tbats` → `run_tbats`; common: `diebold_mariano_tscv` (the generic), `accuracy` (a post-check).

**When:**
- `run_auto_arima`: standard univariate forecasting with an automatic (p,d,q)(P,D,Q) selection by AICc/AIC/BIC via the stepwise Hyndman–Khandakar procedure. A good default for SARIMA on a monthly/quarterly macro series. It accepts `xreg` (ARIMAX).
- `run_ets`: exponential smoothing in state-space form (the model "ZZZ" = automatic error/trend/season). Strong when trend+seasonality dominate rather than an autoregressive structure.
- `run_theta`: the Theta model (Assimakopoulos–Nikolopoulos 2000); robust, minimal parameters, an excellent baseline on short series (the M3 winner).
- `run_tbats`: **multiple/non-integer seasonalities** (Box-Cox + ARMA errors + Trend + Seasonal, De Livera–Hyndman–Snyder 2011) — e.g. weekly+yearly simultaneously.

**When NOT:** a multivariate structure/relationships (→ `04` VAR/VECM); calendar holiday effects (→ `#9 prophet`); intermittent/non-gaussian data (→ `#10 smooth`). `tbats` for a single simple seasonality is overkill — prefer `auto.arima`/`ets`.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- No formal precondition for forecasting: all methods perform differencing/order selection internally. (A manual `d` → then `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test` + a confirmatory KPSS.)
- **Hard gate `run_auto_arima`**: `xreg` must **not** be a data frame, and `NROW(xreg) == length(y)` (the auto.arima documentation).
- **Hard gate `run_tbats`**: `NCOL(y) == 1` — univariate only.
- `y` must be a `ts` with the correct `frequency` for seasonality to be detected (otherwise a non-seasonal fit).

**Alternatives + criterion:** the same ARIMA/ETS in tidy form → `#8 fable` (when you want a `<distribution>` output or several models together). ADAM (`#10`) when you need ETS+ARIMA+regression unified or a non-gaussian error. prophet (`#9`) when holidays/the calendar dominate.

**Reading the output** (the same named list for all 4; via L2 `to_mcp`):
- `mean` — the point forecasts, a `ts` → `{values, start, frequency}`. The central result.
- `lower`/`upper` — the prediction-interval bounds per `level` (a matrix: the columns = the levels 80/95). Serialised as nested rows + dimnames.
- `level` — the confidence levels (80, 95).
- `fitted` / `residuals` — the in-sample one-step values; used for diagnostics (autocorrelation, normality).
- `accuracy` — a matrix of training-set measures (ME, RMSE, MAE, **MAPE**, **MASE**, ACF1). MASE<1 ⇒ better than naive.
- `model` — the whole fitted object (`to_mcp` keeps a compact stub — the heavy internals do not leak).
- **Interpretation traps:** (1) `accuracy(fc)` here is **in-sample** (training set), **not** out-of-sample — it is not a reliable measure of generalisation; for out-of-sample use `15-model-evaluation` (`tsCV`/Diebold-Mariano) or a holdout. (2) MAPE is unstable/infinite when `y≈0` (common for growth rates around zero) — prefer MASE. (3) the ETS/ARIMA prediction intervals assume gaussian innovations; they understate uncertainty on heavy-tailed series. (4) `tbats` is slow (a parallel AIC search) and its intervals do not decompose easily into components.

**Sources:** Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, *Forecasting: Principles and Practice* (FPP3, the ARIMA/ETS chapters); Hyndman & Khandakar 2008 (JSS, the `diebold_mariano_tscv` package, auto.arima); Assimakopoulos & Nikolopoulos 2000 (Theta); Hyndman & Billah 2003 (Theta = SES+drift); De Livera, Hyndman & Snyder 2011 (JASA, TBATS); Hyndman, Koehler, Ord & Snyder 2008 (the ETS state space); the `diebold_mariano_tscv` reference manual (`diebold_mariano_tscv` exports both `theta_model` and `thetaf`; the wrapper `run_theta` calls `theta_model`, the newer addition with a `forecast.theta_model` method; `thetaf` remains as a legacy convenience — live-verified).

---

### #8 fable (tidy ARIMA/ETS) — `fable` (`c02_univariate_forecasting/fable.py`)
**Functions:** `ARIMA` + `model` → `run_fable_arima`, `ETS` + `model` → `run_fable_ets`; diagnostics: `diebold_mariano_tscv`, `glance`, `tidy`, `fitted`, `residuals`, `components` (ETS only).

**When:** the same families (ARIMA/ETS) as `#7` but in the **tidyverts** framework: a `tidy_temporal_frames` input + a `formula`. Prefer it when (a) you want **structured `<distribution>` forecasts** (not only lower/upper; the whole distribution → a quantile grid), (b) a manual order specification with `pdq`/`PDQ`, (c) a tidy downstream (joins, several keys/series in one mable). `components` gives the estimated ETS states (level/slope/season) — a clean decomposition.

**When NOT:** you have a plain `ts` and do not want the tsibble overhead → `#7 forecast`. Theta/TBATS/multiple seasonality → not covered here (→ `#7`). Non-gaussian/intermittent → `#10 smooth`.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- The input = a **ready `tidy_temporal_frames`** (a regular index, one measured variable) + a `formula` (e.g. `value ~ pdq(0,1,1) + PDQ(0,1,1)`). The wrapper does not call `as_tsibble` — the caller supplies it ready.
- **Hard gate `run_fable_ets`**: `anyNA(data)` → stop ("ETS does not support missing values") — fill the gaps first with the imputation tool (`#80`, `c00_data_utilities/replacement_missing_values.imputets_kalman`). (`run_fable_arima` has no such gate.)
- `run_fable_arima`: no formal precondition — if a seasonal specification is given with <2 seasons, `ARIMA` reverts with a warning (not an error). The automatic selection requires `time_series_decomposition`/`unit_root_suite` (the unit-root tests for d/D).

**Alternatives + criterion:** `#7 forecast` for a non-tidy quick use or for Theta/TBATS. `#10 smooth` ADAM when you want ETS+ARIMA+xreg together or a different error distribution.

**Reading the output:**
- `diebold_mariano_tscv` — a **fable** (a tsibble with a `<distribution>` column): `to_mcp` serialises each cell into a **quantile grid** (`probs` c(.05,.1,.25,.5,.75,.9,.95) + `mean`/`sd`). The median (.5) ≈ the point forecast.
- `glance` — a 1-row summary: `sigma2`, `log_lik`, `AIC`, `AICc`, `BIC`, and (for ARIMA) `ar_roots`/`ma_roots` (**complex** → `{re, im}` via `to_mcp.complex`). A lower AICc ⇒ better among models on the same y.
- `tidy` — the coefficients tibble (`term`, `estimate`, `std.error`, `statistic`, `p.value`) → a list of records.
- `components` (ETS only) — a dable with the estimated states (level, slope, season) over time.
- `fitted`/`residuals` — in-sample; `type="innovation"` (default) vs `"regression"` for ARIMAX.
- **Interpretation traps:** (1) the `<distribution>` is **not** a plain number — do not read it as a point; take the median or the `mean` field. (2) `ar_roots`/`ma_roots` come out complex; stationarity/invertibility ⇒ a **modulus > 1** (outside the unit circle) — check `sqrt(re^2+im^2)`. (3) the fable `glance` does NOT compute accuracy — for out-of-sample you need `new_data` + `accuracy` (→ `15-model-evaluation`). (4) an NA is a hard error in ETS but not in ARIMA — do not confuse the two.

**Sources:** Hyndman & Athanasopoulos FPP3 (the tidy edition, the `fable` chapters); the `fable` reference + vignette (`ARIMA`, `ETS`); the fabletools docs (`model`, `glance`, `<distribution>`).

---

### #9 prophet — `prophet` (`c02_univariate_forecasting/prophet.py`)
**Functions:** `run_prophet` = `prophet` → `add_country_holidays`/`add_seasonality`/`add_regressor` → `fit.prophet` → `make_future_dataframe` → `predict` (+ `regressor_coefficients`); `run_prophet_cv` = `cross_validation` → `performance_metrics`.

**When:** a decomposable additive model of trend + seasonality (Fourier) + holidays + regressors, with automatic changepoint detection. Ideal when **calendar effects** dominate (holidays, day of week), the series has **gaps/an irregular index**, or you want an interpretable trend/seasonal/holiday decomposition. Business-friendly, robust to outliers/missing values.

**When NOT:** "clean" monthly/quarterly macro series without calendar structure — there ARIMA/ETS (`#7`/`#8`) are more accurate and more parsimonious (prophet tends to overfit the trend on short macro series). Autoregressive dynamics → ARIMA. A short series (prophet needs enough points for the Fourier terms/changepoints).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- Input mapping: it **requires** the columns `ds` (a Date) + `y`. `.pr_to_dsy` maps a long-format `period`/`value` → `ds`/`y` (a defensive `as.Date`: unparseable → NA → a clean gate "invalid dates").
- **Hard gate:** `seasonality.mode ∈ {additive, multiplicative}`.
- **Hard gate:** `growth="logistic"` → the df (**and** the future df) must have a `cap` column.
- **Hard gate:** with `regressors`, the columns must exist in the df **AND** an explicit `future` df with their future values is required (`make_future_dataframe` supplies only `ds`).
- **A project auto-gate (macro spacing):** a median spacing ≥28 days ⇒ auto-disable the `weekly`/`daily` seasonality (when "auto") + auto-infer `freq` (day/week/month/quarter/year). This prevents spurious high-frequency seasonality on a monthly series.
- No stationarity/formal precheck is needed (prophet models the trend explicitly).

**Alternatives + criterion:** ARIMA/ETS (`#7`/`#8`) for clean low-frequency macro series; `#10 smooth` ADAM with explanatory regressors when you want state-space rigour; `18-*` (structural/intervention) when the target is causal impact rather than a forecast.

**Reading the output:**
- `diebold_mariano_tscv` — a DataFrame → a list of records; the key columns: `ds`, `yhat` (the point forecast), `yhat_lower`/`yhat_upper` (the interval at `interval.width`, default 0.8 = 80%!), `non_parametric_trend`, and the `*_terms` (the seasonal/holiday/regressor components + additive/multiplicative).
- `future` — the future df that was used (ds + the regressors).
- `regressor_coefficients` (only with regressors) — the center/coef per regressor (the same fit as the yhat).
- `run_prophet_cv.cv` — per cutoff: `yhat`, `y` (the actual), `cutoff`, `ds`, `horizon`. `.metrics` — `horizon` + `mse`/`rmse`/`mae`/`mape`/`mdape`/`smape`/`coverage`.
- **Interpretation traps:** (1) the default `interval.width=0.8` ⇒ **80%** intervals, NOT 95% — do not read them as 95%. (2) Without `mcmc.samples>0` the intervals reflect **only** trend uncertainty (a MAP estimate), not the full Bayesian one — they understate. (3) `run_prophet_cv` is **expensive** (many re-fits). (4) `horizon`/`units` in `cross_validation` are in time units (e.g. days) — 180 days ≠ 180 periods on a monthly series. (5) `coverage` in the metrics should be ≈ `interval.width` for well-calibrated intervals.

**Sources:** Taylor & Letham 2018, *Forecasting at scale* (The American Statistician / the PeerJ preprint); the `prophet` reference manual + the Facebook Prophet docs (`add_regressor`, `cross_validation`, `make_future_dataframe`).

---

### #10 smooth (ADAM / ES variants) — `smooth` (`c02_univariate_forecasting/smooth.py`)
**Functions:** `adam` → `run_adam`, `auto.adam` → `run_auto_adam`, `ces` → `run_ces`, `auto.ces` → `run_auto_ces`; common: `diebold_mariano_tscv` (→ `forecast.adam`/`forecast.smooth`), `accuracy` (→ `accuracy.smooth`).

**When:**
- `run_adam`/`run_auto_adam`: **ADAM** — it unifies ETS + ARIMA + regression in one state-space framework (Svetunkov 2023). Use it when you want (a) ETS+ARIMA together, (b) a **non-gaussian** error (dnorm/dlaplace/ds/dgnorm/dlnorm/dinvgauss/dgamma), (c) **intermittent demand** (occurrence models), (d) explanatory variables with select/adapt. `auto.adam` tries a **vector** of distributions + selects the ARIMA orders.
- `run_ces`/`run_auto_ces`: **Complex Exponential Smoothing** — it does not separate trend/season explicitly (complex-valued exponential smoothing); useful when the trend/season is unclear. `auto.ces` tries a **vector** of seasonality types (none/simple/partial/full).

**When NOT:** a simple gaussian monthly series where `auto.arima`/`ets` (`#7`) suffices — ADAM is heavier. Holidays/calendar → `#9`. A tidy `<distribution>` workflow → `#8`.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **Data-agnostic:** it accepts a vector/`ts`/`msts`/matrix/DataFrame **as it is** (the 1st column = the response, the rest = regressors) — **no** long-format→ds/y conversion. A `ts` with the correct `frequency`/`lags` for seasonality.
- **Hard gate (in all 4):** `holdout=TRUE` → `h>0` (otherwise a holdout of size 0).
- No formal "must-not-be-a-data-frame" requirement (the documentation does not state one).
- No stationarity precheck is needed (ADAM performs the ARIMA selection internally).

**Alternatives + criterion:** `#7 ets`/`auto.arima` for the "classical" gaussian route; `#8 fable` for tidy; `#9 prophet` for the calendar. Between ADAM and CES: ADAM when you want explicit ETS/ARIMA/xreg control; CES when the trend/season is hard to distinguish.

**Reading the output** (a unified named list via `.sm_forecast_accuracy`):
- `mean` — the point forecasts (the conditional mean), a `ts`.
- `lower`/`upper` — the bounds of `interval="prediction"` at `level=0.95` (the project default; `side="both"`).
- `level` / `interval` — the level and a binary flag for whether an interval was produced.
- `fitted`/`residuals` — in-sample.
- `accuracy` — the error measures via `accuracy.smooth`: it **auto-extracts holdout** measures (MASE/RMSSE/…) when the model was estimated with `holdout=TRUE`; otherwise in-sample ones.
- `model` — the whole adam/ces object (states, persistence, phi, the complex smoothing parameters) — a compact stub in `to_mcp`.
- **Interpretation traps:** (1) the `level=0.99` in the **fit** arguments is the **outlier-detection** level — **NOT** the forecast confidence; the forecast interval is controlled by `interval.level` (0.95). Do not confuse them. (2) `h`/`holdout` are **fit-time** arguments; the forecast horizon has its own `forecast.h` (resolution: explicit → the fit `h` if >0 → 10). (3) `accuracy` is **holdout** (out-of-sample) only if `holdout=TRUE` — otherwise in-sample, as in `#7`. (4) the `auto.adam` `distribution` and the `auto.ces` `seasonality` are **vectors to try** (not a single choice) — they are passed whole, no `match.arg` is applied.

**Sources:** Svetunkov 2023, *Forecasting and Analytics with the Augmented Dynamic Adaptive Model (ADAM)* (the online monograph, openforecast.org); Svetunkov & Kourentzes (CES / complex exponential smoothing); the `smooth` reference manual + vignettes (`adam`, `ces`, `forecast.adam`, `accuracy.smooth`).


---

## §6. Multivariate and nowcasting — `c03_multivariate_nowcasting/`

This category applies when you have **several (>=2) interacting time series** and want joint dynamics (VAR/BVAR), shock transmission, or forecasting/nowcasting — especially when the series are many (dfms), of mixed frequency (mfbvar/midasr) or have time-varying parameters/volatility (bvarsv). It is the reduced-form / predictive layer: the **structural identification** (SVAR/IRF/FEVD/BQ, #19) lives in the separate button `c04_structural_shocks/svar_irf_fevd.py` and is **not mixed** in here.

A quick decision map:

| Situation | Method |
|---|---|
| Few series (2–6), a classical frequentist VAR + diagnostics + Granger | #11 `reduced_form_var` |
| Few/moderate series, you want shrinkage/priors (short samples) | #12 `BVAR` (Minnesota) or #13 `bayesian_var_2` |
| Time-varying coefficients + stochastic volatility | #14 `tvp_var_stochastic` (TVP-VAR-SV) |
| Many series (a large n), common factors, a nowcast with ragged edges | #15 `dynamic_factor_nowcasting` (DFM) |
| Mixed frequency, Bayesian, a nowcast of latent monthly GDP | #17 `mixed_frequency_bayesian` |
| One low-frequency dependent variable explained by high-frequency regressor(s) | #18 `midas_regression` (MIDAS) |

**A universal serialization trap (L2 `to_mcp`):** all the fitted objects of this category (`varest`, `vec2var`, `bayesian_var`, `dfm`, `midas_r`, `mixed_frequency_bayesian`, the raw list of `bvar.sv.tvp`) are foreign fitted S3 objects → `to_mcp` returns them as a **compact stub** (`@mcp_class`, `@mcp_serialized=FALSE`), not a full serialization. So the `model` field of every wrapper is **only a handle for the next call** (predict/irf/fevd/summary) — the numeric results (fcst/quants/factors/coef/htest) are what reach the LLM. Source: `the reference/to_mcp` (the dispatch: "foreign fitted S3 -> compact stub").

---

### #11 Reduced-form VAR — `reduced_form_var` (`c03_multivariate_nowcasting/reduced_form_var.py`)
**Functions:** `vr_varselect` (VARselect), `vr_var` (VAR + roots), `vr_predict` (predict), `vr_causality` (causality), `vr_serial_test` (serial.test), `vr_arch_test` (arch.test), `vr_normality_test` (normality.test), `vr_vec2var` (vec2var).

**When:** you have 2–6 stationary series and want a classical frequentist VAR(p): order selection by an information criterion, estimation, forecasts with fan-chart data, a Granger causality test, and full residual diagnostics (autocorrelation/ARCH/normality). `vr_vec2var` is the bridge: it converts an estimated VECM (`ca.jo`) into a level VAR for forecasting when the series are cointegrated.

**When NOT:** many series (a large n → over-parameterization; go to `dynamic_factor_nowcasting` or `BVAR`); short samples where you need shrinkage (→ `BVAR`/`bayesian_var_2`); mixed frequency (→ `mixed_frequency_bayesian`/`midas_regression`); a structural analysis of shocks (IRF/FEVD with identification → `c04_structural_shocks/svar_irf_fevd.py`, a separate button).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- The **stationarity** of every series → `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test` (+ a **confirmatory KPSS**, `run_kpss_test`). The `causality` help warns explicitly: "The Granger-causality test is problematic if some of the variables are nonstationary" (Pfaff, the vars reference). If the series are I(1) and cointegrated → go through a VECM (`c05_cointegration/johansen_restricted_vecm.ca.jo`) and `vr_vec2var`.
- **No NA**, **K>=2 columns** (project gates, hard `stop`): a VAR does not accept missing values, and a univariate VAR is meaningless.
- **A stability post-check** (NOT a precondition): `vr_var` returns `stable = all(moduli(roots) < 1)`. An unstable VAR is a valid estimate but makes the IRF/FEVD **unreliable** — check `stable=TRUE` before trusting any structural analysis in #19.

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| `BVAR`/`bayesian_var_2` (#12/#13) | a moderate n or a short sample → Minnesota shrinkage wins on MSFE |
| `dynamic_factor_nowcasting` (#15) | a large n (dozens of series) → a factor structure instead of a full VAR |
| `tvp_var_stochastic` (#14) | suspected structural instability/changing volatility → a TVP-VAR-SV |
| `c04_structural_shocks/svar_irf_fevd.py` (#19) | you want identified shocks (Cholesky/BQ/sign) — IRF/FEVD |

**Reading the output:**
- `vr_varselect`: `selection` = the suggested p per criterion (AIC/HQ/SC/FPE); `criteria` = a matrix (→ `to_mcp` nested rows + dimnames). Trap: SC/BIC picks a more parsimonious p than AIC — for residual diagnostics prefer the larger one.
- `vr_var`: `roots` (the moduli), `stable` (a logical — **the critical post-check**), `logLik`, `Phi`/`Psi` (the MA representation arrays), `coefficients`. `model` (a varest) → a stub.
- `vr_predict`: `fcst` = a list per variable with the columns `fcst/lower/upper/CI` = the data of the fan chart (the frontend draws it, not the wrapper).
- `vr_causality`: `Granger` and `Instant`, two **htest** objects → `to_mcp` gives `{statistic, p.value, parameter, method}`. **Interpretation trap:** Granger = **predictive** causality (x helps to predict y), **NOT** a structural/causal relationship; H0 = "does not Granger-cause", so p<0.05 → there is predictive causality. `Instant` (a Wald chi-square test) is a contemporaneous error correlation, not a direction.
- The diagnostics (`serial`/`arch`/`jb`): htest objects, H0 = "clean residuals" (no autocorrelation / no ARCH / normal). p<0.05 → a **rejection** → the model is mis-specified (raise p or revise it).

**Sources:** the vars 1.6-1 reference (Pfaff); the `causality` help (Granger 1969; Lütkepohl 2006; Hamilton 1994); Enders, *Applied Econometric Time Series* (VAR/Granger).

---

### #12 Bayesian VAR (Minnesota) — `BVAR` (`c03_multivariate_nowcasting/bayesian_var.py`)
**Functions:** `bvar_estimate` (bvar + bv_priors/bv_minnesota/bv_lambda), `bvar_predict` (predict.bvar), `bvar_irf` (bv_irf + irf.bvar), `bvar_fevd` (irf with fevd=TRUE), `bvar_companion` (companion), `bvar_summary` (summary.bvar).

**When:** a multivariate VAR with few observations or a moderate n, where a frequentist VAR overfits; you want **Minnesota prior shrinkage** (hierarchical, GLP 2015) for more stable forecasts and fan charts with posterior quantiles. It supports IRF with Cholesky **or sign restrictions** inside the same button (without a separate SVAR step).

**When NOT:** you need mixed frequency (→ `mixed_frequency_bayesian`); time-varying parameters/SV (→ `tvp_var_stochastic`); a very large n where a factor model is more natural (→ `dynamic_factor_nowcasting`); you want frequentist inference/p-values (→ `reduced_form_var`).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **Stationarity — methodological, NOT a hard gate:** the Minnesota prior centres the coefficient on the first own lag at **1 (a random walk)** — the default, fixed in the button (`bv_minnesota(b = 1)`, confirmed live; the wrapper does not expose `b`). So BVAR naturally applies to data in **LEVELS (log levels), typically I(1) — do NOT difference them beforehand** (differencing I(1) series with b=1 ⇒ you impose a RW on the already-stationary differences = a de facto I(2) prior on the levels, over-shrinkage). Testing the order of integration serves for information/cointegration awareness (if I(1) and cointegrated → consider a VECM, `c05_cointegration/johansen_restricted_vecm.ca.jo`), not to trigger differencing → `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test` (+ a confirmatory KPSS).
- **Hard gates (project):** `data` a numeric matrix/df/ts, `ncol>=2`, without NA, `nrow>lags+1`; `lambda>0` (the Minnesota tightness mode); `n_burn<n_draw`.
- **Determinism:** `bayesian_var` has no seed argument → the wrapper calls `set.seed(seed)`. Always supply a `seed` for reproducibility.

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| `bayesian_var_2` (#13) | you want full control of the Gibbs sampler / alternative IRF types (gir/sir) |
| `reduced_form_var` (#11) | a short sample is not a problem, you want frequentist Granger/diagnostics |
| `tvp_var_stochastic` (#14) | suspected changing volatility/parameters |

**Reading the output:**
- `bvar_estimate`: `acceptance_rate` (an **MH tuning diagnostic** — the target is ~0.20–0.40; outside that range → poor mixing, resample); `variables`, `n_vars`, `n_save`. `model` (a bvar) → a stub.
- `bvar_predict`: `quants` = an array **[quantiles x horizon x variables]** → `to_mcp` `{values, dim, dimnames}`; a chart-ready fan.
- `bvar_irf`: `quants` = an array **[quantiles x horizon x impulse x response]**. **Trap (a post-gate):** if all the quants are NA, the identification (sign/zero) failed within sign_lim → the wrapper calls `stop`; relax the restrictions. `sign_restr` must be MxM ∈ {1,-1,0,NA}.
- `bvar_companion`: `eigen_mod`, `stable` (modulus<1) — the same stability logic as `vr_var`.
- `bvar_summary`: `coef` = the posterior **median** coefficients (not the MLE), `vcov`, `logLik`.
- **Collision trap (implementation):** **both** `BVAR` **and** `bayesian_var_2` define `predict/irf/summary.bvar` for the class `bayesian_var`; the wrapper calls `getS3method(.., asNamespace("BVAR"))` explicitly — a non-namespaced call would dispatch to the wrong one.

**Sources:** BVAR 1.0.5 (Kuschnig & Vashold 2021, *JSS*); Giannone-Lenza-Primiceri (2015) hierarchical Minnesota priors; the BVAR vignette (`introduction`).

---

### #13 Bayesian VAR (Gibbs) — `bayesian_var_2` (`c03_multivariate_nowcasting/bayesian_vartools.py`)
**Functions:** `bt_var` (gen_var → add_priors → draw_posterior), `bt_predict` (predict.bvar), `bt_irf` (irf.bvar), `bt_fevd` (fevd.bvar), `bt_summary` (summary.bvar).

**When:** a Bayesian VAR where you want an **explicit, transparent Gibbs pipeline** (gen_var → priors → draw_posterior in one safe call) and flexible IRF/FEVD types — feir/oir/gir/sir/sgir (generalized and structural). A good choice when you want a generalized IRF (independent of the ordering).

**When NOT:** you want a ready hierarchical Minnesota with auto-tuning (→ `BVAR`); mixed frequency (→ `mixed_frequency_bayesian`); TVP/SV (→ `tvp_var_stochastic`).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **Stationarity** → `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test` (+ a confirmatory KPSS).
- **Hard gates:** `data` of class **`ts`/`mts`** (not a matrix!), `ncol>=2`, without NA; `burnin<iterations`; `deterministic ∈ {const,none,trend,both}`.
- **Determinism:** **both** `draw_posterior` **and** `predict.bvar` are MCMC → a seed in both `bt_var` and `bt_predict`.

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| `BVAR` (#12) | you want a hierarchical Minnesota with minimal tuning + sign restrictions |
| `reduced_form_var` (#11) | a frequentist workflow, diagnostics, Granger |

**Reading the output:**
- `bt_predict`: `fcst` = a list of ts per variable, each ts **[n.ahead x 3] = lower/median/upper** → `to_mcp` ts→`{values,start,frequency}` per component.
- `bt_irf`: `irf` = a `bvarirf` ts [0.n.ahead x 3] (median + CI). **Trap (`type`):** `feir` = forecast-error (non-orthogonalised); `oir` = orthogonalized (Cholesky — **it depends on the ordering**); `gir` = generalized (Pesaran-Shin, order-independent); `sir/sgir` = structural. Choose `gir` when you have no theoretical ordering.
- `bt_fevd`: `fevd` = a ts [0.n.ahead x n_vars]; **the rows sum to ~1** (variance shares). The default is `type="oir"`.
- `bt_summary`: `coefficients`/`sigma` = the posterior statistics per parameter.
- **Collision trap:** the same as #12 — an explicit `getS3method(.., asNamespace("bvartools"))`; in addition, `bayesian_var_2` defines a `summary.dfm` that clashes with `dynamic_factor_nowcasting`.

**Sources:** bvartools 0.2.4; the vignette `bayesian_var` (Mohr); Pesaran & Shin (1998) generalized IRF; Lütkepohl 2006 (FEVD/orthogonalization).

---

### #14 TVP-VAR-SV — `tvp_var_stochastic` (`c03_multivariate_nowcasting/bayesian_varsv.py`)
**Functions:** `sv_estimate` (bvar.sv.tvp), `sv_predict_density` (predictive.density), `sv_predict_draws` (predictive.draws), `sv_irf` (impulse.responses), `sv_parameter_draws` (parameter.draws).

**When:** you suspect that the relationships **change over time** (time-varying parameters) **and/or** that the volatility of the shocks changes (stochastic volatility) — e.g. changes of monetary-policy regime, the Great Moderation, crises. It gives posterior predictive **distributions** (a density/CDF on a grid) and an IRF at a specific point in time `t`.

**When NOT:** a small sample (TVP-VAR-SV is heavily parameterized, it needs a decent T); you want constant coefficients (→ `BVAR`/`reduced_form_var`); many series (in practice 2–4 variables; it is computationally heavy).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **Stationarity** → `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test` (+ a confirmatory KPSS).
- **Hard gates:** `Y` numeric, `ncol>=2`, finite (no NA/Inf); the training split `tau >= ncol*p+1` **AND** `tau < nrow(Y)` (Primiceri's LS-prior training sample); `scenario ∈ {1,2,3}`.
- **Determinism + save.parameters:** stochastic → `set.seed(seed)`; the wrapper **always** sets `save.parameters=TRUE` (required by `sv_irf`/`sv_parameter_draws`).

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| `BVAR`/`bayesian_var_2` (#12/#13) | constant coefficients suffice → far cheaper |
| `10-trend-cycle-statespace` (KFAS/dlm/bssm) | you want a general custom state space with TVP |
| Markov switching (`MSwM`, outside this category) | discrete regimes instead of smooth evolution — **note: `MSwM` handles gaussian/lm only** |

**Reading the output:**
- `sv_predict_density`: `{grid, value}` — **`predictive.density` returns a closure f(z); the wrapper evaluates it on a numeric grid** (it NEVER returns a function — that would be unserializable). `cdf=TRUE` → the cumulative version.
- `sv_predict_draws`: `draws` (the MCMC sample), `quantiles` (a named vector → a fan chart), `mean`.
- `sv_irf`: `irf` [draws x nhor], `bands` [probs x nhor]. **`scenario`:** 1=no orthogonalization, **2=Cholesky at time t (the default)**, 3=the DNP variant. `t=NULL` → the default point in time; change it for an IRF in a specific period.
- `sv_parameter_draws`: `draws` [draws x time] = the **path** of one coefficient over time (an inspection of the drift). `type ∈ {intercept, lag1.lagP, vcv}`.

**Sources:** bvarsv 1.1 (Krueger); **Primiceri (2005)** *Time Varying Structural VARs and Monetary Policy, ReStud*; **Del Negro & Primiceri (2015)** the corrigendum (the sampling order).

---

### #15 Dynamic Factor Model / nowcasting — `dynamic_factor_nowcasting` (`c03_multivariate_nowcasting/dynamic_factor_nowcasting.py`)
> #16 (`nowcasting`) is routed here: the `nowcasting` package is archived on (a dead `matlab` dependency); the DFM-nowcasting functionality is fully covered by `dynamic_factor_nowcasting`.

**Functions:** `df_icr` (ICr — Bai-Ng), `df_dfm` (DFM, EM/2S, mixed frequency), `df_predict` (predict.dfm), `df_summary` (summary.dfm).

**When:** you have **many series** (dozens; a "fat" panel) sharing a few common factors; you want to nowcast/forecast by drawing on the whole panel, robust to **missing data / ragged edges** (the BM algorithm) and to **mixed frequency** (monthly + quarterly via `quarterly.vars`). The standard route for nowcasting GDP from high-dimensional indicators.

**When NOT:** few series (2–6 → a full VAR is more natural, `reduced_form_var`/`BVAR`); you want an explicit Bayesian mixed-frequency VAR with latent monthly states (→ `mixed_frequency_bayesian`); one low-frequency y from one high-frequency regressor (→ `midas_regression`).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- The **stationarity** of the panel's series (the DFM assumes stationary data — "numeric data matrix of stationary time series", the DFM help) → `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test` (+ a confirmatory KPSS); difference/log-difference first.
- **NO pre-scaling:** the standardization (center/scale) is done **internally** by the DFM — do not standardize the input.
- **Hard gates:** `ncol>=2`, `nrow>=10`; `df_icr` **requires an X without NA** (PCA); the **automatic selection of r** (r=NULL) also requires no NA; with an **explicit r**, NA are allowed (the BM EM handles them).

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| `mixed_frequency_bayesian` (#17) | you want a full Bayesian posterior + a steady-state prior in a mixed-frequency VAR |
| `BVAR` (#12) | a moderate n, you want full VAR dynamics rather than a factor summary |
| `midas_regression` (#18) | one dependent variable, few high-frequency regressors (not common factors) |

**Reading the output:**
- `df_icr`: `r_star` = a **vector of length 3** (the IC1/IC2/IC3 of Bai-Ng 2002); `IC` (an r.max x 3 table); `eigenvalues`. **Trap:** the 3 criteria often disagree in finite samples; the penalty of **IC2 is the largest** → the most parsimonious r (the `df_dfm` automatic mode uses IC2).
- `df_dfm`: `factors` (the T x r estimated factors — the preference order is QML→2S→PCA); `loadings` (C, n x r); `transition` (A); `Q`/`the reference`; `loglik`; **`converged`** (an EM post-check — non-convergence does not block but is flagged). **Sign trap:** the factors/loadings are identified only up to a rotation/sign (`pos.corr=TRUE` helps, but the sign of a factor has no absolute interpretation).
- `df_predict`: `X_fcst` (the h x n variable forecasts = the nowcast/forecast), `F_fcst` (the h x r factor forecasts). `standardized=FALSE` → the original units. **There is no newdata** — predict extends the fitted model.
- `df_summary`: `R2` per series (how much the common component explains), `R2_stats`.
- **Collision trap:** an explicit `getS3method("summary","dfm",asNamespace("dfms"))` — `bayesian_var_2` defines a same-named `summary.dfm`.

**Sources:** dfms 1.0.1 (rOpenSci); **Bai & Ng (2002)** *Econometrica* (ICr); Doz-Giannone-Reichlin (2011 two-step, 2012 QML); **Banbura & Modugno (2014)** (EM with ragged/missing data — mixed frequency); Stock & Watson (2016) *Handbook of Macro*.

---

### #17 Mixed-Frequency BVAR — `mixed_frequency_bayesian` (`c03_multivariate_nowcasting/mixed_frequency_bayesian.py`)
**Functions:** `mf_estimate` (set_prior [+interval_to_moments] → estimate_mfbvar), `mf_predict` (predict.mfbvar), `mf_mdd` (mdd — the marginal data density).

**When:** a Bayesian VAR where the series have **different frequencies** (monthly indicators + quarterly GDP) and you want to **nowcast** using latent monthly states + a **steady-state prior** (prior information about long-run means, Schorfheide-Song). The wrapper folds the multi-step sequence (prior → moments → estimate) into **one call** so that the LLM cannot leave the prior half-specified.

**When NOT:** all the series are of the same frequency (→ `BVAR`/`bayesian_var_2`); a very large n where a factor model scales better (→ `dynamic_factor_nowcasting`); one dependent variable on high-frequency regressors without a latent VAR (→ `midas_regression`).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **Input structure (a hard gate):** `Y` = a **list of >=2 `ts` objects**, with the **higher-frequency (monthly) ones FIRST** and the quarterly ones last (non-increasing frequencies); NA in the quarterly series are allowed **only at the end** (the ragged edge for nowcasting).
- **Aggregation gate:** with `aggregation="average"`, `n_lags>=3` is required (intra-quarterly averaging).
- **Prior gates:** `ss`/`ssng` → requires `prior_psi_mean & prior_psi_Omega` (or `prior_psi_int` → automatically via `interval_to_moments`); `fsv` → requires `n_fac`.
- **Stationarity:** the same logic as the other VARs (→ `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.py`); the steady-state prior helps with trending series but the VAR dynamics want stationary ones.
- **Determinism:** MCMC → `set.seed(seed)`.
- **Masking trap (implementation):** an explicit `set_prior` — `bayesian_regression` (category 14) exports a `set_prior` that masks `set_prior` in the full suite environment.

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| `dynamic_factor_nowcasting` (#15) | many indicators, you want a factor nowcast (frequentist EM, faster) |
| `midas_regression` (#18) | you target **one** low-frequency variable with a few high-frequency regressors |
| `BVAR` (#12) | the same frequency, you do not need latent states |

**Reading the output:**
- `mf_predict`: `diebold_mariano_tscv` = a **DataFrame** (`variable, time, fcst_date, lower, median, upper`) → `to_mcp` a list of records; the lower/upper are set by `pred_bands` (e.g. 0.8 → 10%/90%). It requires `n_fcst>0` at estimation.
- `mf_mdd`: `log_mdd` = the **log marginal data density** for model comparison (higher = better). **Trap:** it is available **ONLY for `variance="iw"`** (a gate on the class `_iw`); ss/ssng → `method ∈ {1,2}`, minn → `p_trunc ∈ (0,1)`.
- `mf_estimate`: `model` (an mfbvar) → a stub; `prior`/`variance`/`aggregation` echo the specification.

**Sources:** mfbvar 0.5.6 (the archive; the deps stochvol/GIGrvg/RcppProgress); **Schorfheide & Song (2015)** *Real-Time Forecasting with a Mixed-Frequency VAR, JBES*; Ankargren, Unosson & Yang (the steady-state / factor SV extensions); the mfbvar vignette.

---

### #18 MIDAS regression — `midas_regression` (`c03_multivariate_nowcasting/midas_regression.py`)
**Functions:** `md_midas` (midas_r + mls + nealmon/nbeta/almonp), `md_haht` (hAh_test / hAhr_test), `md_forecast` (forecast.midas_r), `md_select` (a rule-based AIC/BIC weight selection).

**When:** you want to forecast **one** low-frequency variable (e.g. quarterly GDP) from **one or a few high-frequency regressors** (e.g. monthly/daily data), without losing information through plain aggregation. Restricted MIDAS condenses the high-frequency lags through a parametric weight scheme (exponential Almon / Beta / polynomial Almon).

**When NOT:** many interacting series / a system (→ the VAR family); you want latent monthly states/a GDP nowcast from many indicators (→ `mixed_frequency_bayesian`/`dynamic_factor_nowcasting`); the same frequency (→ an ordinary regression/ARDL, `05-cointegration/ARDL`).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **The defining MIDAS condition (a hard gate):** `length(x) == m*length(y)` (m = the frequency ratio) — the wrapper checks it explicitly and builds the formula/data/start **internally** (LLM safety: the user never writes a formula/start by hand, the #1 source of errors in midasr).
- `y`/`x` numeric vectors **without NA**; `length(y)>=10`; `k < length(x)`.
- **A start of the correct length per scheme:** nealmon=3, nbeta=4, almonp=poly_degree+1 (a gate).
- The **stationarity** of the series → `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test` (methodological, not a hard gate).
- **Determinism:** NLS (optim) is deterministic for given starting values → **no seed**.

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| `mixed_frequency_bayesian` (#17) | you want a mixed-frequency VAR system + a posterior + a nowcast of latent states |
| `dynamic_factor_nowcasting` (#15) | many high-frequency indicators → a factor summary instead of explicit lags |
| A plain ARDL (cat. 05) | the same frequency, no weight scheme needed |

**Reading the output:**
- `md_midas`: `coefficients` (the restriction parameters + the intercept/trend); `midas_coefficients` = the **implied weights theta** (the shape of the high-frequency lags — this is what you interpret); `fitted`/`residuals`; **`converged`** (an NLS post-check — non-convergence is flagged with a `message`, it does not block; the results are unreliable).
- `md_haht`: an **htest** → `{statistic, df, p_value, method}`. **H0: the functional restriction (the weight scheme) is adequate** (Kvedaras-Zemlys 2012). **Trap:** p<0.05 → a **rejection** → the scheme is wrong (try another weight function or an unrestricted model). `robust=TRUE` → the HAC version (hAhr).
- `md_forecast`: `mean`/`lower`/`upper`/`level` — it requires a `newx` of future high-frequency values of length `h*m` (and a `newtrend` of length h if the model has a trend).
- `md_select`: `table` (per scheme: n_params/AIC/BIC/converged), `best` = a **rule-based** choice of the weight function by information criterion (the choice is made by a criterion, NOT by the LLM — determinism).

**Sources:** midasr 0.9; **Kvedaras & Zemlys (2012)** *Testing the functional constraints…, Economics Letters* (the hAh test); Ghysels, Santa-Clara & Valkanov (the MIDAS foundations); the midasr vignette (Ghysels-Kvedaras-Zemlys, *JSS* 2016).

### #256 PCA for MIXED I(0)/I(1) variables (Hamilton–Ma–Xi) — `stats` (`c03_multivariate_nowcasting/pca_mixed_variables.py`)

**Functions:** `pn_cyclical_components` [`lm.fit`] — ONLY step (7): an OLS per series on a constant + `p` own lags at horizon `h` → the **cyclical components** (the residuals) + full per-series diagnostics. `pn_pca_nonstationary` [`lm.fit` + `composite_index_dimensionality`] — the **full procedure**: (7) → PCA **on the residuals** → sign-normalized loadings/scores for all components + a variance decomposition + the Bai–Ng `IC_p2`.

**When:** when the **common cyclical factors** behind a panel of macro series are wanted and the stationarity of that panel is **unknown or mixed** — I(1) levels (industrial production, credit, prices) together with I(0) series (unemployment, spreads, PMI) in the **same** panel. The method **does not require the user to classify the series into I(0)/I(1)** nor to choose a transformation per series: "The method does not require knowing which variables are nonstationary or the nature of the nonstationarity" (the abstract). The **same** regression is applied to **all** of them. Defaults: `h=24, p=12` (monthly), `h=8, p=4` (quarterly).

**When NOT:** when **all** the series are demonstrably stationary and on a common scale → classical PCA (#117); when a latent factor with **dynamics**, mixed frequency or ragged-edge nowcasting is needed → a DFM (`dynamic_factor_nowcasting` #15, `sparseDFM` #144); for charts (frontend, charter §5); for **one** series (N≥2 is a hard gate — PCA looks for *common* factors); for an unbalanced panel with NA (a balanced sample is required); for isolating the cycle of **one** series → the Hamilton regression filter (cat 10).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** a numeric **matrix/mts/DataFrame** with ROWS = time, COLUMNS = variables; **T ≥ 2** rows, **N ≥ 2** columns; **without NA/NaN/Inf**; **no constant** series; **no deterministic** series (`y_t = a + b·t`, an index, a running number — its lags are collinear); `h`, `p`, `r_max` **positive integers**; and the **sample size**: `T_eff = T − h − p + 1 ≥ p + 2` ⟺ **`T ≥ h + 2p + 1`** (at least 1 residual degree of freedom). The check before the PCA: `pn_cyclical_components` (look at `r_squared`/`residual_sd`/`short_sample`); evidence of non-stationarity: `c00_data_utilities/composite_index_dimensionality.pca_stationarity_precheck` (KPSS per column) — if it flags, **this** is the right node, not #117.

**Alternatives + criterion:** `pca_composite` (#117) **only** if all the series are stationary — on non-stationary levels the standardization is **mathematically undefined** ("For a nonstationary variable, the population mean is undefined and the sample standard deviation diverges to infinity as the number of time-series observations gets large", §1) and the Bai–Ng criteria are **corrupted** (they selected >1 factor at T=100 when the truth was **0**, Table 1). `dynamic_factor_nowcasting` (#15) / `sparseDFM` (#144) when a state-space DFM with dynamics/mixed frequency/missing data is needed. `h = 12` or `h = 1` when `short_sample = TRUE` (T_eff < 600): a larger `h` ⇒ more autocorrelation in `c_it` ⇒ a greater risk of a spurious factor (Onatski & Wang 2021). `scale_residuals = "none"` **only** if the series are already on a common scale.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `factor1` / `scores` = the estimated **common cyclical factors** over time (T_eff × k) — the main chart-data, with `time` on the x-axis (it survives from an `mts`). `loadings` (N × k, sign-normalized) shows which series loads on which factor. `loadings_hmx`/`factors_hmx` = the normalization of the paper (lambda-tilde'lambda-tilde/N = 1 and f-hat = N^-1 lambda-hat' C-hat, eq. 9–12).
- `residuals` (T_eff × N) = the **cyclical components** c-hat_it of eq. (7); `residual_sd`/`r_squared`/`sigma`/`rss`/`rank` per series.
- **Fit/apply externalization (§3b gate 6):** `coefficients` (N × (p+1)) + the `lag_terms` of regression (7) **and** the `residual_center`/`residual_scale` of the PCA step **and** `loadings` are returned as **numeric** fields ⇒ the out-of-sample apply (new observations → residual → scale → projection) is fully reproducible **outside** the node (the KNIME "Normalize Model" pattern).
- `pca_matrix` = `"correlation"` (the default) or `"covariance"`. **Trap:** with `scale_residuals="none"` the `var_explained` (covariance-based) does **not** coincide with `r2_eigen` (eq. 18, which is always correlation-based) — read `pca_matrix` before comparing them. With the default they coincide **exactly** (a post-check: the sum of sdev² = N).
- `eigenvalues`/`r2_eigen` = xi-hat_j and R²_j = xi-hat_j/N (eq. 18); `ic_p2`/`n_factors_icp2` = the Bai–Ng `IC_p2` (eq. 19) — **valid here** because it runs on the (stationary) residuals; `r_max_effective` = the actual bound min(r_max, N−1, T_eff−1).
- `short_sample`/`short_sample_threshold` (600)/`short_sample_advice`: a **diagnostic, not a gate**.

**Critical traps:**
- **Do NOT difference / detrend beforehand.** Equation (7) in **levels** *is* the transformation; pre-differencing transforms twice.
- **NEVER standardize the raw series.** The scaling is applied **only** to the residuals — which are stationary, so their sd **converges**. The default `unit_variance` is the procedure of the paper.
- **T ≥ h + 2p + 1.** With fewer, `lm.fit` **does not error**: it returns residuals of **exactly 0** (silent-wrong) and the PCA would run on zeros.
- **A deterministic series ⇒ rank < p+1** with **silently NA** coefficients; **a constant series ⇒ `cor` → NA with only a warning**. Both are hard gates here.
- **The PC signs are arbitrary** (the prcomp help Note) → an explicit sign normalization (the max-|loading| positive, the same rule as #117).
- **logs vs levels**: the paper takes logs of whatever is described in rates and leaves rates as they are — an **upstream decision** (cat 00), never a silent one here. **Outliers:** explicitly "make no corrections" for h=24 (the h itself reduces the kurtosis); for extreme values → #246.

**Sources:** Hamilton, Ma & Xi, *Principal Component Analysis for a Mix of Stationary and Nonstationary Variables*, **NBER WP 32068** (rev. 2026-04-08, `econweb.ucsd.edu/~jhamilto/HX.pdf`) — eq. (7) `y_it = k_i + a_i1 y_{i,t−h} + … + a_ip y_{i,t−h−p+1} + c_it`, "Our procedure is to perform PCA on the regression residuals {c-hat_1t,…,c-hat_Nt}", "with h = 8 and p = 4 for quarterly data and h = 24 and p = 12 for monthly data", §6.3 "Since c-hat_it is normalized to have unit variance…", §5 + eq. (18)–(19) on the **correlation matrix** of the residuals, §5 "provided the number of time-series observations is 600 or larger"; Hamilton (2018), *Why You Should Never Use the HP Filter*, REStat 100(5); Bai & Ng (2002), Econometrica 70(1) (IC_p2; Stock & Watson 2016 p. 436); Onatski & Wang (2021), *Spurious Factor Analysis*, Econometrica 89(2); the `composite_index_dimensionality`/`lm.fit` the reference help (version 4.6.1).
