## §17. Model evaluation and selection — `c15_model_evaluation/`

> **when this category applies:** **after** the fit — when we already have one or more estimated models and want to (a) **compare predictive accuracy** between them out of sample (Diebold-Mariano, tsCV, the Model Confidence Set) or (b) **diagnose whether the model assumptions hold** in the residuals (serial correlation, heteroskedasticity, ARCH, a wrong functional form). It produces no forecasts (→ `02`/`04`) and does no estimation — it works on **errors/residuals/loss series** that the other buttons have already produced.

**The common selection logic inside the category (a decision rule):**

| Question | Preferred tool |
|---|---|
| two models, which forecasts better out of sample? | `#74 dm.test` (Diebold-Mariano) |
| one model, how robust is its out-of-sample accuracy per horizon? | `#74 tsCV` (a rolling backtest) |
| **many** (>2) models, which subset is statistically indistinguishable from the best? | `#75 MCS` (the Model Confidence Set) |
| regression residuals: autocorrelation? heteroskedasticity? a wrong functional form? | `#76 lmtest` (BG / BP / RESET) |
| time-series residuals: is there conditional heteroskedasticity (ARCH)? | `#77 ArchTest` (the Engle ARCH-LM test) |

**The difference between a test and a backtest:** `#76`/`#77` are **misspecification tests** (one residual series → an htest, H0 = "the model is fine along this dimension"). `#74`/`#75` are a **relative comparison of accuracy** (they need out-of-sample errors from ≥2 methods). First the diagnostics (do the assumptions hold?), then the comparison (which one wins?).

**Preconditions — the general rule:** all the tools work on **errors/residuals the caller has already produced** — the quality of the diagnostic depends on the errors being genuinely **out-of-sample** (for DM/MCS) or genuine residuals (for BG/BP/RESET/ARCH). Using in-sample residuals as "forecast errors" in DM/MCS is a methodological error (it understates the uncertainty; Diebold 2015). There is no formal statistical precondition tool beforehand — only the correct provenance of the errors.

---

### #74 forecast (Diebold-Mariano + tsCV) — `diebold_mariano_tscv` (`c15_model_evaluation/diebold_mariano_tscv.py`)
**Functions:** `dm.test` → `eval_dm_test`, `tsCV` → `eval_tsCV`.

**When:**
- `eval_dm_test`: a **comparison of the forecast accuracy of two** methods through two error series `e1`, `e2` (of equal length, aligned in time). H0: equal accuracy. It uses the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold 1997 modification (a small-sample correction) — which is why it is appropriate even on a moderate sample.
- `eval_tsCV`: a **rolling-origin (time-series) cross-validation** of a forecasting function — an expanding or fixed (`window`) window; it returns the errors per time point and per horizon (h=1.H). The classical honest out-of-sample backtest for **one** model/pipeline.

**When NOT:** for **>2 models** at once → `#75 MCS` (DM only does pairwise comparisons; multiple DM tests → a multiple-testing problem). For the assumption diagnostics of one model (not a comparison) → `#76`/`#77`. DM does **not** test which model is "correct" — only which forecasts better under the given loss.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- `eval_dm_test`: `e1`, `e2` numeric, of the **same length**, without NA/Inf, `length ≥ 2`, `h` a positive integer `< length`, `power > 0`. The errors must be **out-of-sample** and **aligned** — the caller guarantees their provenance.
- `eval_tsCV`: `y` a numeric/`ts`; `forecastfunction` a **function** with the signature `function(y, h)` (or `+ xreg`) returning a `diebold_mariano_tscv` object — it is not validated internally, `tsCV` handles it; `h`/`initial`/`window` integers within their bounds.
- No formal stationarity is required (we work on errors); but if the `forecastfunction` specifies an ARIMA manually, the preconditions of `02` apply.

**Alternatives + criterion:** `#75 MCS` when you compare **many** models (it generalises DM without the multiple-testing bias). The same loss-based ranking can also come from the `accuracy` of `02-univariate-forecasting`, but **without** a statistical significance test — prefer DM/MCS when you want to say "statistically better", not merely "a lower RMSE".

**Reading the output:**
- `eval_dm_test` (an `htest` → atomic fields via `to_mcp`): `statistic` (the DM statistic, ~a t distribution); `p_value` — if `< alpha` the equality of accuracy is rejected; `parameter` = (the horizon, the power); `alternative`/`varestimator` echoes; `htest` = the raw object (compact).
- **The direction trap (critical):** for `alternative="less"` the alternative is "**method 2 is less accurate than method 1**" (i.e. `e1` is better); for `"greater"` the reverse (`e2` is better). The sign of the `statistic` and the direction depend on the **order** `e1, e2` — do not confuse it. (The `dm.test` docs.)
- `eval_tsCV`: `errors` — a `ts` (h=1) or an `mts` (h>1) of errors of the same length as `y`, with **leading NAs** (the first positions lack enough history); `to_mcp`: ts→`{values,start,frequency}`, mts→nested rows+dimnames. `accuracy` — a DataFrame (1 row per horizon) with `rmse`/`mae`/`me`/`n_eff` computed **over the finite values only**.
- **Interpretation traps:** (1) a `me` (mean error) ≠ 0 signals **bias** in the forecast; (2) `n_eff` falls as the horizon grows (fewer valid points) — the large-h RMSE rests on few points and is less reliable; (3) tsCV is **slow** (a re-fit at every origin).

**Sources:** Diebold & Mariano 1995 (JBES); Harvey, Leybourne & Newbold 1997 (IJF, the small-sample DM); Diebold 2015 (the careful use of DM: not for in-sample/nested model comparison); Hyndman & Athanasopoulos *FPP3* (tsCV, time-series CV); the `diebold_mariano_tscv` reference manual (`dm.test`, `tsCV`).

---

### #75 MCS (the Model Confidence Set) — `MCS` (`c15_model_evaluation/confidence_set.py`)
**Functions:** `MCSprocedure` → `run_mcs_procedure`, `LossLevel` → `compute_loss_level`, `LossVol` → `compute_loss_vol`.

**When:** when you compare **many (≥2, typically many) models at once** and want the **subset** of models that are statistically indistinguishable from the best at confidence `(1-alpha)` (Hansen, Lunde & Nason 2011). It works on a **loss matrix** (rows = time points, columns = models), with a block bootstrap. The helpers `compute_loss_level` (point forecasts, SE/AE) and `compute_loss_vol` (volatility forecasts, SE1/SE2/**QLIKE**/R2LOG/AE1/AE2) build the loss matrix from the realized vs the evaluated series.

**When NOT:** for **exactly two** models, a pairwise test → `#74 dm.test` (simpler, no bootstrap needed). MCS does **not** say which one is "the best" — only which cannot be excluded; a large final set means low discriminating power (little data), not "all are fine".

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- `run_mcs_procedure`: `Loss` a **numeric** matrix/DataFrame, with `≥2` columns (models) and `≥2` rows, **all finite** (no NA/Inf; the bootstrap crashes on NA); `alpha ∈ (0,1)`; `B` a positive integer; `min.k`/`k`/`seed` integers; `match.arg(statistic)` ∈ {Tmax, TR}.
- The loss series must come from **out-of-sample** forecasts (the same argument as for DM).
- **A `seed` must be supplied for reproducibility** — the result depends on the block bootstrap.

**Alternatives + criterion:** `#74 dm.test` for 2 models. Superior Predictive Ability (Hansen 2005, SPA) when you compare many models **against one benchmark** (not covered here) — MCS presupposes no benchmark, it finds the set. For a simple ranking without a test → `accuracy` (`02`).

**Reading the output:**
- `show` — a DataFrame (one row per model that **survived**), with a `model` column + `Avg_Loss`, the statistics `Rank_M`/`Rank_R`, and the **`MCS p-Value`** (and the `p-Value for H_{0,M_k}`). Column names with spaces or symbols are preserved verbatim. `to_mcp`: a DataFrame → a list of records.
- `included` — the names of the models in the final confidence set (the main result).
- `n_models`/`alpha`/`statistic`/`B` — echoes; `ssm` = the raw S4 SSM (`to_mcp` keeps a compact stub — the S4 slots do not deep-serialize).
- **Interpretation traps:** (1) `show` contains **only the survivors**, not those excluded — the excluded models are absent from the table; (2) the **`MCS p-Value` is not** the p-value of an individual model — a model belongs to the set if `MCS p-Value > alpha`; (3) a different `seed`/`B` → a slightly different set (bootstrap variability); (4) `Tmax` (semi-quadratic) and `TR` (range) can give different sets — state which one was used.
- **A package quirk (implementation):** `LossLevel`/`LossVol` are non-conformable for a multi-column `evaluated` against a vector `realized` ("non-conformable arrays") — the wrapper calls them **per model column** (`drop=FALSE`) and `cbind`s the results; numerically identical to the documented formula.

**Sources:** Hansen, Lunde & Nason 2011 (Econometrica 79(2):453-497, the MCS); Bernardi & Catania 2014 (The MCS package for the reference); Patton 2011 (robust volatility loss functions, QLIKE); the `MCS` reference manual (`MCSprocedure`, `LossLevel`, `LossVol`).

---

### #76 lmtest (Breusch-Godfrey / Breusch-Pagan / RESET) — `breusch_godfrey_breusch` (`c15_model_evaluation/breusch_godfrey_breusch.py`)
**Functions:** `bgtest` → `run_bg_test`, `bptest` → `run_bp_test`, `resettest` → `run_reset_test`.

**When:** **residual diagnostics of a regression** (an `lm`/`glm`, or a `formula`+`data`):
- `run_bg_test` (**Breusch-Godfrey**): serial correlation in the residuals up to order `order`. H0: no autocorrelation. Preferred over Durbin-Watson because it handles **lagged dependent variables** and higher-order autocorrelation (Enders 2015).
- `run_bp_test` (**Breusch-Pagan**): heteroskedasticity — the error variance depends on the regressors. H0: homoskedasticity. `studentize=TRUE` (Koenker) = robust to non-normality (the default).
- `run_reset_test` (**Ramsey RESET**): a wrong **functional form** (omitted non-linear terms). H0: the linear specification is adequate. It adds powers (`power=2:3`) of the fitted values/regressors/principal components.

**When NOT:** for **ARCH** (the conditional heteroskedasticity of a time series, not a cross-sectional one) → `#77 ArchTest`. For unit roots/stationarity → `01`. For models other than `lm`/`glm` (e.g. a VAR) → the serial-correlation test of `reduced_form_var` (`04`). RESET does **not** say **which** non-linearity is missing — only that something is.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- The first argument: a **`formula` (+ `data`) or a fitted `lm`/`glm`** — the wrapper does **no refit**, it only validates and passes through (`.lt_check_model`).
- `run_bg_test`: `order` a positive integer; `run_bp_test`: `studentize` a scalar logical; `run_reset_test`: `power` integers **≥ 2** (of length ≥ 1).
- **No stationarity is required** — but note: if `y` is non-stationary, the OLS regression itself may be spurious (→ check first with `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test` + a confirmatory KPSS, and prefer cointegration `05` if needed).

**Alternatives + criterion:** the White test (a more general heteroskedasticity test) — BP with a suitable `varformula` approximates it. The Ljung-Box test (autocorrelation without regressors, on a pure residual series) → `diebold_mariano_tscv`/`stats` instead of BG when there is no regression design matrix. The ARCH-LM test (`#77`) when the heteroskedasticity is **time-dependent** (volatility clustering) rather than a function of the regressors.

**Reading the output** (all three are `htest` → atomic fields via `to_mcp`):
- `statistic` — BG: `LM = n·R²` (a Chisq) or an F; BP: a Chisq; RESET: an F. `p_value` — **if `< alpha` H0 is rejected** ⇒ **there is a problem** (autocorrelation / heteroskedasticity / misspecification). `parameter` = the df. `method`/`data_name`; `htest` = the raw object.
- **The polarity trap:** here **a rejection = bad** (the model fails the diagnostic) — the opposite of a forecast test, where you do not necessarily want a rejection. H0 = "all is well", so a **small p ⇒ a violated assumption**.
- **Interpretation traps:** (1) BG with a wrong `order` (too small) misses higher-order autocorrelation; (2) BP with `studentize=FALSE` (the original Breusch-Pagan) is sensitive to non-normality — prefer `TRUE`; (3) a RESET rejection ⇒ misspecification but **not** of what kind (a nonlinearity, an omitted variable, a wrong link); (4) a rejection for serial correlation ⇒ the OLS standard errors are **invalid** (you need HAC/Newey-West), not necessarily biased coefficients.

**Sources:** Breusch & Godfrey 1978; Breusch & Pagan 1979; Koenker 1981 (the studentized BP); Ramsey 1969 (RESET); Enders 2015 *Applied Econometric Time Series* (BG > DW with a lagged y); the `breusch_godfrey_breusch` reference manual (`bgtest`, `bptest`, `resettest`).

---

### #77 FinTS (ARCH-LM) — `FinTS` (`c15_model_evaluation/arch.py`)
**Functions:** `ArchTest` → `run_arch_test`.

**When:** testing for **ARCH effects** (conditional heteroskedasticity / volatility clustering) in one univariate series — typically in the **residuals** of a mean model or in returns. Engle's LM test: an auxiliary regression of `x²` on `lags` of its own lags; H0: **no ARCH** up to order `lags` (Engle 1982). An essential pre-check **before** fitting a GARCH: if there are no ARCH effects, GARCH is superfluous.

**When NOT:** for cross-sectional heteroskedasticity (a function of the regressors) → `#76 bptest`. For autocorrelation in the **level** (not the variance) → `#76 bgtest`/Ljung-Box. The test needs **univariate** input — for multivariate volatility → MGARCH (outside this category).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- `x` **univariate** (`NCOL(x)==1`) and **numeric** (a class-based `is.numeric` — logical/factor/character are rejected; relying on `as.numeric` alone would let a logical→0/1 and a factor→codes pass **silently wrong**), without NA/Inf.
- `lags` a positive integer **`< length(x)`**; `demean` a scalar logical.
- `x` must be the **residuals of a mean model** (or returns with a zero/constant mean) — if there is unmodelled autocorrelation in the level, the ARCH test may confuse mean dependence with variance dependence (hence `demean` when needed). Clean the mean first with `02`/`04`.

**Alternatives + criterion:** a Ljung-Box test on the **squared** residuals (McLeod-Li) — equivalent evidence of ARCH, available in `stats`/`diebold_mariano_tscv`. The ARCH-LM test is preferred as a **formal LM test** with clear df. After a positive ARCH-LM → fit a GARCH-family model (the volatility category `06`).

**Reading the output** (an `htest` → atomic fields via `to_mcp`):
- `statistic` — the **Chi-squared** `LM = n·R²` of the auxiliary regression; `parameter` = the **df = `lags`**; `p_value` — **if `< alpha` H0 is rejected ⇒ ARCH effects ARE PRESENT** (volatility clustering, you need a GARCH). `lags`/`demean` echoes; `htest` = the raw object.
- **The polarity trap:** as in `#76`, **a rejection = there is a problem/an effect** (H0 = "no ARCH"). A small p ⇒ conditional heteroskedasticity, not "a good model".
- **Interpretation traps:** (1) the test runs on the **residuals**, not on the original series — ARCH in the raw series may be due to an unmodelled mean; (2) a large `lags` → lower power; (3) a wrapper post-check: the `p.value` is validated to be a proper probability in `[0,1]` (otherwise a `stop`).
- **A namespace trap (implementation, documented):** `FinTS` **exports `ARIMA`**, which **masks `ARIMA`** inside the data mask of `model` as soon as it is attached → it broke a test of `c02_univariate_forecasting/fable.py`. The fix: the consumer calls a qualified `ARIMA`/`ETS`/`model`. Always run the WHOLE `./run_verifications.sh` — the break shows up in **another** category.

**Sources:** Engle 1982 (Econometrica, ARCH · the LM test); McLeod & Li 1983 (the squared-residual Ljung-Box test); Tsay *Analysis of Financial Time Series* (the ARCH-LM pre-GARCH check); the `FinTS` reference manual (`ArchTest`).

---

### #94 scoringRules (CRPS / LogS / PIT — evaluating density forecasts) — `scoringRules` (`c15_model_evaluation/density_forecast_evaluation.py`)
**Functions:** `sr_crps_sample` [`crps_sample`, method=edf/kde], `sr_logs_sample` [`logs_sample`], `sr_crps_parametric`/`sr_logs_parametric` [`crps_norm`/`crps_t`/`crps_mixnorm` + `logs_*`], `sr_crps_tailweighted` [`twcrps_sample`/`owcrps_sample`], `sr_pit_sample` (an empirical PIT — a project addition).

**When:** you have a **predictive DISTRIBUTION** (posterior/ensemble draws or an explicitly parametric one) and want to score it as a *whole distribution*, not as a point. The natural consumer of the draws from `#12` BVAR, `#13` bvartools, `#14` bvarsv (TVP-SV), `#17` mfbvar, `#60` bssm, and of the quantiles/densities of `#64` GaR. **CRPS** (proper, negatively oriented, in the same units as y) = the default for samples; **LogS** when you want a local/likelihood-based score; **PIT** for calibration (the histogram ~ Uniform if well calibrated); **tail-weighted CRPS** (`twcrps`/`owcrps`) for a GaR-style focus on the left tail.

**When NOT:** a **point** forecast comparison ⇒ `#74` Diebold-Mariano (NOT CRPS); a choice among many point models ⇒ `#75` MCS; binary classification/AUC ⇒ `#84` pROC; a simple in-sample goodness of fit ⇒ `#76`/`#77`. Multivariate ES/VS (`es_sample`/`vs_sample`) are outside the surface.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **A draws-producing tool first**: `c03_multivariate_nowcasting/bayesian_var.py` (or bvartools/bvarsv/mfbvar/bssm) produces the posterior predictive draws; `c12_distribution_risk/quantile_regression.qr_growth_at_risk` produces the quantiles (→ a density via `#95`).
- **The shape**: `dat` = a matrix `[n_obs × n_draws]` (one row of draws per observation, ≥2 draws) or a vector only for a single observation; `y` = the realisations (out of sample). Hard gates: no NA/Inf; `bw>0`; `sd/scale/df>0`.

**Alternatives + criterion:** `sr_crps_sample` (edf) = the robust default for draws; `sr_logs_sample` when you want a likelihood-based score (but it is **sensitive to the KDE bandwidth in the tails**); `sr_*_parametric` when the distribution is explicitly normal/t/mixnorm (e.g. an analytical BVAR predictive); `sr_crps_tailweighted` when the cost is asymmetric in the tail (GaR).

**Reading the output:**
- `scores` — the **per-observation** score vector (chart-data: the score over time); `mean_score` = the mean score (the comparative number).
- `score` = "CRPS"/"LogS"/"twCRPS"; `method` (edf/kde)/`family` (normal/t/mixnorm); `weighted`, `side`, `a`, `b`, `kind` for the tail-weighted variants.
- `sr_pit_sample.pit` — the PIT values ∈[0,1]; a histogram ~ Uniform ⇒ good calibration (a U shape ⇒ underdispersed, an inverted U ⇒ overdispersed).
- **Interpretation traps:** (1) CRPS/LogS are **negatively oriented** — **LOWER = BETTER** (do not read them as accuracy). (2) LogS = −infinity if y falls outside the support of the draws; a KDE smooths this but it is **sensitive to the bandwidth in the tails** — for heavy-tailed samples prefer **CRPS (edf)**. (3) The CRPS of a single observation is NOT comparable across series of different scale (it is in the same units as y). (4) A low tail-weighted CRPS may be due to **few** observations falling in the tail — read the per-observation `scores`.

**Sources:** Jordan, Krüger & Lerch 2019 *JSS* 90(12) "Evaluating Probabilistic Forecasts with scoringRules"; Gneiting & Raftery 2007 *JASA* 102 (proper scoring, CRPS/LogS); Gneiting & Ranjan 2011 *JBES* 29 (the threshold-weighted CRPS); Krüger et al. 2021 *Int. J. Forecast.* (predictive-distribution scoring); **PIT** (`sr_pit_sample`, custom): Diebold, Gunther & Tay 1998 *Int. Econ. Rev.* 39(4):863-883 (PIT calibration); Berkowitz 2001 *JBES* 19(4):465-474 (the PIT density-forecast test); the `scoringRules` reference manual.

---

## §18. Limited dependent / recession probability — `c16_limited_dependent/`

> **When this category applies:** when the outcome is **not** a continuous quantity but a **binary
> event** (recession / no recession, a crisis dummy) and the question is **"what is the *probability* of the
> event"** — typically the classical **yield curve → recession probability** exercise (Estrella-Mishkin):
> a binomial GLM (**#83 feglm**, probit/logit) estimates the probability of a recession from the
> yield-curve spread, and a ROC/AUC tool (**#84 pROC**) evaluates **how well** the in-sample/out-of-sample
> probability score separates the recession quarters from the rest. The two cards are a
> **pair**: #83 produces the `fitted_probabilities` score, #84 scores it. Neither is a
> time-series dynamic method — they do not replace VAR/VECM (cat. 04-05); they are **cross-sectional /
> pooled classification** over a binary target.

---

### #83 Binomial GLM (probit/logit) — the recession probability — `fixed_effects_ols` (`c16_limited_dependent/binomial_glm_recession.py`)
**Functions:** `run_feglm_binom` → `feglm(family = binomial(link))`, with the helpers
`coeftable`, `predict(type="response")`, `fitstat(., "pr2")` (the McFadden pseudo-R²),
`logLik`/`AIC`/`BIC`/`deviance`/`nobs`/`coef` (the S3 methods for `fixed_effects_ols`).

**When:** you have a **binary** outcome (a recession dummy 0/1, crisis / no crisis) and want to estimate
its **probability** from one or more predictors — pre-eminently the **Estrella-Mishkin
yield-curve** exercise: `recession ~ term_spread` with a **probit** (the default) or a **logit** link. `fixed_effects_ols`
adds **high-dimensional fixed effects** (`fixef=` or `| fe` in the formula) and **clustered SE**
(`cluster=`) cheaply — useful for a panel of countries / regions with country/time effects, or for a weighted
estimation (`weights=`).

**When NOT:**
- ⛔ A **continuous outcome** → OLS/IV (`c07_causality_policy/fixed_effects_ols.py`, `feols`) or forecasting (cat. 02),
 not a binomial GLM. The wrapper locks to `binomial` — it does not expose `feols`/`fepois`/`fenegbin`.
- ⛔ **>2 categories** (e.g. an expansion/slowdown/recession regime) → an ordered/multinomial model or Markov
 switching (`MSwM`, cat. 06), not here (the wrapper rejects a factor with ≠2 levels).
- ⚠️ **Endogenous dynamics in the recession state itself** (an autoregressive latent recession probability,
 e.g. the Kauppi-Saikkonen dynamic probit) → not covered; `feglm` is a **static** cross-sectional
 GLM (any dynamics enter only as a lagged regressor on the RHS, supplied by the user).
- ⚠️ A count outcome → Poisson/NegBin (outside the surface here).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** **no formal stationarity/distributional** precondition — the IRLS
of the GLM is deterministic and **cross-sectional** (it is not time-series inference). Instead there are
**hard data-shape gates** (all live-verified against the docs `feglm.Rd`/`predict.fixest.Rd`/
`fitstat.Rd`, built into the wrapper):

| Gate | Why | Glyph |
|---|---|---|
| a valid formula (a string/formula → a clean message, covering the `\| fe` syntax) | a defensive parse instead of a cryptic base `str2lang` error | ⛔ |
| data a DataFrame, non-empty, with **all** the variables (the formula + the `fixef`/`cluster` characters) present and **without NA** | `feglm` would throw a cryptic error or drop rows silently | ⛔ |
| the LHS a **plain column** (not an expression `log(x)~…`) | a requirement of the response-coercion step | ⛔ |
| the response **binary**: numeric with **only {0,1} (both values present)**, logical (→0/1), or a **2-level factor** (→0/1, the first=0/the second=1) | ⚠️ `feglm` REQUIRES a numeric single-column LHS; a **factor LHS → a cryptic "not numeric" error** (live-verified) → a defensive conversion to 0/1 BEFORE the call | ⛔ |
| a constant response (a single value) is rejected | estimation needs both 0 **and** 1 to occur | ⛔ |
| the `fixef` character columns exist; the `cluster` (character/formula) columns exist | the documented FE/cluster surface | ⛔ |
| `weights` numeric of length nrow, non-negative, without NA/Inf, with a **sum > 0** | ⚠️ all-zero weights used to pass the gate → a cryptic wrapped error (an adversarial-review LOW fix) | ⛔ |
| `link` via `match.arg` (**probit** by default, or logit) | a documented constrained choice | ⛔ |

**Alternatives + criterion:**
- ⤷ **probit vs logit:** numerically almost equivalent for prediction; the **Estrella-Mishkin tradition
 uses probit** (hence the default), while logit is preferred when you want an interpretation in **odds ratios**.
 The sign and the statistical significance are practically unchanged; what changes is the scale of the coefficients.
- ⤷ **Base `glm(family=binomial)`** does the same job; you choose `feglm` when you want many
 **high-dimensional fixed effects** (countries×years) or **clustered SE** cheaply — otherwise they are equivalent.
- ⤷ A **Markov-switching recession probability** (`MSwM`, cat. 06) when the recession state is
 **latent/unobserved** and you want the model to **extract** the regime probabilities rather than regress
 on a known dummy. ⚠️ `MSwM` is gaussian/`lm` only — it does not do binomial.
- ⤷ A **dynamic probit** (Kauppi-Saikkonen 2008) when the autocorrelation of the recession state is critical
 — outside the surface here (a static GLM only).

**Reading the output** (a named list; `.coeftable` = a DataFrame → `to_mcp` a **list of records**; the scalars →
atomic fields; `.object` = the raw fit → a **compact stub** `@mcp_serialized=FALSE`):

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `coefficients` | the named vector of betas on the **scale of the link** (the probit/logit index), **NOT** probabilities/marginal effects |
| `coeftable` | `term`/`estimate`/`std_error`/`z_value`/`p_value` — a z-test (GLM), with the SE clustered if a `cluster` was supplied |
| `fitted_probabilities` | the **recession probabilities** `P(y=1\|x)` (`predict(type="response")`) — the score that feeds #84 |
| `obs_kept` | the **1-based indices** of the rows that were kept; ⚠️ with `fixef`/separation `feglm` **DROPS** rows → `length(fitted_probabilities) < nrow` — use it to align with the original dates |
| `n_input_rows` | the input rows (before the drop) — to verify the alignment |
| `pseudo_r2` | the **McFadden pseudo-R²** (a ratio of log-likelihoods, `fitstat "pr2"`) — NOT an OLS R²; typical values of 0.2-0.4 are considered very good |
| `loglik`/`aic`/`bic`/`deviance`/`nobs` | the fit statistics; `aic`/`bic` for comparing links/specifications |
| `link`/`family`/`fixef_names` | metadata (probit/logit; binomial; the FE names) |

**Interpretation traps:**
- ⚠️ **The coefficients are not marginal effects.** In a probit/logit the beta gives the effect on the **latent index**,
 not on the probability; the effect on the probability depends on the point (it fades at the extremes). For
 "how many percentage points" you need marginal effects (not exposed here) — only the **sign and the
 significance** are read directly from the `coeftable`.
- ⚠️ **`fitted_probabilities` alignment:** do NOT assume `length == nrow(data)`. With fixed effects that
 cause separation, rows drop silently; **always** align through `obs_kept`.
- ⚠️ **A pseudo-R² ≠ an R².** A McFadden of 0.3 is excellent (it is not comparable to an OLS 0.3). Do not read it
 as "it explains 30% of the variance".
- ⚠️ **Perfect separation / quasi-separation** (e.g. the spread separates the recessions perfectly) → the coefficients →
 ±infinity with enormous SE; `feglm` may drop them (see `obs_kept`) or fail to converge — check the SE.
- ⚠️ **An in-sample AUC (via #84 on the same sample) overstates** the predictive ability; for a real-time
 recession call you need an out-of-sample / real-time vintage evaluation.

**Sources:** 📦 `fixed_effects_ols` — (the help pages `feglm`, `fitstat`,
`predict.fixest`; `pr2` = the McFadden pseudo-R², live-verified via btw). 📖 Bergé (2018) *Efficient
estimation of maximum likelihood models with multiple fixed effects* (a CREA DP, the fixest reference).
📖 Estrella & Mishkin (1998) *Review of Economics and Statistics* 80(1):45-61 — the probit recession
probability from the yield spread. 📖 Estrella & Hardouvelis (1991) *J. Finance* 46(2):555-576 — the yield
curve → real activity. 📖 Kauppi & Saikkonen (2008) *Rev. Econ. Stat.* 90(4):777-791 —
the dynamic probit (an alternative, outside the surface). 📖 McFadden (1974) "Conditional logit analysis of qualitative choice behavior", in P. Zarembka (ed.) *Frontiers in Econometrics*, Academic Press, 105-142 — the pseudo-R².

---

### #84 ROC / AUC — binary forecast evaluation — `pROC` (`c16_limited_dependent/roc_auc_binary.py`)
**Functions:** `run_roc` → `roc` (the AUC), `ci.auc` (the **DeLong** CI of the AUC),
`coords(x="best")` (the **Youden** optimal operating point).

**When:** you have a **numeric score/prediction** (typically the `fitted_probabilities` of #83, or
any leading indicator) and a **binary target** (recession 0/1) and want to measure
**discriminatory ability** independently of any threshold: the **AUC** (the probability that a random recession
quarter receives a higher score than a non-recession one), the **CI of the AUC** (DeLong), the whole **ROC
curve** (sensitivity vs specificity across all thresholds, chart-ready), and the **optimal threshold**
(Youden). The natural evaluation companion of #83.

**When NOT:**
- ⛔ **>2 classes** → a multiclass ROC (not exposed; the wrapper requires exactly 2 levels).
- ⚠️ A **point/interval forecast of a continuous quantity** → forecast-accuracy metrics (RMSE/MAE, Diebold-
 Mariano — cat. 15), not a ROC. The ROC concerns **binary classification**.
- ⚠️ A **comparison of two ROC curves** (which model is better) → `roc.test` (a paired DeLong test) — **not
 exposed** here (one curve per call); the wrapper also omits smoothing/bootstrap CI/power.
- ⚠️ **Calibration** (are the probabilities correctly calibrated?) → the AUC measures **discrimination**,
 NOT calibration; you need a reliability diagram / a Brier score (not here).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** the input is the `fitted_probabilities` of **#83
`run_feglm_binom`** (or any numeric score) + the binary target. **No statistical** precondition;
instead there are **hard gates** (live-verified against the pROC docs) — critical because of **silent label inversion**:

| Gate | Why | Glyph |
|---|---|---|
| `response`/`predictor` not NULL; `predictor` a **numeric vector** (not a matrix/array); of the **same length** | basic types | ⛔ |
| `predictor` without Inf; not entirely NA; **non-constant** after the NA removal | a constant score → an undefined ROC | ⛔ |
| **≥2 complete** observations after the NA drop | otherwise a cryptic error | ⛔ |
| `response` with **EXACTLY 2 levels** | a ROC is binary | ⛔ |
| **CRITICAL — the (control, case) order:** without an explicit `levels`, **ONLY** a logical (FALSE=control/TRUE=case) or a numeric {0,1} (0=control/1=case, the recession dummy) is allowed. For **arbitrary factor/character labels an explicit `levels = c(control, case)` is REQUIRED** | ⚠️ alphabetical order does NOT coincide with (control, case) — e.g. `"case" < "control"` → a **SILENT inversion** of cases/controls and, at a fixed `direction`, **AUC → 1 − AUC**. Correctness does NOT depend on the LLM (an adversarial-review CRITICAL fix) | ⛔ |
| `levels` (if supplied) of length 2, distinct, non-NA, present in the response | a clean gate | ⛔ |
| `ci` a single logical; `conf_level` ∈ (0,1); `direction` via `match.arg` (**auto** by default) | documented | ⛔ |
| **A POST-gate:** the returned object is of class `roc` | a safety net | ⛔ |

**Alternatives + criterion:**
- ⤷ **The AUC vs single-threshold metrics** (accuracy/precision/recall at one cutoff): the AUC when you want a
 **threshold-independent** measure of separation; a single threshold when you have a **specific cost**
 of a false alarm/miss and want to operate at one point (→ use `best_threshold`).
- ⤷ **A DeLong CI vs a bootstrap CI:** the wrapper gives the **DeLong** one (analytic, fast, the default for the full
 AUC — DeLong 1988). A bootstrap CI (ci.se/ci.sp) is **not exposed**; you would want it only for a partial AUC
 or smoothed curves (outside the surface).
- ⤷ **Youden vs a cost-weighted threshold:** `best_threshold` is **Youden** (max sens+spec−1,
 with equal weight on the two errors). If the cost of a missed recession ≫ that of a false alarm, the optimal point
 differs — pick a threshold from `roc_curve` manually.
- ⤷ **A comparison of models** → `roc.test` (outside the wrapper).

**Reading the output** (a named list; `.roc_curve` = a DataFrame → `to_mcp` a **list of records**; `.auc_ci`/
`.best_threshold` = named lists; `.roc_object` = the raw `roc` → a **compact stub**):

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `auc` | the Area Under the Curve ∈ [0,1]; **0.5 = random**, 1 = perfect separation; the "C statistic" |
| `auc_ci` | `{low, high, conf_level, method="delong"}` — the **DeLong** CI of the AUC; if `low` > 0.5 → significantly better than random |
| `roc_curve` | a DataFrame `threshold`/`sensitivity`/`specificity` — **chart-ready** (the frontend plots sens vs 1−spec); ⚠️ the ±Inf sentinel thresholds at the ends are **removed** so that the column stays uniformly numeric |
| `best_threshold` | a named list of numeric vectors `threshold`/`sensitivity`/`specificity` at the **Youden** point; **several rows** if there are ties |
| `n_cases`/`n_controls` | the number of positive (recession) / negative observations after the NA drop |
| `controls_level`/`cases_level` | **WHICH label** is the control/case — check it so as not to read the result backwards |
| `direction` | `"<"` (controls < cases, the normal case for a probability score) or `">"`; it sets the orientation |
| `percent` | whether the AUC/sens/spec are in % (here always FALSE) |

**Interpretation traps:**
- ⚠️ **CRITICAL — label inversion and AUC = 1 − AUC:** if the control/case labels are mixed up, the AUC
 inverts (0.8 → 0.2). The wrapper blocks this by requiring an explicit `levels` for a non-0/1/logical
 response; **always** read `controls_level`/`cases_level` to confirm. (An AUC < 0.5 does not mean
 "a bad model" — it often means **inverted labels or direction**.)
- ⚠️ **The silent adjustment of `direction="auto"`:** `"auto"` picks the direction that gives an AUC ≥ 0.5,
 hiding a possible inversion; for a strict evaluation set `direction="<"` (a probability score →
 higher = a more likely recession) so that an AUC < 0.5 surfaces as a genuinely bad model.
- ⚠️ **An in-sample AUC is over-optimistic:** if the `predictor` comes from the same sample that estimated
 #83, the AUC is optimistic. For an honest evaluation → an out-of-sample / real-time predictor.
- ⚠️ **Youden ≠ operationally optimal:** it weights false alarms and misses equally; in macro recession calling the
 cost is asymmetric — do not adopt `best_threshold` blindly.
- ⚠️ **The AUC measures discrimination, NOT calibration:** two models with the same AUC may have very
 different probability calibration. The AUC does not say whether a "60% probability" really is 60%.

**Sources:** 📦 `pROC` — (the help pages `roc`, `ci.auc`, `coords`;
DeLong is the default for the full AUC, `coords(x="best")` = Youden, live-verified via btw). 📖 Robin et al.
(2011) *pROC: an open-source package for the reference and S+ to analyze and compare ROC curves*, BMC
Bioinformatics 12:77. 📖 DeLong, DeLong & Clarke-Pearson (1988) *Biometrics* 44:837-845 — the variance
of the AUC (the CI method). 📖 Youden (1950) *Cancer* 3(1):32-35 — the J index (the best operating point).


---

## §19. Forecast combination — `c17_forecast_combination/`

this category applies when you already have (or can produce) several competing univariate forecasting models for the SAME series and want ONE more robust combined forecast — a combination almost always reduces the error and the variance relative to picking a single "best" model (Bates-Granger 1969; Timmermann 2006). It is NOT a category for modelling structure/causality — it is a purely predictive layer on top of the components.

---

### #85 Ensemble forecast combination (equal / in-sample / CV weights) — `forecastHybrid` (`c17_forecast_combination/ensemble_forecast_combination.py`)
**Functions:** `hybridModel` (the fit), `diebold_mariano_tscv` (the method `forecast.hybridModel`, an h-step forecast with PI). The wrapper: `run_hybrid`.

**When:** when you want a robust combination of 2-7 established univariate models of the `diebold_mariano_tscv` ecosystem on ONE series — the letters: `a`=auto.arima, `e`=ets, `f`=thetam, `n`=nnetar, `s`=stlm, `t`=tbats, `z`=snaive. Ideal for baseline macro forecasting (inflation, GDP, unemployment) where stability matters more than interpretability, and when you do not know in advance which single model works best. `weights="equal"` (the default) is empirically the most robust; `insample.errors`/`cv.errors` when you have enough data and want data-driven weights.

**When NOT:** for a multivariate/structural analysis (VAR/VECM → sections 04/05), for causal/predictive Granger testing, or when you need statistically EXACT prediction intervals — the PI of `hybridModel` are heuristic and OVER-CONSERVATIVE (see the traps). Also NOT when you have ONE clearly dominant model (a combination then only adds noise), or for very short series (`length(y) < 4` → a hard gate).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **no formal statistical stationarity precondition** — the components (auto.arima/ets/tbats) handle the differencing/seasonality themselves; no unit-root pre-test is needed. (Optionally, to understand the series: `c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test` + a confirmatory KPSS.)
- **structural preconditions (hard gates in the wrapper):** `y` a numeric vector/ts (NOT a matrix/DataFrame), `length(y) >= 4`, without NA/NaN/Inf (clean it first). `models` = ONE non-empty string with letters ⊆ `{a,e,f,n,s,t,z}` and **≥ 2 distinct** components.
- **the seasonal components (`s`/`t`/`z`) require `frequency(y) >= 2`** (otherwise a stop). In addition `s` (stlm) and `n` (nnetar) require **`length(y) > 2*frequency`**; if that is not met, the wrapper removes them EXPLICITLY (they are recorded in `dropped_models`) — a stop only if fewer than 2 remain.
- **`weights="cv.errors"` requires `length(y) >= windowSize + cvHorizon`** (the default windowSize=84) — otherwise a stop.

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| A single model (`auto.arima`/`ets`/`fable`, sections 03/16) | when one model clearly dominates or you want interpretable parameters/diagnostics |
| Online/adaptive combination (e.g. `opera` — ARCHIVED on ) | a streaming/regret-based combination with time-varying weights; unavailable here |
| Multivariate models (VAR/VECM, sections 04/05) | when there are cross-series dependencies/cointegration — a univariate combination ignores them |
| Bayesian model averaging (section 14) | when you want a posterior-weighted combination with full uncertainty quantification |

**Reading the output** (a named list, JSON-safe via `to_mcp`):

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `method` | fixed to `"hybridModel"` |
| `included_models` | which components ACTUALLY took part (after any automatic removal) |
| `n_models` | the number of actual components |
| `dropped_models` | those requested but NOT included (a length-based removal or a drop by `hybridModel` itself) — **always check it**, it shows whether the ensemble was silently downgraded |
| `weights_method` / `weights` | the weighting method + the per-model weights (a named list summing to ~1) |
| `error_method` | RMSE/MAE/MASE (relevant only if the weights ≠ equal) |
| `h`, `level`, `frequency` | the horizon, the PI levels, the seasonality |
| `point_forecast` | a `ts` → `to_mcp`: `{values,start,frequency}` — the central forecast |
| `lower` / `upper` | a matrix (h × length(level)) → `to_mcp`: nested rows + dim + dimnames — the PI bounds per level |
| `pi_combination` | `"extreme"` (the most extreme bounds of the components) or `"mean"` |
| `pi_disclaimer` | an EXPLICIT statement that the PI are OVER-CONSERVATIVE |
| `fit` | the raw hybridModel (stubbed by `to_mcp` — it keeps a compact summary) |

**Interpretation traps:**
- **The PI are OVER-CONSERVATIVE:** `lower`/`upper` have no guaranteed nominal coverage — they come from a combination heuristic (`extreme` = the most extreme bounds, `mean` = the average). Do not take them as strict statistical bounds (see `pi_disclaimer`). The reference itself points this out.
- **The silent downgrading of the ensemble:** `hybridModel` removes on its own the components that do not suit the series (e.g. `stlm`/`nnetar` when `length < 2*frequency`, `ets` when the seasonal period > 24). Always read `dropped_models`/`included_models` — you may have asked for 6 models and had 3 run.
- **The stochasticity of `nnetar` (`n`):** random initial weights → non-reproducible. The wrapper enforces a local `seed` (the default 42L, without contaminating the global RNG); if you change it, the forecasts with `n` change.
- **`insample.errors` is not recommended** (per the docs): it tends to overfit the weights; `equal` is more robust. `cv.errors` is theoretically better but SLOW and needs enough data.
- **Weights ≠ model importance:** a large weight means a low in-sample/CV error, NOT that the component is structurally "correct" — it is a purely predictive criterion.

**Sources:** the forecastHybrid ref manual — the `hybridModel` help page (David Shaub); Shaub & Ellis, the "forecastHybrid" vignette (, ); Bates & Granger 1969 "The Combination of Forecasts" (OR Quarterly); Timmermann 2006 "Forecast Combinations" (the Handbook of Economic Forecasting); Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, *Forecasting: Principles and Practice* (the component models ETS/ARIMA/STL/TBATS).


---

## §20. Yield curve / term structure — `c18_yield_curve/`

this category applies when you have a **cross-section of yields by maturity** (for one or more dates) and want to condense the whole curve into a few interpretable factors (level / slope / curvature) — typically as an input to a recession probit (#83) or as a spread-based risk indicator, not to test stationarity or time-series relationships.

---

### #87 Nelson-Siegel / Svensson / Diebold-Li factors — `YieldCurve` (`c18_yield_curve/nelson_siegel_svensson.py`)
**Functions:** `fit_nelson_siegel` → `Nelson.Siegel`, `NSrates` · `fit_svensson` → `Svensson`, `Srates`

**When:** when you have observed yields (spot yields) at a vector of maturities (pillars) and want to fit a **parametric curve** and extract the factors:
- **Nelson-Siegel (3 factors)** — `beta_0` (level), `beta_1` (slope), `beta_2` (curvature) + `lambda` (the decay). Parsimonious, stable, ideal for macro factor extraction and for feeding a probit/VAR. Diebold-Li (2006) is exactly this NS formulation with the level/slope/curvature interpretation (Diebold-Li 2006).
- **Svensson (4 factors)** — it adds `beta_3` + a second decay (`tau1`,`tau2`) for curves with **two humps**; it requires more pillars and a wider maturity range (Svensson 1994).

**When NOT:** (a) when you want an **arbitrage-free / affine** term structure (e.g. ACM/ABG term premia) — NS/Svensson is a descriptive fit, not a no-arbitrage model. (b) When you care about a simple **slope indicator** (the 10y-2y spread) — do not overkill it with a 3-4 factor fit. (c) When the yields are a time series of a single tenor and you want stationarity/cointegration — that belongs to 01/05, not here.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** no formal statistical precondition (it is cross-sectional curve fitting per date, not time-series inference — it presupposes no stationarity). But there are **hard structural gates** (in the wrapper):
- `maturities` numeric, without NA/Inf, **all > 0**, **strictly increasing**.
- the number of pillars **>= 4** (Nelson-Siegel) / **>= 6** (Svensson) — otherwise it is underdetermined.
- `rates` numeric, without NA/Inf; `ncol(rates) == length(maturities)` (a plain vector → 1 row/one date).
- `dates` (if supplied) convertible to a `Date`, of length `n_obs`, without NA; otherwise a synthetic deterministic calendar index.
- the maturities in **months** per the package convention (the docs: "maturity in months"), but the estimator works with the vector as it stands — be consistent with the unit (Guirreri, the YieldCurve manual).

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| `fit_nelson_siegel` (NS/Diebold-Li) | the default macro factor extraction; few pillars, stability, an interpretable level/slope/curvature |
| `fit_svensson` | curves with a second hump, a rich tenor grid (>= 6 pillars, a wide range); a better fit at the long end |
| A simple spread (10y-2y), outside the category | you want only a slope indicator for recessions — you do not need a factor fit |
| An affine / no-arbitrage term premium (ACM/ABG) | you want a decomposition into expectations vs a term premium — outside this package |
| The recession probit #83 | the natural consumer of the NS/Svensson factors — run it AFTER the fit |

**Reading the output:** the wrapper returns a named list. Via L2 `to_mcp`: the `indexed_time_series`/`ts` objects serialise as `{values,start,frequency}`, the `DataFrame` objects as a list of records.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `model` | `"Nelson.Siegel"` or `"Svensson"` |
| `factors` (an xts) | the factors per date: NS → `beta_0,beta_1,beta_2,lambda`; Svensson → `beta_0.beta_3,tau1,tau2` |
| `factors_df` (a DataFrame) | the chart-ready version with a `date` column + the factors |
| `fitted_rates` (an xts) | the fitted yields per maturity (the curve the model produces) |
| `residuals` (an xts) | observed − fitted per pillar (fit diagnostics) |
| `which_rate` (Svensson) | `"Spot"` (the default) or `"Forward"` |
| `interpretation` | the explicit mapping `beta_0=level, beta_1=slope, beta_2=curvature,..` |
| `n_obs`, `n_maturities` | the number of dates / pillars |

**Interpretation traps:**
- **The Svensson `which_rate` wrong-quantity trap (an adversarial-review HIGH):** `Svensson` estimates the observed **spot** curve; `fitted_rates`/`residuals` are meaningful **only** with `which_rate="Spot"`. The wrapper default is deliberately `"Spot"` — with `"Forward"` `Srates` returns instantaneous forward rates, so the residuals silently become the **wrong quantity** (a comparison of an observed spot with a fitted forward). Leave the default; set `"Forward"` only if you genuinely want the forward curve and do NOT interpret the residuals as a fit error.
- **Interpreting the slope:** in the NS convention `beta_1` is the short-run component; whether its sign is negative or positive depends on the direction of the definition — read the `interpretation` field, do not assume.
- **`lambda`/`tau` are not yields:** they are decay rates (the position of the hump), not interest rates — do not feed them into a probit as a spread.
- **Descriptive, not no-arbitrage:** the factors do not separate expectations from the term premium; do not read them as pure interest-rate expectations.
- **The maturity unit:** an inconsistent mix of months/years in `maturities` produces a distorted `lambda` and a poor fit — keep to one unit.

**Sources:** Diebold-Li 2006 (*Forecasting the Term Structure of Government Bond Yields*, J. Econometrics 130); Nelson-Siegel 1987 (*J. Business* 60); Svensson 1994 (*IMF WP 94/114*); the `YieldCurve` reference manual (Guirreri) — the `Nelson.Siegel`/`NSrates`/`Svensson`/`Srates` help pages; the wrapper footer "IMPLEMENTATION NOTE" + the adversarial-review HIGH (the which_rate default = Spot).


---

## §21. Business cycle dating — `c19_business_cycle_dating/`

it applies when the target is the **non-parametric dating of turning points** (peaks/troughs) and **phases** (expansion/recession) in a quarterly macro series — that is, "when did the recession start/end" — and not the estimation of a regime model or a filtered cyclical component.

### #88 Harding-Pagan BBQ (the quarterly Bry-Boschan turning points) — `BCDating` (`c19_business_cycle_dating/harding_pagan_bbq.py`)
**Functions:** `date_business_cycles` → `BBQ`, `average_over_phases` → `avgts`

**When:** when you have a **quarterly** univariate level series (real GDP, industrial production, an activity index) and want **peak/trough dates** and **phase durations** without a model — the classical "NBER-style" cycle dating of Harding-Pagan (Harding-Pagan 2002). `avgts` gives the mean value of **another** series (e.g. growth, inflation) per dated phase — for a descriptive comparison of expansions vs recessions.

**When NOT:** (a) a **non-quarterly** frequency — the BBQ is explicitly a quarterly Bry-Boschan; monthly data are not covered here (the gate `frequency == 4`). (b) When you want **probabilistic** regimes with endogenous switching probabilities → Markov switching (`MSwM`, section 10/regimes) — but note, `MSwM` covers gaussian/lm only. (c) When you want to **extract a cyclical component** (a gap) instead of dates → filters (`mFilter`/`sided_hp_filter`, section 10). (d) A multivariate composite cycle (a composite reference cycle from several series) — the BBQ is univariate.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- The BBQ is a **level-based turning-point** algorithm (local maxima/minima with minphase/mincycle rules), **not** a statistical test → **no formal stationarity is required**; it is applied to levels, not differences. No unit-root pre-test is needed.
- **A clean series**: the wrapper rejects `NA`/`Inf` (a hard gate); `avgts` in particular errors on an **internal NA** (documented in the help). Ensure a complete series before the call.
- **Sufficient length**: `length(y) > 2*mincycle` (a gate) — otherwise a full cycle does not fit.
- **Frequency consistency** for `average_over_phases`: `series` and `dates@states` of the same frequency (a gate).
- No transformation precondition (log/detrend) is imposed; the choice is the analyst's, depending on whether they date a "classical cycle" (levels) or a "growth cycle" (a deviation from trend).

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred over the BBQ |
|---|---|
| Markov switching (`MSwM`, regimes) | you want **regime probabilities** per period + endogenous transitions, not deterministic dates; gaussian/lm only |
| HP/band-pass/Hamilton filters (`mFilter`/`sided_hp_filter`, 10) | you want a **cyclical gap** (a continuous component), not discrete turning points |
| State space/DFA (`KFAS`/`MARSS`, 10) | a latent common cycle from **several** series |
| A monthly Bry-Boschan | monthly data (outside the surface of this package) |

**Reading the output** (the `date_business_cycles` structured list, after `to_mcp`):

| Field | Meaning (after serialization) |
|---|---|
| `states` | a regime `ts` **+1 = expansion / -1 = recession** per quarter → `{values,start,frequency}` |
| `peaks_index` / `troughs_index` | the **index positions** inside the series (not dates) — 1-based indices of `time` |
| `peaks_date` / `troughs_date` | the same peaks/troughs as quarter labels **"YYYYQn"** (a deterministic conversion) |
| `phases` | a `DataFrame` → records: `type` (Expansion/Recession), `start`, `end`, `duration` (in quarters), `state`, **`complete`** |
| `avg_expansion_duration` / `avg_recession_duration` | the mean duration **over complete (non-censored) phases only** |
| `n_complete_phases` | the number of complete peak-to-trough / trough-to-peak phases |
| `param`, `mincycle`, `minphase` | the rules that produced the dating (an audit trail) |
| `harding_pagan_bbq` | the raw S4 `BCDating` fit — `to_mcp` turns it into a **stub** (a heavy object) |

**Interpretation traps:**
- **The sign convention:** `+1 = expansion`, `-1 = recession` — do not read it the other way round (it is not a z-score/anomaly).
- **peaks/troughs = position indices, NOT dates.** For dates use `peaks_date`/`troughs_date`. A peak means *the end of an expansion / the start of a recession*.
- **Censored end phases:** the first phase (the start of the series → the 1st turning point) and the last one (the last turning point → the end) are **censored** (`complete = FALSE`) — they are not complete Harding-Pagan durations and are **excluded** from the averages. The package's native `summary` reports only complete durations; do not compare censored durations with complete ones.
- **An internal NA in `avgts` → an error** (not a silent omission): trailing/leading NA are dropped, but an internal NA errors — the wrapper rejects an all-NA input and warns.
- **mincycle/minphase determine the number** of turning points: values that are too large → "smoothing" and fewer phases; `mincycle > minphase` is enforced (a gate). The dating is not unique — it depends on these rules, which is why they are returned in the output.
- The package (v0.9.8, last updated 2019; archived/legacy) is deterministic, with no RNG — no seed is needed.

**Sources:** Harding-Pagan 2002 "Dissecting the Cycle" *JME* 49(2), 365–381 [the BBQ methodology]; Bry-Boschan 1971 [the algorithmic dating ancestor]; the `BCDating` v0.9.8 ref manual — the `BBQ`, `avgts` help pages (<); the wrapper footer "IMPLEMENTATION NOTE" (`c19_business_cycle_dating/harding_pagan_bbq.py`).

### #213 Change-point detection in the mean / variance / mean+variance — `change_point_detection` (`c19_business_cycle_dating/change_point_detection.py`)
**Functions:** `detect_changepoints` → `cpt.mean` / `cpt.var` / `cpt.meanvar` (the dispatch is via `statistic`), `changepoint_segments` → an accessor node (`cpts`/`param.est`/`seg.len`)

**When:** when you have a **univariate** series (of any frequency) and want to locate **WHERE** its structure changes — the **level** (`statistic="mean"`), the **volatility** (`statistic="variance"`, volatility regimes) or **both at once** (`statistic="meanvar"`). It returns the **positions** of the structural breaks, their number, the per-segment parameter estimates and the segment lengths, through a penalized segmentation (PELT/BinSeg/SegNeigh/AMOC). Ideal for detecting regime shifts, breaks in volatility, or structural breaks in the level of macro indicators without a regression model.

**When NOT:** (a) you want **cycle dating** (peaks/troughs, expansion/recession phases NBER-style) on a quarterly series → the BBQ (`BCDating`, `#88`). (b) You want breaks in **regression coefficients** (structural stability) with dates/a number → Bai-Perron/CUSUM (`structural_change`). (c) You want **probabilistic** regimes with endogenous switching → Markov switching (`MSwM`). (d) You want a **continuous cyclical gap** instead of discrete breaks → filters (`mFilter`/`sided_hp_filter`, section 10).

**Preconditions:**
- **A clean, regularly spaced series:** the wrapper rejects `NA`/`Inf` (a hard gate); an interior NA causes a package error (changepoint assumes regularly spaced data).
- **Univariate only:** changepoint treats a matrix input as **several datasets** (it returns a `list`, not a `cpt`) — blocked.
- **test.stat ↔ method compatibility:** the non-parametric `CSS`/`CUSUM` do **not** work with PELT (a gate: they require AMOC/BinSeg/SegNeigh).
- **Penalty rules:** `Manual` requires `pen_value>0`; `Asymptotic` requires `pen_value ∈ (0,1]` (a type-I error); `pen_value` **a number only** (the package's text-formula path does an internal eval/parse → blocked as an injection surface).
- **Q (BinSeg/SegNeigh):** the maximum number of breaks/segments must satisfy `Q < n/minseglen` (a gate).

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| The BBQ (`BCDating`, #88) | cycle dating (peaks/troughs/phases) on a quarterly series, not break positions in the mean/variance |
| Bai-Perron / CUSUM (`structural_change`) | breaks in regression **coefficients** (structural stability) |
| Markov switching (`MSwM`) | regime **probabilities** + endogenous transitions instead of deterministic positions |
| `statistic` = mean/variance/meanvar | a change in the level / the volatility / both at once |
| `method` = PELT/BinSeg/SegNeigh/AMOC | exact-linear (the default) / approximate-fast / exact-slow / at most 1 break |

**Reading the output** (the `detect_changepoints` structured list, after `to_mcp`):

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `changepoints` | 1-based **SEGMENT-END INDICES** (the last obs of a segment); **NOT** the final n, **NOT** dates |
| `n_changepoints` / `n_segments` | the number of breaks and of segments (= breaks + 1) |
| `segments` | a `DataFrame` → records: `segment`, `start`, `end`, `length` + the per-segment parameter columns |
| `segment_params` / `global_params` | the per-segment vs the global estimates (e.g. the Gamma `shape`, the variance-assumed `mean` = global) |
| `param_est` | the raw named list of `param.est` (the names depend on the test.stat) |
| `penalty`/`method`/`test_stat`/`minseglen`/`Q`/`pen_value_used` | the rules that produced the segmentation (an audit trail) |
| `fit` | the raw S4 `cpt` fit — `to_mcp` turns it into a **stub**; a register field for `changepoint_segments` |

**Interpretation traps:**
- **`changepoints` = SEGMENT-END indices, 1-based, WITHOUT the final n.** A change point i means "the segment ends at obs i; the next one starts at i+1". They are not dates.
- **The names of param.est CHANGE with the test.stat:** `mean`/`variance` (Normal), `scale`+`shape` (Gamma), `rate` (Exponential), `lambda` (Poisson). The wrapper classifies them generically (length==nseg → per segment, otherwise global) — do not always assume mean/variance.
- **`cpt.var`: the mean is handled** (estimated via MLE or supplied with `know_mean`/`mu`) and is **global** (an assumed mean), not per segment — only the variance is per segment.
- **`penalty="Manual"` with `pen_value=0` silently over-segments** (no penalty at all); `"None"` makes every point a change point. Gated/documented footguns.
- **`CSS`/`CUSUM` do not work with PELT** (the package's "Invalid Method") — a hard gate requires AMOC/BinSeg/SegNeigh.
- **Deterministic** — no RNG; no seed is needed (verified live with `identical`).

**Sources:** Killick, Fearnhead & Eckley 2012 "Optimal detection of changepoints with a linear computational cost" (PELT) *JASA* 107(500), 1590–1598; Killick & Eckley 2014 "changepoint: An the reference Package for Changepoint Analysis" *JSS* 58(3), 1–19; Scott & Knott 1974 (Binary Segmentation) *Biometrics* 30(3); Auger & Lawrence 1989 (Segment Neighbourhoods) *Bull. Math. Biol.* 51(1); Zhang & Siegmund 2007 (MBIC) *Biometrics* 63; Hinkley 1970 (a change in the mean) *Biometrika* 57; the `change_point_detection` v2.3 ref manual — `cpt.mean`/`cpt.var`/`cpt.meanvar`/`cpts`/`param.est` (the args/values confirmed live) (<); the wrapper footer "IMPLEMENTATION NOTE".

### #214 Bayesian change point (the Barry-Hartigan PPM, MCMC) — `bayesian_change_point` (`c19_business_cycle_dating/bayesian_change_point.py`)
**Functions:** `detect_change_points` → `bayesian_change_point` (the univariate mean-change case)

**When:** when you have a **univariate sequential** series (real GDP, industrial production, an activity index, a spread) and want a **Bayesian** detection of changes in the **mean** — that is, the **posterior probability of a change at EVERY position** and a **smoothed posterior level**, through the Product Partition Model of Barry-Hartigan (1993) with MCMC. Ideal when you want **soft/posterior probabilities** and Bayesian model averaging over partitions, rather than deterministic dates or one single "best" segmentation.

**When NOT:** (a) when you want **NBER-style peaks/troughs and dated** expansion/recession phases → the Harding-Pagan BBQ (`BCDating`, #88). (b) A change in the **variance / the whole distribution** or a **multivariate** one → `energy_statistics_nonparametric` (E-Divisive) / `change_point_detection` (PELT). (c) A **regression/panel/graph** change point (`x`/`id`/`adj`) — **scoped out** here (the univariate mean-change case only). (d) Probabilistic **regimes** with endogenous transitions → Markov switching (`MSwM`). (e) A length **< 4** (a hard gate — segfault protection).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- bcp is a **Bayesian PPM** over levels — **no formal stationarity** is required; it is applied to the level series, not to differences. No unit-root pre-test is needed.
- **A clean series**: `bayesian_change_point` accepts `NA`/`Inf` **silently** and produces an invalid result (live-verified) → the wrapper **rejects** them (a hard gate).
- **A minimum length** of `length(y) >= 4` (a gate): anything smaller causes a **segfault** in the C core `rcpp_bcpM` (live-verified crashes at n=2,3).
- **Stochastic (MCMC)**: the `seed` (default 20240719) is set **inside** the wrapper → full reproducibility.

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred over bcp |
|---|---|
| The Harding-Pagan BBQ (`BCDating`, #88) | you want **dated peaks/troughs and phases** (deterministic dates) rather than a posterior probability of change |
| PELT/BinSeg (`change_point_detection`) | you want an exact **MAP segmentation** with a penalty (mean/var/meanvar), not Bayesian averaging |
| E-Divisive / ECP (`energy_statistics_nonparametric`) | a non-parametric change in the **whole distribution**, multivariate |
| Markov switching (`MSwM`) | **regime probabilities** + endogenous transitions instead of a partition |

**Reading the output** (the `detect_change_points` structured list, after `to_mcp`):

| Field | Meaning (after serialization) |
|---|---|
| `posterior_prob` | an array of length `n`; the posterior probability of a change **at each position**; the **LAST ONE = NA** (the last position cannot host a change) → a JSON null |
| `posterior_mean` | the smoothed **posterior level** per position (model-averaged, NOT constant within a block) |
| `posterior_var` | the posterior variance per position |
| `changepoint_index` | the **1-based positions** where `posterior_prob > threshold` (the final NA is excluded automatically) |
| `changepoint_prob` / `n_changepoints` | the probabilities at the detected positions / their number |
| `posterior_expected_blocks` | `mean(blocks)` per MCMC iteration — the expected number of segments |
| `threshold`,`p0`,`w0`,`burnin`,`mcmc`,`seed` | the rules/parameters that produced the result (an audit trail) |
| `bcp_fit` | the raw S3 `bayesian_change_point` fit — `to_mcp` turns it into a **stub** |

**Interpretation traps:**
- **The last `posterior_prob` is NA** by construction (the last position cannot host a change — there is no following block); **do not read it as a 0**. The wrapper confirms that **ONLY** the last one is NA; any interior NA ⇒ a degenerate fit ⇒ a `stop`.
- **A change AT position i ⇒ a boundary AFTER i** (a new segment starts at i+1); it is a **position index**, NOT a date.
- **`posterior_mean` is NOT constant within a segment** — it is a Bayesian average over all the partitions (a Barry-Hartigan characteristic, deliberate); no single "best" partition emerges.
- **Stochastic (MCMC):** the same `seed` ⇒ an `identical` output (live-verified); without a reseed two calls differ.
- **`bayesian_change_point` accepts NA/Inf silently** and produces garbage (live-verified) → a hard gate; **`n < 4` ⇒ a segfault** → a hard gate (`>= 4`).
- `p0` = the prior probability of a change (larger ⇒ more changes); `w0` = the signal-to-noise prior; the detection depends on `p0`/`w0` + `threshold` — it is **not unique**, which is why they are returned in the output.

**Sources:** Barry & Hartigan 1993 "A Bayesian Analysis for Change Point Problems" *JASA* 88(421), 309–319 [the PPM]; Erdman & Emerson 2007 "bcp: An the reference Package for Performing a Bayesian Analysis of Change Point Problems" *J. Stat. Software* 23(3); Wang & Emerson 2015 [the bcp ≥ 4.0 methods]; the `bayesian_change_point` v4.0.4 ref manual — the `bayesian_change_point` help page (<, live-verified); the wrapper footer "IMPLEMENTATION NOTE" (`c19_business_cycle_dating/bayesian_change_point.py`).

### #215 Energy-statistics non-parametric multivariate change-point detection — `energy_statistics_nonparametric` (`c19_business_cycle_dating/energy_statistics_nonparametric.py`)
**Functions:** `detect_changepoints_divisive` → `e.divisive`, `detect_changepoints_agglo` → `e.agglo`

**When:** you have a **multivariate** series (an n×d numeric matrix — e.g. several macro indicators together) and want to locate **multiple change points in the distribution** (a structural change in the mean/variance/higher moments) **without a parametric assumption**. The method rests on the **energy distance** (Székely-Rizzo): a non-parametric measure of the equality of distributions, sensitive to changes in moments of any order. Two complementary algorithms: `e.divisive` (a top-down division with **permutation-test significance**, a data-driven number of changes) and `e.agglo` (a bottom-up **agglomerative** merging with a penalized goodness of fit from an initial segmentation).

**When NOT:** (a) **univariate turning-point dating** (peaks/troughs, expansion/recession phases) → `BCDating` (#88) — ecp gives distributional change points, not the cycle. (b) You want **probabilistic regimes** with endogenous switching → Markov switching (`MSwM`). (c) You want a **cyclical gap** (a continuous component) → filters (`mFilter`/`sided_hp_filter`, #10). (d) A break in **regression coefficients** (not in the distribution of the data) → `structural_change`/CUSUM. (e) A very small sample: `nrow(X) < 2*min.size` (a hard gate).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **A clean matrix:** the wrapper rejects `NA`/`NaN`/`Inf` (a hard gate) — a **live-verified silent-wrong**: ecp with an NA does not error, it silently returns no change point.
- **Sufficient length:** `nrow(X) ≥ 2*min.size` (a gate) — otherwise two segments of the minimum size do not fit (a silent no-CP in ecp).
- **A valid permutation budget:** `the reference` a positive integer (a gate) — the reference=0 runs but gives meaningless p-values.
- No formal stationarity/normality is required — the method is non-parametric; it is applied to the levels.

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| `detect_changepoints_divisive` (E-divisive) | a data-driven number of changes + a **formal permutation-test** significance (p-values per split); the **default** choice; stochastic → seeded |
| `detect_changepoints_agglo` (E-agglomerative) | you have an **initial segmentation** (`member`) or want a **deterministic** bottom-up procedure with a penalized GOF; no permutation test |
| The Harding-Pagan BBQ (`BCDating`, #88) | **univariate quarterly** data; you want peaks/troughs and phases (turning points), not distributional change points |
| Markov switching (`MSwM`) | you want **regime probabilities** + endogenous transitions; gaussian/lm only |
| `structural_change`/CUSUM | a break in the **coefficients** of a linear model, not in the distribution |

**Reading the output** (a structured list, after `to_mcp`):

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `changepoints` | the interior change points (sorted); a position `p` = a change **BEFORE** observation `p` (2≤p≤n); **WITHOUT** the boundaries 1 and n+1 |
| `n_changepoints` / `n_segments` | the number of changes / segments (divisive: `n_segments == k_hat`, `n_changepoints == k_hat-1`) |
| `cluster` | an integer vector of the segment assignment per observation (of length n) |
| `estimates_raw` | the raw ecp `.estimates` **WITH** the boundaries (an audit trail) |
| `p_values` / `n_significant` (divisive) | the p-value per split in `order.found` order; the **last one** = the terminal non-significant split; `n_significant` = the number with `p < sig.lvl` |
| `gof_progression` / `gof_final` (agglo) | the penalized goodness of fit per merging step |
| `alpha`, `sig_lvl`, `the reference`, `min_size`, `k`, `penalty` | the rules that produced the result (an audit) |
| `seed` (divisive) | the seed that was used (reproducibility) |

**Interpretation traps:**
- **The ecp `.estimates` include the boundaries** (position 1 and n+1 for divisive; a circular wrap for agglo) — they are **NOT** change points. The wrapper removes them; report **only** `changepoints`.
- **`e.divisive` is STOCHASTIC** (the reference permutations): without a seed the p-values (and marginal splits) change from call to call — the wrapper calls `set.seed(seed)` **inside** (the default 20240101). `e.agglo` is **deterministic** given X/member.
- **Silent-wrongs** that are blocked: `NA`/`Inf` in X → silently no CP; `2*min.size > nrow(X)` → silently no CP; `the reference=0` → meaningless p-values; a vector instead of a matrix → a cryptic error; a wrong-length `member` → a silent matrix recycling.
- **`p_values` do NOT align with the sorted `changepoints`** — they are in `order.found` order with one extra terminal (non-significant) split; for the number of significant ones use `n_significant`.
- **`alpha`** is the moment index of the energy distance in `(0,2]` (the default is 1), **NOT** a significance level — do not confuse it with `sig.lvl`.
- **`e.agglo` with `penalty="none"`** can over-segment noisy data; `"num_cp"` penalises the number. The dating is **not unique** (it depends on `alpha`/`member`/`penalty`), which is why they are returned in the output.

**Sources:** Matteson & James 2014 "A Nonparametric Approach for Multiple Change Point Analysis of Multivariate Data" *JASA* 109(505) 334-345 [E-divisive]; James & Matteson 2014 "ecp: An the reference Package for Nonparametric Multiple Change Point Analysis of Multivariate Data" *JSS* 62(7) 1-25 [E-divisive and E-agglomerative]; Székely & Rizzo 2005 "Hierarchical clustering via joint between-within distances" *J. Classification* 22 151-183 [the energy distance]; the `energy_statistics_nonparametric` v3.1.6 ref manual — the `e.divisive`, `e.agglo` help pages (live-verified, <); the wrapper footer "IMPLEMENTATION NOTE" (`c19_business_cycle_dating/energy_statistics_nonparametric.py`).
