## §22. Inequality — `c22_inequality/`

when this category applies: when the question is not about the level or the dynamics of a time series but about **how unequally a quantity is distributed across a population at a given moment** — that is, you have a **cross-section** of non-negative values (incomes, wealth, shares, weights) and want a **scalar inequality index** (Gini, Theil, Atkinson, Ricci-Schutz, Kolm, the coefficient of variation, generalized entropy) or the **Lorenz curve as purely numeric data** for the frontend. It is **descriptive/distributional**, not inferential: no null hypothesis, no stationarity, no regression. A single method covers the category (#91, `inequality_indices_lorenz`). If instead you want to model **how covariates shift the tail** of an outcome distribution (Growth-at-Risk) go to cat. 12 `quantile_regression` (#64); if you want tail metrics of **returns** (VaR/ES) go to cat. 12 `PerformanceAnalytics` (#65). Here you measure **distributional inequality**, not tail risk.

---

### #91 Inequality indices + the Lorenz curve — `inequality_indices_lorenz` (`c22_inequality/inequality_indices_lorenz.py`)
**Functions:** `compute_inequality` [`ineq(x, parameter, type, na.rm)`], `lorenz_curve` [`Lc(x, plot=FALSE)` + `ineq(type="Gini")`]

**When:** you have a cross-sectional vector (of length ≥ 2, without NA/Inf) and want either (a) a **scalar inequality index** — `Gini` (0=complete equality, 1=maximum), `Theil`/`entropy` (generalized entropy, **additively decomposable** into within/between groups), `Atkinson` (with an explicit inequality-aversion parameter), `RS` (Ricci-Schutz / Pietra: the share that must be redistributed), `Kolm` (absolute inequality, invariant to adding a constant), `var`/`square.var` (the coefficient of variation) — or (b) the **Lorenz curve** (`p`, `L`, `L_general`) as numeric data for a chart. Ideal for comparing inequality across countries/periods/groups.

**When NOT:** (a) the tail of a distribution of **returns** (VaR/ES/downside) → cat. 12 `PerformanceAnalytics` (#65), not an inequality index. (b) How **exogenous conditions** shift the lower tail of an outcome (Growth-at-Risk) → cat. 12 `quantile_regression` (#64). (c) **Poverty** indices (headcount/gap/FGT) or **concentration** indices (a concentration index) → `pov`/`conc` are **not exposed** in the wrapper (out of scope). (d) A **within/between decomposition** of the Theil index by groups: the wrapper gives only the overall index of one vector — the decomposition must be done manually per subgroup. (e) Theoretical/grouped Lorenz curves (`Lc.mehran`, `theorLc`, a weighted `n`) — excluded (the plain empirical Lc only).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** **no formal statistical precondition** (it is not a test/regression — it is a deterministic descriptive index over a cross-section; stationarity/normality are meaningless here). The only gates are **structural/mathematical** and the wrapper imposes them itself:

| Gate | Requirement | Why |
|---|---|---|
| numeric + `length ≥ 2` + no NA/Inf | every input `x` | the index needs ≥2 units; `na.rm=FALSE` deliberately (the NA are blocked before `inequality_indices_lorenz`) |
| **non-negativity** `x ≥ 0` | **only** for `Gini/Atkinson/Theil/entropy` + `lorenz_curve` | the mathematical definition / the Lorenz curve; **note:** `inequality_indices_lorenz` does NOT error by itself on negatives — the gate comes from the project. `RS/Kolm/var/square.var` **allow** negative values |
| **`sum(x) > 0`** | `lorenz_curve` | all zeros pass the `≥0` gate but `Lc` divides by 0 → a `NaN` that silently becomes a JSON `null` (an adversarial-review MEDIUM) |
| `parameter` a finite length-1 scalar | when supplied | otherwise a stop |
| a post-check: the index a finite scalar; the Lc has the fields `p`/`L` | every output | an invalid result does not escape |

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| `type="Gini"` | a headline single-number inequality measure, sensitive mainly to the **centre** of the distribution; the most widespread/comparable |
| `type="Theil"` / `type="entropy"` | you want an **additive decomposition** into within/between groups (the GE family); `entropy@param=1`/`Theil@param=0` == Theil's T / GE(1) (more sensitive to the upper tail); `entropy@param=0`/`Theil@param=1` == the mean log deviation / GE(0) (sensitive to the lower tail) |
| `type="Atkinson"` | you want an **explicit** inequality-aversion parameter epsilon (`parameter`): a larger epsilon ⇒ more weight on the lower tail; a normative/welfare interpretation |
| `type="Kolm"` | you want **absolute** inequality (invariant to adding the same amount to everyone), not relative |
| `type="RS"` | you want the "Robin Hood" interpretation (the share of the total to redistribute for equality) |
| `lorenz_curve` (+ Lorenz dominance) | a visual/non-parametric comparison: if curve A lies **everywhere** above B, A unambiguously has less inequality (dominance) — stronger than any scalar index |
| cat. 12 `quantile_regression`/`PerformanceAnalytics` | a conditional-on-X tail (GaR) or risk metrics of returns — **a different question** |

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp` — a named list → recursion → atomic fields):
- `compute_inequality` → `index` (the scalar index), `type` (which index), `parameter` (`NA_real_` if the package default was used), `n` (the sample size). **The scale**: `Gini/Atkinson/RS ∈ [0,1]` (0=equality); `Theil/entropy ≥ 0` (with no upper bound of 1 — do **not** read it as a percentage); `Kolm` is in **units of x** (absolute, not 0-1); `var`=the CV, `square.var`=the CV². **A parameter trap:** the defaults are `Atkinson` 0.5, `Kolm` 1, `entropy` 0.5, `Theil` 0 — if you do not pass a `parameter`, the `NA_real_` in the output means "the package default", **not** "no parameter". **A Theil-vs-entropy trap:** in `inequality_indices_lorenz` the parameter is inverted between the two `type` values — `entropy@1 == Theil@0` (== the `Theil` default; Theil's T / GE(1), the upper tail), `entropy@0 == Theil@1` (the mean log deviation / GE(0), the lower tail) — the same number under a different name; choose deliberately which tail you emphasise.
- `lorenz_curve` → `p` (the cumulative population share 0.1), `L` (the cumulative share of the total / the ordinary Lorenz curve 0.1), `L_general` (the generalized Lorenz curve = `L × mean` — in units of x, incorporating the **level** as well, not only the shape), `gini` (the Gini coefficient of the same series, for consistency), `n`. The interpretation: `p*100%` of the population holds `L(p)*100%` of the total; the distance from the diagonal = the inequality. `p`/`L` are **chart-ready arrays** (`to_mcp` serialises the atomic numeric vector as a JSON array) — the frontend draws the curve, the wrapper does **not** make a chart. **An ordinary-vs-generalized trap:** two countries may have the same ordinary `L` (the same shape of inequality) but a different `L_general` because their means differ — for a **welfare** comparison look at `L_general` (Shorrocks), for a **relative inequality** comparison look at `L`/`gini`.

**Sources:** the `inequality_indices_lorenz` ref (`help("ineq")`, `help("Lc")`, live-verified) < Cowell 2000 "Measurement of Inequality" (the Handbook of Income Distribution, Atkinson-Bourguignon eds.); Cowell 1995 *Measuring Inequality*, Prentice Hall; Atkinson 1970 (*JET* 2:244, the Atkinson index and inequality aversion); Theil 1967 *Economics and Information Theory* (the Theil/entropy indices); Arnold 1987 *Majorization and the Lorenz Order*, Springer (Lorenz dominance); Shorrocks 1983 "Ranking Income Distributions", *Economica* 50(197):3-17 (the generalized Lorenz curve); Kolm 1976 "Unequal Inequalities I", *JET* 12(3):416-442 (absolute inequality).


---


### #224 Tax progressivity/redistribution + a subgroup decomposition of inequality — `IC2` (`c22_inequality/tax_progressivity_redistribution.py`)
**Functions:** `ic2_sgini` [`calcSGini(x,w,param)` — the extended/S-Gini], `ic2_sconc` [`calcSConc(x,y,w,param)` — the concentration index], `ic2_atkinson` [`calcAtkinson(x,w,epsilon)`], `ic2_gei` [`calcGEI(x,w,alpha)` — generalized entropy], `ic2_lorenz` [a REPRODUCTION of `curveLoCo` as numeric data, WITHOUT a plot], `ic2_decomp_sgini` [`decompSGini(x,z,w,param,decomp,ELMO)`], `ic2_decomp_gei` [`decompGEI(x,z,w,alpha,ELMO)`], `ic2_decomp_atkinson` [`decompAtkinson(x,z,w,epsilon,decomp,ELMO)`]

**When:** you have a cross-section of non-negative values (income/wealth/tax/expenditure) and want: (a) an **extended/single-parameter Gini** with an explicit tail weight (`param`), an **Atkinson** index (the inequality aversion `epsilon`), or a **GEI** (Theil-T `alpha=1` / the mean log deviation `alpha=0`); (b) a **concentration index** ranked by ANOTHER variable (e.g. the tax by pre-tax income) → the building blocks of **Kakwani progressivity** and **Reynolds-Smolensky redistribution**; (c) the **Lorenz curve** (`p`, `L`, `L_general`) as numeric data; (d) a **SUBGROUP decomposition** of an index into within / between / (overlap|stratification|cross|residual) by a factor.

**When NOT:** (a) a plain scalar Gini/RS/Kolm/var **without** an extended parameter or a decomposition → #91 `inequality_indices_lorenz`. (b) The tail of **returns** (VaR/ES) → #65; a conditional-on-X GaR → #64. (c) **Poverty** indices (FGT/headcount) — not exposed. (d) Time-series dynamics. (e) `curveConcent` is plot-only — not exposed (the numeric concentration is covered by `ic2_sconc`).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** **no formal statistical precondition** — the indices are deterministic/closed-form (no seed). All the gates are **structural** and the wrapper imposes them (IC2 very often returns **silently NULL/a wrong result** instead of an error):

| Gate | Requirement | Why (live-verified IC2 1.0.1) |
|---|---|---|
| `x` numeric, `length ≥ 2`, no NA/Inf, `x ≥ 0`, `sum(x) > 0` | every input | a negative `x` → IC2 returns an ENTIRE `NULL`; NA → IC2 **silently removes** rows; a zero mean → NULL |
| **strictly** `x > 0` | Atkinson with `epsilon==1`, GEI with `alpha ∈ {0,1}` | a zero at those parameters → IC2 NULL (a geometric mean/log); `epsilon≠1`/`alpha∉{0,1}` accept zeros |
| `w`: numeric, `length==length(x)`, no NA/Inf, `w > 0` | when supplied | a wrong length → IC2 **silently recycles**; NA weights → a silent removal; `w≤0` → an error deep inside |
| `param`/`epsilon` finite and `> 0`; `alpha` finite (any sign) | the parameter | `param≤0` → NULL; an extreme `alpha` → an **overflow to Inf** (a post-gate) |
| `z` a factor or atomic (→a factor), `length==n`, no NA, **≥ 2 non-empty groups** | the decomposition | a non-factor → IC2 silently NULL; 1 group → `between=0`, pointless |
| a post-check: the index a finite scalar; the **recomposition** \|total − the sum of the components\| ≤ 1e-6 | every output | overflow/NULL and a wrong decomposition do not escape |

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| #91 `inequality_indices_lorenz` | a headline Gini/Theil/Atkinson/Kolm **without** an extended parameter or a group decomposition |
| `ic2_sgini` with `param>1` | an extended Gini with an explicit weight on the poor (`param=2`=the classical Gini) |
| `ic2_gei` with `alpha=1/0` | you want a **fully additive** within+between decomposition (the GE family) |
| `ic2_decomp_atkinson` BDA vs DP | BDA is **multiplicative** (`1-(1-w)(1-b)`) vs DP **additive** (`within+between+residual`) |
| `ic2_sconc` + `ic2_sgini` (the difference) | Kakwani = `C_tax − G_preTax`; Reynolds-Smolensky = `G_preTax − C_postTax` (the redistribution of taxes/benefits) |
| `ic2_lorenz` + dominance | a non-parametric comparison of distributions (curve A everywhere above B) |

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `ic2_sgini`/`ic2_sconc`/`ic2_atkinson`/`ic2_gei` → `index` (the scalar), `index_name` (`SGini`/`SConc`/`Atk`/`GEI`), `parameter`+`parameter_name` (`param`/`epsilon`/`alpha`), `n`, `weighted`.
- `ic2_lorenz` → `p` (the cumulative population share 0.1, **chart-ready**, n+1 points including `(0,0)`), `L` (the ordinary Lorenz curve 0.1), `L_general` (the generalized one = `L × mean`, in units of x — it incorporates the **level**, Shorrocks), `gini`, `mean`, `n`.
- `ic2_decomp_*` → `within`/`between`, `third_component`+`third_name` (`overlap` SGini-BM / `stratif` SGini-YL / `cross` Atk-BDA / `residual` Atk-DP), `between_elmo` (the Elbers "maximum" between component; `NA` if `ELMO=FALSE`; **outside** the identity), `reconciled_total`+`reconcile_error`, `decomp_method`, `groups` (a DataFrame per group: `group`/`index`/`share`/`weight`[/`contribution`]), `n_groups`.

**Traps (live-verified):** (1) **the extended-Gini `param`**: `param=2`=the classical Gini; `param>1` is positive; `param→1`=0; `0<param<1` is **NEGATIVE** (a valid S-Gini but unconventional — for a headline use `param≥1`). (2) **The Atkinson decomposition**: BDA is **MULTIPLICATIVE** (`total=1-(1-within)(1-between)`) — do **NOT** sum `within+between+cross`; DP is **ADDITIVE**. GEI/SGini are additive. (3) **Kakwani/redistribution = a DIFFERENCE** of a concentration index and a Gini, not a single output — the wrapper gives the building blocks. (4) `betweenELMO` is not part of any recomposition identity.

**Sources:** the IC2 ref (`help(calcSGini/calcSConc/calcAtkinson/calcGEI/curveLorenz/decompSGini/decompGEI/decompAtkinson)`, IC2 1.0.1, live-verified) < Kakwani 1977 (*Economic Journal* 87:71, tax progressivity); Atkinson 1970 (*JET* 2:244); Blackorby-Donaldson-Auersperg 1981 (*Canadian J. Econ.* 14:665, BDA); Das-Parikh 1982 (*Empirical Economics* 7:23, DP); Bhattacharya-Mahalanobis 1967 (*JASA* 62:143, BM) & Yitzhaki-Lerman 1991 (*Review of Income and Wealth* 37:313, YL); Shorrocks 1980 (*Econometrica* 48:613, GE decomposability) & Elbers et al. 2005 (World Bank WP 3687, ELMO); Reynolds-Smolensky 1977 (redistribution).

### #225 The drivers of inequality change: RIF regressions + a regression-based decomposition — `drivers_inequality_change` (`c22_inequality/drivers_inequality_change.py`)
**Functions:** `rif_influence` [`rif(x, weights, method, quantile, kernel)`], `rif_regression` [`rifr(..)`], `rif_regression_se` [`rifrSE(.., Nboot, confidence)` — a SEEDED bootstrap], `gini_decomposition` [`gini_decomp(x, z, weights)`], `mld_decomposition` [`mld_decomp(x, z, weights)`], `dineq_regression_decomp` [`dineq_rb(formula, weights, data)` — Fields], `dineq_change_decomp` [`dineq_change_rb(..)` — the Yun price/quantity decomposition]

**When:** you have **income microdata** (survey weights + covariates) and the question is not "how much inequality" but **"WHAT drives it / how did it change"**: (a) `rif_influence`/`rif_regression` — the marginal effect of covariates on a **distributional statistic** (a quantile/gini/variance) through an unconditional-quantile / RIF regression (Firpo-Fortin-Lemieux); `rif_regression_se` adds bootstrap inference. (b) `gini_decomposition`/`mld_decomposition` — the decomposition of an index into **within / between (/ overlap)** by one categorical grouping. (c) `dineq_regression_decomp` (Fields 2003) — the contribution of **several** characteristics (+ a residual) to total inequality, summing to 100%. (d) `dineq_change_decomp` (Yun 2006) — the decomposition of the **CHANGE** in the variance of log income between two years into a **price effect** (a change in the coefficients) vs a **quantity effect** (a change in composition).

**When NOT:** (a) a plain scalar index or a Lorenz curve without covariates → #91 `inequality_indices_lorenz`. (b) Tax progressivity / a single-index decomposition (Kakwani/Reynolds-Smolensky) → #224 `IC2`. (c) A parametric fit of the income distribution (GB2/Dagum) → #227 `GB2`. (d) How **exogenous conditions** shift the tail of an outcome (Growth-at-Risk) → cat. 12 `quantile_regression` (#64); tail metrics of **returns** (VaR/ES) → #65. (e) The time-series dynamics of an index.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** **no formal statistical precondition** (descriptive/decompositional, not a hypothesis test). The gates are structural/mathematical and the wrapper imposes them:

| Gate | Requirement | Why |
|---|---|---|
| numeric `x`, `length ≥ 2`, no NA/Inf | every income input | the package **silently** does a complete.cases drop on NA → blocked here |
| **non-negativity** `x ≥ 0` | `gini_decomposition` (+ `method='gini'` in the RIF functions) | `gini_decomp` does **NOT** filter negatives → a silently wrong Gini; the gate is imposed project-side |
| weights: `length == n`, no NA, **STRICTLY > 0** | wherever supplied | a `length` mismatch → a silent recycling (live: a z of length 250 vs an x of 500 → n=500); NA weights → silently 0; a 0 → an NA RIF |
| `z` (the group): `length == n`, no NA, `≥ 2` groups | the decomposition | a single group → between≡0 (degenerate) |
| the formula: a numeric response + `≥ 1` covariate; all the variables in the data | rifr/rifrSE/dineq_rb/dineq_change_rb | otherwise a stop; a `y ≤ 0` is **silently** deleted (a log) → a **hard stop only if all** `y ≤ 0`, otherwise `n_deleted` is reported |
| `method`/`kernel` via `match.arg`; `quantile ∈ (0,1)` (a scalar only for rifrSE); `Nboot`/`seed` positive integers; `confidence ∈ (0,1)` | the configuration | rifrSE with a vector quantile → "condition has length > 1" |
| a post-check: finite indices/coefficients | every output | a degenerate/collinear fit or `dq=0` (the rectangular kernel) → Inf/NA → a stop |

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| `rif_influence` | you want the RIF **vector** (an input for a downstream RIF regression / a health-inequality decomposition); the recentering: the weighted mean == the index |
| `rif_regression` (deterministic) | the marginal effects of covariates on a quantile/gini/variance, fast, without inference; it supports **vector quantiles** |
| `rif_regression_se` (a bootstrap, SEEDED) | you need SE/CI/Z/P on the RIF coefficients; **one** quantile only |
| `gini_decomposition` | within/between **+ overlap** (the interaction) of the Gini by one categorical variable; the overlap ≠ 0 when the groups overlap |
| `mld_decomposition` (GE(0)) | a **clean** within+between decomposition (no overlap); the mean log deviation is additively decomposable |
| `dineq_regression_decomp` (Fields) | **several** characteristics at once: the contribution of each covariate (+ the residual) to total inequality (4 indices); they sum to 100% |
| `dineq_change_decomp` (Yun) | **two years**: the change in inequality per characteristic split into **price** (a change in the coefficients) vs **quantity** (a change in composition) |

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp` — a DataFrame → records, a named numeric → atomic fields, a raw fit → a stub):
- `rif_influence` → `rif` (a chart-ready array), `recentered_stat` (== the index, live-verified), `method`/`quantile`/`kernel`/`weighted`/`n`.
- `rif_regression` → `coefficients` a **UNIFIED** DataFrame (`term, quantile, coef, se, t, p`) — **normalised** by the wrapper because `rifr` **changes shape by method** (quantile: `Coef/SE/t/p` matrices + an `adjusted_r2` matrix; gini/variance: a `coefficients` matrix + a scalar `adjusted_r2`); `adjusted_r2` a df; `fit`=the raw object (a stub).
- `rif_regression_se` → `coefficients` a df (`term, coef, lower, upper, se, z_value, p_value, signif`); **deterministic given the `seed`** (a bootstrap via `boot`, `identical` verified).
- `gini_decomposition` → `decomposition` a named numeric (`gini_total, gini_within, gini_between, gini_overlap`) — **within+between do NOT sum** to the total without the `overlap`; `by_group` a df (the `gini_group_contribution` sums to `gini_within`).
- `mld_decomposition` → `decomposition` (`mld_total, mld_within, mld_between` — **within+between == the total**, with no overlap); `by_group`; **`n_deleted`** (the x≤0 that were deleted, a log) + a `note`.
- `dineq_regression_decomp` → `inequality_measures` (`gini, mld, theil, variance_logincome`); `decomposition` a df (`variable, contribution` — they **sum to 1**); `adjusted_r2`/`r_squared`; `n_deleted`/`n_used`.
- `dineq_change_decomp` → `variance_logincome` (`year1, year2, change`); `change_absolute`/`change_relative` dfs (`variable, price, quantity, total`) + `residual_*`; **the Yun identity:** `sum(price+quantity) + residual == the change` (live-verified to 2e-15).

**Traps:** **(1) A DUAL weights convention** — `rif`/`gini_decomp`/`mld_decomp`: a numeric **vector** (the node: a `matrix_handle`); `rifr`/`rifrSE`/`dineq_rb`/`dineq_change_rb`: a **column name** (a string) in the data (the node: a `string`). **(2)** The log-based methods **silently** delete `y ≤ 0` → always read `n_deleted`. **(3)** The Gini `overlap` ≠ 0 (overlapping groups) — do not ignore it; the MLD is purely additive. **(4)** The `rifrSE` bootstrap → the **seed** is exposed (the default is 42) for reproducibility.

**Sources:** the `drivers_inequality_change` ref (`help("rif")`/`help("rifr")`/`help("rifrSE")`/`help("gini_decomp")`/`help("mld_decomp")`/`help("dineq_rb")`/`help("dineq_change_rb")`, live-verified v0.1.0) < Firpo, Fortin & Lemieux 2009 (*Econometrica* 77:953, Unconditional Quantile Regressions — the RIF); Fields 2003 (*Research in Labor Economics* 22:1, the regression-based inequality decomposition); Yun 2006 & Brewer & Wren-Lewis 2016 (*Oxford Bull. Econ. Stat.* 78:289, price vs quantity); Mookherjee & Shorrocks 1982 (*Economic Journal* 92:886, the MLD within/between decomposition); Heckley, Gerdtham & Kjellsson 2016 (*J. Health Economics* 48:89, the general RIF decomposition).

### #226 Complex-survey inequality and poverty (linearized SE) — `complex_survey_aware` + `design_complex_survey` (`c22_inequality/complex_survey_aware.py`)
**Functions:** `svy_inequality` [`svydesign` + `convey_prep` + `svygini`/`svyqsr`/`svyzenga`], `svy_poverty` [the same + `svyfgt`/`svyarpr`]

**When:** you have **survey MICRODATA** (a DataFrame; one row per household/person) with **sampling weights**, and optionally **strata / PSU clusters / an fpc**, and want an **inequality** index (`gini`, `qsr`=S80/S20, `zenga`) or a **poverty** index (`fgt` FGT(g), `arpr` the at-risk-of-poverty rate) **WITH a correct design-based (linearized) standard error + a CI + degrees of freedom**. The node takes the COLUMN NAMES of the design (`income`/`ids`/`weights`/`strata`/`fpc`) and **builds the `svydesign` + `convey_prep` INTERNALLY** — the user does not set up the design by hand. It supports **domain estimation** (`subset_var`/`subset_level`) with correctly reduced df.

**When NOT:** (a) a plain vector without a complex-survey design → **#91 `inequality_indices_lorenz`** (a scalar index/Lorenz curve **without** an SE). (b) Replicate-weight designs (`svrepdesign`) — not exposed here. (c) The tail of **returns** (VaR/ES) → cat. 12 `PerformanceAnalytics` (#65); a conditional-on-X Growth-at-Risk → `quantile_regression` (#64). (d) The other convey estimators (`svygei`/`svyatk`/`svyrenyi`/`svywatts`/`svypoormed`/`svyjdiv`) — future candidates, not in this node.

**Preconditions (+ gates):** no formal statistical precondition — the gates are **structural** and the wrapper imposes them (through the shared path `.cvy_build_design`):

| Gate | Requirement | Why |
|---|---|---|
| data a DataFrame with ≥2 rows | every call | microdata are needed |
| the income/weights/ids column names exist | every call | `ids="1"` ⇒ `~1` (no clustering) |
| income numeric, **non-negative** (≥0), without Inf, with ≥2 non-NA values | every call | the Gini/FGT etc. presuppose non-negative income; `svygini` does **not** error by itself on negatives |
| an NA in the income + `na_rm=FALSE` ⇒ a **hard stop** | every call | otherwise `coef`=NA SILENTLY — an invalid result does not escape |
| weights numeric, without NA/Inf, **all >0** | every call | `svydesign` accepts negative weights SILENTLY |
| strata/fpc a column name or NULL (an fpc numeric) | optional | |
| **convey_prep ALWAYS** | internally | fgt/arpr/qsr error without it; gini/zenga compute a silently wrong linearization |
| g an integer ≥0; `type_thresh∈{abs,relq,relm}`; abs_thresh>0 **only** when type_thresh='abs' (otherwise NULL) | `svy_poverty[fgt]` | relq/relm SILENTLY ignore abs_thresh |
| alpha1,alpha2∈(0,1) and alpha1<alpha2; level/percent/quantiles∈(0,1) | respectively | |
| a post-check: the estimate a finite scalar; the SE ≥0 and finite; the CI a finite pair | every output | |

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| `svy_inequality measure=gini` | a headline single-number inequality with a design-based SE |
| `svy_inequality measure=qsr` | the Quintile Share Ratio S80/S20 (Eurostat); the ratio of the shares of the upper/lower quantile |
| `svy_inequality measure=zenga` | the Zenga uniformity index ∈[0,1]; sensitive across the whole distribution |
| `svy_poverty measure=fgt g=0/1/2` | FGT: the headcount / the poverty gap / the severity; an absolute or a relative threshold |
| `svy_poverty measure=arpr` | the At-Risk-Of-Poverty Rate (Eurostat: 60% of the median) |
| `subset_var`/`subset_level` | domain estimation per group with correctly reduced df |
| #91 `inequality_indices_lorenz` | a plain vector without a survey design/weights — no SE |

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`): `estimate` (the index; Gini/Zenga/ARPR/FGT∈[0,1], QSR≥1), `se` (a **linearized** design-based SE — a Deville influence function, **not** iid), `ci_lower`/`ci_upper` (a **t-based** CI with the design `df`), `df` (`degf`, reduced in a domain), `n_total`/`n_used`/`n_na`, `measure`/`income`, + the measure-specific fields (`g`/`type_thresh`/`abs_thresh` for FGT; `alpha1`/`alpha2` for QSR; `percent`/`quantiles`). The raw `svystat` goes into `.svystat` (`to_mcp` turns it into a stub). **An SE trap:** the SE depends on the CORRECT design — a wrong `ids`/`weights`/`strata` ⇒ a correct estimate but a WRONG SE. **An FGT monotonicity trap:** severity(g=2) ≤ gap(g=1) ≤ headcount(g=0). **Deterministic:** an analytical linearization, no RNG.

**Sources:** the `complex_survey_aware` ref + vignettes (`svygini`/`svyfgt`/`svyarpr`/`svyqsr`/`svyzenga`, live-verified 1.0.1) < `design_complex_survey` (Lumley 2010 *Complex Surveys*, Wiley; live-verified 4.5); Foster-Greer-Thorbecke 1984 *Econometrica* 52:761; Osier 2009 *Survey Methodology* 35:193 (linearization); Deville 1999 *Survey Methodology* 25:193 (influence functions); Zenga 2007 *Statistica & Applicazioni* 5:3; Eurostat EU-SILC (the ARPR at 60% of the median, S80/S20).

### #227 GB2 (the Generalized Beta of the second kind) — a parametric income distribution + Gini/ARPR — `GB2` (`c22_inequality/gb2_parametric_income.py`)
**Functions:** `fit_gb2` [`mlfit.gb2(z, w)` — the full ML + the profile log-likelihood], `gini_gb2` [`gini.gb2(a, p, q)`], `arpr_gb2` [`arpr.gb2(prop, a, p, q)`]

**When:** you have **positive income microdata** (optionally with survey weights) and want a **parametric model of the whole distribution** instead of a non-parametric index. The **GB2(a,b,p,q)** is the 4-parameter umbrella family of income-size distributions (McDonald 1984; it contains Singh-Maddala, Dagum, Fisk/log-logistic and Beta-2 as special cases): `a`=the tail shape, `b`=the scale, `p`/`q`=the Beta-2 shapes. `fit_gb2` fits it by **ML** (the full + the profile log-likelihood via `optim`) and returns the 4 parameters, the log-likelihood, the **convergence status**, and **analytical closed-form** Gini and ARPR indices on the fitted parameters — which smooth the sampling noise, allow simulation/tail prediction, and give consistent EU-SILC/Laeken poverty indicators. `gini_gb2`/`arpr_gb2` are also exposed **standalone** for when you already have (a,p,q).

**When NOT:** (a) you want a **non-parametric** Gini/Theil/Atkinson or Lorenz curve **directly from the sample** with no distributional assumption → #91 `inequality_indices_lorenz`. (b) The tail of **returns** (VaR/ES) → #65 `PerformanceAnalytics`; the conditional-on-X lower tail of an outcome (Growth-at-Risk) → #64 `quantile_regression`. (c) Income with **zeros/negatives** → the GB2 is defined on **x>0**; they are rejected (`mlfit.gb2` does **not** error by itself). (d) A **small sample** where the 4-parameter ML does not converge (heavy-tail identifiability) → the convergence gate blocks. (e) A within/between decomposition by group.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** **no formal statistical precondition** (it is a distributional fit, not a test); the gates are **structural/mathematical** and the wrapper imposes them:

| Gate | Requirement | Why |
|---|---|---|
| numeric (or a 1-column matrix) + `length ≥ 10` + no NA/Inf | the `z` input of `fit_gb2` | a 4-parameter heavy-tail fit; **NA do not error** in `mlfit.gb2` (they silently understate n) |
| **`z > 0`** (strictly positive) | `fit_gb2` | the GB2 support; zeros/negatives do not error by themselves — the gate comes from the project (the docs example filters `inc>0`) |
| `w` of the same length as `z`, positive, no NA/Inf | the weights (if supplied) | a wrong length **is silently recycled**; zero `w` silently exclude observations |
| `prop ∈ (0,1)` | `fit_gb2`/`arpr_gb2` | the poverty line as a share of the median (typically 0.6); outside the range → a silently wrong ARPR |
| positive shape parameters | `gini_gb2`/`arpr_gb2` | `gini.gb2`/`arpr.gb2` with negatives → NA/a warning |
| **a post-check: FUNCTIONAL CONVERGENCE** — the full ML `convergence == 0` | `fit_gb2` | a non-converged 4-parameter fit returns parameters **as if it had succeeded** (silently wrong); a hard stop unless `allow_nonconvergence=TRUE` (then a `converged=FALSE` flag) |
| a post-check: 4 finite, positive (on convergence) parameters; a finite index | every output | a heavy-tail Gini (`a*q≤1`) → NA: the standalone `gini_gb2` errors, inside the fit → `gini_defined=FALSE` |

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| #91 `inequality_indices_lorenz` (non-parametric) | you want no distributional assumption; a descriptive index/Lorenz curve directly from the sample |
| `fit_gb2` (the full GB2) | you want smoothing / tail prediction / analytical poverty-welfare metrics from one unified model; it needs a sufficient n to converge |
| `gini_gb2` / `arpr_gb2` standalone | you already have (a,p,q) [+prop] and want only the scale-free index without a re-fit |
| `allow_nonconvergence=TRUE` | **only** to diagnose a non-converged fit (`converged=FALSE`) — NEVER in production |
| cat. 12 `quantile_regression`/`PerformanceAnalytics` | GaR or risk metrics of returns — a different question |

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp` — a named list → atomic fields):
- `fit_gb2` → `a`,`b`,`p`,`q` (+ the `params` named vector): the estimated GB2 parameters from the **full** ML; `loglik`/`loglik_profile`; `converged` (TRUE only if the full ML `convergence_full==0`); `convergence_full`/`convergence_profile` (the optim codes); `gini` (the analytical Gini ∈[0,1] at the fitted parameters, with a `gini_defined` flag); `arpr` (the ARPR at `arpr_prop`×the median, with an `arpr_defined` flag); `n`; `indicators` (a DataFrame of the empirical estimate vs ML-full vs ML-profile: median/mean/ARPR/RMPG/QSR/GINI/a/b/p/q — a **chart-ready** comparison of the empirical and the GB2-fitted values); `gb2_fit` (the raw fit — `to_mcp` turns it into a stub). **A convergence trap:** `converged=FALSE` is not a valid result — a non-converged 4-parameter heavy-tail fit is silently wrong.
- `gini_gb2` → `gini` (scale-free, it depends only on a,p,q); `arpr_gb2` → `arpr` (scale-free); `prop`. **An argument-order trap:** `(shape1=a, shape2=p, shape3=q)` — swapping p↔q changes the result. **A heavy-tail trap:** for `a*q≤1` the expected value does not exist → the Gini is NA (a standalone hard stop). **Determinism:** `mlfit.gb2` is deterministic (`optim` + method-of-moments starting values; `identical` verified) — no seed.

**Sources:** the `GB2` ref (Graf & Nedyalkova; `the mlfit. documentationgb2`, `the gini. documentationgb2`, `the arpr. documentationgb2`, live-verified 2.1.2) < McDonald 1984 "Some generalized functions for the size distribution of income", *Econometrica* 52(3):647-663 (the GB2); Kleiber & Kotz 2003 *Statistical Size Distributions in Economics and Actuarial Sciences*, Wiley, ch.6; Graf & Nedyalkova 2014 "Modeling of Income and Indicators of Poverty and Social Exclusion Using the GB2 Distribution", *Review of Income and Wealth* 60(4):821-842; the EU-SILC / Laeken indicators (ARPT/ARPR/RMPG/QSR, the Social Protection Committee 2006).

### #228 Affluence / richness indices (the top-tail mirror of poverty) — `affluenceIndex` (`c22_inequality/affluence_richness_indices.py`)
**Functions:** `richness_index` [`r.hc/r.cha/r.fgt/r.med(x, weight, k, [beta|alpha])`, dispatched by `index`], `income_share_top` [`r.is(x, weight, p)`], `affluence_line` [`line.med(x, weight, k)`]

**When:** you have a cross-section of **positive incomes** (of length ≥ 2, without NA/Inf, optionally with population weights) and want to quantify the **UPPER tail** — wealth/affluence, as the "mirror" of the poverty indices: (a) `richness_index` with an affluence line `rho = k × the median` (**k > 1**, an UPPER threshold) → `hc` (how many are rich, the headcount ratio), `cha` (the intensity, a concave axiom **T1**: it increases under a progressive transfer among the rich), `fgt` (the intensity, a convex axiom **T2**, `alpha>1`), `med` (the **absolute** mean affluence gap, in income units); (b) `income_share_top` → the income share of the richest `(1-p)` fraction (the top 1%/10% shares); (c) `affluence_line` → the **Medeiros** affluence line, constructed from a poverty line.

**When NOT:** (a) the inequality of the **whole** distribution (Gini/Theil/Atkinson/Lorenz) → #91 `inequality_indices_lorenz` — here we focus only on the upper tail. (b) **Poverty** indices / the lower tail (the FGT poverty family) — the opposite direction. (c) The tail of **returns** (VaR/ES/downside) → cat. 12 `PerformanceAnalytics` (#65). (d) A conditional-on-X **Growth-at-Risk** → cat. 12 `quantile_regression` (#64). (e) Wolfson polarization / Palma (S90S40) / a weighted Gini (`polar.aff`/`S90S40`/`gini.w`) — **not exposed** (the Gini is covered by #91). (f) **Bootstrap SE** (`boot.sd1`/`boot.sd2`) — stochastic, outside the deterministic core of "an index + a threshold + n", not exposed. (g) A **subgroup** decomposition (`*.sub`) — not exposed.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):** **no formal statistical precondition** (deterministic descriptive indices on a cross-section). The gates are **structural/mathematical** and the wrapper imposes them:

| Gate | Requirement | Why |
|---|---|---|
| numeric + `length ≥ 2` + no NA/Inf + **`x > 0`** | every input `x` | income must be positive; `r.cha` divides by `x`; **the package does NOT error on negatives/zeros** (live: `r.hc(-5,…)` returned a number — silently wrong) |
| **the threshold direction: `k > 1`** | `richness_index` | `rho=k×median` is an **UPPER** threshold; `k ≤ 1` → a line at or below the median → "everyone is rich" (live: `k=0.5` → `r.hc=0.9`) |
| **`0 < k < 1`** (the opposite meaning) | `affluence_line` | here `k` is a **POVERTY** line (BELOW the median); a bounded `k` also protects against the internal infinite `while` loop of `line.med` |
| `beta > 0` (only for `cha`), `alpha > 1` (only for `fgt`) | the index parameters | the package does **NOT** check the domain (live: `alpha=0.5` was computed silently) |
| `p ∈ (0,1)` | `income_share_top` | the endpoints degenerate (`p→0` ⇒ ~1, `p→1` ⇒ 0) |
| the weights of the same length, `> 0`, no NA (or `NULL` ⇒ equal) | every `weight` | **no recycling**; the weighted median/quantile is the SAME `spatstat.univar` the package calls internally |
| a post-check: `hc/cha ∈ [0,1]`, `fgt/med ≥ 0`, `r.is ∈ [0,1]`, `line.med` with complete/finite fields | every output | an invalid result does not escape (live: an `fgt` overflow → `Inf` is blocked) |

**Alternatives + criterion:**

| Alternative | When it is preferred |
|---|---|
| `index=hc` (`r.hc`) | **how many** are rich — the weighted share above `rho` (the headcount); it does not capture intensity |
| `index=cha` (T1, concave) | the **intensity** of affluence, which **increases** under a progressive transfer among the rich; bounded in `[0,1]`; `beta>0` |
| `index=fgt` (T2, convex) | an intensity that **decreases** under a progressive transfer among the rich; `alpha>1`; it is **NOT** bounded by 1 |
| `index=med` (Medeiros) | the **absolute** mean affluence gap (in income units) — the size of the excess wealth |
| `income_share_top` (`r.is`) | the income share of the richest `(1-p)` — the top 1%/10% shares; the threshold = the `p` quantile, not `k×median` |
| `affluence_line` (`line.med`) | you want the affluence **line** (not an index), constructed from a poverty line (`0<k<1`) |
| #91 `inequality_indices_lorenz` (Gini/Theil/Lorenz) | the inequality of the **whole** distribution, not a focus on the upper tail |

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp` — a named list → atomic fields):
- `richness_index` → `index` (**the scale:** `hc/cha ∈ [0,1]` are proportions; `fgt ≥ 0` with **no** upper bound of 1; `med ≥ 0` is **absolute**, in income units), `index_type`, `affluence_line` = `rho = k×median` (the UPPER threshold), `median_income`, `count_rich` (`#{x>rho}`), `share_rich` (the weighted share of the rich), `k`, `n`.
- `income_share_top` → `income_share ∈ [0,1]` (the share of the total held by `x>q_p`), `threshold_quantile` = `q_p`, `top_fraction` = `1-p` (**a trap:** `p=0.9` ⇒ the **top 10%**; `p` is the quantile threshold, not "the top p%"), `count_top`, `n`.
- `affluence_line` → `affluence_line` = `rho_medeiros` (the derived affluence line, **ABOVE** the median: `median_multiple > 1`), `median_multiple`, `median_income`, `poverty_gap` (`Gp`), `k`, `n`.

**Determinism:** all the exposed paths are **pure** (no RNG); the stochastic bootstrap-SE path (`boot.sd*`) is not exposed → no seed. The numeric fields are chart-ready (the frontend draws, the wrapper does not).

**Sources:** the `affluenceIndex` v2.2 (`help(r.hc/r.cha/r.fgt/r.med/r.is/line.med)`, live-verified on version 4.6.1) < Peichl, Schaefer & Scheicher 2008 (IZA DP 3790, "Measuring richness and poverty", the axioms T1/T2); Chakravarty 1983 (*Mathematical Social Sciences* 6:307-313, the concave mirror); Foster, Greer & Thorbecke 1984 (*Econometrica* 52:761-766, the convex FGT family); Medeiros 2006 (*Social Indicators Research* 78:1-18, the affluence line from a poverty line); Brzezinski 2010 (*Social Indicators Research* 99:285-299, income affluence and the top income share).

### #173 Fixed-Effects Individual-Slopes (FEIS) + a slope-heterogeneity Hausman test — `fixed_effects_individual` (`c08_panel_data/fixed_effects_individual.py`)
**Functions:** `feis_fit` [`feis`+`summary.feis`, a producer], `feis_test` [`feistest` — an artificial-regression / Mundlak-CRE Hausman test], `feis_bstest` [`bsfeistest` — a pairs-cluster bootstrapped Hausman test, STOCHASTIC], `feis_slopes` [`slopes` — the individual slopes `alpha_i`]

**When:** you have a panel `(i,t)` and the effect of a **trend/slope variable** (time, experience, age, …) **differs by unit**. FEIS "detrends" the data with the predicted individual slope of each unit (instead of the simple demeaning of a within FE), giving consistency even when the unit-specific slope is correlated with the regressors (Bruederl & Ludwig 2015; Ruettenauer & Ludwig 2020; Wooldridge 2010). A two-part formula: `y ~ x1 + x2 | slope1 + slope2`; for a conventional FE write `y ~ x | 1` explicitly.

**When NOT:** (a) no theoretical slope heterogeneity → a conventional FE (#46 `pd_fit model="within"`) suffices and is more efficient. (b) Units with **fewer than q+1** observations (q = the number of slope parameters including the intercept) → they are dropped silently (a warning); if there are many, the panel collapses. (c) A dynamic panel / a lagged dependent variable on the RHS → the Nickell bias, go to #47 `pd_gmm_fit`. (d) You care about the coefficient of a **time-invariant** regressor → the detrending wipes it out.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **A two-part formula** (the gate `.feis_as_formula`): the `|` is mandatory; otherwise a clean stop (`feis` would otherwise throw "No individual slopes specified").
- **A panel in long format** with a valid `id` column (the gate `.feis_check_data`: a DataFrame, the id a single string naming an existing column, all the formula variables present).
- **Is the slope heterogeneity actually significant?** run `feis_test(m.object, type="art1")` — H0: FEIS can be reduced to a conventional FE; a rejection → keep FEIS. `art2`=FE vs RE, `art3`=FEIS vs RE. With a small N prefer `feis_bstest` (a pairs-cluster bootstrap).
- Before you even consider FEIS: the classical `c08_panel_data/static_panel_estimators.pd_hausman_test` (FE vs RE).

**Alternatives + criterion:**
- **#46 `pd_fit` (`model="within"`)** — when the `feis_test` art1 does not reject (no slope heterogeneity): it is more efficient.
- **#47 `pd_gmm_fit`** — a dynamic panel / endogenous regressors.
- **Bayesian random slopes (`bayesian_regression`, category 14)** — hierarchical shrinkage of the slopes, a full posterior, or a non-gaussian likelihood instead of fixed individual slopes.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `coefficients` — a named numeric vector of the regressor effects, **in the detrended space**. `coef_table` — a matrix `Estimate/Std. Error/t-value/Pr(>|t|)`; the SE are cluster-robust when `robust=TRUE` (`vcov_arg` states the method).
- `slopevars` — the slope variables (the RHS of the `|`). `r2`/`adj.r2` — **in the detrended space** (not comparable with a within/pooling R²). `n_groups`/`nobs` — after dropping the units with `<q+1` obs; **a trap**: compare `n_groups` with the original N.
- `feis_test`/`feis_bstest` — `art_feis_vs_fe` (art1/bs1), `art_fe_vs_re` (art2/bs2), `art_feis_vs_re` (art3/bs3), each `{chi2, df, p.value}` from `wald.test`. **The components other than the selected `type` are NULL** (art1 → only `art_feis_vs_fe`). Read `p.value` for the decision.
- `feis_slopes.slopes` — an `N x J` matrix of the `alpha_i` (the rownames = the ids), including the `(Intercept)`. A slope collinear within a cluster → `0` (documented).
- **Determinism**: `feis_fit`/`feis_test`/`feis_slopes` are deterministic; `feis_bstest` is **STOCHASTIC** → the same `seed` (the default 2025) ⇒ the same p; a low `rep` ⇒ a noisy p.

**Sources:** the feisr help (`help("feis","feisr")`, `feistest`, `bsfeistest`, `slopes` — feisr 1.3.1) — Ruettenauer & Ludwig 2020 *Sociological Methods & Research* (FEIS) <https://doi.org/10.1177/0049124120926211>; Bruederl & Ludwig 2015 *Sage Handbook of Regression Analysis* (Fixed-Effects Panel Regression); Mundlak 1978 (Econometrica 46:69, the CRE specification behind feistest); Wooldridge 2010 *Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data* 2nd ed. §10.7 (the regression-based Hausman test) and §11 (heterogeneous slopes).

### #174 Beck-Katz Panel-Corrected Standard Errors (PCSE) for a pooled TSCS — `beck_katz_panel` (`c08_panel_data/beck_katz_panel.py`)
**Functions:** `pcse_fit` [`lm`+`beck_katz_panel`, a PRODUCER], `pcse_vcov` [`beck_katz_panel` over a raw_handle `lm`, a PRODUCER], `pcse_summary` [`summary.pcse` AS structured data]

**When:** you have a **pooled OLS** on time-series cross-section data (N units × T periods, with T not much smaller than N) and want **standard errors robust** to (a) panel heteroskedasticity (a different variance per unit) and (b) **contemporaneous (cross-unit) correlation** of the residuals — while keeping the plain OLS coefficients. This is the classical Beck-Katz prescription for macro/political-economy panels where the units (countries) co-move over time.

- `pairwise=FALSE` (**casewise**, the default): it uses only the **balanced rectangle** (the units present in all periods) to estimate the cross-unit covariance — suitable for (nearly) balanced panels.
- `pairwise=TRUE`: it uses all the **overlapping** observations per pair of units — preferable for **unbalanced** panels.

**When NOT:** (a) a lagged dependent variable on the RHS or endogeneity → a dynamic panel bias, go to #47 `pd_gmm_fit`. (b) When you need **within/random effects** (unit-specific intercepts) → #46 `pd_fit` (FE/RE) — the PCSE is an SE correction, not an effects estimator. (c) When **N >> T** (a micro panel with few periods): the Beck-Katz estimate of Sigma becomes unreliable → prefer clustered or Driscoll-Kraay SE (`vcovSCC`). (d) When the main problem is serial correlation → Prais-Winsten/Newey-West.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- A **pooled OLS equation** with a valid panel index `(groupN=the unit, groupT=the time)`. In `pcse_fit` you supply **column names**; in `pcse_vcov` you supply **numeric vectors** of length `nobs`. A gate: the group index without NA and of length == the rows of the `model.matrix` (otherwise `beck_katz_panel` crashes with a cryptic message).
- **Complete cases**: an NA in the model/index columns drops rows in the `lm` → a length mismatch in `beck_katz_panel` → the wrapper blocks it explicitly (it demands complete cases).
- **T not << N**: the PCSE presupposes enough periods to estimate the N×N contemporaneous covariance.

**Alternatives + criterion:**
- **#46 `pd_fit`** (within/random) — when there are unit-specific effects you want to model (not merely to correct the SE for).
- **Driscoll-Kraay** (`vcovSCC`) — when N >> T or there is strong cross-sectional dependence with a large N.
- **`vcovBK`** — the same Beck-Katz logic but over a `panel_unit_root` panelmodel instead of a pooled `lm`.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `coefficients` — a named numeric vector; **a trap:** they are plain pooled **OLS** coefficients — the PCSE correction changes ONLY the SE, not the point estimates.
- `coef_table` — a matrix `Estimate/PCSE/t value/Pr(>|t|)`; the SE are panel-corrected. `beck_katz_panel` — a named vector of the PCSE. `vcov` — the **PCSE** covariance matrix (NOT the classical OLS vcov); chart/inference data.
- `df`/`nobs`/`nmiss` — the degrees of freedom, the valid observations, the **missing panel cells** (nmiss>0 ⇒ unbalanced). `balanced` = `(nmiss==0)`.
- `pairwise` — TRUE=pairwise / FALSE=casewise; record it in the report because it changes the estimate of Sigma.
- **A trap:** `pairwise=NA` runs silently wrong in `beck_katz_panel` — the wrapper rejects it (a non-NA logical scalar). `pcse_summary` exposes `summary.pcse` **as data** (the original only prints — the GLOBAL INVARIANT: no print).

**Sources:** Beck & Katz 1995 "What to Do (and Not to Do) with Time-Series Cross-Section Data", APSR 89(3):634-647; the `beck_katz_panel` package (Bailey & Katz, JSS 2011 42(9)), `help("pcse","pcse")` + the `beck_katz_panel` source; Beck 2001, Annual Review of Political Science 4:271-293.

---

### #175 Hierarchical / multilevel (mixed) models — linear and generalized (partial pooling) — `hierarchical_multilevel_linear` (`c08_panel_data/hierarchical_multilevel_linear.py`)
**Functions:** `lme_lmer` [`lmer`+`summary`, a PRODUCER→object], `lme_glmer` [`glmer`+`summary`, a PRODUCER→object; the family is a closed set {binomial,poisson,Gamma,inverse.gaussian} via match.arg], `lme_ranef` [`ranef.merMod` → tidy BLUP records], `lme_varcorr` [`VarCorr.merMod` → tidy variance/correlation records]

**When:** you have **hierarchical/nested** data (regions within countries, years within units, pupils within schools) and want **partial pooling** — random intercepts/slopes per group with shrinkage — instead of complete pooling (which ignores the structure) or entirely separate models per group (which overfits small groups). A linear response → `lme_lmer` (`y ~ x + (1 | grp)`); a non-gaussian one → `lme_glmer` with a `family`. Both are PRODUCERS: they return a model handle that feeds `lme_ranef`/`lme_varcorr` (Bates et al. JSS 2015; Gelman & Hill 2007).

**When NOT:** (a) when the group effects are **correlated** with the regressors (endogeneity) → partial pooling biases, go to within/FE (#46 `pd_fit model="within"`). (b) A lagged dependent variable on the RHS (the Nickell bias) → #47 GMM. (c) A single hierarchical level in a plain panel `(i,t)` where the RE variance components of `panel_unit_root` suffice → #46 `pd_fit model="random"`. (d) You want priors / a full posterior / uncertainty quantification on the variance components → `bayesian_regression` (category 14).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **A random-effects structure in the formula**: a `(.. | group)` term is mandatory — the gate `.lme_check_re` (a stop if the `|` is missing). `.lme_check_data` hard-gates NA (a unified policy with feisr/pcse).
- **Uncorrelated effects (as in RE)**: partial pooling PRESUPPOSES that the random effects are uncorrelated with the regressors — if in doubt, compare with FE (#46) / run a Hausman test (`pd_hausman_test`).
- **Enough groups**: too few groups or zero between-variance → a boundary (singular) fit; the wrapper flags it explicitly (`singular=TRUE`).

**Alternatives + criterion:**
- **#46 `pd_fit` (within/FE)** — when the individual effects are correlated with the regressors (endogenous) → FE is consistent, the mixed model is biased.
- **#46 `pd_fit` (random)** — one level, a linear panel; the GLS variance components suffice without a full mixed-model machinery.
- **`bayesian_regression` (category 14)** — priors, a full posterior, a more complex likelihood, or hierarchical shrinkage with uncertainty quantification.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `fixef` — a named vector of the population-level (fixed) coefficients.
- `coef_table` — `Estimate/Std. Error/t value` (lmer; **NO p-value by design** — there is no default df, judge by a CI/LRT) or `+z value/Pr(>|z|)` (glmer).
- `varcorr` — tidy records `{grp,var1,var2,vcov,sdcor}`: the variance/covariance/correlation of the random effects. `sigma` — the residual scale (== `attr(VarCorr,'sc')`).
- `ranef` — records `{grpvar,term,grp,condval,condsd}`: the BLUPs (the shrunk group deviations) + the conditional SD. **A trap**: they are conditional modes, NOT parameters — they are shrunk towards 0; do not read them as separate fixed effects per group.
- `singular`/`converged`/`conv_messages` — they **record degeneracy and convergence IN the output** (the stateless node contract: stderr is lost, the warning "boundary (singular) fit" does not reach downstream — check these fields). `singular=TRUE` ⇒ degenerate variance components.
- `logLik/AIC/BIC` — **a trap**: REML=TRUE likelihoods are NOT comparable across models with different fixed effects; for an LRT/AIC on the fixed effects set `REML=FALSE` (ML). `family` (glmer) = a closed set (gaussian is NOT allowed — use `lme_lmer`).

**Sources:** Bates, Mächler, Bolker & Walker, "Fitting Linear Mixed-Effects Models Using lme4", *JSS* 2015 67(1) < `help("lmer","lme4")`, `help("glmer","lme4")`, `ranef.merMod`, `fixef.merMod`, `VarCorr.merMod` (live introspection); Gelman & Hill 2007 *Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models*; Pinheiro & Bates 2000 *Mixed-Effects Models in S and S-PLUS* (BLUP/partial pooling).

### #190 Price index numbers (bilateral / multilateral / spliced) + CPI-subindex contribution decompositions — `PriceIndices` (`c11_decomposition_accounting/price_index_numbers.py`)
**Functions:** `pi_bilateral` [`jevons/dutot/carli/laspeyres/paasche/fisher/tornqvist/walsh` via an enum], `pi_multilateral` [`geks/ccdi/gk/tpd` rolling-window], `pi_splice` [`geks_splice/…` movement/window/half/mean splicing], `pi_contributions` [`bennet`/`montgomery` — the CPI-subindex value/price/quantity contributions per product]

**When:** you have **long-format scanner/CPI microdata** (the columns `time,prices,quantities,prodID`) and want either (a) a **price index** — bilateral (Jevons…Walsh) or multilateral (GEKS/CCDI/GK/TPD) — or (b) a **decomposition of the change in the value** of a CPI subindex into price/quantity contributions **per product** (Bennet/Montgomery). `pi_contributions` is the node's reason for existing in macro use: it explains "how much of the change in the subindex is due to prices vs quantities, per product" (the identity `Value_difference = Price_indicator + Quantity_indicator`).

**When NOT:** (a) you already have a ready **index-level series** (an index-level ts) — that is a transform/growth-rate question (cat. 00), not index-number construction. (b) A macro aggregate without product-level microdata. (c) A need for model-based (SPQ) or chained-bilateral batch indices — outside the curated surface (deliberately not exposed).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **Long-format microdata** with the mandatory columns (`time` as a Date, `prices`>0, `quantities`, `prodID`) — hard-gated explicitly (a missing column / a non-Date time / a non-positive price / an NA → a clean stop). Load them via `c00_data_utilities/readers.read_delimited`.
- **A valid window**: `start <= end` (in the format `'YYYY-MM'`); a `start > end` returns a **silently inverted** index in the package → blocked (a gate). `window >= 2` and `<=` the available months.
- A bilateral baseline (`pi_bilateral`) before you choose a multilateral one: a large Laspeyres–Paasche gap ⇒ substitution/new-goods bias ⇒ go multilateral.

**Alternatives + criterion:**
- **`pi_multilateral` (GEKS/CCDI/GK/TPD)** — high product turnover / new-goods bias; the bilateral indices have chain drift and you want a transitive multilateral one.
- **`pi_splice`** — a non-revisable extendable multilateral series beyond a fixed window (a rolling-window splice).
- **#62 `prod_fareprim` (productivity)** — if you want a TFP / quantity index (Färe-Primont) rather than a price index.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `pi_bilateral`: `index` (a scalar, or a vector when `interval=TRUE`, with base=start=1); `formula`; `dates` (the month labels when interval).
- `pi_multilateral`: `index` (a scalar, end vs start over the window); `method`; `window`; `wstart`.
- `pi_splice`: `index` (a scalar, or the full series when `interval=TRUE`); `method`; `splice`; `dates`.
- `pi_contributions.aggregate`: 1 row `{Value_difference, Price_indicator, Quantity_indicator}` (the identity value = price + quantity); `.contributions`: per product `{prodID, value_differences, price_contributions, quantity_contributions}`; `n_products`.
- **Traps**: `gk` = the rolling Geary-Khamis index (≠ `geary_khamis`, the fixed-base one, which is not exposed); a per-product `price_contribution` can be 0 when the price did not change (a contribution to the **value difference**, an indicator not an index ratio); `interval=FALSE` ⇒ one index end vs start, `interval=TRUE` ⇒ a series with dates for a chart.

**Sources:** the `PriceIndices` vignette/help (`jevons…walsh`, `geks/ccdi/gk/tpd`, `geks_splice`…, `bennet`, `montgomery` — live introspection) < ILO/IMF/OECD/Eurostat/UNECE/World Bank (2004, 2020) *Consumer Price Index Manual: Theory and Practice*; Diewert 1976 "Exact and superlative index numbers", *J. Econometrics* 4:115; Bennet 1920 (*JRSS* 83:455); Montgomery 1937; Krsinich 2016 (FEWS, UNECE-ILO); de Haan & Krsinich 2014 (the multilateral GEKS).

### #165 Instrumental variables / 2SLS (the modern standalone `instrumental_variables_2sls`, a three-part formula) — `instrumental_variables_2sls` (`c07_causality_policy/instrumental_variables_2sls.py`)
**Functions:** `iv_fit` [`instrumental_variables_2sls` + the S3 `summary.ivreg(diagnostics=TRUE)` + `confint.ivreg`]

**When:** you have one or more **endogenous regressors** — a regressor correlated with the error term (simultaneity, an omitted variable, measurement error) — and you have valid **external instruments** (correlated with the endogenous regressor, uncorrelated with the error). You want a consistent causal estimate by two-stage least squares **together with the three standard diagnostics** (weak instruments, endogeneity, over-identification) in one call. The node is explicitly the **modern three-part interface** `y ~ exog | endog | instruments`: to the left of the 1st `|` the exogenous regressors (+ the constant), between them the endogenous ones, to the right of the 2nd `|` the excluded instruments.

**When NOT:** (a) all the regressors are exogenous → a plain OLS/`lm` (IV merely loses efficiency). (b) Fewer instruments than endogenous regressors (**under-identified**) → the estimate is not defined. (c) **Weak instruments** (a first-stage F < 10) → 2SLS is biased towards OLS and the classical CIs are invalid; you need weak-IV-robust inference (Anderson-Rubin). (d) A panel with fixed effects + IV → `#33 fx_feols`. (e) Many/non-linear controls with ML nuisance functions → `#45 DoubleML`. (f) The classical **2-part** interface `y ~ x | z` → `#34 wrap_ivreg` (AER) — it is deliberately blocked here.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **The data as a `DataFrame`**: load them with `c00_data_utilities/reading_delimited_fixed.read_delimited` (or `read_csv_data`) and pass the handle. The gate `.ivr_check_data`: a non-empty DataFrame, all the formula variables present, **no NA** in the model variables.
- **A three-part formula (mandatory)**: the gate `.ivr_check_three_part` — exactly **two** `|` (3 RHS parts); a 2-part or 1-part formula is blocked with a clean message stating the number of parts and pointing to the AER node (#34).
- **Identification**: for the Sargan over-identification test you need `n_instruments > n_endogenous` (over-identified); otherwise it is just-identified and the Sargan test does not exist (`df1=0`, `NA` are returned).
- **Test the endogeneity before trusting the IV**: `iv_fit` itself returns the **Wu-Hausman** test — if it is NOT rejected, the regressor is not endogenous in practice and OLS is consistent+efficient.

**Alternatives + criterion:**
- **#34 `wrap_ivreg` (AER)** — the classical 2-part interface `y ~ x1 + d | x1 + z`; the same 2SLS mathematics, a different syntax.
- **#33 `fx_feols` (fixest)** — when you need high-dimensional fixed effects **and** IV in the same fit (a panel).
- **#45 `wrap_doubleml_plr`/`irm` (DoubleML)** — many or non-linear controls, ML nuisance functions, debiased/orthogonal inference.
- **`method="M"`/`"MM"`** (it requires `robustbase`) — outliers/heavy tails → a robust IV.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `coefficients` / `coef_table` — the 2SLS estimates of the structural equation + `Estimate/Std. Error/t value/Pr(>|t|)`. **A trap**: if `weak_instruments_flag=TRUE`, do NOT trust these SE/CIs.
- `conf_int` — the coefficient CIs at `conf_level`; `sigma`, `df.residual`, `nobs`, `r.squared`, `adj.r.squared`.
- `n_endogenous` / `n_instruments` — the identification counts; `overidentified=TRUE` ⇔ the excluded instruments > the endogenous regressors.
- `weak_instruments` — a **list** `{df1, df2, statistic, p.value}` **per endogenous regressor** (the first-stage F test; with several endogenous regressors you get several rows `Weak instruments (<var>)`). `weak_instruments_flag` = TRUE if any F < 10 (the Staiger-Stock rule).
- `wu_hausman` — `{df1, df2, statistic, p.value}`, the endogeneity test; **a rejection ⇒ the regressor really is endogenous** (the IV is justified); a non-rejection ⇒ prefer OLS.
- `sargan` — `{df1, df2, statistic, p.value}`, the over-identification test; it is **meaningful only when over-identified** (`df1>0`); just-identified ⇒ `df1=0` + `NA` (not an error). A rejection ⇒ some instrument is invalid (correlated with the error).
- `diagnostics` — the full diagnostics table (chart-data); `fitted`/`residuals` — chart-data.
- **A masking trap**: the standalone `instrumental_variables_2sls` masks `instrumental_variables_2sls` in the shared `source` env; the wrapper calls `instrumental_variables_2sls` explicitly (namespaced, without `library(ivreg)`). Do not confuse it with #34.

**Sources:** the ivreg vignette *"Diagnostics for 2SLS Regression"* + `help("ivreg","ivreg")`, `help("summary.ivreg")` — Fox, Kleiber & Zeileis, *ivreg: Instrumental-Variables Regression by 2SLS* < Sargan 1958 (Econometrica 26:393) over-identification; Wu 1973 / Hausman 1978 the endogeneity test; Staiger & Stock 1997 (Econometrica 65:557) the weak-instruments F>10 rule.
### #167 The Goodman-Bacon decomposition of the TWFE DiD coefficient — `goodman_bacon_decomposition` (`c07_causality_policy/goodman_bacon_decomposition.py`)
**Functions:** `bacon_decompose` [`bacon`]

**When:** you ran a two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) DiD — `outcome ~ treated | unit + time` — on a panel with **staggered adoption** of the intervention, and want to see **what that single coefficient is made of**. The Goodman-Bacon (2021) decomposition shows that the TWFE beta is a weighted average of **all** the possible 2x2 DiD comparisons, and gives you the weight + the estimate of each type of comparison. It is a **diagnostic tool**, not an estimator: it answers "how much can I trust my TWFE?".

The types of 2x2 comparison (the `type` column):

| `type` | who is treated / control | safety |
|---|---|---|
| `Treated vs Untreated` | an early/late cohort vs the **never-treated** (coded `untreated=99999`) | **clean** — the desired comparison |
| `Earlier vs Later Treated` | an early cohort (afterwards) vs a late cohort **before** it receives the intervention | clean (the control is still untreated) |
| `Later vs Earlier Treated` | a late cohort vs an early cohort that is **ALREADY** treated | **DANGEROUS** — the forbidden comparison; it uses already-treated units as controls |
| `Both Treated` (only with covariates) | it combines the two treated-vs-treated comparisons | see above |

**When NOT:** (a) an **unbalanced panel** — it fails deliberately (the method requires a strongly balanced panel; the same number of periods per unit). (b) All the units adopt simultaneously (no staggered variation → a trivial decomposition). (c) You want an **unbiased estimator** under heterogeneous treatment effects — that is `staggered_did`/`did_imputation`, not this diagnostic. (d) A continuous/non-binary treatment (bacon requires 0/1).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **The TWFE coefficient being decomposed** comes from `c07_causality_policy/fixed_effects_ols.fx_feols` (`y ~ treated | unit + time`) — the decomposition explains EXACTLY that number.
- **A strongly balanced panel**: the `bacon_decompose` gate checks that all the units have the same number of observations (the same condition as the internal `stop("Unbalanced Panel")`), and gives a clear message instead of a cryptic error.
- **id_var/time_var/the formula variables exist** as columns (otherwise a cryptic `object 'id' not found`), `id_var ≠ time_var`, no `NA` in the columns used — all explicit gates.
- On a **macro panel** (large T) run a stationarity test first (`c01_preparation_prechecks/panel_unit_root.run_purtest`). If the panel comes from a file, `c00_data_utilities/reading_delimited_fixed.read_csv_data`.

**Alternatives + criterion:**
- **`c07_causality_policy/staggered_did.wrap_att_gt`** (Callaway-Sant'Anna) — when you want an **unbiased** group-time ATT rather than a diagnostic; there is a never/late-treated control group.
- **`c07_causality_policy/staggered_didimputation.wrap_did_imputation`** (Borusyak-Jaravel-Spiess) — an efficient imputation estimator robust to heterogeneity.
- **`c07_causality_policy/fixed_effects_ols.fx_feols`** with `sunab` — a cohort-interacted event study, when you want dynamic estimates rather than a simple diagnostic.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `two_by_twos` — a DataFrame per 2x2 comparison: `treated`/`untreated` (the activation times; **`untreated=99999` = the never-treated group**), `estimate`, `weight`, `type`. This is the chart-data table (a scatter of weight vs estimate by type).
- `type_summary` — the aggregates `{type, weight (the sum), avg_estimate (the weighted mean), n_comparisons}` per type. **The main diagnostic**: if `Later vs Earlier Treated` carries a large weight, your TWFE is contaminated by forbidden comparisons.
- `twfe_estimate` — the overall TWFE beta **as an identity**: without covariates `= sum(weight*estimate)`; with covariates `= Omega*beta_hat_w + (1-Omega)*sum(weight*estimate)`. It is verified bit-exact against `lm(y ~ treated + factor(id) + factor(time))`.
- `total_weight` (~1); `n_2x2` (the number of comparisons).
- `has_covariates` / `within_estimate` (`beta_hat_w`) / `within_weight` (`Omega`) — the within component when there are time-varying covariates; `NA` otherwise.
- **Interpretation traps**: (1) a large weight on `Later vs Earlier Treated` = negative-weighting/heterogeneity bias → your TWFE may have the wrong sign; move to an unbiased estimator. (2) `99999` = never-treated, not an actual time. (3) Negative weights/estimates under staggered adoption = a red flag. (4) With covariates the decomposition approximates the TWFE through FWL (the identity holds). (5) Unbalanced → a hard error, not a silent mistake.

**Sources:** Goodman-Bacon 2021 "Difference-in-Differences with Variation in Treatment Timing" (J. Econometrics 225:254–277); bacondecomp `help("bacon","bacondecomp")` + the `math_reform` dataset; de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfœuille 2020 (AER 110:2964, negative weights); the TWFE identity was verified numerically against `lm(y ~ treated + factor(id) + factor(time))` (exact, no-cov & cov) <

### #166 Heterogeneity-robust dynamic DiD event study (de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfoeuille) — `DIDmultiplegtDYN` (`c07_causality_policy/staggered_didmultiplegtdyn.py`)
**Functions:** `didm_dyn` [`did_multiplegt_dyn`]

**When:** you have a long-format panel `(group, time)` and want **dynamic event-study** treatment effects in a design where the treatment may be **non-binary** (e.g. a continuous dose/intensity) AND/OR **non-absorbing** (it may switch off or change), and past treatments affect the current outcome. The estimator is **robust to heterogeneous effects** — it does not suffer from the negative weights of TWFE OLS. It returns: the event-study effects `Effect_1.ℓ` (`effects=`), placebo (pre-trends) estimators (`placebo=`), the average total effect per unit of treatment (ATE), and joint tests.

**When NOT:** (a) when the treatment is **binary AND absorbing** (plain staggered adoption, a single irreversible change) → prefer `#36 did` (Callaway-Sant'Anna, doubly robust) or `#37 didimputation` (analytical SE, speed), which are more direct there. (b) A simple 2x2 (one treated group, two periods) → `#33 fixest` interaction/`sunab`. (c) Heterogeneity **across covariates** (CATE) rather than across relative event time → `#44 grf` causal forest.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **A long panel**, evenly spaced in time: load it with `c00_data_utilities/reading_delimited_fixed.read_delimited`. The columns `group/time/outcome/treatment` must exist and be **free of NA** — the gate `.didm_check_data` (a live-verified trap: an NA in a core column makes the package **silently** drop rows and return a partial-sample result; it is blocked explicitly).
- **Parallel trends + no anticipation**: they are not checked beforehand — use the placebos (`placebo>=1`) as a check; `p_jointplacebo` (for `placebo>=2`) tests their joint nullity.
- **`placebo <= effects`**: a hard gate (live-verified: the package silently clamps `placebo->effects` with a warning and returns; here it is blocked so the result is not silent).

**Alternatives + criterion:**
- **`#36 did`** — necessarily preferable if the treatment is binary & absorbing and you want a doubly robust ATT(g,t) + uniform bands.
- **`#37 didimputation`** — an absorbing design with an emphasis on analytical SE / speed.
- **`#44 grf`** — when the question is which units have a larger effect (CATE across covariates), not the dynamics across event time.
- **HonestDiD (a consumer)** — for robustness to violations of parallel trends (Rambachan & Roth 2023); **CAUTION**: `coef_b`/`coef_vcov` are in the order `[Effects…, Placebos…]` (post first); HonestDiD wants **chronological** order (pre-periods=placebos first, `numPrePeriods`=the number of placebos); reorder first, otherwise you get silently wrong robust CIs.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `effects` — a list with `estimate/se/lb_ci/ub_ci/N/switchers` (numeric vectors of length `effects`) + `table` (the raw matrix). It is the **event-study path**: the effect `ℓ` periods after the first change in treatment.
- `ate_estimate` / `ate_available` — the average cumulative (total) effect per unit of treatment. **A trap**: when `trends_lin=TRUE` the ATE is **not computed** (by documentation) → `ate_available=FALSE`, `ate_estimate=NA`; do not read it.
- `placebos` — the same structure; `estimate` should be ~0 under parallel trends/no anticipation. It **SUPPORTS, it does not prove** the assumption.
- `p_jointeffects` (only for `effects>=2`) / `p_jointplacebo` (only for `placebo>=2`) / `p_equality_effects` (only for `effects_equal=TRUE`) — joint-test p-values (NULL otherwise).
- `coef_b` (a named numeric) / `coef_vcov` (a matrix) — the full coefficient vector + vcov in the order `[Effects…, Placebos…]`; **FOR HonestDiD reorder chronologically** (placebos first) — they are not ready as they stand.
- `n_switchers_effect` — the number of switchers per effect; `delta_D_avg_total`, `max_pl`, `max_pl_gap` — diagnostics.
- **Determinism**: analytical SE (`bootstrap=NULL`) is deterministic (live-verified: identical successive calls); `bootstrap=N` is stochastic → `set.seed(seed)` + the `seed` is passed into the bootstrap option itself (`c(reps, seed)`) for reproducibility in a stateless node. `seed` defaults to 2025.
- **Runtime**: `DIDmultiplegtDYN 2.4.0` requires `polars` to be **attached** (a bare `pl` in its core); the wrapper attaches it **transiently** only for the duration of the call (on.exit detach) so that it does not pollute the shared source env — polars masks only `plot`/`kronecker`/`body<-`/`an install step` (no econometric generic).

**Sources:** de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfoeuille 2020 *AER* 110(9):2964-2996 (fuzzy DiD / heterogeneous effects); de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfoeuille 2024 *Econometrics Journal* (dynamic/event-study non-absorbing DiD); the `DIDmultiplegtDYN` vignette + `the did_multiplegt_dyn documentation` (v2.4.0); Rambachan & Roth 2023 *ReStud* (the HonestDiD sensitivity analysis, a consumer of `coef_b`/`coef_vcov`).
### #170 Sensitivity analysis to unobserved confounding / OVB (robustness value + OVB bounds) — `sensitivity_unobserved_confounding` (`c07_causality_policy/sensitivity_unobserved_confounding.py`)
**Functions:** `sens_analyze` [`sensitivity_unobserved_confounding` — which internally composes `robustness_value` (RV_q / RV_{q,alpha}), `partial_r2` (r2yd.x) and `ovb_bounds` (adjusted estimates/SE/CI) into one object]

**When:** you have a treatment effect estimated by **OLS under selection on observables** and want to quantify its robustness to an **unobserved confounder**. `sens_analyze` returns: (a) the **robustness value** — how strong (in partial R²) a confounder, correlated with BOTH the treatment AND the outcome, would have to be in order to reduce the effect by `q·100%` (RV_q) or to render it statistically insignificant at `alpha` (RV_{q,alpha}); (b) the **partial R² of the treatment** (an upper bound on explanatory power); (c) the **OVB bounds** table — the adjusted estimate if the confounder were `kd`/`ky` times stronger than each **benchmark covariate**. Two input routes: `formula` + `data` (it builds the `lm` internally) **or** `object` (a raw_handle to an already fitted `lm`).

**When NOT:** (a) there is no credible linear/OLS design — for RD/DiD/IV/synthetic control use #38–45. (b) You want **point identification** under confounding — that requires an instrument/design (#34 IV), not sensitivity analysis; the tool **does not correct** the bias. (c) A non-linear/GLM outcome — the `lm` route does not apply. (d) Sensitivity to a violation of **parallel trends** in an event study — go to the HonestDiD-type flow.

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **A fitted `lm`, or formula+data**: the gate `object XOR formula+data` (exactly one source). On the consume route the `object` must be of class **`lm`** (fixest/glm are blocked). Produce it with `lm` upstream, or pass `formula`+`df_handle` (load the cross-section with `c00_data_utilities/reading_delimited_fixed.read_csv_data`).
- **`treatment` = ONE coefficient name** of the model (not the intercept): the gate gives an explicit message listing the available coefficients (`sensitivity_unobserved_confounding` itself emits a cryptic "Variables not found").
- **`benchmark_covariates` = a non-empty subset** of the covariates \ `{treatment}`: a gate; if you pass the treatment itself or an unknown name, it is blocked cleanly (otherwise the package fails with "Variables not found: XXd").
- **`kd`/`ky` positive**: for `kd<=0` the package emits `NaN` + "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed" — a hard gate. `ky` defaults to `kd`. `q>0`, `alpha∈(0,1)`.

**Alternatives + criterion:**
- **#44 `wrap_causal_forest` (grf)** — when you want **heterogeneous** effects under unconfoundedness, not a diagnosis of its violation.
- **#45 DoubleML** — high-dimensional controls / debiased estimation instead of post-hoc sensitivity.
- **#34 `wrap_ivreg` / AER 2SLS** — if a valid instrument exists, it gives point identification instead of bounds.
- **Manual `r2dz.x`/`r2yz.dx` bounds** (a feature of `sensitivity_unobserved_confounding`) — hypothetical confounding scenarios **without** a benchmark covariate; deliberately scoped out here (the flow focuses on the benchmark-based bounds).

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `robustness_value` (RV_q) — **a trap**: it is NOT a p-value. A **small** RV ⇒ a **weak** confounder suffices to overturn the effect ⇒ **fragile**. A value of, say, 0.57 means that a confounder with >57% partial R² in both directions is needed to make the effect vanish.
- `robustness_value_alpha` (RV_{q,alpha}) — the analogue for the loss of **statistical significance** at `alpha`.
- `partial_r2_treatment` (r2yd.x) — the partial R² of treatment~outcome; it serves as the comparison scale for "how strong is strong".
- `ovb_bounds` — a DataFrame per `(benchmark × kd/ky)` with `adjusted_estimate/adjusted_se/adjusted_lower_CI/adjusted_upper_CI` (+ `bound_label`, `r2dz.x`, `r2yz.dx`): the estimate **if** the confounder were `kd`/`ky` times stronger than the benchmark covariate. Chart-data for a contour-style display in the frontend.
- `unadjusted_estimate`/`unadjusted_se`/`t_statistic`/`dof` — the original OLS estimate.
- **Traps**: `reduce=TRUE` (the default) assumes the confounder **reduces** the effect — set `reduce=FALSE` if the confounding would inflate it; the bounds are **conditional on** "kd times the benchmark", so their credibility hangs on the suitability of the benchmark covariate as an analogue of the plausible confounder; **sensitivity ≠ identification** — the tool does not correct the bias.

**Sources:** Cinelli & Hazlett (2020), "Making Sense of Sensitivity: Extending Omitted Variable Bias", *JRSS-B* 82(1):39–67; the sensemakr vignette + `help("sensemakr","sensemakr")`, `the ovb_bounds documentation`, `the robustness_value documentation`, `?partial_r2` < Cinelli, Ferwerda & Hazlett (2020), "sensemakr: Sensitivity Analysis Tools for OLS " (SSRN 3588978).
### #169 RD with multiple cutoffs / multiple scores (multi-cutoff & multi-score, robust bias-corrected) — `rd_multiple_cutoffs` (`c07_causality_policy/rd_multiple_cutoffs.py`)
**Functions:** `rdmc_fit` [`rdmc` — multiple cutoffs, pooled + per cutoff], `rdms_fit` [`rdms` — multiple/cumulative cutoffs on one score]

**When:** an RD design with **multiple cutoffs** (`rdmc`: the cutoff `C` varies by unit) or **cumulative cutoffs on one score** (`rdms`); you want a **pooled estimand + per-cutoff estimates**, robust bias-corrected (Cattaneo-Titiunik-Vazquez-Bare, built on top of `rdd_robust`).

**When NOT:** (a) a single cutoff → `#38 rdrobust`. (b) A manipulation/density (McCrary) test. (c) A two-score design with `X2/zvar/C2` (deliberately out of scope — a fragile `rangemat`).

**Preconditions (+ checking tool):**
- **`rdmc`**: `>= 2` distinct cutoffs in the per-observation `C` (the same length as `X`); a single cutoff is blocked explicitly (go to `rdd_robust`).
- **`rdms`**: a vector of cutoffs; for the pooled estimand you need `xnorm` (otherwise `pooled.available=FALSE`).
- **An NA gate**: `rdd_robust` ignores NA in `Y/X/fuzzy` silently (N drops) → the gate forbids NA.
- Autonomous bandwidth: `c07_causality_policy/rdd_robust.wrap_rdbwselect`. Loading `Y/X/C`: `c00_data_utilities/reading_delimited_fixed.read_delimited`.

**Alternatives + criterion:**
- **#38 `wrap_rdrobust`** — a single cutoff (a single-cutoff sharp/fuzzy RD).
- **#39 `rdd`** — parametric/non-parametric RD with an IK bandwidth, one cutoff.
- **`rdms_fit` + `xnorm`** — cumulative cutoffs on ONE score and you want the pooled estimand.
- **`conventional=TRUE`** — conventional (not robust bias-corrected) p-values/CI for comparison.

**Reading the output** (aligned with L2 `to_mcp`):
- `pooled` — `{tau, se, pv, ci_l, ci_r, hl, hr, Nhl, Nhr}` (rdmc always; rdms only with `xnorm`, otherwise `available=FALSE`).
- `per_cutoff` — a DataFrame `{cutoff, coef, se, ci_l, ci_r, pv, Nh_left, Nh_right, Nh_total[, weight]}` = chart-data per cutoff.
- `weighted` (rdmc) — `{coef, se, pv, ci_l, ci_r}`, the weighted average of all the cutoff-specific estimates.
- `cutoffs / n_cutoffs`; `cfail / n_failed` (the cutoffs where rdrobust failed — `n_failed>0` ⇒ a suspect estimate); `kernel/p/bwselect/level/conventional`.
- **Traps**: for `rdmc` C = a per-observation cutoff variable, whereas for `rdms` C = a vector of values — a wrong length ⇒ silent recycling (blocked); `rdms` pooled = NA without `xnorm` (check `pooled.available`); a robust bias-corrected CI is **NOT** symmetric around the coefficient (do not read it as coef±1.96·se); cutoffs with a small `Nh_total` are noisy.

**Sources:** Cattaneo, Titiunik & Vazquez-Bare 2020 "Analysis of RD Designs with Multiple Cutoffs or Multiple Scores", *Stata Journal* 20(4):866-891; `rd_multiple_cutoffs` `the rdmc documentation the rdms documentation` (2.0.0) < Calonico, Cattaneo & Titiunik 2014 (*Econometrica* 82:2295) robust bias-corrected inference; Cattaneo, Idrobo & Titiunik 2024 "A Practical Introduction to RD Designs: Extensions" (CUP Elements).
